News.title: Family’s heartbreaking plea over canal bike mystery after dad found  on school field by girl, 11, with fatal head injury
News.content:
CANAL RIDDLE Family’s heartbreaking plea over canal bike mystery after dad found on school field by girl, 11, with fatal head injury







Next

THE family of a dad who was found fatally injured on the grounds of a school have made a heartbreaking plea after his e-bike was found in a canal.

Neil Thompson – known as Chuck – was discovered at Smestow Academy in Wolverhampton by an 11-year-old girl earlier this year as she prepared for a PE lesson.



It’s believed Mr Thompson, 45, was injured after coming off his e-bike while riding along Smestow Canal in the early hours of January 19.

Officers subsequently carried out searches of the area where the dad’s bike was found left by a bridge near to the canal.



Now, on what would have been Neil’s 46th birthday, his loved ones are appealing for the person who discovered the bike to come forward.

Det Sgt Amie Petford, of West Midlands Police, said: “His family are now asking the person who got the bike out of the water gets in touch so that they can have a place where they can go to grieve.



“The bike was rusty and appeared that someone had pulled it out of the canal and left it by a bridge at a lock so it is likely it would have been near there, but his family are hoping to know exactly where so they can lay flowers.”

The coroner concluded that Mr Thompson had died from head and facial injuries of an “unknown cause”.



West Midlands Police say there is no further criminal investigation into this matter.

The force initially launched a homicide investigation but the inquest was told mystery still surrounds exactly how he came to sustain his fatal injuries.

The court heard Neil had left his home on an electric bike at around 8.17pm on January 18 to visit a friend.

He left at around 1am the next morning, with CCTV capturing the dad travelling along a canal towpath at 1.26am.

A member of the public walking his dog through Smestow Valley Nature Reserve photographed him in the school grounds at around 7.15am.



He was believed to still be alive at that point but what happened during the intervening hours remains unclear, the inquest was told.

The probe placed Neil on the canal towpath between approximately 1am and 1.26am but there was no CCTV showing how he suffered his injuries.

The inquest also heard there was no clear understanding of how Neil got from the towpath to the school playing field where his body was found.

He would have had to negotiate or scale a fence to enter the school grounds but investigators were unable to establish how or when he made that journey.

Police also found no confirmed damage or blood evidence along the towpath during their investigation nor any evidence that he had been robbed.



In a statement at the time of his death, Neil’s family said: “Our beautiful son, brother, father and friend Chuck, very much loved in the community of fishing, his one true love.

“His love for life and funny stories touched the lives of so many people.”

The dad of the 11-year-old girl who found the body told previously how she was left “really shaken up” after making the grim discovery.

He said: “My daughter phoned her mum up, screaming, and told her that she found a dead body by the goal posts on the field.

“She’s only 11 years of age. They went out for PE and it was very foggy. It’s terrible what she’s had to see.”



RECOMMENDED STORIES

The person who pulled the bike from the canal is urged to contact the police quoting crime reference log 1452 of January 19.

The force added: “We appreciate the efforts of the person who pulled the bike from the water which led us to be able to locate it, and the family just now want to know where that place was.”

News.title: Woman collapses in pain as couple convicted of adultery are flogged 100 times each under brutal Sharia law in Indonesia
News.content:
CRUEL PUNISHMENT Woman collapses in pain as couple convicted of adultery are flogged 100 times each under brutal Sharia law in Indonesia







Next

A WOMAN was pictured crying out in pain after she was flogged over 100 times alongside a man as punishment for violating barbaric Sharia laws.

Shocking photos show her begging for mercy before collapsing to the floor in pain after the brutal flogging in Banda Aceh, Indonesia.



The horrifying spectacle unfolded in front of a crowd – including children – on Thursday.

People who have sex before marriage can be caned under the harsh decrees – only enforced in the Aceh province of Indonesia.



Violent punishments are also dished out for gambling, adultery, drinking alcohol, gay sex and holding hands outside of marriage.

The couple were convicted of adultery at Banda Aceh Sharia Court last month and sentenced to 100 lashings each.

Heartbreaking photos show the woman wincing with pain and holding up her hand for mercy while the cane hangs behind her, about to strike.

The man’s beatings were so severe that they had to be halted at strike 60, according to news outlet AJNN.

“Perhaps his health was a little compromised, or he simply couldn’t handle the whipping. So we stopped him first to give him a chance to rest”, said Darma Mustika, a senior official of the regional attorney’s office.



The caning then continued – up to 100 lashings total.

Eight others were beaten – receiving between 16 and 21 lashes – for mingling at a birthday party.

Under Sharia law, the mixing of men and women who are not family is strictly forbidden.

The pain of the punishment – as well as the public shaming – is intended to deter horrified onlookers from committing the same “crimes”.



It comes just weeks after four people were brutally punished for having sex outside marriage in the same Aceh province.

Two men and two women were each lashed 100 times for violating Sharia law.

At one point, the masked official carrying out the beatings – known as the algojo – appeared to take pity on one woman and whisper words of support in her ear.

The woman – whose face was partially covered by a white scarf – was photographed weeping as she fell to the ground in agony.

The floggings took place in front of a crowd, including children, that gathered to watch.



In the course of the brutal spectacle, four other people were lashed 22 times for the lesser crime of physical intimacy, which can mean hugging and kissing.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Two others received seven lashes each for being too close to each other, which can include holding hands.

Another man was flogged 20 times for consuming alcohol.

News.title: Twisted student, 25, tells court ‘I enjoy killing children’ after ‘stabbing three kids on their way to nursery’
News.content:
CHILD 'KILLER' Twisted student, 25, tells court ‘I enjoy killing children’ after ‘stabbing three kids on their way to nursery’







Next

A TWISTED student told the court “I enjoy killing children” after allegedly stabbing three five-year-olds with a kitchen knife.

Han L, 25, stands accused of knifing three boys while they were on their way to nursery in Zurich, Switzerland.



The horror attack had been weeks in planning, according to prosecutors.

Chinese national Han reportedly asked ChatGPT about the “legal consequences of… killing random victims by stabbing”.



Chillingly, he also asked “where to find children” in Zurich.

One little boy was knifed in the heart and barely survived, according to Swiss paper Blick.



A second was raced to hospital in critical condition and the other had wounds to his ear and lung after the stabbing spree on October 1, 2024.

Two years later on September 17, his defence lawyers have argued that he holds no criminal blame – and should be set free.

Psychiatrist Elmar Habermeyer told the court that Han was suffering from acute schizophrenia, psychosis, and depression at the time of the crime.

The university student was unable to control his actions, claimed his lawyers, and so should not be held responsible for attempted murder.



But the prosecution has slammed this narrative as false.

They point to the meticulous preparation allegedly carried out by Han prior to the attack – and to his frequent trips abroad.

A sickening indictment said that Han had bought beef the day before the attack in order to practice stabbing and slashing techniques.

He had also “studied anatomical depictions of the human head, neck and upper body as well as the blood vessels via Google and ChatGPT with a view to their killing“, claim prosecutors.

Lawyer Hanno Wieser added: “Anyone who can travel abroad, book hotels, and find their way around a foreign city can also decide against murder”.



But in a dramatic twist, Han’s lawyers claim that the travels to Prague and Warsaw were an attempt to distract himself from his murderous fantasies.

His unfamiliar surroundings in Switzerland – where he moved to in 2023 for his master’s degree – were also blamed for the horror stabbings.

Han had been unhappy with his new European life and was feeling “disrespected”, according to his indictment.

The expert psychiatrist told the court that Han’s risk of re-offending was low – but only if he was in a “stable environment or in China”.

The prosecution is now demanding a 15 year prison sentence and 15 year ban from the country.



They say that Han acted out of “pure vindictiveness, a thirst for recognition, and ideological blindness.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

At the end of the hearing, Han L stepped up to the lecturn and said: “I am very, very sorry. I sincerely apologize to the victims and their families.

“I wish the children good health and a good life. And I apologize to the Swiss people.”

News.title: Shocking moment enraged historian, 80, smashes cars with scaffolding pole in feud with two hoteliers over parking spaces
News.content:
Next

THIS is the dramatic moment an 80-year-old military historian “snapped” and went on a car-smashing rampage after a bitter feud with his hotelier neighbours turned toxic.

Alexandre Binda took a steel scaffolding pole to two cars outside a hotel in Rothbury, Northumberland, causing more than £6500 of damage, after months of tit-for-tat rows over parking spaces.



The former Rhodesian soldier walked free from Newcastle Crown Court with an 18-month conditional discharge after a judge said there were “clearly two sides” to the saga.

Binda and his wife had been in a neighbours-at-war battle with a hotel manager and his husband, whose premises back onto the couple’s mews home.



The feud escalated so badly that the hotelier and his husband were both charged with common assault against Binda and his wife, though they were later cleared.

But before that case even reached court, Binda walked up to the hotel armed with a pole and began smashing up the vehicles he believed were parked on his property.

Shocking footage shows him approaching one vehicle with a pole as he appears to argue with another person nearby.

He is then shown swinging the pole and striking the front of the motor.



Binda wrecked a van to the tune of £4500 and caused a further £2000 of damage to a Range Rover – all caught on camera by the hoteliers.

According to The Telegraph, Prosecutor Saba Shan told the court the couple “looked outside and saw the defendant smashing two vehicles with a metal scaffolding pole”, with one filming while the other dialled 999.

The van owner received a £4500 payout, but the Range Rover wasn’t insured.

The hotel manager’s husband said he “could no longer live in my property due to the anxiety and depressions it’s caused”.

It was also heard at court that the pair had left the hotel.



Binda, who has no previous convictions, pleaded guilty to two counts of criminal damage and was ordered to pay £1000 compensation at £50 a month.

Defending, Nick Lane said: “He is deeply ashamed and embarrassed that, at the age of 80, he finds himself before your honour today.”

He added: “He simply snapped and acted in the way he did”.

News.title: Baby boy whose skeletal remains were found wrapped in newspaper from 1910 was deliberately ‘garrotted’ with twine
News.content:
GRIM DISCOVERY Baby boy whose skeletal remains were found wrapped in newspaper from 1910 was deliberately ‘garrotted’ with twine







Next

MYSTERY remains over the skeleton of a newborn baby boy found wrapped in a newspaper from 1910 with twine looped around his neck, an inquest heard.

The tragic discovery was made during renovations on a home in Bishop Auckland in July 2024.



The newborn – named as Baby Auckland – had been wrapped in newspaper then buried under floorboards.

Twine had been looped three times around his neck, knotted, then looped again.



Coroner Crispin Oliver said the tot was garrotted while he was still alive and recorded a verdict of unlawful killing.

He said the most likely explanation was that the “person in a position to care for him while he was most vulnerable” took the decision to end the boy’s life “by means of strangulation using twine as a garotte”.

The coroner added: “As such, this was homicide.”

Given the passage of time, there was no prospect of any criminal proceedings, the coroner said, despite lengthy police inquiries.

The hearing was told that the investigation involved DNA testing, a radio carbon expert and a forensic anthropologist as well as public appeals.

Mr Oliver said – unusually – all elements of the inquest process were engaged, meaning it was necessary to establish who the deceased was, as well as how, where and when he died.



The coroner said there was no record of the baby existing.

He said: “This is a very sad and singular case.”

Giving his conclusion, he said that Baby Auckland died in or shortly after 1910 “having been garrotted with twine” shortly after his birth, then concealed under the floorboards.



Mr Oliver said: “This was a terrible thing to have happened to a defenceless infant.

“It happened in our community but it happened over a century ago and it is heart-warming how the public and individuals in this community have stepped up to do the right thing by Baby Auckland.”

The coroner praised the painstaking police investigation, and Durham County Council for organising a funeral, supported by a funeral director who gave their services for free and a memorial firm which provided a headstone.

The baby was wrapped in a newspaper called The Umpire, dating from 1910.

Renovations were being carried out in a second floor room at the building at Fore Bondgate by owner Peter Moody, who made the discovery under a floorboard.



He told police that the skeletal remains had what looked like a metre of garden twine around the neck.

Records established that the property, used as a cafe at the time, was built in the late 19th century.

Detective Chief Inspector Mel Sutherland, who led the police inquiry, said forensic anthropologist Dr Micol Zuppello worked at the scene and established that the remains were human and male.

Dr Zuppello believed the body, since mummified, was placed face-down.

She judged the remains were that of a baby of 38-40 weeks gestational development.



It was not possible to say if the baby was stillborn.

Home Office pathologist Dr Louise Mulcahy told the inquest she could not ascertain the cause of death.

There was no sign of trauma on the skeletal remains, but there was no soft tissue left to establish if poisoning was a factor.

She confirmed to the coroner that the twine was looped and knotted directly around the baby’s neck, then wrapped in newspaper, rather than the chord being used to tie the wrapping, like a parcel.

That finding led the coroner to judge that the baby had been strangled with the twine.



DNA testing did not reveal any known living relatives, Mr Sutherland said.

The detective said public appeals in the media led to two sisters to come forward believing that they could be related to a servant who worked at the property, but a DNA test did not match.

Mr Oliver asked Mr Sutherland if the twine could have been used to hang a religious artefact around the baby’s neck, or if string could have been used in midwifery practices at the time, but the detective said neither was likely.

The inquest also heard from Dr Brian Tripney, a radio carbon dating expert from Glasgow University, who used a bone sample to establish that the baby was born in a period between the mid-1600s and 1955.

Speaking to reporters after the hearing, Mr Sutherland said the two-year investigation had been frustrating and challenging due to the passage of time.



Without modern sources of evidence such as CCTV or phone records, he said investigators had to think laterally and use different techniques.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

He said: “It was heart-warming to see how many people gave Baby Auckland the send-off that he got.”

After the funeral in April, Cathy Hunt, Durham County Council’s cabinet member for children and young people’s services, said: “Sadly, for reasons we will never know, this little boy was never given the dignified and appropriate burial he deserved, so it was important that he was laid to rest in a way that honoured a life that could have been.”

News.title: Police suspects who look eerily like your favourite celebs – can you name them all?
News.content:
YOU MUGS Police suspects who look eerily like your favourite celebs – can you name them all?







Next

POLICE suspects over the years have stunned the public with their eerie resemblance to some of the world’s most recognisable stars.

And it certainly doesn’t help being the spitting image of a celebrity if you’re a wanted criminal on the run – especially not if your mugshot goes viral and ends up plastered across the internet.



The most recent celebrity lookalike was hauled into custody last month after allegedly shoplifting £430 worth of power tool batteries from a store in Minnesota.

But Cyrena Anne Quast, 35, ended up stealing the spotlight for a completely different reason – her uncanny resemblance to superstar singer Jennifer Lopez.



She doesn’t look thrilled to have been arrested – but on the plus side, half the world is now saying you look just like J-Lo.

It’s certainly one sort of silver lining.

So who else has seen their doppelganger get up to no good?

Abdulah Husseini went viral for his likeness to David Schwimmer after Blackpool police posted CCTV footage of him on Twitter carrying a beer crate, prompting the Friends star to post “It wasn’t me!” and even reenact the hilarious video.

Harry Styles lookalike Jason Sanderlin, 21, has definitely taken his life in the wrong direction, with his mugshot going viral after he was accused of assaulting a woman during a robbery in Pennsylvania.

Someone needs to tell Walter White lookalike Todd W. Barrick that Breaking Bad was supposed to be entertainment, not an instruction manual.



Illinois cops were on the hunt for Todd for methamphetamine possession – and he’s even the same age as the character played by Bryan Cranston.



Devon police were on the hunt for this dead ringer of Eastenders star Dean Gaffney back in 2018.

Police launched the appeal after Derek Giff failed to appear in court following a string of burglaries.

Don’t worry, the former Prime Minister hasn’t fallen on hard times – Bojo lookalike and career criminal Jason Watson from Hull went viral after admitting to burgling a cafe.



They might both like to sport a bit of tousled swept-back hair, but that’s where the similarities end between footballer Jack Grealish and Kaine Blissett, who in 2024 was wanted by Kent Police on recall to prison.

Bear Grylls was another who found out he had an unfortunate doppelganger, when security footage was released showing a burglar with a definite likeness to the survivalist.

Equipment worth thousands of pounds was stolen from a modelling studio office by the SAS hero’s lookalike.



His mug was made public by raging finance manager Iain Blank who appealed for social media users to track down the robbers.



But Twitter sleuths were quick to point out the uncanny resemblance, with one saying: “Good question… @BearGrylls, can you account for your whereabouts on Thursday evening?”

A George Clooney look-alike was caught on video nabbing a package from a porch in Tallahassee.

In a Facebook post, the Police Department said Geoffrey Hall has caught the attention of the public because of his resemblance to Clooney.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

He was later arrested on charges of burglary, petit theft and violation of probation.

Perhaps he could learn a thing or two from the Oceans 11 gang.

News.title: ‘Happily’ married mum, 46, admits having sex with her SON ‘only about 100 times’ since he was a teen
News.content:
INCEST HORROR ‘Happily’ married mum, 46, admits having sex with her SON ‘only about 100 times’ since he was a teen







Next

A MARRIED mum and her son have been charged with incest after she admitted the pair had sex “only about 100 times”, police revealed.

Christina Clemens, 46, hid the sick relationship from her husband for several years, allegedly having sex with son Shane Williams, 22, since he was a teenager at their Florida home.



It first came to light after Clemens called the police and accused Williams of sexually assaulting her last month, according to Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd.

Revealing details in a video address on Wednesday, Judd said: “He got mad because she called and we arrested him for hitting mama.”



The cop told him: “Shane, you ought not ever lay a hand on your mama.

“And then he said, ‘Well, I’ll tell you what — I’ve been having sex with my mama since I was 18 years old.’

“So we asked mama, ‘Have you been having sex with your son since he was 18?’

“She says, ‘Only about 100 times. I didn’t stutter’ — that’s what she told us.”

Investigators spoke with her husband, who told them the couple were “happily married” and living together.

When asked if he knew that his wife and her son were having sex, he said no.



He did admit to feeling “a little suspicious” when he spotted them going into the master bedroom together and locking the door, police said.

“What else can you say? That’s nasty” said the sheriff.

“And it’s illegal”, he added.

Highly explicit court documents detail the disgusting relationship and alleged that the intercourse consisted of “oral sex, regular sex and anal sex”.

The son also alleged that the pair used sex toys – and filmed their x-rated rendezvous on cameras in the bedroom and living room.



According to the bombshell docs, Williams did not grow up with his biological moher – but only rekindled his relationship with her at age 18.

Disgraced mum Clemens, from Lakeland, has now been charged with one count of incest and and one count of domestic battery.

She has also been accused of living in open adultery.

Inmate records seen by People report that she is being held on a $5,250.00 bond for both charges.

Her son Williams has also been charged with incest and with one count of domestic violence battery.

News.title: Couple jailed over ‘depraved’ plans to sexually abuse young girl in Wales
News.content:
Couple jailed over ‘depraved’ plans to sexually abuse young girl in Wales

Victoria and Shaun Lewis, both 40, have been jailed after planning to sexually abuse a young girl in what has been described as a 'particularly depraved' case

View Image Victoria Lewis and Shaun Lewis have both been jailed (Image: South Wales Police)

A couple has been jailed after making "depraved" plans to sexually exploit a teenage girl.

Victoria Lewis, 40, arranged for the girl to meet her partner, Shaun Lewis, also 40, knowing he would sexually exploit her. The woman also arranged for an indecent photograph to be taken of the child and for her to travel to an area where the abuse would take place.

Shaun Lewis, from Sandfields in Port Talbot, made "numerous sexual requests and demands" of the victim directly to her and also through Victoria Lewis. Detective constable Amanda Jenkins, of South Wales Police, described what the Neath Port Talbot couple put the child through as "horrifying".

DC Jenkins said: "This has been a particularly depraved case which has involved Victoria Lewis arranging for a child to meet with a man she knew would sexually exploit her. What Victoria Lewis has done is sickening and to think about what the child has gone through because of Victoria Lewis is horrifying.

Moment man drives on wrong side during police chase before running into A-road READ MORE :

"We cannot praise the victim enough for the bravery she has shown to tell police what happened to her and secure justice against a despicable woman – and that is before even mentioning Shaun Lewis’ part in the offending."

Victoria Lewis, from Neath, pleaded not guilty to arranging the sexual exploitation of a child aged 13 to 17, arranging sexual activity with a child, and arranging travel with a view to exploitation.

She was found guilty of all three charges following a trial in April and sentenced to four years in prison, Wales Online reports.

Shaun Lewis pleaded guilty to arranging the sexual exploitation of a child, arranging a child sexual offence, and arranging travel with a view to exploitation.

He was handed an extended sentence of 12 years comprising seven years in prison and a licence period of five years.

A South Wales Police spokesman said: "We never underestimate how difficult it is for survivors of sexual abuse to speak out and report.

"But we hope cases like this one provide reassurance that victims will be listened to, treated with dignity and respect, and will be supported throughout the judicial process.

"If you have been sexually abused, and you are not yet ready to report to police, please don’t suffer in silence." Both defendants will have notification requirements for life.

News.title: Royal Family live: Prince Harry says it's 'good to be back' on first public outing since UK return
News.content:
Prince Harry said "it's good to be back on British soil" as he made his first public appearance since moving back to the UK.

The Duke of Sussex appeared in an exuberant mood as he arrived for the inaugural Spirit of Invictus awards at the Old Naval College in London.

Asked how things were going before be went into the venue, he said: "Good! It’s good to be back on British soil.” In a speech tonight Harry told the audience of armed forces veterans "your service matters".

The duke spoke about his journey setting up the global Invictus Games and how competitors have gone on to achieve the impossible and join "the best community in the world".

He said: "Tonight you will hear extraordinary stories, but I hope we don’t simply applaud them. I hope we recognise what they ask of us.

"Because Invictus was never created so that the rest of us could sit back and admire resilience. It was created so that people who have served know that when their lives change, we don’t disappear.

"They served us. We must continue to show up for them, and I guarantee you, we all benefit when we do.

"And to the veterans here tonight, and those wherever you are around the world, I want to say this as one soldier to another: your service matters. What you gave in uniform matters. And people far beyond the military community who see in your example what courage, resilience and leadership actually look like.

"People are watching. The teammate who is struggling. The young soldier wondering what life after uniform might look like. The family trying to find its way forward.

"At a time when societies around the world are being tested, the Invictus spirit has something to teach all of us. This community doesn’t just demonstrate resilience. It helps build it. Never underestimate what your example gives to the world."

News.title: 'Earl Spencer's memoir strikes at the King but will also plunge dagger into Diana's sons' hearts'
News.content:
The devastating manner in which Diana, Princess of Wales was tragically killed, opened wounds for her loved ones that will never heal.

For her two sons, just 15 and 12 at the time their mother was cruelly and catastrophically taken from them, it has shaped almost every facet of their life since then.

William and Harry have frequently spoken of their lifelong desire to honour her legacy, in their charity work, their roles in public life and indeed after having families of their own, to keep her spirit alive.

How shattering it must be then, to have her memory excavated in such wounding detail. The content of Diana’s brother, Earl Spencer's memoir, not only strikes at the heart of the monarchy, with his lethal character assassination of King Charles, and the wild allegations of his reaction to his ex-wife’s death, but plunges a dagger into the heart of Diana’s beloved sons.

‌



View 3 Images Diana, Princess of Wales, died nearly 30 years ago (Image: WireImage)

It is without question that despite their differences since Harry decided to walk away from his royal role, of which Diana would no doubt have been disturbed over had she lived to see them as men, husbands and fathers, both William and Harry will be deeply disturbed over their uncle’s claims.

Spencer’s claims of the then Prince Charles not only suggesting he - and the royal family - would “forget her soon enough”, and that he was “giddily elated” and sounded like a “lottery winner” when he called him after Diana’s death, are harmful on multiple counts.

Of course, if taken at face value, they threaten not only public perception of the King, who has undergone three decades of carefully cultivated image repair, but could also could have devastating consequences for his relationship with his children.

‌



View 3 Images Earl Charles Spencer has penned a bombshell new book (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

William and Harry have in the past been incredibly open about their father’s misgivings. He was of course the polar opposite parent in many ways to Diana. A product of his own cold upbringing in an unforgiving institution that is not without fault. But what they do acknowledge is after being plunged into becoming a single parent, aside from burying himself in work, he did at least try to shield them from more heartache as best he could in those immediate years following their mother’s passing.

Whereas Harry has used his exit from the monarchy to criticise his family and lay the blame at them for his mental health issues when he was at his most vulnerable, William is an entirely different man. He believes in actions and not words to fulfil his duties as a father and a future king, and will be devastated that his mother’s legacy is being talked about in such terms as we approach the 30th anniversary of her death.

Whether Earl Spencer has any regard for that is a matter for him. What is undeniable is that the King and his heir are united on many matters concerning the business of the family playing out in public and after the monarch's stinging rebuke of Spencer’s claims, in that grief may have clouded his judgement in such recollections, they will unanimous in their despair at this latest war of words.

News.title: Beloved US radio host dies 'peacefully' at Swiss clinic with family by her side
News.content:
Beloved US radio host dies 'peacefully' at Swiss clinic with family by her side

Judy Markey, the beloved co-host of the popular Chicago radio programme 'Kathy and Judy Show', has died at the age of 82 after undergoing a voluntary assisted death in Switzerland

View 3 Images Judy Markey died on Friday in Switzerland at the age of 82 (Image: Corbis via Getty Images)

The beloved co-host of a popular Chicago radio programme has died after travelling to Switzerland for a "voluntary assisted death", her family said.

‌



Judy Markey, who hosted the daily "Kathy and Judy Show" with Kathy O’Malley on WGN-AM 720 from 1989 to 2009, died on September 11 at the age of 82 with her family by her side. The show returned as a weekly Saturday morning programme from 2013 to 2017.

‌



Markey suffered from a degenerative neurological disorder and chose to have an assisted death, the Chicago Sun-Times reports. The name of the clinic was not revealed.

‌



An online obituary set up by Markey's husband, Tom Collinger, described her as a "genuine one-of-a-kind" and said she made the choice to "[go] out on her terms with a voluntary assisted death in Switzerland" after "some years with her body in decline".

View 3 Images Markey suffered from a degenerative neurological disorder

"This choice was made having lived a full and rich lifetime in which she got 'more from it than she ever imagined'," the obituary said.

‌



In the moments before her death, she ate several bites of a Snickers bar and said she had a headache, according to the Chicago Sun-Times. Collinger told the newspaper: "I said, ‘Do you want some Advil?' And she said, ‘I kind of want something a little stronger.'" He added that everyone in the room found her last joke funny.

Her death came on the same day as MPs in the UK rejected a proposal to legalise assisted dying for terminally ill people, bringing the latest attempt to change the law to an end. The House of Commons rejected the legislation by 286 votes to 270 on Friday.

The Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill would have allowed mentally competent adults with fewer than six months to live to apply for assistance to end their lives, subject to approval from a panel of professionals.

‌



View 3 Images Pro-assisted dying campaigners react after MPs voted against the assisted dying bill on Friday (Image: TOLGA AKMEN/EPA/Shutterstock)

Markey was named one of Chicago's "One Hundred Most Influential Women" by Crain's Chicago Business.

Before becoming a radio personality, Markey was a columnist for the Chicago Sun-Times. She also wrote for The New York Times and magazines including Cosmopolitan, and authored several books, including The Daddy Clock and How to Survive Your High School Reunion and Other Mid-Life Crises.

Article continues below

Markey is survived by her husband, daughter Erin Markey, son Adam Markey, stepson Zach Collinger, stepdaughter Kate Collinger Buxton and son-in-law Pat Buxton. She also leaves behind two granddaughters.

News.title: Moment man drives on wrong side during police chase before running into A-road
News.content:
Moment man drives on wrong side during police chase before running into A-road

Duran Amet was seen driving a Ford Focus into the path of oncoming traffic near Bristol before being detained by officers, asking 'what's the problem?'

View 2 Images Duran Amet had a minor passenger who was not wearing a seatbelt in the car (Image: Avon and Somerset Police)

Shocking footage shows a man driving a car the wrong way on a roundabout as he was chased by police officers.

‌



The red Ford Focus, driven by 36-year-old Duran Amet, is seen swerving between lanes and mounting a pavement as he travelled on the A4174 near Wick Wick Roundabout outside Bristol. This took place after officers attempted to stop the car last Thursday due to intelligence held about the vehicle.

‌



Amet tried to evade the police, making a number of dangerous manoeuvres which also included driving into the path of oncoming traffic and travelling at excessive speeds. This was all happening while a minor passenger was in the car with Amet, not wearing a seatbelt.

‌



Met Office names areas facing heavy rain on Friday with 19 counties at risk READ MORE :

Ex-West Ham star Michail Antonio found guilty over Lamborghini incident in London READ MORE :

Amet then entered the Emerald Park area and abandoned his car there, running off towards the A4174 dual carriageway, Bristol Live reports.

Following a short foot chase, Amet was caught and handcuffed by an officer, saying "Sorry, sorry" and "What's [the] problem?".

‌



Amet was charged with dangerous driving, driving while disqualified, driving without insurance, failing to stop for police and using a vehicle without a valid MOT certificate.

View 2 Images Footage showed him running between cars on the busy A-road (Image: Avon and Somerset Police)

He was remanded into custody and appeared at Bristol Magistrates' Court last Friday where he received an immediate custodial sentence of 28 weeks.

Article continues below

PC Jack Fare, of Avon and Somerset Police, said: "Amet’s driving showed a complete disregard for the safety of other road users and pedestrians. Throughout the incident, his actions created significant risk to members of the public.

"It is particularly concerning that he carried out these dangerous manoeuvres while a passenger, who was a minor and not wearing a seatbelt, was in the vehicle.

"We welcome the custodial sentence, which reflects the seriousness of his offending."

News.title: UK risks total breakdown of law and order due to justice failures, PM warned
News.content:
UK risks total breakdown of law and order due to justice failures, PM warned

The leaders of six justice sector unions and royal colleges have issued a bombshell warning to Andy Burnham - telling the PM their members have had enough of being 'set up to fail'

View 2 Images Andy Burnham has been given a dire warning about the state of the justice system (Image: Finnbarr Webster/Getty Images)

The UK is at risk of a total breakdown of law and order, chiefs at several of the UK's biggest justice sector unions and royal colleges have warned Andy Burnham.

‌



In a bombshell intervention, leaders told the Prime Minister that prisons, probation, police and courts are unable to perform their key functions and keep the public safe. The dire warning from the heads of six national bodies - including the Prison Officers Association (POA), the National Association of Probation Officers and the Police Federation of England and Wales - calls for a Royal Commission to carry out a top-to-bottom review.

‌



In a letter to the PM they said: "Our members have had enough of being set up to fail and blamed when things go wrong." They warned that the controversial early prison release scheme, expected to free up around 5,000 spaces in England and Wales, will fail if probation services are not made fit for purpose.

‌



View 2 Images Mark Fairhurst of the Prison Officers’ Association said the entire criminal justice system is in meltdown (Image: BBC )

Their letter states: "From arrest to trial, incarceration to release, the cycle of reoffending continues to spiral out of control, in part because rehabilitation is simply impossible in violent, squalid and overcrowded jails.

"Sticking-plaster solutions such as early release schemes are doomed to fail unless probation is made fit for purpose, while plans to restrict jury trials are a dangerous and wrong-headed response to case backlogs caused mainly by cuts and mass court closures under the last Government.

‌



"Despite early warnings by the new Labour Government they had inherited a 'ticking time-bomb' in our prisons and that failure to act would mean the prospect of a total breakdown of law and order, the response by ministers since has been piecemeal, timid and contradictory."

Mark Fairhurst, national chair of the POA, said: “The entire Criminal Justice System is in meltdown, from Prisons to Probation from Courts to policing. Our call for a Royal Commission is appropriate and will prove how brutal the cuts to these vital public services has ended in a perpetual crisis that clearly puts the public at risk. You cannot have justice on the cheap."

The leaders, also including the heads of the University and College Union, the Public and Commercial Services Union and the Royal College of Nursing, said the government must establish a royal commission to look at the problems running through the justice system.

‌



The move was promised by the Tory manifesto in 2019, but was never delivered. The letter states: "As leaders of trade unions, Royal Colleges and staff associations representing workers in prisons and the wider criminal justice system, we hear daily from our members about the dire state of the vital public services they deliver.

"Years of underinvestment, organisational failures and an obsession with outsourcing have left prisons, probation, police and courts in crisis, unable to perform the core functions of state needed to reduce crime and keep the public safe."

A commission would be required to take evidence from a range of experts - including judges, lawyers, frontline workers, prisoners and ex-prisoners.

Article continues below

The government is grappling with the state of the justice system. As well as the early release of prisoners to tackle the capacity crisis in British jails, fomer Justice Secretary David Lammy proposed reducing the number of jury trials to tackle enormous backlogs.

A government spokesman said: “We inherited a justice system on the brink of collapse, and while there is more to do, we are already taking action.

“We’re building 14,000 more prison places, cutting court backlogs, imposing the toughest-ever controls on offenders, and investing record sums in probation and victim support. That’s on top of putting thousands more police officers into communities and delivering the biggest reforms to policing in 200 years.”

News.title: 1980s voted Britain's favourite decade - here's what Brits miss most
News.content:
1980s voted Britain's favourite decade - here's what Brits miss most

The 1980s has been crowned Britain's most standout decade - and many say they'd love to see a permanent comeback of 80s trends

View 4 Images The decade came top in six out of eight categories (Image: PinPep)

The 1980s has been named Britain's most iconic decade, new research reveals. The era topped the rankings in six out of eight categories in a poll of 2,000 Britons. These included hair, music, pop culture, TV shows, theme tunes, and catchphrases.

‌



The survey found that many Brits would welcome a lasting return of 1980s trends including denim jackets (11%), big-volume hair and curls (9%), and retro trainers (8%). Almost a quarter (23%) would even be prepared to experiment with a modern take on an 80s mullet or perm - with nearly half of Gen Z stating they would consider sporting one of these throwback hairstyles.

‌



View 4 Images Brits miss the TV and styling trends of the 80s (Image: PinPep)

‌



When it comes to entertainment, 38% across all age groups wish big family TV nights remained part of daily life as they were in the '80s. They long for the era when everyone tuned into the same episode and discussed it the following day.

Other cherished moments included watching the programme with your family (36%), belting out the theme tune (27%), and waiting for cliff-hangers to be resolved (20%).

The research was commissioned by UKTV to mark the 40th anniversary of Neighbours, with the first two series making their comeback on U.

‌



To celebrate its return, viewers can win the ultimate Neighbours fan box filled with 80s-inspired treats and playful nods to the show’s early years including tributes to Charlene’s garage look, Scott’s mullet, and Ramsay Street’s most recognisable details.

The study revealed 47% have watched a rerun of a classic TV programme over the past 12 months to seek comfort or transport them back to their younger years (38%).

Yet, the appetite for old-school TV isn't purely about nostalgia. Turns out, 49% agreed classic soaps deliver a level of drama and escapism they still relish today. This feeling was even stronger amongst younger generations, climbing to 68% of Gen Z and 60% of Millennials.

‌



View 4 Images U is offering fans the chance to win one a limited-edition 80s inspired Neighbours styling kits (Image: PinPep)

View 4 Images The kit includes a mullet wig, shoulder pads, a custom tote bag, and much more (Image: PinPep)

According to the study, these series remain most firmly lodged in people's memories due to their iconic characters (45%), dramatic storylines (39%), and catchy theme tunes (36%).

‌



When asked what might inspire them to watch an early episode of Neighbours, for 32% of Gen X it was all about tapping into the '80s nostalgia. Whereas 28% of Gen Z want to discover classic storylines they've never seen before.

Fashion also plays a significant role, with 30% of all generations admiring Kylie Minogue's curly perm as Charlene. Others highlighted her tomboy style (17%), wedding outfits (16%), and Scott's double-denim look (14%).

Emma Tibbetts, director of programming, Scripted, UKTV said: "First arriving on screens in 1985, Neighbours quickly became a daily ritual for UK viewers, turning Ramsay Street into one of TV's most recognisable addresses.

‌



"As the soap celebrates its 40th anniversary and its first two series return to screens on U, fans can go back to the friendships, romances and cliff hangers that helped make the show a global phenomenon.

"Neighbours has always been more than a TV show, it's part of a cultural memory of a generation.

"Bringing the original episodes back to U, gives fans the chance to relive where it all began, while inviting a new audience to discover the characters, drama and unmistakable 80s style that made Ramsay Street iconic. ".

News.title: Thames Water is introducing more regular bills for thousands of customers
News.content:
Thames Water is introducing more regular bills for thousands of customers

The majority of Thames Water customers are billed every six months, but between 110,000 and 120,000 are being moved to monthly billing by December

View 2 Images Thames Water is making a change to billing for thousands of customers (Image: SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images)

Hundreds of thousands of Thames Water customers are being switched to monthly payments as part of a major shake-up.

‌



The majority of Thames Water customers are billed every six months, but between 110,000 and 120,000 are being moved to monthly billing by December. It follows a trial involving 5,000 households that ended last November.

‌



The customers that will be included in the scheme are those with smart meters, which calculate how much water they actually consume, according to This is Money.

‌



The newspaper reports that customers are able to opt out of monthly billing and return to six-monthly billing. 11% of customers opted out during the initial pilot last year. Thames Water has around 16 million customers.

UK heatwaves will cause food prices to skyrocket this winter, report finds READ MORE :

View 2 Images Find out ways to save money on your water bill below (Image: Getty)

A Thames Water spokesperson said: “Monthly billing can help customers track their water usage more regularly, identify periods of high consumption sooner, assist their budgeting by aligning with other household bills, avoid larger less frequent bills and better understand how their usage changes throughout the year.

‌



“We expanded monthly billing to a larger group of eligible smart meter customers following a successful pilot and customers are able to opt out and return to six-monthly billing if they prefer.”

Thames Water is fighting to secure a rescue deal proposed by its senior creditors to avoid collapse and being placed in temporary nationalisation by the Government. The company is struggling under a reported £20billion debt pile.

How to save money on your water bill

If you're on a low income, check if you qualify for a social tariff, which is a discounted rate. Who is eligible and the level of support varies depending on the firm.

Article continues below

If you live in England and Wales then your water bill is still based on the rateable value of your home in 1990. All new homes have been fitted with water meters since then, and you can ask to get for free, though it is not always beneficial for everyone.

Consumer champion Martin Lewis refers to this rule of thumb for those considering getting one: “If there are more bedrooms in your home than people, or the same number, check out getting a meter.”

It sounds obvious, but reducing your water usage can also have a big impact on your bill - and it doesn't have to be big changes. For example, reduce your shower time by one minute or invest in water-saving gadgets to help your consumption.

News.title: Remains found after wildfire identified as mother-of-three missing since 2019
News.content:
Human remains discovered in woodland in south-west London following a wildfire have been identified as a woman who has been missing since 2019.

Mother-of-three Joanne Sheen, then aged 44, was last seen when she travelled from Fareham to Southampton with a friend on 5 December 2019.

Metropolitan Police officers were called to Padstow Walk in Feltham on 12 August after bones were discovered in an area of shrubland damaged by a fire the previous week.

A 56-year-old man from Southampton has been arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit murder and he remains in police custody.

Detectives in London have now handed the investigation over to Hampshire Police after the remains were identified as those of Sheen.

Sheen's disappearance sparked a major police investigation, which the force described as "long and complex".

News.title: Charles 'sounded giddily elated' after Diana died, Earl Spencer claims
News.content:
Earl Spencer, brother of Diana, Princess of Wales, has claimed King Charles "sounded giddily elated" when he called him after her death in 1997.

In a controversial book about Diana, he alleged the then-Prince Charles sounded like a "lottery winner" after the news.

Buckingham Palace strongly pushed back on Wednesday against the credibility of the book, after an initial extract claimed Charles had said of Diana: "We'll forget her soon enough."

A spokesperson said: "While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss."

The latest claims are once again highly personal in their attacks on King Charles and the royals, interpreting their motives in a very harsh light.

The evidence is Earl Spencer's own recollection of conversations about that emotional time around his sister's death, almost 30 years ago.

What remains to be seen is how the public might respond to the allegations, whether they might support this book as a new and different Spencer perspective, or whether they might feel it to be inappropriate to be sharing such private disputes.

Representatives of Prince Harry have said they do not want to comment on the book and Buckingham Palace has pointed back to its response from Wednesday, when it rejected the account of Prince Charles in the wake of Diana's death in Paris.

In excerpts from Earl Spencer's memoir published in the Daily Mail, external, he recounts being alerted to the car crash on 31 August, 1997, by a phone call from his sister Jane in the middle of the night at his home in Cape Town, South Africa.

During the calls that followed, which confirmed the death, the then-Prince Charles telephoned him, he writes.

The book alleges: "Unlike my other callers, who were stunned, barely able to articulate their condolences and offers of help, he sounded giddily elated - like a lottery winner, I remember thinking at the time."

According to Earl Spencer, Charles informed him he had told Princes William and Harry of their mother's death first thing that morning, in their bedrooms at Balmoral.

The royal couple had divorced in August 1996.

Swan Song: Diana, My Sister is due to be published next week. BBC News has not seen the book in full.

News.title: Interest rates held but Bank signals rise if energy prices stay high
News.content:
The Bank of England has held interest rates at their current rate of 3.75% for the sixth time in a row but said they were likely to rise if high energy prices persist.

The US-Israel war with Iran has disrupted global energy supplies leading to a sharp increase in petrol and diesel prices and an uptick in inflation.

But Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey said energy price volatility made it more likely that interest rates would rise.

The Bank also announced it was slowing its sales of UK government debt, prompting an easing in the UK's long-term borrowing costs.

The Bank of England's main interest rate is a crucial benchmark for banks and other lenders in setting interest rates for individuals and businesses who want to borrow or save money. Higher rates can help dampen inflationary pressures, while lower rates can help boost spending and investment.

The UK's central bank aims to keep inflation at a target of 2%, but it has been above that rate for nearly two years, with inflation hitting 3.1% in August.

On Thursday the Bank of England raised its forecast for inflation predicting it would be "slightly above 4%" at the start of next year. It warned that the price cap on household gas and electricity bills for January was "now expected to rise substantially further".

Speaking after the Bank's decision, Bailey said the direct impact of higher energy prices was clear, but officials were still assessing how far those costs would feed through into wider inflation across the economy.

News.title: Father's tribute to 'sweetest little boy' Noah Woods
News.content:
People from as far afield as Birmingham and Hampshire turned up to help with the search for Noah, who was from nearby East Bergholt.

Helicopters, dog units and members of the public had been scouring the area, close to the River Stour on the Suffolk-Essex border.

Reflecting on the community response, Woods wrote in his Facebook post: "It seems he has made an impact across the whole nation.

"You have all taken Noah into your own hearts, with all the overwhelming help, we were all just trying to bring him home to us safe and sound."

He thanked everyone who came together to search for "our boy" - listing emergency services, businesses and venues in the village - and "all of the people who gave up their time in their busy schedules to help us when we most needed it".

"The compassion shown by all of you will never be forgotten by us, and brought us comfort and strength at the darkest time of our lives."

He finished the post by addressing his son.

"It has been a privilege to be your parents and be able to have packed so much love in the short three years you were with us."

Suffolk Police said his death was not being treated as suspicious, but that officers still had inquiries to complete before submitting a file for the coroner.

Supt Tom Pearse thanked the family for their "patience and understanding throughout the searches".

"It was clear from the media coverage we saw that they not only had all of Suffolk behind them, but an outpouring of goodwill from across the entire country and beyond.

"I know how grateful Noah's family are for all the support and kind messages they have received, but would reiterate our plea to now allow them the time, space and privacy they need at this deeply distressing time."

News.title: King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands
News.content:
King Charles has warned AI executives of the "existential dangers" posed by the technology falling into the wrong hands.

He made the comments at a summit he had convened at Dumfries House in Ayrshire to discuss how the tech can be used to benefit society.

Those gathered at the meeting also included Kanishka Narayan, the UK's AI Minister, the Pope's advisor, and participants from AI giants such as Nvidia, OpenAI and Anthropic.

It comes amid a series of recent warnings from people inside the industry about the rapidly evolving capabilities of advanced or "frontier" AI models and the regulation needed to keep them in check.

"Those who have created these technologies are now increasingly warning that AI risks developing darker capacities - perhaps even to take life," the King told the executives.

He said there seemed to be an "urgency" in "adequately considering the existential dangers of such technologies falling into the wrong hands, and being used in potentially catastrophic ways".

"The task before you is not merely to advance technology, but to ensure that it remains firmly in the service of humanity, community and the natural world," he told the group.

The summit has been called to consider whether a "shared set of principles" can be developed to "help guide the future application" of AI.

News.title: Warm words on Canada's EU 'associate membership' but no guarantees
News.content:
Is Canada about to join the EU? Headlines across Europe indicate a lot of confusion right now.

The EU constitution rules that possibility out as Canada is geographically outside Europe.

But in a speech on Thursday to the European Parliament, Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney said: "Canada and Europe should secure our strategic autonomy through deep cooperation in the full range of strategic capabilities."

Mark Carney was responding â extremely warmly â to an invitation by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen for Canada to become the EU's first associate member.

The EU and Canada already have a far-reaching trade deal (Ceta) in place but Carney insisted additional cooperation on energy and economic security, on critical and raw materials, education, tech and AI innovation, and defence would help safeguard all countries involved.

Canada and the EU feel increasingly squeezed by the superpowers USA on the one side and China on the other â and by tech giants, too, that seem to operate supranationally.

The idea of associate EU membership, Carney emphasised, would not be to form a third superpower or to create a bloc against anyone else.

"We do not pursue zero sum deals," he said. Instead he suggested like-minded nations should club together to create a new form of multilateral global governance in an increasingly turbulent world where â in the minds of some others - might is right.

Only by countries joining forces and shunning isolationism, Carney suggested, could they close key capability gaps, build strength and ensure national sovereignty.

This last may have been a nod to upcoming elections across Europe and the continent's increasingly powerful nationalist politicians. Their slogans â whether "Italy First" or "France for the French" or "Make Poland Great Again" â echo Donald Trump's call to Make America Great Again.

Carney's words were hopeful and warm; the applause in the European Parliament rapturous and apparently heartfelt.

News.title: Ed Sheeran's tour in 'damage control mode' after Macklemore backlash
News.content:
Robert Kraft, the US stadium owner who had pro-Palestinian rapper Macklemore removed as Ed Sheeran's opening act, says Sheeran asked him to match his own $2m (Â£1.5m) donation for "aid in the region".

It came after Macklemore said he would donate $1m (Â£750,000) to Palestinian organisations, challenging Kraft to match him.

Kraft, who owns the New England Patriots, wrote on Wednesday: "Earlier today, before Macklemore challenged me to match his donation, Ed called me and asked me to commit $2 million to match his donation to aid in the region to fight this humanitarian crisis.

"Ed now plans to reach out to other venue owners and our goal is to continue to work together to build bridges."

The BBC's Mark Savage looks at the controversy over Sheeran's US tour and why it is in "damage control mode".

News.title: UK Youth Parliament looks set to be axed
News.content:
The UK Youth Parliament is at risk of being axed within months, BBC News has learned, as the government is not committing to funding it any longer.

The parliament was launched in 2000 to boost interest in politics among young people and has more than 300 elected members aged between 11 and 18.

Once a year, the young politicians are allowed to hold debates in the House of Commons chamber, on a day when MPs are not sitting.

Some MPs and young people say axing it would be a blow for youth democracy, while others say it is not providing value for money.

The Department of Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS), which funds the parliament each year with taxpayer cash, is not committing to giving any more grants to it.

A spokesperson for the DCMS praised the youth parliament's "important legacy... giving elected young people a national platform to represent their peers, engage with decision-makers and develop confidence, leadership and skills for life and work".

It received Â£453,000 in taxpayer funding in the last year alone with about Â£2.4m public money spent on it among other youth initiatives between 2017 and 2024.

While no final decision has been made on funding beyond March 2027, a government source said: "The government has not committed to continuing the programme in its current form."

UK Youth Parliament insiders told the BBC that without government funding, it is likely to close.

It follows a government review, external published in October last year, which concluded that while the parliament was delivering on its intended goals, only a quarter of young people know about it - and some schools felt "excluded from the process."

The government says it is working with young people and youth organisations to design a new scheme that increases their involvement in democracy and decision-making, with further announcements to be made this autumn.

Any new scheme will have a "particular focus on under-represented groups", a government source said.

Bobby Forbes, the recently departed chair of the UK Youth Parliament's Youth Select Committee, which works with officials in Westminster, said it gives teenagers "a direct way to scrutinise government and hold decision-makers to account".

News.title: UK needs 'credible path' on defence spending, says Nato chief
News.content:
Nato chief Mark Rutte has said he is confident the UK government understands the need for a "credible path" to increase defence spending.

The alliance's secretary general told the BBC he was "absolutely confident" in the UK's commitment to hit a Nato-wide spending target of 3.5% of GDP by 2035.

Speaking after meetings in London, he said British ministers accepted the need to make yearly steps towards hitting the target.

But he accepted that the exact "pathway" towards the goal would not be set out until next year.

Andy Burnham has followed predecessor Sir Keir Starmer in committing to reach Nato's 3.5% spending target by 2035, up from an estimated 2.6% this year.

He has said date for reaching a planned 3% interim target will come next spring, when the long-term budgets of government departments are due to be set.

But he has faced pressure to immediately commit to reaching the milestone by the end of the decade. His chancellor and ex-defence secretary John Healey has previously argued this would show Britain was serious about the Nato goal.

Former Dutch PM Rutte has been encouraging members of the alliance not to pencil in large spending increases shortly before the deadline.

Speaking to BBC political editor Chris Mason after meeting Defence Secretary Wes Streeting and Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband in London, Rutte said he was confident British ministers understood the 2035 target could not be met "in one go in 2034".

"I am absolutely confident that when it comes to the 3.5[%] they are there," he said.

"I am absolutely confident that when it comes to the yearly increments, they totally take it and accept it, that they have to be there.

"There has to be a credible path. What that credible path exactly will be, we will see with the spending review next year," he added.

News.title: Andy Burnham urged to set dementia waiting-time target
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham is facing calls to set a national waiting-time target for dementia care in England.

An Alzheimer's Society proposal to set an 18âweek referralâtoâtreatment target has been backed by Professor Sir Mike Richards, England's former national cancer director, and Baroness Louise Casey, who's leading a major review of adult social care.

In a report, Alzheimer's Society and the King's Trust said a "cancer-style revolution" was needed to improve dementia care, which they described as being "stuck in the 20th century".

In a speech at Alzheimer's Society conference on Thursday, Social Care Minister Alison McGovern expressed support for the report, external.

She said: "The report that the Alzheimer's Society published today on going on the journey that we've been on with cancer, with Alzheimer's and dementia, I think that's spot on."

The minister said dementia had been "neglected for far too long".

She added: "And nowhere is this division between health and social care felt more sharply than by people living with dementia in their families, too often left to navigate a shattered system at the most difficult time in their lives."

The government has committed to appointing a top official to oversee dementia care and publish a new plan - a modern service framework - to speed up support for those with the disease by the end of the year.

McGovern said the government would "appoint a dementia tsar, backed with real expertise".

Currently there is no waiting-time target for dementia in England.

In contrast, the NHS sets waiting-time targets for cancer diagnosis and treatment.

Professor Richards was the national cancer director when these cancer targets were introduced in 2000, and said he thought an 18âweek referralâtoâtreatment target for dementia patients was achievable.

He said setting such a target would require "political initiative" and extra funding.

"All of that is going to cost more money but remember the toll that this condition is taking at the moment, both on the people affected by dementia themselves and their relatives," the professor said.

The same proposal has been made by Baroness Casey.

In a letter to former Health Secretary Wes Streeting in March, she said the government should look at "how dementia can be put on a level playing field with other conditions, for example by setting national standards for dementia diagnosis, including an 18âweek referralâtoâtreatment target".

Speaking to the BBC, Baroness Casey said she agreed with the proposal to emulate cancer care.

She said: "I think the National Health Service and more generally all of us have stuck our heads in the sand about it, and it's time we started saying, yes, we should have a similar mission, and we should do as much as we possibly can on dementia, and now."

Baroness Casey is expected to publish her recommendations on social care reform next summer.

About one million people are living with dementia in the UK, a figure expected to reach 1.4 million by 2040.

Burnham cancelled his engagements earlier this week after the death of father, Roy, who had Alzheimer's disease.

Returning from compassionate leave, he said his father would have wanted him "back out there" to bring forward "the changes that he always pushed me to make".

In July, Burnham spoke about his father's condition and said it had influenced his drive to reform adult social care in England.

Burnham has said he will wait for Baroness Casey's recommendations before deciding what changes to make to social care and how it's funded.

News.title: Man, 29, jailed for raping two 14-year-old girls
News.content:
A man has been jailed for 14 years for raping two teenage girls after encouraging them to drink alcohol at his flat.

Sultani Bakatash, 29, an Afghan, met one of the girls on Snapchat before inviting her and her friend to his home in Georgina Court, Bolton, Greater Manchester, on 6 December.

Bolton Crown Court heard the 14-year-old girls drank vodka and Coke and became so intoxicated they were passing in and out of consciousness before Bakatash raped and sexually assaulted them.

Following a four-week trial, he was convicted of two counts of rape, one of sexual assault and one of assault by penetration. The judge said his work with the British Army in Afghanistan might mean he was not deported.

One of the girls managed to escape from the flat and knocked on a neighbour's door, the court heard.

She said: "He's trying to rape my friend. She's locked in. He's raping her."

The court heard Bakatash encouraged the girls to keep drinking while taking only a sip himself and complimenting them on their appearance.

Charlotte Rimmer, prosecuting, said he had arranged to meet the girls, encouraged them to drink and then seized the opportunity to rape them.

She described him as "a man, intent on sexual gratification, regardless of what they wanted".

The court heard both girls became so drunk they passed out and each witnessed the other being raped and sexually assaulted.

News.title: Ukrainian guilty of vandalism at mosques linked to Russian network behind Starmer arson attack
News.content:
A Ukrainian man has pleaded guilty to spraying abusive graffiti on mosques in east London, in a case linked to the Russian state network behind arson attacks against the former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer.

Illia Bilyk, 21, entered guilty pleas at Thames Magistrates' Court to five counts of racially and religiously aggravated criminal damage.

Bilyk sprayed graffiti on the Stratford Islamic Association, Al-Birr Mosque and Leyton Jamia Masjid on 23 January 2025. Two days later he targeted Noor Ul Islam Primary School and the Islamic Shariah Council.

The BBC has learned that Bilyk told police he was recruited into spraying the graffiti by a Russian speaker after being approached on the messaging app Telegram.

Bilyk said the Russian speaker told him where to target and paid him afterwards.

In June this year two Ukrainians - Roman Lavrynovych and Stanislav Carpiuc - were jailed for conspiring to carry out arson attacks targeting a property and a car connected to prime minister Sir Keir Starmer.

An investigation by the BBC and Hope not Hate revealed that Russia was behind the arson attacks and had also generated Islamophobic vandalism throughout London, including on the east London venues which Biluyk has now admitted vandalising.

News.title: Former MI6 spy takes Trump to Scottish court for £800,000 legal payout
News.content:
A company founded by a former spy is pursuing Donald Trump at a small Scottish court for more than Â£800,000 in unpaid legal costs.

The US president was named in a hearing at Ayr Sheriff Court as Orbis Business Intelligence seeks funds from the Trump Turnberry golf resort.

The case concerns legal costs owed by Trump from a 2024 English data protection case against Orbis's director Christopher Steele - a former MI6 agent.

But SLC Turnberry Limited - which owns the course - is disputing Trump's role as the "ultimate owner", arguing that his stake in the course is held by a trust.

Steele was the author of a salacious "dossier" linking Trump to Russia during his 2016 election campaign.

London's High Court of Justice ruled Trump's action out of time and a judge ordered him to pay Orbis Â£680,000 in legal costs.

Orbis is targeting the president's financial interests at Turnberry in order to claim the funds.

The case called at Ayr Sheriff Court because the resort falls within its jurisdiction, while Steele and Orbis have no connections there.

News.title: RNLI station out-of-service after anti-migrant protests
News.content:
Portsmouth's lifeboat station remains temporarily out of service following anti-migrant protests.

Protesters blocked roads in the city on 6 September after about 120 people arrived at the Eastney Landing ferry port area following a Channel small boat crossing. The RNLI helped bring them ashore.

The RNLI also said it helped to ensure the safety of anti-migrant demonstrators who went into the sea.

Following the protest, the charity's chief executive said staff had faced "unacceptable" online and physical abuse. The lifeboat station was taken out of service on 10 September, meanwhile, abuse aimed at volunteers also forced the lifeboat museum in Poole to shut for several days.

The RNLI said: "Search and rescue cover continues to be provided through established contingency arrangements, including flank RNLI stations and other declared assets.

"We hope to have the lifeboat station back on service as soon as possible."

After abuse was directed at its crews tasked to assist the incident, its chief executive issued a statement.

Peter Sparkes said: "Recent events have generated deliberate misinformation and a misunderstanding about the RNLI â our purpose, our tasking, and particularly our lifesaving work in the Channel.

"Sadly, as a result, some of our volunteers and staff have been the subject of online and, in the worst cases, physical abuse.

"The RNLI's people represent the very best in our society, they selflessly give up their time to keep others safe."

He added: "Stand by them, not against them and their families. I am extremely proud of and grateful for their vital lifesaving work."

The protest in Portsmouth followed a separate demonstration the previous day, in which hundreds of masked "stop the boats" protesters brought the Port of Dover to a standstill.

The protests led the RNLI to also review its security procedures. As part of this, volunteers were told to consider not wearing RNLI-branded clothing in some circumstances while representing the charity.

News.title: Marooned Lord Byron statue returns to Hyde Park
News.content:
A statue of the 19th-century poet Lord Byron has been returned to Hyde Park, nearly 70 years after it was isolated on a traffic island when new roads were built through the area in the early 1960s.

The Grade II-listed statue was erected as a national memorial in 1880 after receiving special permission from Queen Victoria. Changes to the Park Lane road layout 80 years later left it inaccessible, leading it to become isolated, neglected and dirty.

The Lord Byron Society launched a campaign to relocate the statue six years ago, arguing it had become neglected.

The move cost more than Â£400,000, funded by a Â£230,000 grant from The National Lottery Heritage Fund and additional donations.

"We are all extremely grateful that our plea to rescue Byron and put him back into full public view was met with so much support by everyone involved," said Lord Robin Byron, the president of the society.

News.title: Family blame police for 'Putney pusher' suspect's death
News.content:
While in police custody in June over the Putney Bridge incident, Brandram was also arrested on suspicion of possession of class A and class B drugs.

Ch Supt Dan Knowles said: "Our thoughts are with Mr Brandram's family and friends at this deeply distressing time.

"We recognise the significant impact his death will have on those who knew and loved him."

He said that following Brandram's release under investigation, "it was made clear that inquiries would continue while officers progressed outstanding lines of inquiry and forensic examinations".

"This remains the position, and further investigative work is ongoing," he added.

Knowles, who leads policing in south-west London, said that cases involving "complex evidential and forensic work" could take "a number of months to complete".

The Independent Office of Police Conduct confirmed it had received the Met's referral, which is being assessed.

Shortly after the Putney Bridge incident on 5 May 2017, investigating officer Sgt Mat Knowles said: "It was only due to the superb quick reactions of the bus driver that she was not hit by the vehicle."

Bus driver Oliver Salbris told the Sunday Times following the incident: "If I hadn't swerved, I would have smashed her head.

"It was reflex. The consequences would have been terrible for her â and for me."

The Met said at the time that about 15 minutes after the push, the jogger came back the other way across the bridge and ignored the victim when she tried to speak to him.

Detectives identified more than 50 people of interest following the incident.

The Met had initially closed its investigation in 2018 after three men had been arrested and released without charge.
