The uncapped duo of Everton’s Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall and Bournemouth’s Marcus Tavernier are dark horses in attacking midfield. There is intrigue over whether the Real Madrid right-back Trent Alexander-Arnold will be picked after more than a year out of the international picture. Kobbie Mainoo’s situation is also a source of debate after Tuchel gave the Manchester United midfielder zero minutes at the World Cup.

Sports.title: FA chair Hewitt demands Infantino release records of failed World Cup plan
Sports.content:
The Football Association’s chair, Debbie Hewitt, has written to Gianni Infantino demanding that Fifa releases all documents relating to his abandoned World Cup sell-off plan and the decision to lift the USA striker Folarin Balogun’s suspension during last summer’s tournament.

The Guardian revealed last month that Hewitt and other members of the Fifa council were lobbying for an independent review of the proposed Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) sell-off and the Balogun controversy. Their requests have been formalised in a letter sent to the Fifa president and his deputy, Mattias Grafström.

The letter, first reported by the Times, has been sent in advance of the Fifa council meeting in Zurich on 15 October. That is due to be the first time since the FFE plan emerged in July that Infantino will meet the other 36 members of the group that acts as Fifa’s board of directors.

A number of members of the council, which comprises 28 representatives of the six confederations, eight vice-presidents and Infantino, attempted last month to call an extraordinary general meeting to hold Infantino to account over FFE and Balogun.

The rebels were unable to get the 19 votes required to trigger such a meeting, however, and Hewitt’s call for the release of documents and an independent review is also likely to fail.

Infantino has not had any contact with the Fifa council since writing to it to withdraw FFE at the start of August and has been lobbying for support before next year’s presidential election, making visits to the Caribbean, South America, Morocco and Qatar.

Balogun’s ban was lifted after a phone call from Donald Trump to Infantino despite the player being shown a straight red card for serious foul play in the USA’s World Cup last-32 win over Bosnia and Herzegovina. That allowed him to play against Belgium in the last 16, a match the USA lost 4-1.

View image in fullscreen Debbie Hewitt is taking the lead in holding Gianni Infantino to task despite the risk that it could affect the UK’s chances of hosting the 2035 Women’s World Cup. Photograph: Eddie Keogh/The FA/Getty Images/PA

Fifa has said it followed due process, with the decision taken independently by its ethics committee, but has yet to publish a written report on the hearing. A request from the Royal Belgian FA for an explanation went unanswered.

Hewitt’s letter is understood to make reference to other governance issues at Fifa, particularly its response to the crisis caused by the FFE controversy this summer.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The FA’s willingness to take the lead in holding Infantino to task comes with some risk because the UK is the currently sole bidder for the 2035 Women’s World Cup. A decision on the hosts of that tournament and the 2031 edition is due to be made at an extraordinary Fifa congress on 23 November.

The deadline for candidates to stand in March’s presidential election is five days earlier. Infantino is the only candidate to publicly reveal his intention to stand, with Uefa and Concacaf – the North and Central American and Caribbean confederation – working to find someone to stand against him.

The FA sent a letter of endorsement for Infantino’s fourth term as president before the World Cup but, along with several other European countries, has since withdrawn its backing.

Sports.title: Football Daily | Michael Carrick risks untimely spell in the ‘crisis’ box seat with Manchester United
Sports.content:
RINSE AND REPEAT?

Following the conclusion of this weekend’s round of Premier League fixtures, football fans have what promises to be an exceptionally long, uninspiring and largely inconsequential international break to endure. In most parts of the world, various nations have nothing more exciting than friendlies scheduled. In Europe, it’s the return of the Nations League. A competition apparently conceived for no other reason than to allow Cristiano Ronaldo to spuriously claim he has won two major international trophies, this Uefa wheeze is about to kick off for the fifth time. Almost unique among tournaments that have enjoyed such longevity, its format remains fairly baffling to many of those who will actually be playing in it and all but the keenest students of the game. In truth, hardly anyone cares about the Nations League and quite literally nobody gives two hoots about its opening games.

As is customary in the absence of anything more interesting to report on, hacks will be keeping their ears cupped towards the continent in the hope that some loose-lipped South American Premier League star cuts a promo about a perceived dissatisfaction with their lot. Otherwise, the first top-flight head coach whose club is deemed to be “in crisis” will be lined up in the collective media crosshairs and, as things stand, it is Michael Carrick who is in the box seat.

“Under pressure?” he replied to assorted reporters in the wake of Manchester United’s dismal capitulation after going 2-0 up against Brighton in the Milk Cup. “That doesn’t bother me one bit.” As words of defiance go, they may have sounded more convincing if they hadn’t been uttered by a man who appears to have aged 20 years across his first six games in proper charge, only two of which have been won. “I understand what goes on and how the world works,” he added with a sigh.

In recent years there has been a recurring rinse-and-repeat cycle as far as what goes on and how the world works at United. Specifically one involving the dismissal of head coaches following widespread media speculation regarding their abilities to paper over the giant chasms caused by boardroom penny-pinching, dismal player recruitment and ongoing fan dissatisfaction, for which somebody – anybody but the owners and their besuited yes-men – must carry the can. Whether it’s Ole, Erik, Ruben, or the new incumbent, the story only ever seems to end one way, and just six games into the new season, it already seems the die has been cast for the cycle to begin again. Outwitted by Fabian Hürzeler, while his players were torn apart out on the field, Carrick can’t be absolved of all blame for United’s many shortcomings on and off the field. Anything but a win in Sunday’s crisis klaxon derby at Fulham and his future, or lack of one at Old Trafford, will be a tedious but unavoidable talking point for what promise to be 16 already very long days.

LIVE ON BIG WEBSITE

Join Michael Butler from 7.30pm for hot Milk Cup minute-by-minute updates from Manchester City 3-1 Norwich, while Scott Murray will be your guide at 8pm for the night’s Bigger Vase action in his clockwatch, featuring Real Sociedad 1-1 Bournemouth, plus Crystal Palace 1-0 Lech Poznan.

QUOTE OF THE DAY

“You can try to kill me here. But it’s my scar, it’s not your scar. No one is more hurt than me, no one wanted it more. They can endlessly torture you and think: ‘If I had done different substitutions, then we would have won the match.’ You just don’t know it” – Thomas Tuchel stands by his heavily criticised defensive regression during the Geopolitics World Cup semi-final defeat by Argentina, adding that the opposition tactics forced his hand: “Sorry for the language, [they played eff]-it football: ‘We have nothing to lose. Let’s [eff] it.’”

View image in fullscreen Thomas Tuchel on the celebrity beat earlier this week. Photograph: Alberto Pezzali/AP

double quotation mark I met Ludek Miklosko once. In fact, shaking my hand was one of the first things he had to endure after signing for West Ham in the summer of 1990. (The history books say he signed earlier, but he wasn’t officially unveiled until the summer.) I was working in the club shop at Upton Park (a cabin by the gates). He seemed baffled that now he was finally here and had escaped the communist regime, he was being introduced to a child as ‘our new goalkeeper’. He was very nice about it, though; I showed him the new kit, and he went on to meet the groundsman and have a look at the pitch. My lasting memory was of his truly massive hands. Lovely fella” – Jimmy O’Brien.

double quotation mark I was struck by the phrase that Madrid’s Carlos Espí ‘dug his side out of a hole’ (yesterday’s Football Daily). Surely, one cannot dig oneself out of a hole? Digging, by definition, takes you further into the ground. Unless the goal was to arrive in China, climbing out of a hole would be more appropriate” – Christopher D’Cruz.

double quotation mark Amalgamating the themes of yesterday’s three letters, Spurs fans can at least be hopeful about one thing. Since a player who spends much of the time rolling around knacked near the corner flag can’t be interfering with play, then at least none of their forward line will be caught offside much this year” – Jon Millard.

If you have any, please send letters to the.boss@theguardian.com. Today’s prizeless letter o’ the day goes to … Jimmy O’Brien. Terms and conditions for our competitions, when we run them, are here.

Sports.title: Hull City’s rise from Championship strugglers to Premier League fliers
Sports.content:
Sixteen months ago Hull City avoided relegation to League One on goal difference. Four months ago, they needed a last-minute goal from Oli McBurnie at Wembley to win the Championship playoff final. Three weeks ago, when the pre-season predictions were published, they were tipped to threaten Derby County’s record of the worst ever points tally in the Premier League. On Saturday night, they left Stamford Bridge third in the Premier League with eight points.

The 2-2 draw extended their unbeaten run to four games. They have beaten Manchester United and Coventry, and picked up draws against Aston Villa and Chelsea. We are in September and there are 34 more games to come. Hull will not be competing with Arsenal and Manchester City come the end of May. But their start has been remarkable. Almost everyone doubted whether the qualities that took them on an improbable run to the Premier League could keep them there.

The scepticism was not entirely unfounded. To understand where they have come from, it is worth going back to the final day of the 2024-25 season in the Championship. Hull were in the bottom three and their whole campaign would come down to 90 minutes against Portsmouth at Fratton Park. Win and Hull were safe; draw and they needed other results to go their way; lose and it was League One. A 1-1 draw, and Luton’s defeat to West Brom, preserved their status in the Championship, but only on goal difference.

View image in fullscreen Oli McBurnie scored the goal that earned Hull City promotion, and remains a key attacking player in the Premier League. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

Most sides look to rebuild after a campaign threatened by relegation, but a transfer embargo – imposed after the club had failed to pay Aston Villa £1m for Louie Barry’s loan fee – meant that the side that had scored the fewest goals in the league (just 44 in 46 matches) could not strengthen. To make matters worse, manager Rubén Sellés, hired just five months earlier, would soon be shown the door. It was hardly the sort of springboard from which to launch a promotion campaign.

And yet, 12 months later, Hull were celebrating promotion at Wembley. Sergej Jakirovic took over at the start of last season and led the club to a sixth-place finish and a place in the playoffs. They picked up 73 points, scoring just 70 goals in the process. To put that in some context, Coventry picked up 95 points while scoring 97 goals. The fact that Hull even made the playoffs defied the statistics. Had their matches been decided by expected goals, they would have finished second-bottom. They shipped 66 goals, giving them the fourth worst defensive record in the league. Given the speed and statistical improbability of their rise, you could hardly blame the naysayers for wondering whether Jakirovic and Hull would struggle in the Premier League.

The early evidence suggests their approach can work. Hull did not play like other promotion contenders last season in the Championship. They did not dominate the ball and drown out opponents – and that has been one of their biggest strengths so far in the Premier League. Speaking after their win against Manchester United on the opening weekend, their assistant manager, Dean Holden, said: “We are comfortable without the ball. It is not like we are coming up here having dominated the Championship and now we have to change.”

They averaged 45% possession in the Championship, the fifth-lowest in the division. In the Premier League, it has fallen to 29.4%, comfortably the lowest. Hull have not had to answer the question that faces other promoted sides: how do we adapt to not having the ball? They are simply playing a slightly more extreme version of a style they were already comfortable with.

Nor have changed what they do on the ball. They are using the same long, vertical, direct approach as last season. The first phase of the attack is often a long ball into McBurnie in the middle of the field; their midfielders then look to win the second ball and switch play to the wings, often targeting Ryan Giles at left wing-back where he delivers quick crosses or finds a target man in the box.

Hull attempted the second-most long passes in the Championship last season (3,057) and made the fewest passes per sequence (2.5). This season they have attempted the second most long passes (237) and are attempting the fewest passes per sequence in the Premier League (2.46). Giles ranked 10th for crosses in the Championship last season (207); he is third in the Premier League in that statistic this season with 28. Some managers change too much after promotion; Hull have benefited from continuity.

View image in fullscreen Hull City fans wave flags before their opening game of the season. Photograph: George Wood/Getty Images

Having shipped the fourth-most goals in the Championship last season, Hull did not concede in their first three matches in the Premier League. Once again, Jakirovic has gone for continuity. The idea is the same one he used to shut out Millwall and Middlesbrough in the playoffs: a 5-4-1 formation in which his players sit in a mid-to-low block, close the gaps between lines, force the opponent wide, and win the next contact in the box.

Regan Slater and Matt Crooks screen in midfield, with John Egan and Semi Ajayi winning the ugly fights in front of the goalkeeper. Their summer arrivals, notably Nobel Mendy, have added to an already physical backline. Their 53.8% ground duel success rate is the sixth-highest in the Premier League and their 52.3% success rate in aerial duels also ranks sixth.

Perhaps the most valuable thing Hull took into the Premier League cannot be measured by statistics. They are a group that has been through plenty together and, in the process, forged a tight-knit unit. Yes, they spent £150m over the summer, but eight of the starting XI at Stamford Bridge were part of last season’s promotion-winning side. They have added Premier League quality and physicality, but have not attempted to replace the group that got them there. Speaking on the transfer embargo and the difficulties Hull faced last season, Jakirovic said: “Maybe it was the best that it happened like this. This group of players became even closer. They had to stick together and help each other.” They have perfected the art of being the underdogs.

Hull fans will not be getting carried away. There is still a lot of football to play and they know how things can deteriorate across a season. In 2008-09, they were third in the Premier League after nine games, but ended up surviving relegation by a single point. Perhaps they would take that this season, but for now they should enjoy being in the upper reaches of the league.

This is an article by WhoScored

Sports.title: Carlos Espí gives Real Madrid hope in the face of Barcelona’s La Liga storm | Sid Lowe
Sports.content:
José Mourinho called and Carlos Espí came to his side. It was late, it was noisy and it was almost over – the match and maybe even something more – when Real Madrid’s coach took the forward who is also his flatmate to one side on Tuesday night. Standing close, Mourinho had a message to deliver; he also had a piece of paper. Small, folded, half-hidden in his hand, it was not big enough for much more than a single word, shown almost surreptitiously, the request written on it, like what he had whispered in Espí’s ear, left to your imagination. Put ball in goal, perhaps. Or: Help. So he did.

Madrid needed him to, which they should not have. Two goals up inside half an hour at Elche on Tuesday night, they could have added a third or a fourth, maybe even a fifth, before half-time. But, thinking it was as done as it really should have been, their minds perhaps on Sunday’s derby at Atlético too, they had stopped again, drifting. Vinícius Júnior had gone, Arda Guler had gone, Aurélien Tchouaméni might as well have done, barely able to move any more, and now, somehow, the game was going. Goals from Abiel Osorio in the 71st minute and Fer Niño in the 83rd had made it 2-2.

View image in fullscreen Fer Niño scored the equaliser for Elche to make it 2-2 against Real Madrid in the 83rd minute. Photograph: Kai Forsterling/EPA

Antonio Rüdiger was parading the touchline, hands on his head, wearing a look that said: wait, what?! And, control long since lost, the ball not theirs, it could still get worse: somewhere in the notebook, amid all the arrows and the scrawls no one can make sense of, the last, barely decipherable scribble said: “88. Elche are going for the winner too!” All around the Martínez Valero a chant went round: Yes, we can! They had more possession and as many shots on target, had deserved to draw level and maybe even to lead after a second half they had dominated, and genuinely thought they could too. Which was of course their first mistake, the hope what killed them.

With crushing inevitability, the next note says something about Espí and just wide, the one after says 4’ and the one after that just ESPÍ. A step forward, the whole Elche line following to their inevitable demise, and there was the space. On as a substitute, rested to begin with, Jude Bellingham’s superb run and pass released Kylian Mbappé who laid off for Espí to score, staff and subs, dressed in pink, racing down the touchline. He had only gone and done it again. It had been 11.16pm, the 88th minute, when Mourinho slipped him that note; it was 11.21pm when he stood in the corner, pumping his fists. On the pitch four minutes, the 21-year-old who scored an injury-time winner on the opening weekend, had saved them.

Born in Tavernes, a little way up the east coast from Elche, his family waiting for him at the side of the pitch after the match on Tuesday night, no one had heard of Espí this time last year. By then the end of the year, there was a case to say that he was the single most important player in Spain last season but even then, even when Madrid paid his buyout clause, he wasn’t exactly famous. The day he scored against Espanyol in the first week of the season, his Wikipedia page was the most read in the whole country. One detail not on there is that he is a trained oboe player.

That night at Cornella he saved Madrid, like he had saved Levante. No one had an impact on a team like he had on them, scoring 11 goals in 25 games to rescue them for relegation. Maybe saving teams is just what he does. Big strong, a traditional No 9, who does not mind mixing it with centre-backs – Thibaut Courtois called him a “beast” for going into battle with Rüdiger in training. At Madrid, teammates have taken to calling him Joselu Junior. He has scored twice in 42 minutes, delivering four points already. No one at the club has a better ratio.

View image in fullscreen Kylian Mbappé assisted Carlos Espí’s winning goal. Photograph: Kai Forsterling/EPA

This was huge, not just about Tuesday night. Matchday six, a full round of midweek matches, has not finished yet. La Liga did the worst first – Real Sociedad and Celta played out a 0-0 draw two weeks ago – and left the best for last. Betis and Villarreal, the two teams Lamine Yamal says he likes watching the most – if only because he is usually too busy to be in front of the telly when Barcelona play – are both in action on Thursday. But plenty has already happened and something amazing did not: Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang did not score, for the first time. As for Levante and Athletic, they did not even play, although they did turn up and, amid the biblical storm and safety alerts, the league did not actually announce it was off until five minutes after it was due to start and long after the referee had taken one look at the knee-high lake at the end of the tunnel and declared it “reckless” to even get to the pitch, let alone play.

This was the week in which Rayo finally played the last of their unexpectedly successful but ultimately empty games in exile at Léganes, leaving the balance at Butarque: three matches, two wins, one draw, thousands of unoccupied seats and something (else) broken for ever. In which Atlético put four past Osasuna. In which Valencia, under new caretaker management, won for the first time and scored for just the second. And in which Sevilla – Sevilla! – went fourth, a third of the points needed for survival already secure and never to be taken from them. It was also the week in which Atlético scored four, and Barcelona scored seven.

Quick Guide La Liga matchday six results Show Real Sociedad 0-0 Celta (played on 3 September), Rayo 2-1 Espanyol, Alaves 0-1 Valencia, Elche 2-3 Real Madrid, Atlético 4-0 Osasuna, Deportivo 0-1 Sevilla, Barcelona 7-2 Racing. Thursday: Betis v Getafe, Malaga v Villarreal. Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

At the end of the match at the Camp Nou the thunder and lightning also came rolling in, if not quite as violently as at Levante, and delivered every headline writer’s dream – Barcelona are the storm, said AS, while El Mundo Deportivo went for “torrential football” – tragically, no one went for liquid football. The Racing Santander midfielder Sergio Canales described his opponents as “madness”. You do not even have to know about football to see it, he said, which is handy: “Barcelona have it all.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

On a night when they had João Cancelo scoring two belters, Karim Adeyemi channeling Pelé and Gabriel Jesus curling in a gorgeous first goal for the club. Barcelona gave Racing a chance, sending on Wojciech Szczesny, and still did not give them a chance. They scored seven and could have scored 17. Lamine Yamal only scored one; he also had one disallowed, hit the post, and missed a penalty.

They also have Raphinha. And while everyone goes on about Lamine Yamal and Mbappé and the Ballon d’Or and Hansi Flick goes on about how he will be happy when the bloody thing is over, Raphinha, who was not even nominated, quietly goes about showing that right now he is better than both of them – and anyone else in fact. The man who is just filling in at No 9 has 11 goals already this season, a start so good only two men have ever done it before: Lionel Messi and Brazil forward Ronaldo. With seven wins from seven competitive games, this is Barcelona’s best-ever start. They scored two against the man who in the summer conceded just one in eight World Cup games. In their other six matches they have scored: five, five, five, five, four and seven. They have won every league match.

View image in fullscreen Raphinha poses like Spider-Man to celebrate his hat-trick against Racing. Photograph: Joan Monfort/AP

Which is why Madrid needed Espí so badly on Tuesday night. Already defeated at Betis – where Espí came on and scored an outrageous volley that would have been the winner, only for it to be ruled out – Madrid faced the prospect of dropping points again. Still not entirely convincing, they had let another team back into the game – last weekend, Rayo too should have finished off but were suddenly alive. Madrid have “lost” three of the last four second halves – and, with two minutes left, faced the prospect of slipping five points behind Barcelona … with the derby to come this weekend. Of course, it would not have been over: there are still 32 weeks left and Billie Joe Armstrong’s mum hasn’t even sneaked into his room yet. But this is not a Barcelona team that looks likely to allow many second chances and five points would have been a significant gap even at this stage. But then Espí did it again.

After that win at Espanyol on the opening day, the first time their new striker saved them, Mourinho said that he and Espí lived together at the club’s Valdebebas training ground: the two of them, the coaching staff and Marc Cucurella, like the characters in some heartwarming sitcom, a bunch of flatmates thrown together and making it work somehow. “Espí’s a funny kid,” Mourinho said; he’s also one he can call on when you need him.

Sports.title: Alessandro Costacurta: ‘San Siro is an icon – it’s incredibly beautiful but it’s not functional’
Sports.content:
Alessandro Costacurta lasted 15 minutes of his first game at San Siro. He was, admittedly, not playing, but tagging along to watch his older brother’s favourite team.

“I grew up in the province of Varese, north of Milan,” he says. “So as a kid I was a Varese fan. It was my brother who supported Milan. The first time I went to San Siro, I was 12, my brother was 14. I think it was Milan-Bologna. But San Siro wasn’t covered back then, and suddenly this downpour started, so much rain. We were with our dad and after a quarter of an hour he just said: ‘No, that’s it, we’ve got to go.’ So that was the first time I saw San Siro.”

But happily, far from the last. Costacurta was recruited into Milan’s academy a year later and played 663 times for their first team – helping them win Serie A seven times and the European Cup five, either side of its Champions League rebrand. Only his fellow defenders Paolo Maldini (902) and Franco Baresi (719) have made more appearances for the Rossoneri. Many of those were alongside him.

At one point, Costacurta refers to that Milan team as the “best in the world for 25 years”. He quickly corrects himself to “one of the best”. If he wanted to avoid boastfulness then let me say it for him: the back four he formed with Maldini, Baresi and Mauro Tassotti might be – for quality and longevity – the greatest ever.

View image in fullscreen Alessandro Costacurta (front row, second right) celebrates with his Milan teammates after they won the 1989 European Cup final. Photograph: PA Images/Alamy

And they played in one of the planet’s most famous arenas. We are speaking in the days leading up to San Siro’s 100th birthday, an occasion that feels more profound for the knowledge it will not host football games much longer. Milan and Inter completed a joint-purchase of the stadium, and a surrounding parcel of land, from the city council at the end of 2025. They plan to begin construction of a new ground early next year.

A necessary step, for Costacurta. “San Siro is not a modern stadium,” he says. “It’s an icon, it’s incredibly beautiful, but it’s not functional.” He reels off a list of shortcomings, from a shortage of elevators to dated lounges. A mention of the stadium’s infamously grim toilets draws a sheepish grin. “That’s the first thing I wanted to say!”

It will be replaced by a multifunction venue designed by the architect firms Foster + Partners and Manica, with the area around the stadium being regenerated with new retail and hospitality facilities. The realisation of a new stadium has been a central pillar of the vision set out by Milan’s owners, RedBird, since its takeover in 2022.

The project is shared with their co-tenants at San Siro, Inter. There is something in that collaboration that reflects the nature of the rivalry – less bitter than we see between neighbours elsewhere.

“Milan is a particular thing,” says Costacurta. “It’s rare to breathe such friendly air when you go to different derbies around the world. There are chants of course, but also a lot of mixing between fans. And when I was playing, between players too.”

View image in fullscreen The camaraderie between the Milan teams was demonstrated in 2005 as Inter’s Marco Materazzi and Milan’s Rui Costa waited together for flares on the pitch to be cleared during their Champions League quarter-final second leg. Photograph: Stefano Rellandini/Reuters

Still, the games against Inter were the best ones to win – especially when your team was officially the “away” one. “When you’re playing in any great team, the biggest satisfaction of all is ‘conquering’ another great team’s home stadium. I remember a 6-0 when we were ‘away’ to Inter [in May 2001]. At 4-0 we could see their fans walking out.”

Construction is intended to be completed in 2031, ready to host games as well at Euro 2032. It will be a boon to Milan and Inter, providing revenue streams that can make them more competitive on a continental stage, at a time when Serie A – like every other league – has struggled to keep up with the Premier League’s earning power.

Even accepting all this, we can acknowledge the sadness of saying farewell to San Siro. Costacurta has visited Europe’s most famous grounds as a player and spectator. What makes San Siro unique, he says, is the steepness of the stands.

“Lots of stadiums are made this way,” he says, holding his hands at a shallow angle. “San Siro is like this.” Now he is pointing his fingers straight downward. “The first time I was out beside the pitch as a ballboy – which everyone does when you get to the youth team – it made me almost afraid. It felt like all those people were going to fall on top of me.”

View image in fullscreen Fans enjoy the atmosphere in the stadium during the Serie A match between Milan and Brescia at the San Siro in May 2004. Photograph: New Press/Getty Images

“Maybe [Real Madrid’s Santiago] Bernabéu is a bit like that. But still, like San Siro? I don’t think so. In Rome, they have a different way of making you feel close – that anthem they sing before kick-off at Roma is beautiful. But it’s different. At San Siro, when you’re up there at the top, it’s like you’re in a tower above the pitch, leaning out of the window.”

San Siro was opened on 19 September 1926, the realisation of the then Milan president Piero Pirelli’s vision for a football-specific stadium unlike anything in Italy at the time. There was no running track, only four stands with capacity for 35,000 spectators.

Pirelli was said to have taken inspiration from stadiums in England, but San Siro was also a product of its setting. Stables, hay barns and storage space were incorporated below the stands to serve the horse racing track next door.

View image in fullscreen The San Siro Stadium seen from the adjacent Hippodrome soon after it was built in 1926. Photograph: Touring Club Italiano/Universal Images Group/Getty Images

The stadium was bought by Milan’s city council in 1935 and expanded with connecting sections between stands. Inter joined Milan as co-tenants in 1947 before a second tier was added, opening in 1955. In 1980 the stadium was renamed for Giuseppe Meazza, the two-time World Cup-winning midfielder for Italy who played 14 seasons with Inter and two with Milan, though it has remained San Siro to most fans.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen A second tier was added to the stadium, opening in 1955. Photograph: Keystone/Getty Images

View image in fullscreen A view of the stadium exterior in the 1950s. Photograph: FC Internazionale Archive/FC Internazionale/Getty Images

Construction of the final third tier, with a roof at last to shield supporters from the rain, was completed before the 1990 World Cup. Costacurta played the first match after its opening, a 1-0 defeat in the return leg of Milan’s Coppa Italia final against Juventus.

“I remember there was more noise, but the main thing I remember is the pitch,” says Costacurta. “They hadn’t understood how to manage the airflow with the extra tier, and the pitch was really ugly. For a year and a half, our pitch was the worst in Europe.”

Clearly, they adapted. Milan went on a record-breaking 58-game unbeaten run in Serie A from May 1991 through to March 1993. Maybe that ugly pitch even became an asset?

“I think it was a disadvantage for visiting teams that came to San Siro,” says Costacurta. “And San Siro is a stadium that puts a lot of pressure on, there’s this incredible noise.”

He switches to the English word, “Roar!”, for emphasis. He’s not wrong. San Siro on a big occasion is astonishingly loud, to the point that you can find it hard to hear people speaking right next to you.

View image in fullscreen The construction of the final third tier was completed ahead of the Italia 90 World Cup. Photograph: Colorsport/Shutterstock

View image in fullscreen Dancers on the pitch during the 1990 World Cup opening ceremony. Photograph: Michael Kunkel/Bongarts/Getty Images

“Nobody’s really talking on the pitch though,” says Costacurta, who insists the real conversations take place on the training ground. Managers bawling from the touchline are engaged in a futile act. “They hope they can pass a message down the line but, trust me, the message almost never gets there.”

But fans have their ways of getting a message across. San Siro still had standing sections when Costacurta made his first-team debut in 1987. “People would be holding on to the railing beside the pitch, sticking their heads out, shouting, shouting, shouting.

“I was lucky because I came through the youth team, so I didn’t take the hardest insults. They said things to me in a Milanese dialect. Insults, but amusing ones. They called me “pè de ghisa”, which means iron foot, because I didn’t have an acceptable level of technical ability for a team like that yet. But my teammates who weren’t from the youth team got proper insults.”

He won them round in the end. Costacurta laughs at the memory of the “rubbish” chant fans made for him. “It was just ‘Billy! [his nickname] Billy! Vai! Vai! Vai!” [Billy! Billy! Go! Go! Go!] The worst chant of any player at Milan.” But on the day of his final game at San Siro, thousands waited outside the stadium to thank him.

View image in fullscreen Milan supporters display a banner paying tribute to Costacurta during his final match for the club in May 2007. Photograph: Luca Bruno/AP

View image in fullscreen Costacurta acknowledges the fans after his last match for the club. Photograph: Alessandro Garofalo/Reuters

Memories like that will always remain, even when San Siro joins him in retirement. Milan and Inter have said that some part of the old stadium will be preserved in the new development. Costacurta, who became a fan of Arsenal over the years too, admiring Arsène Wenger’s teams from affair, finds encouragement in their move away from Highbury, now converted into apartments.

“I played there in the European Super Cup,” he says. “Nil-nil. [Milan won 2-0 in the return leg at San Siro.] Great. Beautiful. Iconic. I think everyone suffered the change at first, but the Emirates is great now. So why not?”

Sports.title: EFL legend still playing aged 51 reveals how he rejected Man United transfer to join Class of 92
Sports.content:
EFL legend still playing aged 51 reveals how he rejected Man United transfer to join Class of 92

Jamie Cureton has revealed why he rejected a move to Manchester United that would have made him part of the 'Class of 92'.

The Class of 92 consists of David Beckham, Paul Scholes, Gary Neville, Nicky Butt, Ryan Giggs and Phil Neville, and Cureton could have been part of that.



4 The Class of '92 formed the backbone of Man United for a long time Credit: Getty - Contributor

The majority of them went on to become huge parts of Sir Alex Ferguson's early and later Man United sides.

In fact, Scholes and Giggs are arguably two of the best players to have ever represented Man United.

But Cureton turned down the opportunity to be involved.

Incredibly, after a storied career at various different levels, he is still playing football at age 51.



Cureton represents Holland in the Eastern Counties League Division One.

Jamie Cureton explains why he turned down Manchester United

And he joined Paul Hawksbee and Perry Groves to discuss lots of topics around his career and wider football discussions, including how he almost joined the Red Devils.



"Sir Alex Ferguson rang my house and put an offer on the table," Cureton said on Hawksbee and Jacobs.

"I was a Man United fan, but my dad never put me under any pressure. He said, 'it's your decision.'



"I was 14."

Hawksbee then asked why he turned down the offer.

4 'Becks' was one of the most high-profile names to emerge from the 'Class of 92' Credit: Getty

"I was at Norwich and had been at Norwich for a year or two, and I was quite comfortable," Cureton replied.

"What the younger generation won't realise is that Norwich were finishing second in the First Division and playing in Europe, and they had a team that was producing youngsters.

"Man United, up until that point, were buying players, and I felt I had a better opportunity going there and playing.



"It was the Class of 92, so I would have been in that group. The one thing they never had was a centre-forward, and I would have been it.

"But I made my debut at 19, played against Man United at Old Trafford, so in my head, I'd done the right thing because I was involved."

And of course, Ferguson wouldn't let Cureton forget.

4 In another life, the legendary Ferguson could have managed Cureton Credit: Getty

"I was playing for Bristol Rovers and played in Lee Martin's testimonial," the 51-year-old said.



"He was chatting to Ole Gunnar Solskjaer, and I was only 22 at the time, and he made a comment.

"He was following my career and knew what I was doing, so that was quite nice."

Legend

Cureton made his first-team debut for Norwich in 1993 and is still playing 33 years later.

The striker has played nearly 1,100 games across all divisions from the Premier League to where he is now.



Goals have never been a problem either for Cureton, netting a whopping 402 across the course of his career.

4 Cureton has played for 25 clubs in his career

Cureton is best known for his stints at Bristol Rovers and Reading, having made over 100 appearances for both.

Why are they called the Class of 92?

The team that won the FA Youth Cup in 1992 was Manchester United.

Within that side were the likes of Scholes, Butt and Beckham, while a few of them officially joined the year prior.



And though some went on to be Man United legends, others didn't but still had successful football careers.

One of those such players is Robbie Savage.

But all of that group received coaching from 1966 England World Cup winner Nobby Stiles as well as Brian Kidd, and eight of the 14 players signed in 1991 made first-team appearances for Man United, and four of them made a total of 2,000.

Sports.title: Cole Palmer set for England squad recall and two uncapped players could get nod from Thomas Tuchel
Sports.content:
Cole Palmer set for England squad recall and two uncapped players could get nod from Thomas Tuchel

Cole Palmer is set to be handed an England recall following his World Cup snub, talkSPORT understands.

Chelsea star Palmer was one of the biggest names left out by Thomas Tuchel this summer but has started the season in excellent form.



4 Palmer already has four goals and two assists this season Credit: Getty

Bournemouth midfielder Alex Scott, part of England’s pre World Cup training camp in the USA, is also in strong contention for a place in the squad for the upcoming Nations League games.

With Dean Henderson sidelined by injury, Coventry goalkeeper Carl Rushworth, highly regarded withing the FA, is also in line for his first senior call-up.

Tuchel names his squad on Friday at 10am.

England have four Nations League fixtures in the upcoming international break, beginning their campaign against Spain at Wembley on Saturday September 26.



They travel to Czechia three days later before facing an away clash at Croatia on October 3.

The final match of the extended international break sees the Three Lions play host to Czechia on October 6.



All of these matches are live on the talkSPORT network.

Palmer back in the mix

A poor 2025/26 season saw the former Manchester City man fail to make it into the 26-man squad at the World Cup in the summer.

In a campaign which saw him get affected by injury, Palmer managed just 11 goals and and three assists in 34 appearances.



However, he's started this term with real purpose having scored four goals, two of them in the Premier League. He also has two assists to his name this season.

4 Palmer is hoping to add to his 14 senior England caps Credit: Getty

New look England?

It remains to be seen who else gets the nod, but there could be first England caps earned by Scott and Rushworth over the coming weeks.

As mentioned, Bournemouth midfielder Scott flew out to America for England's pre-World Cup training camp but did not join them once the tournament started.



Scott, heavily linked with transfers to Arsenal, Chelsea and Manchester United during the summer, has represented England at under-18, under-19, under 20 and under-21 level.

Coventry City goalkeeper Rushworth has made just four appearances in the Premier League conceding ten goals upon what's been a difficult return to the top flight for the Sky Blues.

However, the 25-year-old has been tipped for a call-up to the England senior squad following his impressive campaign in the Championship last season.

talkSPORT understands Rushworth was disappointed not to be selected by Tuchel in the summer with Brighton's Jason Steele serving as England's fourth goalkeeper during the pre-tournament training camp.



4 Scott is understood to be valued at £80million by Bournemouth Credit: Getty

4 Rushworth joined Coventry on a permanent transfer from Brighton in a £22.5m deal, a club record Credit: Getty

Explaining the decision to pick Steele over Rushworth, Tuchel said: "Jason is a bit of a particular one because we’re planning to take four goalkeepers to the World Cup and the fourth goalkeeper then has a special role.

“The three goalkeepers will compete and support each other for the matches but they will also compete for a place in goal.



“The fourth goalkeeper in a World Cup is then a specialist. He will support the goalkeeper group, he will support the goalkeeper coach, he will support a penalty-taking group and take a lot of workload off the other shoulders and that’s why we need an experienced guy.

“We need a guy with quality, with experience and with the right energy and attitude and we believe that Jason is this guy, so this is kind of a trial to find out how this group works together for the World Cup."

Sports.title: Todd Boehly takeover was ‘horrific’ as full scale of £1.7billion Chelsea chaos laid bare
Sports.content:
Todd Boehly's reign as Chelsea chairman has been branded a catastrophe after his exit was announced on Wednesday.

After taking over from Roman Abramovich in 2022, the American tycoon and director Mark Walter have sold their 25 per cent stake to majority owners Clearlake Capital, fronted up by co-founder Behdad Eghbali.



7 Boehly has grabbed his coat and left Chelsea four years after he arrived Credit: Getty

It comes after a chaotic four years at Stamford Bridge, characterised by wild transfer business, managerial upheaval, and not a lot of success on the pitch.

talkSPORT host Andy Goldstein said: "From my understanding, every single Chelsea fan says good riddance.

"Every single one. There won't be one tear shed from any Chelsea fan.

"It's been pretty horrific, hasn't it, since he's come in?"

Ex-England striker Darren Bent responded: "The majority of their signings have been atrocious. Even the way they've run the club, the football operation, where it was buying these young players rather than buying ready-made superstars, because that was what Chelsea were.



"They still had deep pockets, but they opted to try and make money out of Chelsea and the club's ambition got put on hold. Simple as that. It was all about turnover and profit, as opposed to what Chelsea were."

Bent added: "When you look back at his [Boehly's] tenure, it just looks like someone who didn't have a clue."



So what sort of legacy does Boehly leave behind? talkSPORT.com takes a look at his most significant contributions to the club and assesses whether they were a hit or a miss.

Interim sporting director - miss

Despite knowing very little about the inner workings of top-level football, Boehly stepped in as the club's transfer chief immediately after arriving at Stamford Bridge.



Any trace of the Abramovich era was quickly eradicated, as director Marina Granovskaia, chairman Bruce Buck, and technical advisor Petr Cech all left.

7 Granovskaia was famously the brains behind much of Chelsea's success under Abramovich Credit: Rex Features

Boehly's first move as interim sporting director was to spend £250million in one summer.

Raheem Sterling, Marc Cucurella, Kalidou Koulibaly, and Wesley Fofana all arrived in big-money deals during the 2022 summer window.



Then in September, manager Thomas Tuchel was sacked and replaced with Graham Potter.

Boehly admitted himself that he was in too deep. Reflecting on that period, he said: "Having taken over in the circumstances that we did, basically the whole management team left, I was stuck being interim sporting director for a summer, having no idea what made a good football player."

Record signings - hit

Before handing over to Laurence Stewart and Paul Winstanley, Boehly spent £300m in the January winter window of 2023.

This included the record £107m signing of Enzo Fernandez from Benfica, which most would consider to be a success.



7 City signed Fernandez for a record-equalling £125million on deadline day Credit: Manchester City FC

Not only was Fernandez a key player for Chelsea across three-and-a-half seasons, they still sold him to Manchester City for profit earlier this month.

It was also around January 2023 when Boehly popularised amortisation - the art of signing players on super long contracts to spread costs and balance the books.

This was coupled with the selling of homegrown talent (and hotels) for 'pure profit' - with Boehly constantly searching for loopholes to avoid breaching financial regulations.



With the professionals now helping Boehly in the technical department, the Blues sacked Graham Potter, got Frank Lampard back for an interim spell, and finished 12th in the 2022/23 season - their worst league position since 1996.

The summer of 2023 saw more record spending as Moises Caicedo arrived for £117m - which, again - proved to be money well spent.

After two years of upheaval, Chelsea appeared to be making progress under Mauricio Pochettino by 2024, as their young team rallied to a sixth-place finish.

7 Caicedo remains one of Chelsea's best players Credit: AFP via Getty



Managerial chaos - miss

As reports emerged of a power shift in the boardroom around 2024, it appeared Boehly became less involved in the decision-making at Stamford Bridge during the final two years of his chairmanship, with Egbahli growing more influential.

Pochettino left due to a difference of opinion with the Chelsea board - and many questioned why this bridge was only crossed one year into his Blues tenure.

Enzo Maresca was appointed and delivered two trophies: the Conference League and the Club World Cup, while guiding Chelsea to a fourth-place finish and a Champions League return.

Cole Palmer and Joao Pedro became perhaps the two strongest examples of shrewd business under Boehly.



Both were signed for a combined £100m, less than Liverpool spent on forwards Florian Wirtz and Alexander Isak individually.

Suddenly, there appeared to be method to Boehly's apparent madness, as his expensively-assembled young squad started to gel.

7 Palmer and Pedro have become one of the most prolific partnerships in the Premier League Credit: Getty

But while the American had built a strong team, Chelsea continued to come unstuck by a lack of stability in the dugout.



Maresca's messy exit led to the disastrous appointment of Liam Rosenior - and the man taken from sister club Strasbourg was sacked within four months as the Blues crawled to a tenth place finish.

Xabi Alonso arrived as a 'manager' rather than a 'head coach' - suggesting Chelsea had completely backtracked on the philosophy that forced Pochettino to leave.

This was backed up by the immediate arrival of experienced, veteran players including Danny Welbeck and Jordan Henderson.

Selling - hit

Chelsea fans took a while to accept the shift from Abramovich's 'Galactico' approach - buying proven talent to win trophies - to the player-trading philosophy of their new owners.



Suddenly, players arrived at Chelsea as long-term investments, rather than ready-made winners.

Season Expenditure (Gross Spend) Income (Sales Revenue) Net Spend / Balance Key Transfers 2022–23 £548.0M £59.0M -£489.0M In: Enzo Fernandez (£105.3M), Wesley Fofana (£70M), Marc Cucurella (£56.8M)



Out: Timo Werner (£17M), Emerson (£13.5M) 2023–24 £389.5M £245.5M -£144.0M In: Moises Caicedo (£117M), Romeo Lavia (£54M), Cole Palmer (£41M)



Out: Kai Havertz (£65M), Mason Mount (£58.8M), Mateo Kovacic (£25M) 2024–25 £225.5M £206.0M -£19.5M In: Pedro Neto (£52.2M), Joao Felix (£45.3M), Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall (£30.8M)



Out: Ian Maatsen (£37.5M), Conor Gallagher (£36M), Lewis Hall (£28M) 2025–26 £204.0M £195.5M -£8.5M In: Joao Pedro (£55.4M), Jamie Gittens (£48.7M), Estevao (£29.6M)



Out: Noni Madueke (£48.7M), Christopher Nkunku (£32M), Joao Felix (£30.4M) 2026–27 (up to Sep 2026) £318.5M £354.5M +£36.0M In: Morgan Rogers (£120M), Maxence Lacroix (£52.8M)



Out: Enzo Fernandez (£125M), Andrey Santos (£49M) TOTALS ~£1.68 Billion ~£1.06 Billion -£625.0M

Still, Boehly did his best to turn the Blues into a sustainable winning machine.

He self-reported misdemeanors under the Abramovich regime, which the FA admitted would have likely gone unnoticed otherwise.

And in a PSR world, Chelsea under Boehly were quite remarkable sellers.



They generated around £1billion in transfer sales during his regime, including more than £375m in the 2026 summer window alone.

So despite some rather questionable signings at the start, the Blues always usually found a way to recoup and ensure no lasting damage.

New stadium - miss

This was arguably Boehly's biggest miss.

7 Chelsea's stadium remains far too small for a club of their stature and blocks them from extra revenue Credit: Getty

Abramovich specifically chose him from a long list of prospective buyers because of his commitment to redeveloping Stamford Bridge or building a new stadium, something that was close to the Russian's heart.



With little more than 40,000 seats and a infamously nightmarish logistical situation in west London, Boehly was expected to at least make some progress.

He did not.

Overall PR - miss

Boehly never did himself any favours when it came to overcoming the 'goofy American billionaire in English football' label.

In his early days, he was ridiculed for calling for a Premier League 'All-Star Game' and claiming Mohamed Salah and Kevin De Bruyne were Chelsea academy graduates.

His attitude towards the club's actual academy graduates - like Conor Gallagher and Trevoh Chalobah - left a lot to be desired among the club's fan base.



7 Many Chelsea fans have wanted Boehly gone for a while Credit: Getty

And his role on the board of Vivid Seats - a secondary ticketing platform that often listed Chelsea home matches at extortionate prices - did little to improve that reputation.

BlueCo has not been particularly popular at Strasbourg either - with the club's fans protesting what they consider to be a feeder club system.

Verdict - miss

Considering the billions involved, all Boehly has to show for four years at Chelsea is one fourth-place finish and two trophies, neither of which were the big four domestic prizes.



Off the pitch, his lack of progress over a new stadium and various unpopular schemes made him difficult for Chelsea fans to like, as shown by widespread protests against BlueCo.

The club's transfer business might not end up being quite as disastrous as it once appeared, with a strong squad and a clear knack for selling unwanted talent.

But at best, Boehly left with the transition from Abramovich still unfinished.

Chelsea league finishes during Boehly reign 2022/23: 12th 2023/24: 6th 2024/25: 4th 2025/26: 10th

At worst, it was a failure.

Sports.title: Millwall star sends warning to West Ham players about ferocious Den atmosphere
Sports.content:
West Ham's stars are set to face an atmosphere unlike anything they've experienced before.

The Hammers travel to the home of their ferocious rivals Millwall on Saturday in what is the first meeting between the two clubs since February 2012.



3 Millwall fans are some of the most vocal in English football Credit: Getty

Given it has been well over a decade since the two clubs last met, the Den promises to be a powder keg waiting for a spark, even if kick-off is scheduled for 12:30pm.

The match has, unsurprisingly, been circled several times over in the calendar of all connected to Millwall, including captain Jake Cooper.

As one of the Lions' longest-serving players, Cooper knows all too well about what Saturday's fixture means to the club.



It's why he predicted the Millwall supporters to generate an ambience like never before the fixture gets underway.

Jake Cooper's verdict on Millwall v West Ham atmosphere

"Since it was confirmed that they would be relegated last season, I think every supporter looked towards this fixture coming up," Cooper said on talkSPORT Breakfast.



"It's great we get them at The Den first, and I'm sure our fanbase will be very excited."

Cooper added: "It will be interesting to see what it's like at their new stadium, how close their fans can impact the game.



"But certainly, at The Den, I think our fans will be incredible. It'll feel like 40,000 in there instead of 20,000. It will be some atmosphere, for sure."

How is the Met Police preparing for Saturday's game?

Given the ferocity between these two teams, the Metropolitan Police have beefed up their operations across the capital.

talkSPORT understands 400 officers will be deployed for the event, underlying the magnitude of the situation.

3 The Met will have a major operation in place to minimise crowd trouble on Saturday Credit: Getty



In a post on X, the Met also confirmed a Section 35 dispersal order will be in place from Bermondsey to as far south as Ladywell, permitting officers to remove anyone causing disorder.

How have West Ham and Millwall performed this season?

West Ham go into Saturday's fixture as the favourites, given they are top of the Championship.

After taking two points from a possible nine in their opening three league fixtures, Nuno Espirito Santo's side have reeled off four wins on the trot.

In that run, the Hammers have scored 16 goals and conceded five, sending a serious warning to rival defences across the Championship.



As for Millwall, they began the season brightly with two wins from as many games.

However, the Lions have gone on to win just once in their last five league games.

3 West Ham have not lost to Millwall since November 2004 Credit: Getty

But, as the old adage goes in football, form goes out the window when it comes to a derby.



And that famous saying will certainly ring true once the game kicks off on Saturday.

Sports.title: Ruben Amorim aims thinly-veiled dig at Manchester United players as he makes excuses for poor AC Milan form
Sports.content:
Ruben Amorim aims thinly-veiled dig at Manchester United players as he makes excuses for poor AC Milan form

Ruben Amorim couldn't help but aim a dig at Manchester United when dissecting AC Milan's 2-0 defeat to Benfica on Wednesday.

Goals from Dodi Lukebakio and Jakub Kaminski saw the Italian giants fall to a home reverse in their first Europa League game of the season.



2 Amorim criticised his players rather than the system following defeat to Benfica

And the Portuguese boss compared the loss to the Liga Portugal side to his struggles at Manchester United.

An issue that Amorim frequently complained about during his ill-fated Old Trafford stint was that the players weren't equipped to abide by his three-at-the-back demands up until his United exit.

Amorim struck a similar chord as he criticised his players rather than the system following the European loss.



What did Amorim say?

"I think you are a little bit right," Amorim said when asked about his squad in the wake of the Benfica defeat.

"I know at Manchester United and Milan, two big clubs with the pressure to win, people expect everything in just a few months, and I feel the same pressure here.



"I think this team is a little bit different, they are more accustomed to working with three defenders, they are a little bit faster, a little bit stronger.

"Of course, I don't have the clear characteristics that are perfect at this moment, but it is impossible when you take on a new team to have those perfect characteristics right away."



The 41-year-old, however, pleaded for patience, though admitted that failure, no matter the stature of the club, is possible.

"I know it will take time, but I also know that there is big pressure at this club, yet I prefer this kind of job because if I need to fail one day, I want to fail big," Amorim added.

"I have a lot of passion for this club, I want to help this club to be better, I don't know if I will have the time, but I look at my players and I think they are listening to everything that I say in training, and that gives me hope we can solve these problems."

2 Amorim is working hard to get his ideas across to his players



AC Milan's season so far

Amorim enjoyed a winning start to life in Italy as he oversaw a hard-fought 2-1 victory at Torino on the opening weekend of the 2026/27 Serie A season.

And the Rossoneri followed that up with 2-0 home win over Venezia.

However, defeat to Benfica extended AC Milan's winless run to three matches after the Italian giants were held to back-to-back draws at Juventus and Lazio, respectively.

Next up for Amorim and AC Milan, they welcome of Lecce on Sunday ahead of the extended international break.

Sports.title: Arsenal complete signing of 16-year-old wonderkid from Liverpool
Sports.content:
Arsenal have confirmed the signing of teenage striker Vincent Joseph from Liverpool.

The Gunners have been on a youth recruitment drive in recent months, with the 16-year-old the latest to make the move to north London.



Joseph established himself as one of the most prolific strikers around at youth level during his time on Merseyside.

"We're delighted to confirm the signing of talented young England U-16s striker Vincent Joseph," a statement read on Arsenal's official website.

"The forward joins us as part of our first year scholarship intake for the 2026/27 season.

"After getting off to a brilliant start at under-18s level for Liverpool last season, Vincent is keen for more opportunities to develop his game.



"Our new striker will be hoping to help us chase trophies at Academy level this season, and his outstanding goalscoring record could prove important in such a push.

"As well as scoring three goals in his first two under-18s games last season, the England youth international has scored eight times in his nine games for the England under-16s side, also providing an assist.



"Vincent will link up with some familiar faces as he begins his time in north London, having worked with Emerson Nwaneri and Charlie Phillips at international level.

"The partnership between himself and Emerson has proved valuable for the Three Lions, something the forwards will look to replicate in north London.



"Everyone at Arsenal would like to welcome Vincent to the club and looks forward to seeing him in action for us this season and beyond."

Joseph's exit post

Joseph confirmed that he was departing Liverpool via Instagram on Tuesday night, bringing a nine-year stint with the Reds to an end.

"After nine unforgettable years, the time has come to say goodbye," the post began.

"Thank you for the memories, and for making my time here truly special. YNWA."



Joseph joins an academy that has strengthened considerably recently.

Emerging Georgian star Andria Bartishvili and young goal machine Mylo Bernard have both moved to the capital side recently.

James Scanlon and Habeeb Ogunneye have also both swapped Old Trafford for the Emirates Stadium.

Arsenal also lured Elijah Upson, son of former centre-back Matthew, away from Tottenham Hotspur earlier this year.

Igor Tyjon, Axel Donczew and Phoenix Blayney have also made the move to Arsenal.



Meanwhile, academy graduate Max Dowman is continuing to make some serious waves in the first-team at the age of 16.

Sports.title: Wigan announce sudden death of goalkeeping coach Kevin Miller as tributes paid
Sports.content:
Wigan Athletic have been rocked by the sudden and unexpected passing of goalkeeper coach Kevin Miller.

Miller only linked up with the Latics over the summer to reunite with former Exeter City boss Gary Caldwell having stepped down as goalkeeper coach for the Grecians in June.

"Everyone at Wigan Athletic is deeply saddened and devastated to learn about the sudden passing of Goalkeeping Coach Kevin Miller," a statement read on Wigan's official website.

"Kevin joined the Club earlier this summer, linking up with Gary Caldwell, a close friend and colleague, and the wider First-Team staff after more than three years as Goalkeeping Coach at Exeter City and an impressive playing career that spanned over 18 years.

"Although Kevin’s time with Latics was far too short, he quickly became a much-loved and respected member of our First-Team staff. His experience, professionalism and passion for goalkeeping were clear for all to see, while his uplifting personality made a lasting impression on everyone who had the privilege of working alongside him.

"In a playing career of almost two decades, Kevin made more than 700 career appearances, including in the Premier League. He began his professional career with Exeter City, helping the Club to the Fourth Division title, before going on to represent Birmingham City, Watford, Crystal Palace, Barnsley, Bristol Rovers, Derby, Southampton and Torquay.

"Following an impressive career, Kevin moved into coaching and management, eventually returning to St James Park as Goalkeeping Coach in 2022, where he was able to pass on the considerable knowledge and experience he had gained throughout his career to the next generation of goalkeepers.

"Kevin’s contribution to football was significant, but for those who worked alongside him, it was the person he was that will be remembered most. Kevin was a husband, father, hugely respected colleague, dedicated coach and someone who made a genuine impact on those around him, both on and off the pitch.

"His sudden passing has left everyone at the Club deeply saddened and devastated.

"Our thoughts and prayers are with Kevin’s wife, Fiona, daughter, Esme, close family, friends, colleagues and all who knew and loved him.

"The Club asks for total privacy for Kevin’s family and friends at this difficult time.

"Everyone at Wigan Athletic sends its deepest condolences to Kevin’s loved ones."

1 Miller only joined Wigan as a goalkeeper coach in the summer Credit: Getty

Crystal Palace pay tribute

His former club, Crystal Palace said in a social media post: "Everyone at the club is deeply saddened to learn of the passing of former player Kevin Miller, aged 57.

"The thoughts of everyone associated with Crystal Palace are with Kevin’s loved ones at this difficult time."

Exeter City's statement

Exeter also paid tribute to the 57-year-old, stating: "Kevin was an incredibly popular figure during his time at St James Park, earning a place in the hearts of supporters with his performances between the posts and his wholehearted commitment to the club.

"At just 57, his passing is a huge loss to his family, friends and everyone who knew him. Exeter City Football Club sends its deepest condolences to Kevin's family and friends at this incredibly difficult time. Our thoughts are also with Gary Caldwell and our former staff at Wigan Athletic.

"The club will be supporting those who were close to Kevin and will be commemorating Kevin’s time with us and his memory in an appropriate way.

"Once a Grecian, always a Grecian."

Teams and individuals pay respects

A number of teams and individuals took to social media to pay their respects to the former Exeter shotstopper.

"Wigan Warriors would like to share our condolences following the sad news of the passing of goalkeeper Coach Kevin Miller," the official Wigan Warriors account posted.

"Our thoughts are with those at Wigan Athletic, Kevin's family, friends and colleagues at this sad time."

Former side Barnsley FC, meanwhile, wrote: "Our thoughts are with everyone at Wigan Athletic and Kevin's family. Tragic news. Once a Red, Always a Red."

Former Alan Tonge, who played for Exeter before retiring at 24, posted: "RIP Big Kev. Devastated."

Sports.title: Brentford vs Chelsea LIVE commentary: Joao Pedro and two Blues stars in doubt for Friday night clash
Sports.content:
Brentford vs Chelsea LIVE commentary: Joao Pedro and two Blues stars in doubt for Friday night clash

Premier League Gameweek 5 kicks off with a West London derby as Chelsea face Brentford on Friday night.

The Blues are looking to bounce back against the Bees following two disappointing results against Hull and Arsenal.



3 Joao Pedro has been crucial for Chelsea so far, and saved them a point last time out against Hull Credit: Getty

Meanwhile, Brentford are unbeaten across six matches in all competitions this season - winning three and drawing three.

Keith Andrews' side are seventh in the Premier League table on six points, and they will now be looking for their second league win of the campaign in their final fixture ahead of the international break.

Additionally, Xabi Alonso faces a significant injury criss after three key first-team players were absent from training, including starman Joao Pedro.



The Brazilian forward missed a majority of Tuesday's training at Cobham.

The 24-year-old has been a standout Chelsea player during this season, registering three goals and three assists in only five appearances.



Additionally, Alonso faces an even bigger injury crisis as captain Reece James and midfielder Moises Caicedo were also missing from the main group.

However, Tuesday's training session did see summer recruits Marco Palestra and Jordan Henderson participate after waiting to make their long-awaited debuts.



How to follow Brentford v Chelsea

The fixture will be played on Friday, September 18.

It is scheduled to kick off at the Gtech Stadium at 8pm.

talkSPORT will have live commentary of the match to open up the weekend of Premier League action.

3 Andrews has enjoyed a fantastic start to the season, including a 3-0 win against Spurs Credit: Getty

Coverage will start at 7pm with Hugh Woozencroft before commentary will be from Joe Shennan and former Arsenal defender Martin Keown.

Listen talkSPORT through the website or find us on DAB digital radio through your smart speaker and on 1089 or 1053 AM.

talkSPORT.com will also have all the action in our dedicated Premier League blog.
