World.title: Three changes confirmed: Orlando Pirates starting 11 vs Durban City
World.content:
Orlando Pirates coach Abdeslam Ouaddou has dropped Sbangani Zulu, Neo Rapoo and Oswin Appollis after the 3-1 win over La Cure Waves. Enter Nkosinathi Sibisi, Nkosikhona Ndaba and Tshepang Moremi.

Orlando Pirates starting line up: Sipho Chaine (24), Nkosinathi Sibisi (5), Lebone Seema (6), Nkosikhona Ndaba (3), Kamogelo Sebelebele (36), Thapelo Mokobodi (33), Mthetheleli Mthiyane (29), Simphiwe Masilela (48), Kabelo Kgositsile (49), Tshepang Moremi (11), Yanela Mbuthuma (19)

Substitutes: Siyabonga Dladla (32), Sbangani Zulu (37), Neo Rapoo (19), Simphiwe Selepe (20), Masindi Nemtajela (15), Bheki Mabuza (41), Mpho Padime (38), Oswin Appollis (12), Sebastian Pedersen (31).



Durban City starting line up: Asare, Shandu, Gcaba, Msomi, Ncanana, Mokone, Sanger, Poggenpoel, Jurgens, Sirino, Lwamba

Substitutes: Dreyer, Maseko, Brooks, Papier, Domingo, Green, Morris, Mthembu, Nodada.

ORLANDO PIRATES IN SOWETO

Orlando Pirates look to maintain their unbeaten start to the Betway Premiership when they welcome Durban City to the Orlando Amstel Arena tonight.



Orlando Pirates have scored 12 goals while conceding just once in the league this season.

Abdeslam Ouaddou’s side will enter the match with confidence after progressing in the CAF Champions League. They defeated La Cure Waves 3-1 on aggregate over the weekend.

Nkosinathi Sibisi is also back in contention after a considerable rest. His presence gives Orlando Pirates another experienced option in defence.



DURBAN CITY LOOK TO CAUSE AN UPSET

Durban City have collected six points from their five league matches under Khalil Ben Youssef. The visitors have also gone four matches without defeat in the Betway Premiership.

Their recent league run has been built around a disciplined defence. Three of their last four matches have ended in draws, with the Citizens keeping games tight.

Durban City will also draw confidence from their recent continental success. They defeated Rukinzo 2-1 away from home to progress in the CAF Confederation Cup.



The two teams have already met this season. Orlando Pirates edged Durban City 2-1 after extra time in the MTN8 quarter-finals.

Jean Lwamba will provide the attacking threat for the visitors, while Gastón Sirino brings experience and creativity to the midfield.

Orlando Pirates are chasing another victory that would move them clear at the top of the table. Durban City, meanwhile, will be looking to produce another disciplined performance and leave Soweto with a positive result.

World.title: ‘The coach is not good enough’: Ex-Chiefs star not convinced by Da Cruz
World.content:
Outspoken soccer anaylyst Junior Khanye says Fernando Da Cruz is not a good fit for Kaizer Chiefs.

The French coach was appointed Amakhosi‘s head coach in July, replacing Khalil Ben Youssef and Cedric Kaze.

So far, Da Cruz has had three league victories and three draws in his opening six fixtures.



Khanye, however, feels the coach is too defensive and lack belief.

“When it comes to Chiefs, I still have question marks about bringing in that coach. To me, he is a coach who is more concerned about not conceding, hence his team is always defending. Even if it means putting five defenders in his line-up, he will do it as long as he believes it is the right strategy to get him the result he wants,” said the ex-Chiefs winger.

Against Polokwane City, Amakhosi dropped two points and Khanye feels Da Cruz was too blame.

“Just look at the most recent match against Polokwane City. His team was too defensive, and they were almost caught by surprise because, in my opinion, Polokwane were the more attacking team,” he said as per Soccer Laduma.

“For me, the coach is not good enough. I don’t think there is any trophy that he is going to win for Kaizer Chiefs,” he added.

Fernando Da Cruz has implemented a solid midfield

Despite dropping points in the last few matches, Amakhosi fans have praised Da Cruz’s defensive structure which has won them games. The likes of Lebohang Maboe, Sphesihle Ndlovu and Sibongiseni Mthethwa have impressed as a midfield trio, dominating most games this season.



What’s your opinion on Chiefs’ new coach?

World.title: Gracious Nkomo identified as fourth Kempton Park victim
World.content:
Gracious Nkomo, 28, has been identified as the fourth publicly named victim in the Ekurhuleni killings after police found her body along the R21 in Kempton Park. Image: SAPS

Gracious Nkomo now has a name in an investigation that has left families across Ekurhuleni waiting for answers.

The 28-year-old became the fourth publicly identified victim on Thursday after her family formally identified her at the Germiston Mortuary.

Police found Nkomo partially clothed along the R21 in Kempton Park on 10 September.



Her identification comes as detectives investigate the deaths of nine women across Ekurhuleni, with several victims still awaiting formal identification.

GRACIOUS NKOMO FOUND ALONG R21

Nkomo was the third woman whose body police discovered in the Kempton Park area during the current spate of killings.

Her family identified her exactly one week after officers found her body.



SAPS has not released further details about the circumstances surrounding her death as detectives continue to work on the case.

Nkomo joins Elizabeth “Tsontso” Moselakgomo, Itumeleng Kekana and Dineo Evelyn Motapane as the women whose families have publicly confirmed their identities.

FAMILY GETS PAINFUL CONFIRMATION

Acting National Police Commissioner Lieutenant-General Puleng Dimpane sent condolences to Nkomo’s loved ones following the identification.



“We extend our deepest condolences to the family and loved ones of Gracious Nkomo during this extremely difficult time,” Dimpane said.

She said detectives remain focused on establishing what happened to Nkomo and the other women.

“Our investigators remain seized with these cases, and we will continue to pursue every available lead to ensure that those responsible for these murders are brought to justice,” she said.



INVESTIGATION INTO NINE DEATHS CONTINUES

Police have assembled a multidisciplinary team to examine the deaths and pursue those responsible.

The investigation has widened rapidly as more bodies have surfaced across different parts of Ekurhuleni since July.

A ninth woman was found in Dawn Park on Thursday, adding another case to the growing investigation.



SAPS has not concluded that one person killed all nine women and continues to examine possible links between the cases.

Police have also intensified operations in Kempton Park while detectives work through forensic evidence, victim movements and other information that could help identify suspects.

World.title: City of Cape Town launches memorial park
World.content:
CAPE TOWN - Safety in public spaces has again taken centre stage following the murders of nine women in Ekurhuleni.

Archbishop Tutu IP Trust Chairperson Dr Mamphela Ramphele said a government committed to tackling societal ills and not increased police presence, will help end the scourge.

Ramphele was speaking at the opening of the Tutu Memorial Park in Cape Town.

The park will be fully transformed in six months with dedicated spaces for recreation as well as walls filled with memories of the former Archbishop.

eNCA's Nobesuthu Hejana has more details in the video above.

World.title: Alleged Sextortionist Awaits Bail Verdict
World.content:
SOWETO - Alleged international sextortionist, Ifeel Simango, remains in custody, after his bail application in the Protea Magistrate's Court was postponed.



Simango faces murder, extortion, money laundering, fraud, and the possession and distribution of child sexual abuse material charges.



He allegedly operated as a cyber predator, targeting minors.



Simango has been in custody since his arrest in July.



Simango was arrested following an investigation into the suicide of a 17-year-old Swiss teenager three years ago.



It's understood that the teenager was manipulated into sending explicit images of himself via WhatsApp by an individual using a fraudulent profile.



Police said they are aware of 52 victims worldwide, including two from South Africa.



All the victims are boys under the age of 18.



The case has been postponed to 28 September for bail judgment. Investigations continue, with Simango remaining the only suspect arrested so far.



eNCA's Bafedile Moerane reports in the video above.

World.title: Removal of billboard unlawful and politically driven- ActionSA
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - ActionSA has lambasted the recent removal of its billboard advert in Diepkloof, Soweto.

In a statement following the removal on Wednesday, ActionSA’s National Chairperson Michael Beaumont said the removal was unlawful and described it as a "politically driven campaign".

He said the billboard featuring party leader Herman Mashaba and the words “Let's Do It Again”, was removed from a privately owned site where a third-party media buyer secured advertising space.

In light of this, Beaumont said the party is engaging its legal teams to determine an appropriate response and will also investigate the compliance of the billboard site in terms of city regulation.

“The removal and damaging of election materials, including billboards, is a criminal offence in terms of the provisions of the Municipal Electoral Act, carrying a sentence of a fine or 10 years' imprisonment, and a breach of the IEC Code of Conduct. These latter legal components are important because the billboard was maliciously damaged in its removal," he said.

Beaumont said other possible courses of action are not limited to an urgent Spoliation Order, criminal charges in terms of the Municipal Electoral Act and a complaint to the IEC in relation to the Code of Conduct.

eNCA reached out to the City for comment on the matter, but they did not respond by the time of publication.

Their response will be added once received.

World.title: Rand in recovery
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - The rand is recovering after an initial negative reaction to the US hiking interest rates for the first time in three years.

The rand weakened significantly after the announcement by the US Federal Reserve last night, and it closed at R16.40.

But it has since strengthened to trade below R16.25.

READ | SA economy under pressure as Q2 GDP figures set for release

Higher rates in the United States make dollar investments more attractive, and that makes rand investments relatively less attractive.

The rand has been resilient despite the war in general.

It was trading below R16 to the dollar earlier this month - exactly where it was before the war began.

World.title: Mapisa-Nqakula denies influencing R80m tender
World.content:
PRETORIA - Former Defence Minister Nosiviwe Mapisa-Nqakula has continued to deny soliciting bribes from military contractor Nombasa Ntsondwa-Ndhlovu.

She returned to the High Court in Pretoria, where she faced cross-examination in her corruption trial.

The former Speaker was questioned about her relationship with Ntsondwa-Ndhlovu and she denied she played a role when the businesswoman was awarded an R80-million contract.

Her salary and spending while she was in public office has also come under scrutiny.

She'll be back in court on 22 September.

World.title: Vandals savage Eastern Cape school
World.content:
KUGOMPO CITY - Pupils at Hlokoma High School in the Eastern Cape continue to face a bleak future ahead of their matric exams.



eNCA has exposed the harsh realities faced by pupils who have been plunged into darkness for years, with the school's electricity infrastructure vandalised.



After our visit last month, the Eastern Cape Education Department met with school management to address the crisis, but it seems nothing has changed.



Hlokoma High School management said it is struggling to encourage its matric pupils to be positive ahead of their exams.



Hlokoma High School matric pupils traditionally gather for study camps ahead of their end-of-year exams and as those fast approach, they are likely to use candles and torches to study, because their classrooms are still without electricity.



The problems faced at Hlokoma are nothing new in communities of Mdantsane, where criminals continue to target schools, hoping never to be caught in the act.



eNCA's Ronald Masinda has more details in the video above.

World.title: 'We trust that justice will be served': Madlanga Commission marks one year
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - A year ago today, the Madlanga Commission of Inquiry was established to investigate allegations of criminality and corruption in South Africa’s criminal justice system.

Since then, the Inquiry has heard extensive evidence and seen senior law enforcement officials arrested.

Commission Chair Justice Mbuyiseli Madlanga said the revelations have exposed serious weaknesses in the justice system and could help drive reforms to prevent similar criminality.

“With such a criminal justice system, those criminals who exert undue improper influence on state functionaries will rarely, if ever, answer for their criminal deeds. “To ask rhetorically over the years how many such criminals have escaped facing criminal charges and sanctions. With the revelations that are coming out, we trust that justice will be served.”

Madlanga said he trusts that the Commission's work, in the end, will yield results that will play a “meaningful role towards putting in place mechanisms that will help significantly towards curbing a recurrence of apparent criminality” that has emerged before the Commission.

World.title: Black women pay the price - Corruption Watch on 'crippled' policing system
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - 'South African Policing has failed.'

That is the scathing assessment from Corruption Watch as the Madlanga Commission marks a year of explosive public hearings.

According to Corruption Watch's Executive Director, Lebogang Ramafoko, it did not have to take a commission to have real accountability in the police sector.

As the inquiry continues to pull back the curtain on high-level rot, Ramafoko claims that it is ordinary citizens who are paying the price for a broken system.

“The commission, in my eyes, gets a 10 out of 10, but policing in South Africa gets a minus five out of 10. If you match what is happening in policing with the discovery of women's bodies all over Ekurhuleni, it tells you that this issue it has real consequences for real people," she said.

Nine bodies of women have been discovered in Ekurhuleni in since July 2026, raising fresh concerns over policing and safety of women in the country.

Ramafoko views the discoveries alongside the revelations that have emerged at the Madlanga Commission and adds that this shows a policing system that has allegedly been "crippled to serve the public by organised crime that has infiltrated the police”.

Ramafoko said If accountability was at the core of governance, the country would not need commissions.

World.title: Ruto faults Uhuru for undermining his government
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President William Ruto join traditional dancers in Homa Bay on September 17, 2026. [PCS]

President William Ruto has renewed his public criticism of former President Uhuru Kenyatta, accusing his predecessor of undermining the government and urging him to withdraw from active political mobilisation.

Ruto said he had supported Uhuru throughout their political partnership and expected reciprocal support when he sought the presidency.

“I stood by you through four elections; I stood by you, helped you, took care of you, and worked for you.”

Ruto claimed the two had discussed an arrangement in which each would serve as president for ten years. He accused Uhuru of failing to honour that understanding, saying:

“When the time came for you to help me, after you said ‘ten years for you, ten years for me,’ not even for a single day did you support me.”

Ruto also appealed to Uhuru to respect the position of former President and withdraw from political activities that he said were aimed at destabilising his administration.

“A former president! Surely, my brother, you are lowering the dignity of the office of the former president. You are a retired president respect your office, go and relax. Let us plan for this country of ours, Kenya,” Ruto said.

Ruto made the remarks on Thursday, September 17, 2026, in Sindo, Homa Bay County, as he concluded a four-day development tour of Nyanza.

The tour covered Kisumu, Siaya, Migori and Homa Bay and focused largely on roads, markets, housing, water and other development projects. The Star+1

The latest confrontation adds another chapter to the complicated political relationship between the two leaders.

Ruto served as Uhuru's deputy from 2013 to 2022, after the two politicians formed a political alliance that won the 2013 and 2017 presidential elections.

Contemporary accounts describe their original arrangement as involving support for Kenyatta for two terms, followed by support for Ruto's presidential ambitions. The Washington Post

The President nevertheless acknowledged Uhuru's democratic right to oppose his government but urged the former president to respect the office he once held.

“You are running schemes to sabotage the government. You are a retired president respect your office, go and relax. Let us plan for this country of ours, Kenya,” he said.

His criticism centred instead on what he described as continued political mobilisation against his administration.

He said his administration had stabilised the economy and pointed to investments in education, housing, markets and infrastructure. During the Homa Bay leg alone, the government highlighted a Sh3.5 billion plan for 21 modern markets.

World.title: Five killed as bandits ambush police search team in Isiolo
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Five people, including two police officers killed by bandits at the troubled grazing field of Gotu in Isiolo County on Wednesday.

The victims are a senior police officer, a police constable who was the driver of the vehicle that was ambushed by bandits, a livestock farmer and two National Police Reservists (NPR). The police officers were attached to an Anti-Stock Theft Unit (ASTU) located near Gotu trading centre.

The victims were part of a search team that was looking for an elderly man who reportedly went missing within the Gotu area and was last seen around Madho Gurba Huka, a grazing area in Chari Ward in Merti sub-county.

Isiolo County Police Commander Isaac Sang said the mentally challenged man from Barambate sub-location, Kulamawe location was reported missing a day ago.

The Isiolo camel keeper, reported to be related to the man who went missing, had requested police to search for him.

The mission turned tragic when the group was ambushed by armed bandits, killing all five on the spot.

The incident took place near the junction of Lososia-Merti road and Gotu-Merti route.

Mr Sang said the bodies of the officers and other victims were removed to Isiolo County Teaching and Referral Hospital awaiting postmortem.

"A reinforcement (of security personnel) had been sent to the area which includes an armoured vehicle to pursue the attackers," said the police chief.

The police boss called for calm and cooperation from the residents while police pursue the suspects.

He said that investigation into the incident had commenced.

On Wednesday afternoon, a gunfight was reported between police reservists and the bandits on the western bank of the river.

"The reservists in the area pursued the attackers minutes after reports of the killings that led to an exchange of gunfire. We are told an unknown number of people have been injured," said a herdsman from Gotu who sought anonymity for security reasons.

A source from Isiolo County and Teaching and Referral Hospital revealed that two ambulances had been sent to Gotu to attend to the injured persons.

Gotu, along with Kom in Merti sub-county is a bandit hotspot in Isiolo that is attributed to competition over scarce pasture by rival herders from Isiolo, Samburu East and parts of Marsabit with local leaders calling for eviction of pastoralists from outside the County. Several people have been killed in the two locations since last year and hundreds of livestock stolen.

On August 1, two people were killed in the Garse Dabata area in Gotu and nearly 700 goats and sheep were stolen. Nearly all the stolen animals were recovered in operation undertaken by a multi-agency security team stationed in various locations along the Isiolo-Meru border.

Interior CS Kipchumba Murkomen on two occasions called for an operation in parts of Isiolo, Laikipia, Samburu and Meru Counties that had experienced frequent cases of banditry and rustling.

However, leaders fault the CS for failure to take decisive action on insecurity that keeps on recurring in parts of Isiolo and Meru Counties. The leaders including Governor Abdi Guyo want herders from outside Isiolo who are in Kom and Gotu areas to be evicted.

World.title: Muthaiga Golf Club restores access after KFS standoff
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Muthaiga Golf Club has restored access to a section of its course that was temporarily taken over by the Kenya Forest Service (KFS), hours after the agency moved into the area, claiming it forms part of Karura Forest.

The disruption affected the Front Nine, covering Holes Two to Nine, before the club’s board intervened to restore normal operations.

In a statement issued Tuesday, Muthaiga Golf Club Chairman Dennis Mwirigi said the board had taken the necessary steps to facilitate the resumption of activities after the temporary disruption.

“We are pleased to confirm that access to the affected part of the course has been restored and members may proceed with their scheduled activities as usual,” Mwirigi said.

He said the board remained committed to protecting the club’s interests, assets and members while addressing the matter through the appropriate channels.

The development follows an earlier communication to members informing them that KFS had taken over access to the affected section, claiming it was part of Karura Forest.

The club had initially said the Front Nine would not be accessible until further notice as it sought to resolve the matter. The driving range and parking areas were not affected.

The incident sparked criticism over the manner in which KFS handled the dispute, with Prof Karanja, Chairperson of Friends of Karura Forest, urging the agency to pursue dialogue and legal channels.

Prof Karanja said KFS should have first engaged the club’s management and clearly explained its claim over the disputed land instead of deploying dogs, guns and heavy security.

“If they don't agree that it was your land, go to court. The court will determine,” he said.

He questioned whether KFS had adequately demonstrated that the disputed section was forest land or explained how it was allegedly acquired by Muthaiga Golf Club.

“They should have come publicly and said, look, Muthaiga, that area and that area belong to the forest,” Prof Karanja said.

He said KFS should identify the specific portion of land it claims belongs to the forest and explain the basis of its claim before taking further action.

Prof Karanja argued that the dispute should be resolved through established legal procedures rather than force. “Trees are not protected by guns,” he said.

He described the deployment of armed personnel as the wrong way of resolving a land dispute and called for engagement between KFS and the golf club.

Prof Karanja also warned that actions by government agencies could have wider implications for the administration of President William Ruto, saying confrontational conduct could lead members of the public to associate such actions directly with the government.

“When government departments behave like this, everybody now starts thinking, oh, it's Ruto's whatever,” he said.

He further recalled a previous dispute involving Friends of Karura Forest, where he said armed personnel were deployed and the group removed from an area before senior government officials intervened.

According to Prof Karanja, officials from the Treasury and forestry departments eventually intervened and encouraged dialogue to resolve the matter.

He urged KFS to adopt a similar approach in the Muthaiga dispute, saying the agency and the club should present their respective claims and seek a court determination if they cannot agree.

For now, the restoration of access means members can resume their scheduled activities, while the underlying dispute over the contested section remains subject to further engagement between KFS and the club.

World.title: Juja couple's surprise blessing of five babies
World.content:
Mercy Kanini, 28, from Juja, Kiambu County, gave birth to five children at Thika Level Five Hospital. [Gitau Wanyoike, Standard]

A couple from Juja, Kiambu County, is celebrating the unexpected arrival of five babies after scans during pregnancy showed they were expecting quadruplets.

Mercy Kanini, 28, delivered four girls and a boy through normal delivery at Thika Level Five Hospital, in a rare case believed to be among only a handful of quintuplet births recorded in Kenya.

World.title: Police to restrict access to CBD during Linda Mwananchi Nairobi rally
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Linda Mwananchi officials during a rally. [Courtesy]

Organisers of the Linda Mwananchi rally and their supporters will not be allowed to access Nairobi’s Central Business District (CBD), Nairobi Regional Police Commander Issa Mohamud has warned.

According to Mohamud, police had received notification of the planned rally, which is scheduled to take place at Jacaranda Grounds on Sunday, through Embakasi East MP Babu Owino.

However, he warned that the CBD would remain off-limits, saying police would not allow Nairobi to become a battleground for political supremacy.

“The National Police Service respects the constitutional right of every Kenyan to assemble, demonstrate, express political views, and participate in public affairs, but that right must be exercised peacefully, lawfully, and with respect to the rights and safety of other Kenyans,” Mohamud stated.

According to Mohamud, they had received a tip that some individuals were planning to mobilise goons to disrupt the rally, prompting the directive to keep the CBD out of bounds.

“We have received some information, some credible information, that some individuals may seek to mobilise groups of unruly youths and goons to outnumber and intimidate and confront rival groups.”

“Therefore, I make a direct appeal to all political leaders, organisers or influencers to restrain their supporters and control their crowds. No political objective is worth the blood of a Kenyan,” he added.

Mohamud assured the organisers and those planning to attend the rally that police would provide security throughout the event and facilitate all lawful activities.

The Linda Mwananchi movement is set to hold its Nairobi rally on Sunday, September 13. The procession will start at All Saints Cathedral before proceeding to Jacaranda Grounds.

World.title: ODM vows not to interfere with Linda Mwananchi rally in Nairobi
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Linda Mwananchi leaders during a rally in Western Kenya. [Linda Mwananchi, X]

The Orange Democratic Movement (ODM) has said it will not disrupt the planned Linda Mwananchi rally scheduled for Sunday at Jacaranda Grounds.

In a statement on Friday, September 11, ODM Nairobi Chairman George Aladwa said the party had no business interfering with the rally, noting that Linda Mwananchi had a right to speak to Nairobi residents.

“I want to make it clear that nobody in ODM has any intention of disrupting or interfering with the Linda Mwananchi rally,” Aladwa stated.

He added: “We believe that political competition should be about ideas, policies and the ability to convince Kenyans, rather than confrontations between supporters of different political formations.”

Aladwa said ODM’s opponents had a right to tell Nairobi residents what they stood for and what they intended to offer Kenyans.

“The people are intelligent enough to listen to different political messages and make their own decisions,” Aladwa said.

At the same time, Aladwa said ODM was engaged in an extensive programme to market and strengthen the party across Nairobi as it prepared for activities to commemorate the anniversary of the death of its former party leader, the late Raila Amolo Odinga.

The chairman lauded Odinga for his contribution to Kenya’s democracy, the struggle for constitutional reforms and the political transformation of the country, saying his contribution could not be erased.

“His legacy remains an important part of ODM and Kenya’s political history. As we approach the 2027 General Election, our responsibility is to ensure that ODM remains strong, organised and firmly rooted across Nairobi,” the chairman stated.

“We will continue engaging residents in all constituencies and wards and explaining the party’s agenda to the people. I appeal to ODM supporters to remain calm and focused. Do not allow yourselves to be provoked into unnecessary political confrontations,” he added.

World.title: Saudi Arabia accuses Huthis of ‘red line’ attack on Mecca as rebels face outrage from Muslim world
World.content:
Saudi Arabia said it shot down a Huthi drone near Mecca, Islam’s holiest city, on Tuesday, drawing swift regional condemnation of the Iran-backed Yemeni rebel group.

Turki al-Maliki, spokesperson for the Saudi-led Coalition Forces, accused the group of targeting the city, saying it was the first time in almost a decade that the Huthis had targeted Mecca.

The security of the holy site is “a red line,” he said, adding that the kingdom “will not hesitate to take the necessary and deterrent measures” against the Yemeni group.

The claim was strongly denied by the Huthis, who follow the Zaydi branch of Shiite Islam and also revere Mecca as a sacred city.

The group’s military spokesman, Yahya Saree, said early Wednesday that its targets were Saudi oil facilities and military bases “far removed from the holy places.”

“The fabrications and lies propagated by the criminal Saudi regime regarding targeting Mecca cannot deceive anyone,” Saree said. “There is no threat whatsoever from Yemen to the holy sites.”

Saudi Arabia said it intercepted and destroyed the drone “before it entered” Mecca’s restricted airspace, without specifying how close it was to the city.

The rebel group’s swift advance in Yemen and attacks on neighboring Saudi Arabia in recent weeks have put the kingdom in an increasingly difficult position, facing the prospect of being drawn into a wider conflict as the US-Iran war drags on.

Mecca is the birthplace of the Prophet Muhammad. All Muslims worldwide are required, if they are able, to make the pilgrimage to the holy city at least once in their life, with millions making the journey each year.

“This hostile attempt will also remain a black mark in the record of violations by the extremist terrorist Huthi militia, as a deliberate act intended to provoke the feelings of millions of Muslims,” al-Maliki said in a post on X.

A ‘dastardly and heinous’ act

The Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), a 57-member body representing 1.5 billion Muslims, also condemned the incicdent, saying the strikes “violate the sanctity of holy sites and mosques” and “instill fear in innocent civilians.”

The prime minister of Pakistan, which recently signed a joint defense agreement with Saudi Arabia, called it a “dastardly and heinous” act. While Shehbaz Sharif did not mention the Huthis in his statement, he affirmed his country’s support for Saudi Arabia.

The interception comes amid heavy fighting. The Huthis launched ballistic missiles and drones at several Saudi cities earlier this week, including Khamis Mushait, Abha and Taif, injuring 13 civilians. On Sunday, they claimed responsibility for an attack on a Saudi military base. And on Wednesday, the Huthis said they attacked a Saudi Aramco facility in Yanbu, a port city on the Red Sea.

In response, Saudi forces launched airstrikes across Huthi-held areas of Yemen last Saturday and this Tuesday, according to the Huthis.

The Huthis have recently stepped up their fighting against Yemen’s Saudi-backed government and have expanded their area of control. Last week, they captured a Red Sea port city in Yemen and an island near an important waterway that has, for months, acted as a backup to the Strait of Hormuz, allowing for the export of Saudi oil and refined products.

Over the weekend, Saudi Arabia suspended oil loadings at Yanbu, its primary Red Sea export terminal, after it came under attack from militant groups within Iraq.

No date has been given for its resumption, Ashley Hikmet, head of crude at Axis Limited, a trading subsidiary of the Onyx Capital Group, told CNN. Satellite tracking indicates no Saudi crude has left the Red Sea ports since Saturday, he said.

On Tuesday, Saudi Arabia also cut supplies to Europe with immediate effect, Hikmet said, adding that Aramco notified some customers that supplies would be halted until mid-November. The supply disruptions to Europe were first reported by Reuters.

CNN has reached out to Aramco for comment.

The Huthis’ tightening grip over shipping in the Red Sea has fueled fears that the main escape valves for the region’s oil are slamming shut, as Iran and the US continue battling for control of the Strait of Hormuz.

Oil prices climbed back above $100 per barrel last week following further US strikes on Iranian oil tankers in the Persian Gulf and the fighting in Yemen, sparking protests around the world as people demand government action and economic relief.

CNN’s Nadeen Ebrahim and Thomas Gould contributed reporting.

World.title: Gaza building collapse kills more than 20, dozens remain trapped under rubble
World.content:
More than 20 people, including several children, have died after a war-damaged residential building in Gaza City collapsed early Wednesday, local authorities said, with dozens more feared trapped under layers of rubble.

Dr. Mohammed Abu Salmiya, the director of al-Shifa hospital, told CNN at least 21 people have been killed in the disaster, including 11 children, and that many others have been injured.

Search and rescue operations are underway at the site of the collapsed al-Sa’ada building in the city’s Rimal neighborhood, where around 100 people are missing, according to Gaza’s Civil Defense agency.

The building, which is six stories high with four apartments on each floor, was targeted by Israeli airstrikes at the beginning of the war in Gaza, the Civil Defense agency said. The Israeli strikes followed the Hamas-led October 7, 2023, attack on Israel.

Around 80 percent of all structures in Gaza have been damaged since the conflict began, with two-thirds of them destroyed, according to the United Nations. The destruction has left Palestinians struggling to find safe shelter amid ongoing Israeli airstrikes and the threat of unexploded ordnance.

The demand for shelter is high, especially as winter approaches. Around 1.9 million Palestinians in Gaza — or about 90% of the population — have been displaced during the war, the UN said. Many people in the territory have been displaced several times.

Rescue workers remove the bodies of victims from the rubble of a collapsed building in Gaza City on Wednesday. Saeed M. M. T. Jaras/Anadolu/Getty Images

Hamas’ media office in Gaza said the building fell onto “dozens of displaced families who had been forcibly driven to seek shelter there, amid the complete absence of alternative and safe places of refuge.”

It accused Israel of obstructing rescue efforts by “maintaining its categorical refusal to allow the entry of sufficient equipment, machinery and rescue supplies needed to respond to such disasters.” Israel restricts the entry of what it calls “dual-use goods” into Gaza, including heavy equipment, which it says Hamas could repurpose for military use.

Ramiz Alakbarov, the UN’s humanitarian coordinator for occupied Palestinian territory, called for “urgent approvals” to be granted for the entry of heavy machinery, engine oil and fuel into Gaza.

“No one should have to risk their life simply to find a safe place to shelter,” he said Wednesday.

‘A tragic, painful scene’

Gaza’s Ministry of Housing said Wednesday that about 3,000 buildings in the territory have been classified as “dangerous” or at risk of collapse, after previous Israeli strikes caused structural damage and cracks.

It said the damage poses a “direct threat to the lives of thousands of families” and called for an immediate regional and international response.

“Since midnight in Gaza City, a tragic, painful scene has unfolded: a brutal humanitarian event, as you can see in front of you under this residential building, where dozens of innocent people were trapped,” Civil Defense spokesman Mahmoud Basal said Wednesday.

“People woke up at 3 a.m. to screams and the crying of children who were inside after the building completely collapsed on them,” he added. “We warn of further collapses like this incident in the Gaza Strip, in the areas where citizens are now sheltering.”

No significant reconstruction has taken place in Gaza since a fragile ceasefire deal was agreed last October between Hamas and Israel. The UN reported in late August that the percentage of damaged buildings in the territory has continued to increase since the ceasefire.

Meanwhile, substantial progress from US President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace, created to advance the US-brokered ceasefire agreement, remains elusive following recent criticism from Israel.

This is a developing story and will be updated.

World.title: Why is China less worried about an AI dystopia than the US?
World.content:
Hong Kong/Beijing — Unlike in the United States, no one in China seems to be openly fretting over the prospect of humanity being destroyed by artificial intelligence soon.

There, citizens access local government services through AI-powered digital employees; students receive instant feedback on written assignments by uploading a photo; and hotel guests collect parcels delivered to their doorsteps by robots.

The wide adoption of AI in today’s China underscores the country’s embrace of the novel technology. A Morgan Stanley survey released Monday found 80% of Chinese respondents used AI at least weekly, far exceeding the 54% in the US.

Even as US tech executives and researchers urge a slowdown in AI development citing its existential threat to humanity, the Chinese public has remained comparatively unfazed.

“This technology was created to serve humanity,” said Xu Jingyuan, 22, a business student from Beijing. “We shouldn’t see it as something to fear, but as something that brings greater conveniences to our lives.”

He said the government is “absolutely capable” of managing its risks.

Xu’s comments echoed those of several people CNN spoke to this week, reflecting a divide in attitudes toward AI in Chinese and American society, as well as differing levels of trust in respective governments’ ability to handle the potential threats posed by the technology.

“In the US, there is a general public perception that without whistleblowing, big corporations could escape accountability or scrutiny due to weak government oversight,” said Lian Jye Su, chief analyst at technology research firm Omdia.

“Whereas in China, I think there is this very strong confidence from the public that if any sh*t hits the fan, the government will step in.”

Chinese technology company Tencent’s data center in Guiyang, southwestern China’s Guizhou Province, on July 24, 2026. Jade Gao/AFP/Getty Images

Analysts also point to differences in exposure to AI, public discourse around the technology, and the broader cultural and historical context as possible explanations for the divide.

In a survey by marketing research firm Ipsos earlier this year, 83% of Chinese respondents found AI-powered products or services exciting, whereas only 33% of those in the US felt similar way. Meanwhile, another survey by marketing consultancy Edelman showed that 86% of respondents in China said they trusted their own government to do what is right, compared with just 39% in the US.

A marked difference between the two nations is their political systems. While whistleblowing is routine in the US and policy debates often become messy, especially in an increasingly polarized democracy, China’s top-down power structure allows the one-party state to set agendas without facing open criticism.

Behind the embrace

In China, the ubiquity of AI, its commercial applications and robots have helped boost the public’s wide acceptance of the technology.

“Everyone I know says AI has already permeated every aspect of our lives,” said 51-year-old Shi Hongchao from China’s northeastern Liaoning province. “Everyone is either talking about it or has already started using it. It feels almost unstoppable at this point.”

In China’s hypercompetitive market, tech companies have been aggressively rolling out free AI chatbots and features built into applications people already use. Industries from filmmaking and e-commerce to manufacturing are also integrating the technology. The productivity gains and convenience have spoken for themselves.

“Most Chinese people meet AI as a cheap product first and as a debate second,” said Poe Zhao, analyst and founder of Hello China Tech, a newsletter focused on China’s tech industry. “When a technology shows up as a useful, low-cost service, people judge it by what it does for them, not by what it might do to them.”

This stands in stark contrast to the US, where industry executives and researchers have raised prominent concerns about the rapid advancement of AI and its potential existential risks. China, another AI superpower widely regarded as capable of rivaling the US, has been noticeably silent on the issue.

“Chinese warnings are quieter and use a different vocabulary. The dominant framing is loss of operational control, malicious use and social disruption, rather than human extinction,” Zhao said.

China’s intelligence chief Chen Yixin published an article last Sunday detailing the need to incorporate AI as a strategic industry into the country’s economic development, while outlining what Beijing sees as the technology’s extensive risks.

Beyond the familiar risks of hostile actors misusing AI to conduct cyberattacks, spread misinformation and steal state and corporate secrets, Chen also warned that the technology could destabilize society and threaten China’s political security. He also cited the risks posed by certain countries’ “monopolistic practices” – an apparent reference to the US for its export controls – as another concern.

Rather than public discussions and open letters about AI’s safety threats, much of the Chinese AI governance takes place behind the scenes through companies’ compliance work with the authorities’ technical standards, security assessments, and administrative filings, Zhao added.

Chinese AI companies’ development trajectories also differ from those of their American counterparts, reflecting different priorities and constraints. While Chinese AI labs have rapidly narrowed the gap with US leaders such as Anthropic and OpenAI, their models still trail the most advanced American systems, in part because of constraints on computing power and capital.

DeepSeek founder Liang Wenfeng said in a leaked conference call with investors in July that the biggest gap between Chinese and American AI labs lies in access to the most advanced AI processors – essential for training AI models – due to US restrictions, as well as lower levels of capital investment.

Chinese AI companies are also driven more by commercial incentives to monetize and turn a profit, potentially making them less focused on developments that could trigger extreme or existential risks.

“The US is really keen on pushing the boundaries more,” Su of Omdia said. “In China, there may be less focus on frontier capability, but more focus on how to make AI more productive and commercial.”

China’s rise

China’s technological advances have coincided with the country’s rapid economic development and its rise on the global stage over the past decades. As the country’s AI industry has grown more capable, many Chinese people have come to see that progress as further evidence of China’s technological rise, Su said.

“In China, there is this very pro-AI culture,” Su said. “Technology has always been viewed as a national pride.”

That view contrasts with the US, where skepticism toward large corporations and the government has grown alongside opposition to AI data centers.

Protestors against AI demonstrate at The Puck Building in New York City on September 15, 2026. Eugene Gologursky/Getty Images

Over the past decade, Chinese technologies – from smartphones and electric vehicles to batteries and supercomputers – have increasingly gone head-to-head with US counterparts, surpassing them in some areas.

For many Chinese people, that history has created an implicit expectation that a new technology can deliver both economic benefits and might, said Grace Shao, a tech analyst and founder of industry newsletter AI Proem.

“The average person has seen how much economic gain, prosperity, and even just convenience that technology has brought to them, so there is an unspoken assumption that AI could do the same for them,” she said.

China’s people also tend to look up to the government for protection, Shao added. The Communist Party has repeatedly demonstrated its willingness to assert its control over the country’s most powerful enterprises.

In 2020, Beijing launched a historic crackdown to curb the power of the country’s biggest names in sectors from tech and gaming to education, wiping out over $1.5 trillion in market value from the companies affected.

“There is built-in trust by the people that the government will act as a parental figure again to draw out the guardrails and guidelines for this new technology,” Shao said.

Shi from Liaoning is one of them.

He believes that AI’s benefits still outweigh the concerns, and the development of AI should not be slowed simply because it carries risks.

“I think we should continue to invest more heavily in AI and keep developing it. After all, restricting the technology doesn’t mean it will stop advancing,” he said. “China is a major country. It has an even greater reason to prioritize the development of AI.”

World.title: Nigeria and South Africa tried to ease tensions after violent anti-migrant protests. But the rift is back
World.content:
Abuja, Nigeria — Protesters in South Africa have given migrants living illegally in the country until the end of the month to leave. If that sounds familiar, it comes months after another deadline came and went. And while the threat carries no legal force, it is causing major ructions between Africa’s richest country and its most populous — Nigeria.

In the wake of anti-migrant protests, rising tensions and even killings, some Nigerians – who are predominantly affected by the unrest – are leaving the country altogether. Others are closing businesses, seeking safety near the Nigerian mission or keeping their children out of school, Nigerian community representatives in South Africa say.

At the heart of these tensions are South Africa’s economic woes, with protesters pointing the finger at migrants — a pattern seen across the globe.

“High unemployment, pressure on public services and anxieties about crime create a political environment in which migrants can become convenient scapegoats,” Fola Aina, an international security analyst who teaches development studies at SOAS University of London, told CNN.

The unofficial deadline calls for undocumented foreigners to leave South Africa, but nor have documented migrants been spared.

Nigerians have emerged as some of its most visible victims. Nigeria says nearly 100 of its nationals have died in mob attacks and other incidents linked to anti-migrant violence in South Africa since 2022.

That hostility comes against a backdrop of longstanding negative perceptions of Nigerians in South Africa, which Pretoria says has been fueled by the alleged involvement of some Nigerian nationals in organized crime, drug trafficking and financial fraud.

The fallout is also being felt hundreds of miles away in Nigeria’s capital Abuja, where a diplomatic rift is reopening. Nigeria’s parliament has suspended official visits and legislative engagements with South Africa as anger mounts over the treatment of Nigerians.

The deaths of two more Nigerians in South Africa this month have only added to those tensions.

Protesters march against illegal immigration, in Johannesburg, South Africa, on June 30. Themba Hadebe/AP/File South African Defence Force members are deployed to Hillbrow, following a march against illegal immigration, in Johannesburg, South Africa, on June 30. Themba Hadebe/AP/File

What sparked the latest unrest?

Anti-migrant rhetoric had been building for months when groups, including March and March, gave undocumented migrants until June 30 to leave the country.

Campaigners blamed foreigners for unemployment, crime and pressure on public services.

As the deadline approached, thousands of foreign nationals sought to leave. Nearly 1,700 Nigerians voluntarily evacuated this year, according to Nigerian officials.

On June 30, demonstrations were held in cities including Johannesburg and Durban. While many were peaceful, reports also described clashes, looting and violence.

The departures continued after the deadline. Between June 14 and August 20, more than 86,000 foreign nationals were processed for repatriation and deportation, according to South African government figures, with Malawians making up the largest group.

As the June 30 deadline neared, two Nigerians were killed. But the campaign is not over as protesters say anti-migrant action will restart on September 30.

“There is significant anxiety and fear within the Nigerian community,” Akindele Olufemi Olunloyo, National Publicity Secretary of the Nigerian Union South Africa, told CNN.

Weren’t Nigeria and South Africa trying to fix this?

They were.

In July, South African Foreign Minister Ronald Lamola traveled to Abuja for talks to ease tensions. Both governments condemned xenophobic violence and discussed protecting foreign nationals.

Members of the Zulu regiment known as the ‘Amabutho’ hold a South African flag as they march during a demonstration by the “March and March” movement marking an unofficial deadline set by citizen-led groups for undocumented foreign nationals to leave South Africa, in Durban, on June 30. Marco Longari/AFP/Getty Images

South Africa has also pushed back against the anti-migrant campaign at home, stressing that immigration enforcement is the responsibility of the state. President Cyril Ramaphosa said in August that his government “firmly and publicly rejected xenophobia, Afrophobia, vigilantism, and all forms of discrimination against migrants.”

Yet two months after the Abuja talks, Nigeria said two more of its citizens had been killed in South Africa – and blamed police for one of the deaths.

According to Nigeria’s foreign ministry, Michael Taiwo Fakunle, a bishop, was shot dead at his Johannesburg home on September 4 after allegedly receiving threats. A day later, James Uchechukwu Nwankwo died following what the ministry described as “gruesome interrogation techniques” by South African police officers.

South African police have given a different account of Nwankwo’s death. A police spokesperson told local media that he was arrested on suspicion of drug possession but developed breathing difficulties on the way to a police station. Police said an inquest was opened and that there were no visible signs that he had been assaulted.

CNN has contacted South African police and South Africa’s foreign ministry for comment.

Femi Fani-Kayode, Nigeria’s ambassador-designate to South Africa, Lesotho and Eswatini, said eight Nigerians have been killed in South Africa this year, four allegedly by police officers.

Nigerian nationals wait for processing outside the Nigerian High Commission on June 10, in Pretoria, South Africa. Per-Anders Pettersson/Getty Images/File

“Our patience is wearing thin,” Fani-Kayode wrote in a post on Facebook. He said South Africans in Nigeria don’t face similar violence “by our people or our security forces,” adding that there would be “consequences” if the killings continued.

Why is Nigeria responding more strongly now?

Aina, the security analyst from SOAS, says that Abuja’s decision to suspend official visits to South Africa and the legislative boycott shows the issue’s growing political weight in Nigeria.

“Nigeria’s response has become more assertive,” Aina said.

But he cautioned against interpreting the move as a breakdown in relations. It does not end government-level contacts or existing agreements.

“Its significance lies in the political signal that business as usual is no longer acceptable,” he said.

The swift return of tensions, Aina added, also exposes the limits of July’s talks.

“Condemnations and assurances are important, but they cannot substitute for effective policing, credible investigations, prosecution of perpetrators and sustained protection of vulnerable communities,” he said.

South Africa’s immigration debate involves migrants from across the continent, and Nigerians are only one community caught up in it.

“This is fundamentally a broader South African debate over immigration, economic insecurity and national identity,” Aina said.

Nigerian passengers, who were repatriated from South Africa, disembark from a chartered plane after landing at the Murtala Muhammed international airport Lagos, Nigeria on June 11. Toyin Adedokun/AFP/Getty Images

Who pays for the fallout?

The tensions have also opened a dispute over who should bear the financial cost.

Nigeria sought compensation for citizens who lost property and businesses amid the June violence. But South Africa has made a financial demand of its own, saying it would seek reimbursement from African governments for the cost of repatriating and deporting their citizens.

As thousands of foreigners sought to leave amid the protests, South African authorities helped process and facilitate their voluntary repatriation. Separately, the government continued deporting people found to be in the country illegally.

Nigeria, however, said it had received no formal request from South Africa to reimburse those costs.

South Africa’s Department of Home Affairs told CNN that it intends to pursue reimbursement — through diplomatic channels rather than the courts.

Why does this matter beyond migration?

Nigeria and South Africa are among Africa’s most influential economies and political powers.

Nigeria supported South Africa’s anti-apartheid struggle. Yet relations have not always been easy.

In 1995, then-South African President Nelson Mandela criticized Nigeria’s military government after the execution of writer Ken Saro-Wiwa and eight others, straining relations between the two countries.

In 2012, another row erupted after South Africa deported 125 Nigerians over allegedly invalid yellow fever certificates. Nigeria retaliated by deporting South Africans before Pretoria apologized.

People are seen on the bus as thousands of Malawian migrants were put on buses to return to their home country following a rise in xenophobic attacks and anti-immigrant protests in the city of Pietermaritzburg in KwaZulu-Natal province, South Africa, on June 26. Ihsaan Haffejee/Anadolu/Getty Images

More recently, xenophobic violence in 2015 caused fresh tensions, while another outbreak in 2019 prompted Nigeria to evacuate hundreds of citizens and boycott the World Economic Forum meeting in Cape Town.

That same year, South Africa temporarily shut its diplomatic missions in Nigeria after retaliatory attacks on South African-owned businesses.

The pattern has become familiar: attacks on foreigners in South Africa trigger anger in Nigeria, tensions rise and eventually both governments try to repair relations.

But repeated flare-ups risk consequences beyond the bilateral relationship.

Aina says prolonged tensions could hurt commercial ties and make cooperation on regional security and economic integration more difficult.

“The wider concern is that a dispute between two influential African states could undermine the credibility of the African Union’s commitment to continental solidarity and free movement,” he added.

World.title: Pope Tawadros: Inauguration of “Kom Maria” project in Mallawi important addition to Minya
World.content:
Pope Tawadros II, Pope of Alexandria and Patriarch of the Coptic Orthodox Church, said that “Kom Maria” project had been a dream for the people of Mallawi and has now become a tangible reality.He stressed that the project represents an important addition to the governorate and contributes to reviving the Holy Family Trail, with its religious, historical and cultural significance.

He made the remarks while attending the inauguration of the first phase of the Kom Maria project in Mallawi, Minya, one of the sites along Egypt’s Holy Family Trail.

The ceremony was attended by Minya Governor Emad Kedwani and Bishop Demetrius, Bishop of the Diocese of Mallawi and Ansina.

Pope Tawadros expressed his sincere thanks and appreciation to President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi for providing an example in consolidating the values of citizenship and ensuring that he serves as a president for all Egyptians.

For his part, Kedwani praised the national and community role of the Egyptian Church, headed by Pope Tawadros II, describing it as an active partner in development efforts across various sectors, particularly healthcare.He noted the contribution of church-affiliated institutions to supporting the governorate’s healthcare system through three major hospitals including Misr Al-Mahabba Hospital in Beni Mazar, Al-Ragaa Hospital in Abu Qurqas, and Al-Raai Al-Saleh Hospital in Samalout. The three hospitals have been accredited in preparation for joining the Universal Health Insurance System.

World.title: GAFI: 3,366 Chinese firms operating in Egypt across multiple sectors
World.content:
The number of Chinese investing companies in Egypt has jumped to 3,366 firms, operating across multiple sectors, including textiles, ready-made garments, solar panels, chemical industries, automotive manufacturing, and logistics services, according to the General Authority for Investment and Free Zones (GAFI).

Speaking during her participation in the Investment Promotion Forum at the 26th China International Fair for Investment and Trade (CIFIT), held in Xiamen from Sept. 8 to 11, GAFI Deputy CEO Eman Mansour highlighted the growth of Egyptian-Chinese investment partnerships.

She described the “TEDA Egypt” project in the Suez Canal Economic Zone as a model for industrial cooperation, local manufacturing integration, and export-oriented production.Mansour said sustainability is a cornerstone of Egypt’s economic development plans, citing plans to raise green public investments to 60% of total public investments in FY2026/2027.

She also touched on promising investment opportunities in green hydrogen, renewable energy, electric vehicles, and advanced industries.On the margins of their participation in the global event, GAFI officials explored cooperation opportunities with international bodies and investment agencies from Saudi Arabia, Malaysia, and China, Mansour said.

Discussions covered bolstering cooperation in sustainable investment fields, enhancing private sector competitiveness and linking it to global value chains, as well as expertise-sharing and institutional cooperation, she pointed out.

World.title: Egypt, Senegal plan direct shipping route between Alexandria, Dakar
World.content:
Minister of Transport Kamel al-Wazir held talks with Senegalese Minister of Fisheries, Maritime Transport, Infrastructure and Ports Amy Mara Dièye on launching a commercial shipping route between Alexandria and Dakar to increase trade between Egypt and West Africa.

During the talks, Wazir said that the proposed route would provide a more direct maritime connection between the two countries, facilitate Egyptian exports to West African markets and improve access for Senegalese products to markets in the Middle East and Arab countries.

He affirmed that the Alexandria-Dakar route could serve as a starting point for broader maritime cooperation and stronger trade and investment ties.The two ministers also discussed cooperation in shipbuilding, fishing vessel production and maritime training.

The talks also addressed possible use of Egyptian shipyards to build fishing boats and vessels for Senegal, as well as training programs for Senegalese personnel through specialized Egyptian institutions.For her part, Dièye expressed Senegal’s interest in expanding cooperation with Egypt and benefiting from its experience in maritime transport and infrastructure.

At the end of the meeting, the two sides agreed to form a joint committee to finalize a maritime transport cooperation agreement between Egypt and Senegal ahead of its planned signing.

World.title: FM, Lebanese PM discuss bilateral relations, developments in Lebanon
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Expatriates Badr Abdelatty discussed the latest developments in Lebanon during a phone call with Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam as part of the ongoing consultations and coordination between the two countries and the exchange of views on regional developments and ways to strengthen bilateral relations.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement on Wednesday, September 16, 2026, that Abdelatty reiterated Egypt’s support for Lebanon’s sovereignty, unity and territorial integrity, stressing Egypt’s complete rejection of all Israeli violations and attacks against Lebanese sovereignty.

He also underscored the importance of Israel’s full withdrawal from the occupied Lebanese territories and the full and non-selective implementation of UN Security Council Resolution 1701.

He stressed Egypt’s support for Lebanon’s state institutions, particularly the Lebanese army.The call also addressed the broader, rapidly evolving regional developments and efforts to de-escalate tensions, as well as the repercussions of developments in the Red Sea on the security and safety of maritime navigation, freedom of international trade and energy supplies.

Abdelatty reviewed the Egyptian diplomatic efforts to prevent the escalation from spreading and to spare the region further tensions and instability.

World.title: Liberia: 2 Billion Tons of Ore- Switches Back to AMR
World.content:
Monrovia – For a decade and a half, the mountain has mostly kept its secrets. Putu, tucked into the forested hills of Grand Gedeh County, holds an estimated 2.37 billion tonnes of iron ore — enough, by some reckonings, to rank among West Africa’s largest untapped deposits. And for just as long, it has sat there: surveyed, licensed, argued over, and never mined.

By Rodney D. Sieh, [email protected]

That may be changing. In a letter dated September 11 and addressed to Mines and Energy Minister R. Matenokay Tingban, Severstal — the Russian steel giant that has held the Putu concession since 2010 — told the government something it had spent much of this year arguing against: that Africa Metallic Resources Inc. has come through with a binding offer, and that it beats the rival bid from Planet One Natural Resources Holdings on price and terms alike.

It is a small paragraph with a long backstory.

A mountain with a complicated past

Putu’s modern history begins in 2010, when the Liberian government signed a 25-year mineral development agreement handing Severstal control of the deposit. The timing was almost immediately unlucky. Feasibility studies dragged on. Then came 2014, and Russia’s annexation of Crimea, and the first wave of Western sanctions that would follow Moscow for the next decade. By the time the war in Ukraine escalated those sanctions further, Severstal was, in practical terms, a foreign operator that couldn’t easily raise financing, sell into Western markets, or move equipment through the usual channels. Putu never got past drilling and paperwork. Twenty thousand potential jobs sat, on paper, in a country that badly needed them.

So Severstal went looking for an exit. And that’s where the story most Liberians have been following since spring actually starts.

A contract, a reversal, and a lot of noise

In December 2025, following a competitive review by Liberia’s Inter-Ministerial Concessions Committee, AMR — a Liberian-led consortium built around Cherif Abdallah’s Conex Group, with the Africa Finance Corporation as a financing partner — was named preferred developer. It scored 88.6 out of 100 in the government’s own evaluation, well ahead of a company called JSW and far ahead of Planet One, which came in last at 55.6.

Then, in the space of a few months, the deal seemed to unravel. Severstal began telling the Ministry of Mines that AMR was moving too slowly — that it hadn’t produced proof of funds, hadn’t cleared U.S. sanctions review, and was, in the company’s words, the “least advanced” of the potential buyers. By March and April, Severstal was actively lobbying for Planet One instead, and on April 22, an acting minister granted consent for exactly that transfer.

“What about us, the affected communities? Are we going to be silenced like before?” — Putu Contact Group chairman Joseph Geebro

It didn’t sit well. The Putu Contact Group, representing communities that live in the shadow of the deposit and have watched outside companies come and go for fifteen years without a shovel touching ground, called foul — loudly. Their argument was simple: the government’s own scoring had ranked Planet One last, and yet Planet One was suddenly winning.

President Joseph Boakai stepped in and hit pause. Citing a binding December memorandum with AMR, he ordered the Planet One transfer halted and directed that the existing agreement be given every chance to work before any alternative was considered.

What actually changed Severstal’s mind

Here’s the part of the story that tends to get lost in the back-and-forth: Severstal’s objections to AMR were never really about who AMR was. They were about two specific, fixable problems — sanctions clearance and proof of funds. Over the summer, AMR appears to have solved both. By May, the company had secured clearance from the U.S. Office of Foreign Assets Control, removing the sanctions uncertainty that had been Severstal’s loudest complaint. Financing commitments through the Africa Finance Corporation, a strategic partner of the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation, filled in the rest.

“The company Severstal spent the spring calling the ‘least advanced’ bidder is now the one it’s endorsing.”

That is presumably why Severstal is now writing letters that read almost like an endorsement — telling the ministry that AMR’s terms are better than Planet One’s, and that both bidders offer roughly the same timeline to production. Whatever the company’s earlier reservations, the practical obstacles behind them have largely disappeared.

The Liberian company behind the letters

AMR’s public face has been John B.S. Davies III, who has described Putu less as a mining deal than a test case for a different kind of resource development in Liberia — one where ownership, procurement, and processing stay closer to home rather than following the familiar path of raw ore shipped out and profit following it. Above Davies sits Cherif Abdallah, the Conex Group chairman whose business footprint in Liberia already runs through energy, logistics, and real estate — he’s the same figure who bought out Total’s Liberia and Sierra Leone operations a few years back. It’s Conex’s balance sheet and regional infrastructure, alongside AFC’s financing muscle, that gives AMR’s bid its weight.

What’s actually on the table for Liberia

If the deal closes on the terms in Severstal’s letter, the pitch is substantial: more than 20,000 jobs, government equity carried free of cost, a share offering open to ordinary Liberian investors, and commitments to build out roads, rail, power, and port infrastructure alongside the mine itself — rather than simply exporting raw ore and leaving the rest to someone else.

It’s worth saying plainly, though, that a binding offer is not a closed deal. The Share Sale and Purchase Agreement still has to be finalized, and the same questions about execution capacity that dogged AMR in the spring haven’t entirely vanished just because the sanctions issue has been resolved. Fifteen years of false starts at Putu have taught the southeast to be patient about promises made on paper.

A skeptic’s caution

Not everyone is convinced this reversal changes the fundamentals. Back when Severstal was still lobbying for Planet One, former Minister of Mines and Energy Wilmot Paye warned publicly against treating any change of ownership at Putu as progress in itself.

“I do not believe that a mere change of control is adequate to achieve any more desirable outcome than maintaining the status quo,” Paye said at the time, questioning what had specifically qualified Planet One over other bidders after Severstal had reportedly “concluded” transfer terms with them — the same abrupt reversal now playing out again, in the opposite direction, in AMR’s favor.

Paye’s broader argument was less about which company wins than about the structure underneath the fight. “Mining is not like harvesting a cassava farm,” he said, cautioning that Liberia won’t fully understand what it has agreed to until a real deal is signed — and warning that a successor could eventually seek to extend the existing Mineral Development Agreement through amendment, leaving the country “tied up” again. “The consequence?” he asked. “The vicious circle continues.”

Whether AMR’s newly cleared sanctions status and financing commitments answer that concern, or simply repeat the pattern Paye described with better paperwork, is likely to be argued over for as long as the deal itself takes to close.

The president’s bet

Seen from a few months’ distance, Boakai’s April intervention looks less like picking a side in a corporate dispute and more like buying AMR the runway it needed to clear the objections that were actually holding things up. Whether that reads as prudent mediation or as a government that nearly reversed a fair, competitive process before catching itself is likely to depend on who’s telling the story — and it’s a question this paper’s readers deserve to see asked plainly, not just answered on the government’s terms.

World.title: Liberia: Swedish Ambassador Pledges Continued Support for Post-War Justice, Sexual and Reproductive Rights Among Other Priorities After Embassy Closure
World.content:
Karl Backéus, Sweden’s ambassador to Liberia, presents the embassy’s annual investigative journalism prize to New Narratives/Okay FM senior reporter Fatu Kamara in a ceremony this month. Anthony Stephens/New Narratives.

Summary:

In an exclusive interview, Sweden’s ambassador Karl Backéus has pledged the country will continue to support Liberia’s postwar justice efforts through the U.N., E.U. and other multilateral institutions even as it ends direct assistance to the country.

Backéus said he hopes lawmakers will pass a bill to establish a war and economic crimes court “in the next few months.” He says international backing will depend on a “robust and strong” court, and financial ownership by the government.

Backéus said he sees progress in fight against corruption, but says major problems remain, citing concerns about corruption cases being delayed.

By Anthony Stephens, senior justice correspondent with New Narratives

Sweden’s ambassador to Liberia has used an exclusive interview with Frontpage Africa/New Narratives marking the end of the country’s sixteen years of direct bilateral support since the end of the war, to reaffirm his government’s commitment to Liberia’s post war justice and accountability process.

Ambassador Karl Backéus said the Swedish government, which was one of the country’s most generous donors until last month, will continue supporting post-war justice efforts through the United Nations, European Union and other multilateral institutions. And he added his voice to international diplomats urging Liberia’s lawmakers to approve legislation establishing a war and economic crimes court within the next few months.

“I really fundamentally do believe that, as part of the reconciliation process in Liberia, there is a need for accountability,” said Backéus. “And even though it has taken a very long time, I do think it needs to move forward.”

Ambassador Karl Backéus attends a gathering of postwar justice actors in Monrovia in February. Source: Swedish embassy Facebook page.

Sweden’s commitment comes at a pivotal moment for Liberia’s long-running quest for accountability. More than two decades after the civil wars ended, no one has been prosecuted in Liberia for the widespread wartime atrocities documented by the country’s 2009 Truth and Reconciliation Commission. Six competing proposals involving a War and Economic Crimes Court and a National Anti-Corruption Court are before the Legislature, while questions remain over how the costly courts will be financed as international development funding shrinks. Sweden has been the major international donor to Liberia’s war crimes court process and was in recent years, the second largest bilateral donor after the United States.

Sweden announced last year that it was ending support to five African countries, including Liberia, in order to bolster support to Ukraine, which has been invaded by Russia. The government sees Russian aggression in Europe as a major threat to its own security.

The decision was a major blow for Liberia. Under its 2021–2025 cooperation strategy, Sweden committed about US$190 million to 39 projects spanning human rights, rule of law, governance, sexual and reproductive health and rights, gender equality, agriculture, infrastructure, independent media and climate and environmental protection. (New Narratives was a recipient of support.)

Liberia could continue to benefit from Sweden’s regional and thematic development programs , covering areas including gender equality, sexual and reproductive health and rights, democracy and human rights, peace and security, climate and sustainable development. Backéus said the European Union would be particularly important because Sweden, as an E.U. member, contributes to its funding. He also pointed to cooperation between Sweden and Liberia at the United Nations, including through the Peacebuilding Commission.

But Sweden’s future commitments to Liberia and Africa in general will depend heavily on the outcome of national elections to elect all 349 seats of the Riksdag held on the weekend. It’s turned into a genuine cliffhanger: early results put the opposition centre-left bloc, led by former Prime Minister Magdalena Andersson’s Social Democrats, narrowly ahead of Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson’s outgoing centre-right coalition. The race is too close to call.

Under Sweden’s outgoing government, Sida — the Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency — has faced four consecutive years of cuts, with its 2026 budget reduced by roughly 20 percent as part of a broader shift that abandoned Sweden’s long-standing target of spending one percent of gross national income (GNI) on aid. Aid to Africa is projected to fall by two-thirds between 2021 and 2026.

Across the opposition bloc, the rhetoric is consistently pro-aid, but the near-term budgets tell a different story. Every opposition party still cuts aid in 2026 relative to pre-2023 levels — just less than the government — and none has taken a specific position on reversing the five-country phase-out that includes Liberia.

For now, Backéus said, post war justice and accountability is a priority. Sweden provided nearly $1 million to the U.N. Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights in Liberia, which has in turn provided furniture and technical support to the government office preparing for the proposed court. Backéus said he hopes that will continue.

“If we can be supportive of that, we want to be,” Backéus said. “We want to continue to stay engaged in this.”

Sweden’s “Stories of Change” on social media sites have documented their support for a range of areas in Liberia including small business. Source: Swedish embassy Facebook page.

A recent FrontPage Africa/New Narratives survey of 1,150 people across 11 of Liberia’s 15 counties found 91 percent wanted the court, while 89 percent said they would not vote for lawmakers who failed to support legislation establishing one. The survey was not conducted under scientific polling standards. Backéus said it was a strong sign of public sentiment.

Civilians flee Lurd fighters on Bushrod Island in 2003. Credit: Tim Hetherington.

“I think it really shows that this is something that’s there’s broad support throughout society in Liberia, through communities all over the country for this important process,” Backéus said.

But he acknowledged the legal complexity of the competing proposals and said lawmakers needed to be confident that whatever legislation they approved was legally sound.

“But at the end of the day, of course, we want to see progress,” he said. “So I hope that we will see that in the next few months.”

Backéus said the precise model was ultimately Liberia’s decision, but international partners would need confidence in the institution before backing it.

“We need, of course, to have something that’s robust and strong,” he said. “And then, with that, I think the international community will continue to be there.”

He identified one potential obstacle to Swedish support: the possibility that the court could impose the death penalty.

“From the Swedish side. We would struggle, I think, to support any court that could, at least in theory, sentence people to the death penalty,” Backéus said. “That would not be consistent with our principles that we stand for.”

Financing presents another challenge. Jallah Barbu, executive director of the Office of the War and Economic Crimes Court, has estimated that establishing and operating the court would cost at least US$20 million .

Backéus warned that international financing for tribunals is far more limited than it was 10 or 20 years ago, pointing to the heavily internationally financed Special Court for Sierra Leone as a model Liberia should not expect donors to replicate.

“Sweden will not be able to provide that kind of funding,” he said. “So there needs to be a stronger ownership for for this also financially from the Liberian side.”

Still, Backéus said he believed political commitment to the court had grown significantly in Liberia and that a less expensive model than some previous international tribunals was possible.

Sweden has been one of Liberia’s most generous donors. Credit: Swedish embassy in Liberia.
