World.title: GOP lawmakers pump brakes on Trump's $5K check promise: 'Where are you getting the money?'
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

President Donald Trump's promise of a big payout for Americans if Republicans win the midterms is getting a rocky reception on Capitol Hill.

Several Republicans outright oppose the $5,000 check promise, while others offered tacit support in comments to Fox News Digital but hesitated on whether it could actually be delivered. It's a sign that the GOP will have an uphill fight to get the "Trump dividend" approved by Congress — with the president and lawmakers divided over whether it even needs the legislative branch's green light.

"I disagree with it. It's pay-to-play," Rep. Ralph Norman, R-S.C., told Fox News Digital. "You shouldn't pay anybody to vote your conscience. Plus, where are you getting the money? I think we're in debt $40 trillion."

House Appropriations Committee Chairman Tom Cole, R-Okla., whose powerful committee would likely play a major role in crafting the $5,000 stimulus if it did run through Congress, said he was "skeptical" it could be achieved.

TRUMP FACES RECKONING AS GOP FIGURES LABEL $5K PROMISE A 'SOCIALIST VOTE-BUYING SCHEME'

"Take a billion dollars ... I'd rather use it to either bolster defense or save Social Security. I think that's a better use of the money. But again, we have to see what we're looking at. Right now, we don't have a bill," Cole told Fox News Digital.

TRUMP DANGLES $5,000 CHECKS AS DEBT SURGES — BUT ONLY IF GOP CAN CLEAR MAJOR MIDTERM HURDLE

He added more optimistically, "We just have an idea that we want to get money back to the American people. I like that."

Rep. John Rutherford, R-Fla., said he could support the idea if the sudden injection of cash wouldn't send inflation rates soaring.

"But it ought to be limited — people that are working, people that are paying taxes. I don't think we should just send paychecks out to everybody willy-nilly," Rutherford told Fox News Digital.

Rep. Beth Van Duyne, R-Texas, simply said, "The devil's always in the details. I prefer to look at ways of getting people job opportunities."

VOTERS HAVE A BLUNT MESSAGE FOR TRUMP ABOUT HIS IDEA TO DOLE OUT $5,000 CHECKS

Rep. Brad Knott, R-N.C., praised Trump's candor but signaled he was not enthusiastic about a stimulus without guardrails.

"If we can structure tax incentives, if we can do some type of — whether it's a cut, whether it's a rebate, something in that vein, I think it's probably a little better policy than mailing people a check just because they're here," Knott said.

But the idea did find support from others, like House Freedom Caucus Chairman Andy Harris, R-Md.

"I think that hardworking Americans, probably taxpayers, deserve a tax rebate, we’re going to have to discuss how large a rebate that’ll be," Harris told Fox News Digital, suggesting the $5,000 figure should be up for negotiation. "That’s a good idea."

He added that it should go through Congress, potentially through the same mechanism that Republicans used to pass the "One Big, Beautiful Bill Act."

"It would probably have to go through reconciliation," he said.

Republican Study Committee Chairman August Pfluger, R-Texas, suggested the money could come from what the federal government recovers in efforts to crack down on waste, fraud, and abuse of taxpayer dollars.

"Why don't we continue the president's approach towards fraud, and give a dividend to the people of this great country who that money was stolen from?" Pfluger posed, arguing that hundreds of billions of dollars were lost to fraud in the last administration.

Giving $5,000 to every American adult could cost at least $1 trillion by some estimates, a significant portion of the U.S. annual budget. A price tag that big historically, would be subject to congressional approval, but the president may disagree.

"I think they will do it if we needed it, but I think not," Trump told CBS News when asked if Congress would need to approve the stimulus.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

But Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., told CNN's "State of the Union" earlier this week, "I would assume, yes, he'd need Congress to act."

World.title: America’s hunters get an exclusive seat at Trump’s White House table as he takes aim at Biden-era rules
World.content:

FIRST ON FOX: President Donald Trump will host more than 100 hunters, anglers and outdoor industry leaders for dinner at the White House on Thursday night, where he is expected to sign executive orders aimed at expanding hunting and fishing opportunities and reversing certain Biden-era restrictions on hunting and fishing.

Trump will deliver remarks to the sportsmen and industry representatives gathered for the dinner in the Rose Garden as his administration moves to open more public lands and waterways, ease regulatory barriers and promote hunting among younger Americans and veterans, Fox News Digital learned.

He is expected to sign a pair of executive orders in the Oval Office Thursday aimed at expanding "America’s public lands and waterways," promoting healthy wild game populations and expanding access to offshore recreational fishing, a White House official told Fox News Digital.

TRUMP WILL WELCOME FARMERS AND RANCHERS TO WHITE HOUSE DINNER TO CELEBRATE TRADE, TAX WINS

Representatives from organizations and companies including Bass Pro Shops, the Cabela Family Foundation, the National Rifle Association, Rocky Mountain Elk Foundation, Yamaha Marine Group, Polaris, Beretta USA, Safari Club International, Primos Hunting, Dallas Safari Club, Outdoor Sportsman Group, Sportsmen’s Alliance, USA Shooting Foundation, Ducks Unlimited, Sportsman Boats, Contender Boats, Taurus Holdings and the Congressional Sportsmen’s Foundation are expected to attend.

America’s outdoor recreation sector generates over $1.2 trillion annually and supports over 5 million jobs, according to a White House official.

Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, representatives from the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and officials from the Commerce Department and NOAA will be present, Fox News Digital learned.

CONGRESS SHOULD HONOR TEDDY ROOSEVELT AND CONSERVE OUR OUTDOORS FOR THE NEXT 250 YEARS

The Secretary of the Interior, the Secretary of Agriculture, the Secretary of War, and the Secretary of Commerce are directed to propose changes to current policies.

One of the policies spotlighted in the order targets Biden-era restrictions on the use of traditional lead ammunition and tackle.

Under Biden, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service adopted station-specific requirements for lead-free ammunition and/or tackle at several national wildlife refuges.

DENNY HAMLIN SAYS FORWARD-FACING SONAR IN PROFESSIONAL BASS FISHING HAS GONE 'A LITTLE OVERBOARD'

Trump’s fishing order seeks to unleash more of America’s coastal waters for recreational fishing while cutting federal red tape and giving anglers a bigger role in how fisheries are managed.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The administration seeks to move charter operators toward multi-year permits, replace mail-in catch surveys with mobile reporting, launching programs for depleted stocks such as Atlantic striped bass, and using eligible offshore oil and gas platforms to create artificial reefs.

World.title: Philadelphia home search uncovers possible human ashes, images of 7 missing women: police
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Philadelphia police found images of seven missing women, including two who appear unconscious and injured, while searching more than 1 million images recovered from a home where investigators also found five urns believed to contain human ashes, authorities said Wednesday.

Initial analysis of the images showed two missing women — 27-year-old Gabrielle Armando and 26-year-old Maribel Fresses — lying unconscious in the Chew Avenue home with apparent injuries, Philadelphia Police Department Deputy Commissioner Frank Vanore said during a news conference.

Metadata from the images show they were taken in 2017.

CALIFORNIA AUTHORITIES IDENTIFY FINAL UNKNOWN VICTIM OF ‘HAPPY FACE KILLER’ KEITH JESPERSON AFTER 34 YEARS

"Both women remain missing and have not been seen," Vanore said. "To date, neither their bodies nor any DNA evidence have been recovered."

The home belonged to deceased pornographer Raymond "R.C." Horsch and was occupied by his son, Eugene Horsch, whose June arrest sparked the investigation.

On June 19, a Federal Park Ranger arrested Eugene Horsch, 44, after investigating him and a female passenger sitting in a BMW outside of Philadelphia's Independence Mall, Vanore explained.

"During the course of that investigation, officers recovered two firearms, narcotics, and identification impersonating a federal law enforcement officer, and he was charged. Task force officers from the DEA were able to develop probable cause that same day and serve a warrant on Mr. Horsch's residence," Vanore said.

The female passenger presented police with a false identification using the name Blair Tonzelli, a woman who has been missing since 2023, a spokesperson for the Philadelphia Police Department confirmed to Fox News Digital.

FOUL ODOR AT NYC SCHOOL LEADS POLICE TO BODY HIDDEN IN CHIMNEY

The true identity of the woman in the vehicle has not been released. Tonzelli's whereabouts remain unknown.

After obtaining a warrant, investigators found "a homemade laboratory of some kind in the basement area, five urns believed to contain human ashes and a large amount of digital evidence — including computers, hard drives, flash drives, DVRs, cameras and phones," Vanore said during the press conference.

Investigators have identified 58 people in the videos and images they found in the home. Vanore said "four of those identified appear lifeless, with video depicting what may have happened to one of them."

NEW CALIFORNIA LAW EXPANDS DNA TOOLS FOR MISSING PERSONS INVESTIGATIONS

One video shows R.C. Horsch handcuffing a woman to a bed and zip-tying her neck until she became unconscious. Police identified this woman as Nicole Fusaro, according to FOX 29 Philadelphia.

Another missing woman connected to the home is R.C. Horsch's ex-wife, Amy McHale, who has been missing since 2016, FOX 29 reported.

Two other missing women have been connected to the home. Police identified one as a 25-year-old woman but did not name her, and the other has yet to be identified, according to FOX 29.

World.title: Far-left streamer Hasan Piker called out by MS NOW hosts in fiery exchange over him being a drag for Democrats
World.content:

Far-left Twitch streamer Hasan Piker clashed with two MS NOW hosts on Wednesday on multiple issues, including his political influence and his anti-Israel stance, as Symone Sanders Townsend told the streamer point-blank she would be telling candidates she worked for to absolutely "disavow" him.

"I used to work campaigns, Hasan, and I have to tell you, if I was a strategist or a consultant or the political director on one of these campaigns, I would absolutely be telling my people to disavow you," Sanders Townsend told Piker in an interview on her "Clock It" podcast, which she co-hosts with Eugene Daniels. "I really would, because we wanna win! We wanna win, and so, like, if you’re not gonna help people win, distance."

Piker acknowledged the disagreement between them as Townsend continued, "I’ve elected people, though. You’ve never elected anybody."

STEPHEN A SMITH WARNS HASAN PIKER WILL ‘CONTAMINATE’ DEMOCRATS IN THE MIDTERMS, ‘COME BACK TO HAUNT THEM’

Piker also maintained his view that Israel is worse than Hamas, though he acknowledged it was a provocative statement. "I do believe that," he said.

"Is Hamas a religious fundamentalist operation that have engaged in violent actions? Of course they have, absolutely," Piker continued. "But that violence is directly born out of, and even that repression is directly born out of, the conditions brought about by the occupation that's been going on for 80 plus years."

Daniels pressed the Twitch streamer on whether he understood that it sounded like he was endorsing violence by making that argument.

"Do you understand that that's how people hear it? And is that what you are endorsing?" Daniels asked.

"So this, again, goes back to the same — this goes back to the same dynamic, right?" Piker said. "Structural violence and state violence is oftentimes made to be invisible. So when Israel as a state is operating its normal state functions, and sometimes it can come across as excessive, right? It's not seen as violent."

"It's no different than when people protest against police violence and police brutality. The brutality of the police is systemic violence, and therefore it's normalized," he added.

"It's made to be invisible," Piker continued. "Whereas when people protest against the police, that is all of a sudden chaotic, that's all of a sudden violent. It's never violent when the police actually release tear gas on protesters. It's violence if the protesters use leaf blowers to blow that tear gas."

Townsend jumped in to reject the comparison to protesting the police.

"I'm gonna let Eugene move on, but I just want to note, it sounds like the example that you just gave that the people who are protesting the police are Hamas. And I just would reject that as somebody who has protested the police before, but we can move on," Townsend said.

HASAN PIKER IS BECOMING THE 'FACE OF THE PROGRESSIVE MOVEMENT,' FORMER DEMOCRATIC OPERATIVE WARNS

"Symone Sanders Townsend is putting her finger on a real tension for Democrats heading into the midterms," David Scharf, chair of Morrison Cohen’s Government Strategies & Controversies practice, told Fox News Digital. "Hasan Piker gives candidates access to a large, young audience that traditional political media often doesn't reach. But he also gives Republicans a ready-made way to force those candidates to answer for statements they didn't make."

"Every candidate on the record defending him, appearing with him, or refusing to distance themselves from him helps turn him into a campaign issue," he added.

"In safe blue districts, that may not matter," Scharf said. "In a race as close as Michigan's Senate contest, it can. That's why Sanders Townsend, who has actually run campaigns, is looking at this very differently than Piker is. He's building an audience. She's counting votes."

RASKIN CALLS PIKER’S RHETORIC 'IRRELEVANT DISTRACTION' AFTER THE STREAMER SAID HE'D VOTE FOR HAMAS OVER ISRAEL

Piker insisted during a Friday livestream it was his "God-given" and "constitutionally protected right" to proclaim hatred for America.

During one of his lengthy shows, Piker responded to an attack ad against Democratic Michigan U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed based on his connection to Piker and his past controversial statements claiming to "hate" America.

"Bro, I hate this country, dude. I hate America," Piker said in clips featured on the ad. "Oh God, I f---ing hate America so much."

Piker argued after showing the clip that it was "clear" that he was angry at "what America as the American government is doing to Americans and to everyone else" but nevertheless defended his right to say he hates the country.

EL-SAYED GRILLED ON PIKER, ISRAEL AND SOCIALIST TIES AFTER MIKE ROGERS SKIPS SENATE DEBATE

"Of course, I'm a Godd--- American. It is my Godd--- God-given and constitutionally protected right to say I hate America if America is actually f---ing over Americans," he said. "You can clip chimp it all day. It doesn't change that. It doesn't change that mentality."

"To present this as like, oh, 'These guys are real America haters' as some liberals have been doing on the timeline, as virtually the entirety of the Republican Party is doing, is so f---ing stupid," Piker added.

World.title: Husband and wife get trapped in premier hiking destination; only one of them makes it out alive
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A sudden and powerful storm over Washington state's Cascade Mountains quickly turned a challenging hike into a fight for survival for an Oklahoma couple.

The pair was navigating the rugged "core zone" of the remote Enchantments wilderness when they were engulfed by heavy, deep snow.

By late afternoon, the freezing, high-elevation conditions brought their trek to a desperate halt.

2 MYSTERY DEATHS AT ZION NATIONAL PARK PROMPT URGENT QUESTIONS ABOUT VISITOR SAFETY

At 5:26 p.m., the husband sent an urgent text to 911.

He reported to dispatchers that their clothes were soaked through from the storm, and his wife was physically unable to continue moving, according to FOX 13 Seattle.

Help could not reach them in time.

The stranded hiker, identified as 45-year-old Sybil Claborn of Oklahoma City, succumbed to the extreme elements and died in the snow Sunday.

Before the rescue team reached them, Claborn's husband tried to carry her out but was unable to do so.

They were stranded at an elevation of roughly 7,000 to 8,000 feet, about 8 to 10 miles from the nearest trailheads.

TEEN HIKER'S DISAPPEARANCE ENDS IN TRAGEDY AT NATIONAL PARK WITH KEY QUESTION REMAINING

The situation prompted a frantic rescue effort involving multiple agencies, but the severe weather repeatedly thwarted attempts to reach the couple by air.

The sheriff's office requested a hoist-equipped helicopter at 6:51 p.m., and an Army helicopter launched from Yakima shortly after 8 p.m.

Stormy conditions forced the helicopter to turn back as the husband remained in contact with 911 and reported that Claborn's condition was deteriorating.

A second Army helicopter attempt around 10:50 p.m. was also unsuccessful, while Chelan County Mountain Rescue crews continued toward the couple on foot.

CLICK HERE TO 

Ground crews finally reached the stranded hikers around 3:30 a.m., finding Claborn dead and her husband suffering from severe hypothermia.

Her husband was warmed inside a tent before he was transported to Cascade Medical Center in Leavenworth for treatment.

Claborn's body was later recovered and taken to the Chelan County Coroner's Office.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

Authorities are actively investigating the cause and manner of Claborn's death.

Fox News Digital reached out to the Chelan County Sheriff's Office for more information.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

While the tragedy in the Enchantments unfolded amid heavy snow and freezing conditions, other hikers have died this year while battling extreme heat.

Earlier this summer, a 68-year-old French tourist died after attempting to hike to safety after his vehicle became stuck in mud in Death Valley National Park.

A similar tragedy unfolded at the Grand Canyon in June.

That month, an 18-year-old hiker died after developing heat-related symptoms on the park’s Bright Angel Trail, the National Park Service said.

World.title: Rubio takes behind-the-scenes role on Iran war, while keeping his options open for the future
World.content:
WASHINGTON — The talks to end the Iran war had hit a snag.

Vice President JD Vance had flown to Pakistan for negotiations with the Iranians, a sign that the two sides had narrowed their differences and the White House might be poised to announce a breakthrough.

As the marathon April meeting unfolded, though, U.S. negotiators began to worry: It looked like the Iranians were changing the terms of a potential deal. So, during a pause, they phoned Secretary of State Marco Rubio to get a “steer” on what they should do next, an administration official with direct knowledge of the matter said in an interview.

Rubio agreed that they couldn’t accept Iran’s offer, the official said. There would be no deal.

Rubio isn’t the face of the Iran negotiations. He’s kept a discreet public distance as the unpopular war grinds on. Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and the president’s longtime friend and special envoy Steve Witkoff are the main protagonists in the push to end both the Iran and Russia-Ukraine conflicts.

The arrangement is an unusual one. Past secretaries of state commanded the spotlight when it came to war and peace. Henry Kissinger won a Nobel Peace Prize in 1973 for negotiating a ceasefire in the Vietnam War during the Nixon administration. John Kerry, in the Obama administration, flew back and forth between Washington and the Middle East as he tried in vain to broker a peace deal between the Israelis and Palestinians.

Still, Rubio has been a hidden hand throughout, helping craft the Trump administration’s strategy while privately advising the officials who play a more public role in the peace talks.

He holds a unique place in the Cabinet, one of the most expansive in the modern presidency. Rubio doubles as national security adviser — first in an acting capacity, now permanent — meaning he has a spacious office in the West Wing and gets more face time with Trump than most Cabinet members.

This account is based on interviews with 12 present and former administration officials and others close to Rubio and the White House. Many spoke on condition of anonymity to talk freely about internal policy and political dynamics.

“The reason that the American people perhaps don’t see Secretary Rubio as front and center on Iran is because he really does have the rest of the world to worry about and pays enormous attention to the Western Hemisphere and our European allies,” White House chief of staff Susie Wiles told NBC News. “President Trump is so busy and active around the world, it takes more than one person. So, Secretary Rubio is leading the other efforts around the world that are so important to America’s stability and future promise.”

Trump has given Rubio wide latitude, allowing America’s top diplomat to be selective when it comes to the public parts of the job. Rubio was more visible in the early phase of the Iran war than in the later stages. That could prove advantageous down the road.

Polls show widespread American disenchantment with the conflict. As public opinion hardens, Rubio may be better positioned to sidestep any political backlash than Vance, who has attended futile rounds of peace talks in far-flung locales.

Rubio has said publicly that he currently has no plans to run in 2028, and two people familiar with the matter have told NBC News he has also said that privately. He has acknowledged behind closed doors that the landscape may be tough for Republicans in 2028 and suggested that a presidential run in 2032 or 2036 may be more promising, a person close to him said.

But Rubio’s comments don’t close the door completely. A second person close to him said that he has not ruled out a potential 2028 presidential run, but he is not discussing his future plans.

“Nobody knows what he’s going to do,” the source said. “Political calculation does not factor into literally anything that he’s doing right now.”

Another consideration is personal. Rubio has also said privately that after nearly three decades in public office he may want to take a job in the private sector when Trump’s term ends, two people familiar with the matter told NBC News.

His financial disclosure form shows his net worth to be no more than $240,000 apart from his house, listed in a range between $1 million and $5 million. Those are modest sums in an administration packed with officials worth $100 million or more.

Rubio could readily land a lucrative job that would be a boon to himself, his wife and their four children if he sat out the race, and at 55, he is young enough to mount a campaign later on.

Relationship with Trump

Once angry rivals, Rubio and Trump have developed a good rapport. Rubio may be in and out of the Oval Office five or six times a day, a White House official told NBC News. Both love sports, and they’ve been overheard jawing about baseball batting averages or a knockout punch in the latest mixed martial arts match, the official said.

Olivia Wales, a White House spokesperson, said in a prepared statement: “As President Trump says, Marco Rubio will go down as one of the greatest Secretaries of State in history. The president and Secretary Rubio have successfully restored American dominance on the world stage and are relentlessly working to advance our foreign policy interests.”

After spending 14 years in the Senate, Rubio grasps the politics and legislative tactics needed to pass bills into law and will advise the president on ways to push his agenda through Congress, the official said.

“I can think of many times in which we’re talking about whatever he [Trump] is focused on that day and he’ll say, ‘What do you think, Marco?’ I’ve heard that more times than I can count,” a person close to the White House said. “They jell well together. I’ve seen people who don’t jell well with the president, and Marco is not one of those people.”

Secretary of State Marco Rubio gets more face time with Trump than most Cabinet members. Kent Nishimura / AFP via Getty Images

Rubio’s influence in the peace talks is largely behind the scenes. Witkoff checks in with him before agreeing to attend negotiating sessions, takes guidance before meetings and briefs him afterward, the administration official said.

Last weekend, the two men spoke by phone multiple times about an escalating conflict involving Iran and Yemen. On Saturday, Witkoff reached Rubio while the secretary of state was at the University of Florida football stadium in Gainesville, watching his son play for the Gators, the official said.

Leaving the Senate last year to work for Trump was a gamble for Rubio. The two faced off in the 2016 Republican presidential primaries, where they one-upped each other in schoolyard taunts. Trump derided the Florida lawmaker as “Little Marco.” Rubio mocked the New York businessman’s hand size.

Time and pragmatic politics have transformed the rivalry into a partnership. The Senate confirmed Rubio by a vote of 99-0, a feat that has impressed even Trump.

“It’s not an easy job to be both the secretary of state and the national security adviser, but Secretary Rubio has managed it beautifully,” Wiles said. “He is an experienced, smart and intuitive adviser to the president and the rest of the team, be it national security or foreign affairs.”

Venezuela and a legacy

Other Cabinet secretaries have flamed out since Trump began his second term. Attorney General Pam Bondi is gone, as are Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, Labor Secretary Lori Chavez-DeRemer and Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard.

Rubio, by contrast, has thrived in a job that aligns with his political and policy interests. One of his main priorities is building American clout in the Western Hemisphere, where he is leaving an imprint.

He helped forge an oil deal with Venezuela this summer that the Trump administration believes will buoy both the U.S. and Venezuelan economies.

Earlier this month, Rubio met with heads of state in Latin America as he sought to combat illegal immigration and drug trafficking.

The son of Cuban émigrés, he is also driving the administration’s effort to transform Cuba and bring an end to the regime in Havana.

If he can nudge Venezuela and Cuba toward democratic governance, that could be an enviable legacy for a secretary of state who is nursing presidential ambitions.

Rubio’s statement to a Colombian radio station earlier this month that he currently has “no plans” to mount another campaign was not a hard-and-fast denial. Even if it was, it might not matter. When Rubio first ran for president, he made clear he was done with the Senate. And he sounded adamant.

“I have only said like 10000 times I will be a private citizen in January,” he wrote on social media in May 2016, two months after he dropped out of the presidential contest. The following month, he did an about-face, ran for re-election and won.

If Vance enters the race and falters in the Republican primaries, Rubio might jump in the contest, the second person close to Rubio said.

Another possibility would be for Rubio to become Vance’s running mate, something he would be inclined to do if asked, this person said. Trump himself has suggested the two men pair up in 2028, and his opinion counts given his grip on the Republican base.

Trump likes to ask people privately who they think should be the GOP nominee.

“Whoever the Republican nominee is in 2028, Donald Trump will decide,” the White House official said. “Of course, the primary process will run. But the president will have such an outsized influence in it, and I think he does wish they would run together.”

After the midterm elections in November, attention will turn to 2028 and the post-Trump era. Rubio won’t have much time to decide his future.

“If he’s serious about running, he would have to say so reasonably soon,” the White House official said. “Once you’re elected, you never really get rid of that bug. Ultimately, if there’s an opportunity and an opening, you’d be almost fighting your instincts not to do it.”

World.title: White House withdraws Trump’s nominee to lead ICE
World.content:
The White House withdrew President Donald Trump’s nominee to lead ICE, former Oklahoma state trooper Lance Schroyer, according to a notice published Thursday.

The White House did not say in the notice why Schroyer’s nomination was withdrawn.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement did not immediately provide a response about the withdrawal, but a spokesperson said a statement from the agency is forthcoming.

Schroyer is a senior adviser to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, and he was the secretary’s top pick to take over as director of ICE after Todd Lyons’ exit from the position in April.

Lance Schroyer. Department of Homeland Security

Mullin was previously a U.S. senator for Oklahoma and knew Schroyer from that time.

Schroyer has decades of experience working in local law enforcement in the state, but not specifically with ICE.

Trump announced Schroyer’s nomination in a Truth Social post in June, saying, “Lance has firsthand experience getting Illegal Aliens OFF our streets and, just like ME and our Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin, he LOVES the men and women of ICE.”

Acting ICE Director David Venturella is expected to remain in his role leading the agency for the time being, according to an ICE spokesperson.

World.title: Most Americans think AI is doing more harm than good in schools
World.content:
Most American adults think artificial intelligence is going to do more harm than good in education, according to this month’s NBC News Decision Desk Poll powered by SurveyMonkey.

And a growing share of U.S. adults believe schools that shun the technology will better help students grow than schools that embrace it.

The survey found that 53% of adults believe AI does more harm than good in K-12 education, compared with 27% who believe it does more good than harm. That’s similar to the 54% who said it does more harm than good in colleges and universities, while 24% said they believed it did more good than harm in higher education.

When it comes to preparing students for the future, 44% of respondents said a school that integrates AI tools into the classroom will better help students than a school that bans using it — down 9 percentage points from June 2025.

On the flip side, 56% of respondents said they believe a school that prohibits using AI will better help prepare students for the future, up 9 points since the June 2025 survey.

Respondents were mixed on what — if any — ways of using AI were acceptable for a student completing a school assignment.

Proofreading and editing was seen as the most acceptable use case among those tested, with 49% of adults saying that was OK. That was followed by 41% who said it is acceptable for students to use AI to help with researching and brainstorming and 38% who believed it is OK to use AI to organize or outline ideas.

About a third of respondents, 31%, said no AI use was acceptable for schoolwork. Just 7% said it was OK for students to have AI do writing and generate content for them.

The subject of AI use in the classroom is raging in school districts and on campuses across the country. Parents and advocates nationwide have raised concerns about AI use, saying it has stunted students’ educational growth, and some school districts have enacted restrictions.

New York City announced this month that the use of AI for students will be restricted until high school, with only limited use cases allowed then.

00:40 Melania Trump says young students 'need to learn' about AI 00:00 00:00

On Tuesday, first lady Melania Trump told NBC News that she believes it is important for students to get hands-on experience with AI, a technology that is likely to shape their futures far beyond the classroom.

“Of course, they need to be vigilant, as well,” she said. “But this is our future, and we need to guide them and teach them what is available. If not, they will stay behind, and we need to be the first, in [the] United States, to lead.”

The NBC News Decision Desk Poll powered by SurveyMonkey surveyed 7,105 adults online from Aug. 20 to Sept. 1 and has a margin of error of plus or minus 3.3 percentage points.

World.title: New wild cat species is identified for first time in 100 years, researchers say
World.content:
Tiger cats — small, wild cats in the Leopardus genus native to South and Central America — face stiff conservation challenges as development and agriculture expand.

The new study says there are five tiger cat species in South America.

“All of them are in habitats that are vanishing fast,” said Tadeu de Oliveira, another co-author of the study and an ecologist at the State University of Maranhão in Brazil.

Leopardus tilcayo might have continued to escape notice if not for Nogales-Ascarrunz’s sharp eyes. She volunteers at a wildlife rehabilitation center near La Paz called the Senda Verde Wildlife Sanctuary.

“I saw this cat. It was really, really small, and I couldn’t believe how small it was,” Nogales-Ascarrunz said. “I thought it was a kitten.”

The tilcayo tiger cat is smaller than a house cat. Fernando Faciole / National Geographic

The cat had been brought in by a man living in a community in the forest near La Paz who had mistaken the cat for a domestic kitten, according to details recorded by the sanctuary. He had fed the animal noodles, rice and eggs, only to realize it was wild and that he could not take care of it. So he brought it to the sanctuary.

Initially, colleagues at the sanctuary thought the animal might be a known tiger cat species from Brazil, but Nogales-Ascarrunz wasn’t convinced.

“If you look at the spots or the tail, they really don’t match,” she said.

Nogales-Ascarrunz did genetic testing, using tissue from the tiger cat and a second animal that also turned up at Senda Verde. The results from those specimens revealed that the two cats were unique and from the same species, which had diverged from other tiger cat lineages about 1.4 million years ago. That’s enough genetic distance to consider it a new species.

Nogales-Ascarrunz said, however, that local communities in Bolivia have been aware of the species’ presence for generations.

“This cat, they call it tilcayo. And when you ask, ‘Does it have some meaning in Quechua or Almyra and other Indigenous languages?’ they say, ‘No, my grandpa told me that’s the tilcayo,’” Nogales-Ascarrunz said. “This is a traditional knowledge that they have in the community. We want to preserve that knowledge and we didn’t want to give it another name.”

Nogales-Ascarrunz is working to install camera traps in the Yungas forest in Bolivia to search for more signs of Leopardus tilcayo. Fernando Faciole / National Geographic

It’s not rare for scientists to add a mammal species to the taxonomy — they do so about 65 times a year, according to a study released last year. But many of those new species — including some recently named wild cats — are the result of a split. That’s when scientists realize what was once considered a single species has sufficient genetic distinctions to become two.

For example, the Sunda clouded leopard found on the island of Borneo — called Neofelis diardi — was first recognized in 2006 when its genome was distinguished from its mainland counterparts. But examples of the Sunda clouded leopard were already in museums at that point.

The tilcayo, on the other hand, was completely novel to scientists.

“We didn’t have specimens in museums,” de Oliveira said. “It had never been collected before.”

Nogales-Ascarrunz said this new species is likely in danger. She views the discovery as yet another argument in favor of conservation.

“It’s a new reason to protect the world,” she said.

World.title: Matthew Lillard ‘ashamed’ he returned to ‘Scream’ after Melissa Barrera fired for Israel-Gaza posts
World.content:
Matthew Lillard expressed regret on Tuesday over his decision to film “Scream 7” after actor Melissa Barrera was fired from the franchise over her social media about the Israel-Gaza war, saying he was “on the wrong side of history.”

Video showed the actor speaking to fans during a Q&A at a 30th anniversary screening for the original “Scream” at a Regal movie theater in Austin, Texas. It’s unclear what the question was, as the video only shows Lillard speaking, but it appears to be related to celebrities taking stances on political topics.

Lillard described it as a “great question” and referred to the ongoing situation with singer Ed Sheeran, who is facing backlash after venues pressured him to drop Macklemore from his tour over his pro-Palestinian remarks.

“I don’t think it’s easy all the time,” he said, before referring to Barrera.

Barrera starred in “Scream 6” and was expected to return for the seventh installment of the hit horror franchise, but was fired in 2023. Spyglass Media Group, the production company behind the film, confirmed it had dropped Barrera after she shared Instagram posts condemning Israel.

Melissa Barrera in "Scream VI." Philippe Bossé / Paramount Pictures

According to a Variety report, Barrera’s post included references to Israel as a “colonized” land and reshared posts that accused Israel of “genocide and ethnic cleansing.” Another post said that “Western media only shows the (Israeli) side.”

“Why do they do that, I will let you deduce for yourself,” the post reportedly said.

Spyglass Media Group told Variety in a statement that it has zero tolerance for “antisemitism or the incitement of hate in any form.” Barrera initially declined to comment, but later told the Associated Press that she was “grateful” for everything that had happened and felt it was an “awakening.”

“Melissa Barrera, who’s a beautiful actor, was fired for what she said after the whole Palestinian— what started happening in Israel,” Lillard said. “It’s really f---ing bulls--- and really hard and she’s on the right side of history.”

“But the whole world should have popped up and said, ‘She’s right.’ And they didn’t. And that’s brutal,” he said.

The “Scream” actor’s remarks come days after rapper Macklemore was dropped from Sheeran’s tour over a speech and performance centered on his pro-Palestinian views.

Macklemore, whose real name is Ben Haggerty, said Monday that venues threatened to cancel Sheeran’s shows in response to the rapper saying “Free Palestine” on stage. Among those involved was New England Patriots and Gillette Stadium owner Robert Kraft, who Macklemore accused of organizing a boycott against the rapper.

While talking about the consequences Barrerra suffered, Lillard said, “And when they start coming after your job, sometimes things are worth it.”

He noted that he “got called out” for returning to the “Scream” franchise in the same film Barrera was set to star in. Lillard described himself as being on “the wrong side of history” for that choice.

“I feel bad about that, I feel ashamed about that,” Lillard said. “Because in that moment I was so excited to go back that I didn’t really think about Melissa and that journey and didn’t say no. And I’m embarrassed, and that’s the truth.”

“I still like being in the movie, but it may not have been the best idea,” he said.
