World.title: D.C. airspace is complicated. Experts say Trump's arch would add one more risk
World.content:
D.C. airspace is complicated. Experts say Trump's arch would add one more risk

toggle caption Al Drago for The Washington Post via Getty Images

The Trump administration is eager to press ahead with its proposed 250-foot arch at Memorial Circle, a traffic island on the historic bridge connecting Washington, D.C. to Arlington, Va.

The grassy roundabout is not far from Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport (DCA): An arch would stand just about two aeronautical miles from the airport's main runway, which is one of the busiest in the country.

"An enormous number of airplanes come over that site, basically every 45 to 60 seconds all day long 'til 11 at night," U.S. Rep. Don Beyer, a Democrat who represents that part of Virginia, told NPR. "Just imagine the disaster that could happen with all of these airplanes coming right across a 250-foot-high arch."

Sponsor Message

Loading...

The Trump administration maintains the arch would not pose an additional risk.

A preliminary Federal Aviation Administration report said in June that the structure would likely not be an issue as long as it has blinking red obstruction lights on top, as the 555-foot-tall Washington Monument does. But it is still in the process of conducting a more comprehensive study, which could lead it to label the arch "a hazard."

An FAA spokesperson told NPR over email in early September that "the standard obstruction evaluation process is under way," both for the arch and cranes that would be used for construction, which the administration has said could be up to 320 feet tall.

Neither the FAA nor the White House shared a timeline or further details about those reviews.

But NPR spoke to three aviation safety experts about the impacts of a potential arch. Their consensus: While the arch itself most likely would not pose a significant risk to most aircraft, it adds yet another variable to a notoriously crowded and complicated airspace.

"It's a small airport with one runway, nestled in a metropolitan area that's surrounded by prohibited airspace [near the White House and U.S. Capitol]," said Jeff Guzzetti, a retired accident investigator with the National Transportation Safety Board and the Federal Aviation Administration.

Sponsor Message

The congestion — and complexity — of D.C.'s airspace is a well-documented concern, especially after the January 2025 midair collision between an American Airlines regional jet and an Army Black Hawk helicopter that killed 67 people. Even so, some experts worry the FAA may be facing political pressure from Trump to rubber-stamp the project.

"The best, and the most basic option, is simply not to build it," Guzzetti said of the arch.

Shawn Pruchnicki, a former airline pilot and accident investigator who now teaches aviation safety at Ohio State University, went even further. He said putting a 250-foot arch in Memorial Circle would be "inherently dangerous."

"This is an unbelievably ridiculous idea, to put this arch so close to this airport just for the sake of his personal needs," Pruchnicki added, referring to Trump.

The president originally said the arch was for himself, though he has since characterized it as a tribute to the country's 250th anniversary. The White House has repeatedly said in statements that it will be "one of the most iconic landmarks not only in Washington, D.C., but throughout the world," and did not respond to NPR's questions about experts' concerns.

Critics of the arch, of which there are many, have a wide range of objections, from its impact on Arlington National Cemetery and disruption of nearby historic sites to questions about its scale, purpose and financial cost.

Beyer, the Virginia congressman, said he has yet to meet a constituent from his district — on either side of the aisle — who wants to see it built.

"The imminent concern, beyond his narcissism … is what it will do to transportation," he said, referring to planes as well as cars.

The Trump administration said earlier this month it would soon begin preliminary excavation work at Memorial Circle, even though questions — about aviation safety and much more — remain unanswered.

Sponsor Message

The arch has not yet been approved by a key federal planning commission. Historic preservation experts say the review process has been rushed. And an ongoing lawsuit asserts that the structure can't be built without Congressional authorization, which Trump denies and has not sought. The White House told NPR it continues "seeking final approval from all applicable entities."

toggle caption Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP

What makes D.C. airspace so complicated

Guzzetti said D.C.'s airport, which opened in 1941, was "never meant … to have this amount of traffic."

Because DCA is owned by the federal government, Congress regulates the number of flights — and lawmakers have historically wanted to facilitate travel to and from their home districts. The airport was designed to accommodate about 15 million passengers a year, but now serves closer to 25 million.

Tom Lintner, who spent 30 years working in aviation safety at the FAA — including as an air traffic controller at New York's LaGuardia Airport — said higher traffic density means a smaller margin of error for air traffic controllers.

"As the traffic gets denser and denser, you may find controllers having to make transmissions every five, six, seven seconds," he said. "There reaches a point where there aren't enough seconds left to make the right decision."

The January 2025 midair collision shed light on a pattern of close calls at DCA, resulting in a slew of rule changes and restrictions on helicopters. But some say those measures are not enough.

Just last week, two Democratic senators from Virginia introduced a bill that would cap hourly arrivals and gradually reduce flights over a four-year window starting in 2028. They cited an "overburdened runway" and "unsustainable traffic levels."

"Since the collision, there have been numerous near misses in DCA airspace," Sen. Mark Warner, a co-sponsor of the bill, said in a statement.

Most recently, in early August, a military helicopter carrying President Trump briefly flew too close to a passenger jet leaving DCA. Federal investigators later found that ongoing construction of the White House ballroom contributed to radio problems that prevented air traffic controllers from hearing a warning of the president's takeoff.

Guzzetti says the August incident exemplifies the unique challenges and variables of D.C.'s airspace — even without a 250-foot arch along the primary flight path.

"This is just adding another hazard," Guzzetti said. "Granted, it might not be significant, but still, it's yet another … opportunity for exposure to something bad happening."

Sponsor Message

How close would planes get?

Guzzetti, like the other experts NPR interviewed, is most concerned about the challenge the arch could pose to planes that are landing, not taking off.

He says the approach to Runway 19 — known as the "River Visual" — is already difficult: Pilots must follow the Potomac River and then make a sharp turn (as abrupt as 40 degrees) at low altitude (less than 500 feet) to avoid prohibited airspace.

"Let's say you pass the area where the arch is going to be. You're probably 60 seconds from touching down on landing," Guzzetti explained. "And then … you've got to make a pretty steep turn to the final approach to get lined up for the runway."

Because of that difficulty, experts said, some airlines require special training to land at DCA or have even designated it as "captain-only," meaning only the more senior officer can do it. They stressed that pilots have to be vigilant and must be able to physically see the river in order to land — which means they would also have eyes on the arch.

"That arch is going to be just a few hundred yards, maybe two or three football fields to the right of where your flight path is," Guzzetti said. "So it's going to look imposing. It's going to be dramatic. But a pilot is not going to mistake that or get too close to it."

The greater risk, experts agree, is in the unknowns.

Lintner is most concerned about helicopters, since they fly lower than planes. He said helicopters operate below 500 feet in some areas, and as low as 200 feet in others — lower than the arch.

Lintner did what he calls "back of the envelope" math, which he outlined in a Substack post in August. Altitude-wise, he said the arch is unlikely to present a problem for airlines. But he said it could further complicate the airspace for helicopters, which he called "the last thing this area needs."

Sponsor Message

Pruchnicki, of Ohio State, says the Runway 19 approach — which he flew many times as a pilot — is even trickier when it's dark or windy out. He worries that a plane inadvertently flying lower than it's supposed to be, facing strong easterly winds, "could easily get blown into" an arch.

"If everything is working perfectly, I don't see that it would be a significant problem," he added. "However, we all know, at all airports, things go wrong all the time."

Pruchnicki said complications arise all the time in the tricky airspace near DCA, and questioned why the administration would want to build something that could "potentially put passengers' lives at risk" in those moments.

"Why would the White House and the secretary of transportation ever think that is a good idea?" he added. "Who is more important here? The public, perhaps?"

toggle caption Finn Gomez/Getty Images

'Nobody's watching the watchers'

The FAA's ongoing aeronautical study is supposed to determine whether the arch would have an adverse effect on the national airspace.

But some aviation experts — and one Democratic lawmaker — worry the agency might be under pressure to greenlight the administration's own project. (The FAA did not respond to NPR's questions about this.)

Part of that is the way the system is set up, Lintner says: The FAA is responsible for operating the U.S. air traffic control system and, at the same time, regulating aviation safety. Critics say this dynamic is unique compared to other countries and ripe for conflict of interest.

"Nobody's watching the watchers," Lintner said. "In other words, anybody who says, 'Wait a minute, how do we know that's safe?' The answer is, 'Well, the FAA decided it's safe.' But did they? What's the checks and balances?"

Under federal regulations, the FAA must be notified before construction of any proposed structure — building, cell tower, crane — that would stand either over 200 feet tall or within a certain slope of airport runways. The agency conducts what is known as an aeronautical study, to determine whether the object would constitute a hazard.

Sponsor Message

"They'll actually put out a memorandum to indicate: 'Yes, this is a hazard and it needs these types of lights' … or 'It's no hazard, you can go ahead and build it,'" Guzzetti said.

At that point, the entity behind the proposed construction — in the case of the 250-foot arch, the National Parks Service — has 60 days to either agree to those conditions, terminate the study or request further study.

"Further study includes opportunities to negotiate or propose mitigations, and the FAA may request public comment," an informational FAA video explains.

An FAA spokesperson confirmed to NPR that the public comment period for the arch ended on Sept. 3. The rest of the timeline is unclear: Pruchnicki says he's generally seen this process take anywhere from several months to nearly a year.

Depending on its findings, the FAA could ultimately issue a "determination of hazard." But since the agency doesn't have land-use authority, its conclusion is not legally binding.

"The president can simply instruct his [transportation secretary] to write a waiver for that, to ignore that," Guzzetti said. "I can see that happening with this president."

He's not alone. Sen. Tammy Duckworth, D-Ill., wrote a public letter to the FAA in June, urging the agency to "be firm in rejecting any improper or irresponsible pressure from President Trump to prioritize the construction of his gaudy, vanity arch over the safety of the American people."

Duckworth told NPR in a statement that "building another golden vanity project ... would needlessly add a safety risk in one of the most complex airspaces in the country."

The White House did not respond to NPR's questions about perceived political pressure.

Either way, Guzzetti said, the FAA would ideally make sure certain steps are taken, such as adding red lights to the arch, clearly labeling the structure on aeronautical charts and monitoring any complaints from pilots and the public about planes getting too close.

Sponsor Message

"We all know that aviation involves risks any time you defy gravity," Guzzetti said. "But it's managing that risk which is the trick."

Few bodies have approval power over the arch. The National Capital Planning Commission, which has granted some preliminary green lights, is poised to consider it for final approval in the coming months.

World.title: Carney says Europe, Canada aren't 'fair-weather allies' while rebuking Trump's tactics
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Prime Minister Mark Carney pushed back against U.S. President Donald Trump's recent comments that Canada seeking a deeper relationship with the European Union was "laughable."

Carney told reporters during a news conference on Thursday that a partnership with the EU would make Canada "a better partner" to the U.S., but he insisted that the relationship with the U.S. must respect Canadian independence.

"We are looking for partnerships that are complementary, that reinforce our sovereignty," he said when asked about Trump's comments.

"Canadians are united that nobody is going to tell us what language we speak, no one is going to dictate our culture or with whom we can strike agreements internationally."

Carney, who has been trying to forge closer ties with Europe amid Canada's ongoing trade war with the United States, made the remarks after delivering an address to the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France, on Thursday morning.

WATCH | Canada-EU alliance not about being a great-power rival 'with better manners,' PM says: Canada-EU alliance not about being a great-power rival 'with better manners,' Carney says | Duration 1:46 Prime Minister Mark Carney, in an address to the European Parliament, says an alliance between Canada and the European Union would strengthen sovereignty while 'safeguarding our abilities to live our lives as we choose.'

The prime minister didn't mention Donald Trump by name, but nodded to the U.S. president's tactics in his speech. Carney echoed his Davos speech from earlier this year, saying economic integration has been used as leverage and suggesting that Europe can be a more reliable ally.

"We are not fair-weather allies. We do not pursue zero-sum deals," Carney said. "We hold common values, for which we have always fought, and in whose defence we must always remain vigilant."

When the U.S. president was asked about Canada and the EU seeking to strengthen their partnership on Wednesday, Trump called the idea "laughable" and threatened the EU with "very serious tariffs" if it makes a trade deal with Canada "with bad intentions."

As Carney stepped up to deliver his address, someone began a "U.S.A." chant. Others in the room booed in response.

WATCH | Trump says closer Canada-EU co-operation is 'laughable': Trump says closer Canada-EU co-operation is 'laughable' | Duration closed caption 0:25 U.S. President Donald Trump threatened the European Union with 'very serious tariffs' or to 'stop trading' if it makes a trade deal with Canada 'with bad intentions.'

Carney called for an "alliance of the future" between Canada and the 27 countries that make up the European Union.

"Together, Canada and the European Union can anchor our ground to hold our values while forming a protective canopy under which our citizens can thrive," he said.

"This is about sovereignty. Our ability to live as we wish. It is about the freedoms we must fight for every day. Sovereignty requires resilience — the ability to withstand shocks."

Carney offered a rebuke of Trump and other hegemonic powers in his address, suggesting that an alliance between Canada and the EU will be a "beacon for other democracies."

"I want to be precise about what I am not proposing. I am not proposing a third bloc in order to become a great-power rival, only with better manners," he said.

"We do not seek power to dominate others. On the contrary, we are pursuing resilience so that no one can control our open markets, impair our sovereignty, threaten our territorial integrity or undermine our freedoms, our democracies, our rule of law."

Over the last year, Canada has signed several new partnership agreements with the EU. It was also the first non-European country to become a member of Security Action for Europe (SAFE), which provides €150 billion in loans for defence spending.

WATCH | EU chief talks about Canada in her state of the European Union address: 'We see the world with the same eyes,' EU chief says of Canada | Duration closed caption 2:57 European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, after highlighting the shifting international order in her state of the European Union address, spoke of the potential of the Canada-Europe relationship. 'This is not a partnership against anyone else, but for our common strength.'

'People-to-people ties'

During his address, Carney proposed that Canada join Erasmus+, the EU's program ⁠supporting education, training, youth and sport. The prime minister also said Canada could expand its participation in the next generation of Horizon Europe, the EU's program that puts funding into various research and innovation projects. The program's budget for 2021-2027 is worth about $150 billion.

"We should deepen our people-to-people ties, allowing our youth to live, work and study where they want on either side of the Atlantic," he said.

Carney's speech comes after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in her state of the European Union address on Wednesday that the door is open for Canada to become an "associate member" of the bloc.

"I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada to be the first associate member of the EU," von der Leyen said, drawing a standing ovation.

What questions do you have about the proposed partnership between Canada and the EU? Send them to ask@cbc.ca.

Carney then nodded, rose from his seat, approached von der Leyen and embraced her. He briefly waved to the chamber before returning to his seat.

The EU chief said the two must "urgently reimagine" their partnership, and move beyond just a free trade agreement.

Carney said he "welcomes the ambition" of that proposal, but he has preferred to use a different term, calling it an "alliance for the future."

"Canada and Europe should secure our strategic autonomy through deep co-operation in the full range of strategic capabilities," he said.

WATCH | Ottawa will debate, vote on 'final structure' of Canada-EU alliance, Carney says: Ottawa will debate, vote on 'final structure' of Canada-EU alliance, Carney says | Duration 1:04 Prime Minister Mark Carney says Parliament will debate and vote on the structure of an alliance with the European Union, saying this is an opportunity to make Canada stronger, 'more sovereign' and more sustainable.

Substance matters more than the label: Carney

Carney and his team have been downplaying the idea of using "associate member" to describe a new partnership since it was first floated in a story in the Wall Street Journal last week that cited unidentified sources.

When asked Thursday about the idea of Canada being an "associate member," Carney said the "substance" of the agreement is more important than the label.

The prime minister said that Canada isn't looking to be a full member of the EU and that the final agreement of the alliance would be debated and voted on in Canada's Parliament.

Jonathan Wilkinson, Canada's incoming EU ambassador, reiterated that Canada isn't looking to be a full member of the EU on Wednesday following von der Leyen's speech.

WATCH | Ambassador focused on 'results' in deepened EU alliance: Canadian ambassador focused on 'results' after EU chief opens door to associate membership | Duration closed caption 1:33 Jonathan Wilkinson, Canada's incoming ambassador to the European Union, says 'we're not there' after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen offered to open the door to associate membership. 'What we're focused on is actually driving results,' he said, adding the government will 'eventually' turn to how to describe the relationship.

"There are a bunch of different things people have used to describe what this [new relationship] could be. I think we've actually got to get to the point where we actually know what we're describing," Wilkinson told reporters following von der Leyen's address.

"It's nomenclature; I mean, at the end of the day, there's lots of different ways you could describe it."

Carney had a meeting with von der Leyen on Wednesday and the two discussed sectors where both leaders feel they can deepen ties, according to a readout from the Prime Minister's Office. Those sectors include critical minerals, AI, defence, energy and finance.

World.title: Judge orders Kennedy Center to give 30-day notice before any major changes — including demolition
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A U.S. federal judge on Thursday ordered the Kennedy Center to provide 30-day notice before making any major physical changes to the building, including demolishing it as President Donald Trump has threatened to do.

U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper said his ruling would "avoid any confusion on that score given more recent events," including the sudden closure of the building to the public on Wednesday.

Matt Floca, the Kennedy Center's executive director and chief operating officer, said he closed the iconic performing arts centre temporarily due to "acute risks to public safety resulting from continued structural deterioration" of the aging building.

The building will be closed for at least seven days to "assess existing safety risks in those portions of the main building exhibiting severe structural deterioration," Floca said.

The temporary closure, which occurred without notice Wednesday, is separate from a vote Tuesday by the Kennedy Center's board to close the performing arts centre indefinitely for repairs, Floca and other officials said. The closure was based on an inspection of the roof terrace canopy and a partial ceiling collapse earlier this month, Floca said. The closure may be extended after evaluation next week, he said.

The announcement of the closure came in response to a court case filed by a Democratic congresswoman who is a trustee and sought an emergency court hearing to prevent what she called the building's "unlawful closing."

Rep. Joyce Beatty, an Ohio Democrat and an ex-officio member of the Kennedy Center board, has led efforts to block Trump's name from being added to the building. Beatty had a verbal confrontation with the Republican president Tuesday during a virtual board meeting.

WATCH | Suddenly shut down: Kennedy Center board votes to close after failed efforts to add Trump name | Hanomansing Tonight | Duration closed caption 3:50 The Trump-aligned Kennedy Center board voted to close most of the performing arts venue just hours after a federal judge blocked the institution from returning President Donald Trump's name to the building.

Beatty's lawyers said in a court filing Thursday that the board members' "rationale that they are only temporarily closing the Kennedy Center is a plain pretext to justify shutting down the Center permanently. The facts before the Court are deeply concerning."

Cooper denied a request by Beatty's legal team to hold a hearing to clarify the board's actions and intent. But he agreed to their request "to make crystal clear" that his order prohibits demolition of the building.

The Trump-aligned board, chaired by the president, voted to close the centre after a federal judge blocked the institution from returning Trump's name to the building.

Trump, who was named the Kennedy Center's chairman last year by loyalists on the board, said Wednesday that his efforts to restore the aging building deserve recognition, "because frankly, if we don't do that, it's going to close. It'll end up being ripped down. It's in very, very bad shape, very dangerous shape."

Barbra Streisand arrives for the Kennedy Center Honors in Washington on Dec. 7, 2008. (Jacquelyn Martin/The Associated Press)

Congress has allocated $257 million US to cover the repairs, but Trump said they only would happen if the board was permitted to move forward with plans to add his name to the building.

Barbra Streisand, a Kennedy Center honoree in 2008, on Thursday questioned the closing of the centre for repairs and called the controversy surrounding its operation "galling and painful to witness."

The Kennedy Center board voted in August to inscribe Trump's name on the Kennedy Center's facade so it would read "The John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts Restored and Renovated By President Donald J. Trump." If the Trump Kennedy Center Fund reached $100 million US, another inscription would be added reading "Endowed by the Trump Kennedy Center Fund."

The plaza in front of the Kennedy Center would also have been renamed in Trump's honour.

All of those proposals were shot down Tuesday by Cooper, who ruled that nothing could happen "without Congress's blessing."

Cooper ruled in May that the Kennedy Center illegally added Trump's name to the building, ordering it removed. The institution's leaders complied in June but left a tarp and scaffolding in place where Trump's name was once displayed.

World.title: Judge denies Tamara Lich's request to travel under house arrest
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A judge has denied Tamara Lich's request to travel internationally while she serves a house arrest sentence, including going on a Caribbean cruise and to the White House.

Lich was found guilty in April 2025 of mischief and other offences for her role in organizing and sustaining the 2022 convoy protest that paralyzed downtown Ottawa for nearly a month.

She was handed a conditional sentence last October that included 12 months under house arrest.

A month after being sentenced, Lich asked for and received permission to leave her home in Medicine Hat, Alta., to attend her grandchildren's school. Since then, she has travelled to other provinces for her job with Rebel News.

In July, Lich asked for permission to travel internationally.

Lich appeared virtually in court from the passenger seat of a vehicle on Thursday, wearing a Rebel News hoodie as the ruling was read.

"The fact that an activity can be described as work does not compel permission to leave the jurisdiction," said Justice Heather Perkins-McVey, spending around 45 minutes sharing her reasons for the decision.

Lich was also told there must be "legitimate circumstances" for temporary travel outside of Alberta. Perkins-McVey instructed Lich to make individual requests to do so.

Against principle of sentence

In her initial request to travel abroad, Lich didn't offer the court a detailed itinerary, but her request mention ed attending press events at the White House, going on a seven-day Caribbean cruise with Rebel News, and travelling to Arizona to speak with Rob Schneider, a right-wing comedian whose controversial content prompted his removal from a Saskatchewan stage in 2024.

Crown prosecutors said the additional exemptions would give her a "blank cheque" to travel internationally. They opposed the request, arguing that granting it was unnecessary and would diminish the impact of her sentence "to an unacceptable extent."

Her defence said in July she had " abided by the terms of her conditional sentence to the letter."

In Perkins-McVey's ruling Thursday, she said there was not enough evidence to show Lich's request is needed, including to maintain employment, and it would go against the principle of her sentence.

The judge characterized the Rebel-sponsored Caribbean cruise as a "commercial event" and "fundraiser." She said the Arizona trip was "promotional" and much of the proposed international work could be completed from Canada.

Speaking after court, Lich's lawyer Lawrence Greenspon said the judge's decision was "very considered"

"There's nothing in what the judge said today, or in the sentence itself, that prevents (Lich) in any way from speaking freely, and associating freely and working to the extent that she can by the conditions that were imposed."

Other legal matters

Fellow 2022 convoy leader Chris Barber, who was convicted and sentenced alongside Lich, travels south of the border through his work as a commercial truck driver.

Sentenced Oct. 7, 2025, the two have already served the bulk of their sentences; but they are far from being done with Ontario courtrooms.

Crown prosecutors are appealing the judge's findings and sentencing, arguing both should have been found guilty of more crimes than they were as well as given harsher sentences. Barber and Lich have accepted their sentences, but are appealing the judge's initial decision.

The Ontario Court of Appeal isn't likely to hear those arguements until early 2027.

Lich and Barber are also involved in civil court matters.

World.title: NASA satellite discovers a new crater on the moon that formed just 2 years ago
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Scientists have discovered a crater on the moon that's bigger than the Roman Colosseum and is the result of a powerful impact two years ago that initially went undetected.

The steep-sided hole — 222 metres across and up to 43 metres deep — is the solar system's biggest known impact crater carved out in recent times.

Such a large-scale event is estimated to occur only once every 132 years, researchers said, making this a treasure trove of information as NASA prepares to build a base for astronauts on the moon.

"This event constitutes a statistically rare, effectively once-in-a-lifetime observation," the scientists wrote in one of two studies appearing on the subject Wednesday in the journal Science Advances.

NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) spotted the crater on the moon's near side in May 2024 soon after it was formed by an incoming fragment of an asteroid or comet. The moon strike escaped real-time detection by telescopes on Earth and in space.

A zoomed-in view of McGetchin Crater, circled on the left, next to a 'before' image on the right. (NASA Goddard/Intuitive Machines/Robert Wagner)

LRO's wide-angle images were not identified in the crush of data until August 2025. The spacecraft gathered more detailed pictures last fall, followed by confirmation of the discovery early this year.

The crater is named for the late Thomas McGetchin, a former director of Houston's Lunar and Planetary Institute.

Like gardening

Pockmarked since ancient times, the moon bears some of the solar system's largest impact craters, including one that stretches more than 2,400 kilometres across.

This latest impact churned the lunar surface for more than 100 kilometres. Dust and rocky soil were hurled away at a higher angle than expected, according to Mark Robinson, chief scientist for the LRO's cameras who works at Intuitive Machines. Robinson was the lead author for one of the studies.

A separate study identified a seven-kilometre-wide cold spot around the new crater, consistent with a loosening of the moon's topsoil. Co-author David Paige of the University of California, Los Angeles, likens it to gardening.

"We're now thinking of impacts as a way to garden the regolith — churning the sediments and putting stuff above that's usually below the surface," Paige said in a statement. (Regolith is the term for the loose, solid material on top of bedrock.)

An overhead, close-up view of McGetchin Crater that was taken on Dec. 5, 2025, by NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter. (NASA Goddard/Intuitive Machines/Robert Wagner)

The LRO's numerous crater discoveries since its launch in 2009 show that the moon's top two centimetres of soil is being overturned by ejected material every 80,000 years, faster than previously thought, according to Robinson.

Contrary to the popular belief that the Apollo moonwalkers' dusty lunar footprints will last forever, they will "definitely be long gone in that time frame," Robinson said in an email.

The next step is to calculate the risk of ejected crater material striking NASA's planned moon base, he added.

"That information will help engineers harden structures so one won't have to worry about damage, or maybe worry less."

World.title: Toronto cop charged in Project South allegedly didn't care if selling information harmed people
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Unsealed Project South court documents reveal new details on the police corruption probe, including allegations one officer knew confidential information he sold could help facilitate ‘serious violence’ but didn’t care.

Toronto police Const. Timothy Barnhardt knew the information he sold to a civilian from police database searches could help facilitate "serious violence and explicitly stated that he did not care if individuals were harmed," according to an Information to Obtain (ITO) application supporting more than 50 warrants in the Project South investigation.

The sweeping corruption probe began in June 2025, when York Regional Police thwarted an alleged plot to kill a senior corrections official from Toronto South Detention Centre (TSDC).

Investigators subsequently discovered Barnhardt allegedly ran an unauthorized search on the official's licence plate less than a month before the attempted hit, and he is accused of then sharing confidential information about that official with civilian Brian Da Costa. The identity of the senior corrections official is covered by a publication ban for their safety.

Both Barnhardt and Da Costa are in custody facing several charges in the probe, which have not been tested in court. Their lawyers declined to comment for this story.

The unauthorized query on the jail official was one of 17 times Barnhardt allegedly accessed the Ministry of Transportation server to do searches while off-duty in the first six months of last year, according to the ITO. Police-intercepted communications revealed to investigators that Barnhardt "routinely sold confidential database information to known criminal associate Da Costa, often at Da Costa's direction."

A publication ban was lifted on those revelations, and many others, from the Project South ITO on Wednesday in a ruling from Ontario Superior Court Justice Laura Bird.

Brian Da Costa is one of four civilians charged in Project South who investigators connected to Toronto South Detention Centre inmate Gurpreet Singh, according to the ITO. (Pam Davies/CBC)

Other new details include why investigators believed TSDC inmate Gurpreet Singh ordered the hit on the senior jail official, along with his alleged connections to a corrections officer and four men charged in Project South, including Da Costa.

Neither Singh nor the corrections officer have been charged in this investigation.

CBC News was part of a group of media organizations fighting to lift a publication ban on the ITO in court. Bird previously lifted the ban on some details earlier this summer. In her decision this week, Bird lifted the ban on the majority of the rest of the court record.

"Permitting the media to publish the vast majority of the ITO while maintaining a temporary publication ban over limited portions of it strikes an appropriate balance between the court openness principle and the fair trial rights of the criminal defendants," wrote Bird.

An ITO is a legal document from a police officer laying out the evidence they have of a criminal offence in order to request judicial authorization for a warrant or production order from a judge or justice of the peace. The allegations in the ITO have not been tested in court.

The search warrants were executed as investigators arrested and charged seven Toronto police officers, one retired cop and 19 civilians in Project South. The charge against one of those civilians has since been stayed, and one of the officers retired and pleaded guilty to two charges in July.

The charges against the others accused in Project South have not yet been tested in court.

Police believed Singh behind attempted hit: ITO

Elsewhere in the ITO, police say Singh had motive to harm the senior corrections official who was targeted, and that he was named by that official as one of a handful of inmates who'd expressed hostility toward them. The official told police that Singh and his former cellmate were angry after the official seized cellphones and steroids from their cell and then separated the pair.

CBC News previously reported that Singh and correctional officer Nishwant Dosanjh were investigated for potential involvement in the alleged conspiracy.

TSDC inmate Gurpreet Singh had motive to harm the senior corrections official who was targeted and was named by that official as one of a handful of inmates who’d expressed hostility toward them, according to the ITO. (U.S. Attorney's Office, Central District of California)

The ITO also states Dosanjh was Singh's former romantic partner and she allegedly took the photo of the senior corrections official's licence plate in the employee area of the jail. The photo was allegedly later provided to Da Costa and then shared with Barnhardt, who's accused of using the image to search a police database on May 27, 2025.

The results of that query were allegedly provided to Da Costa, then shared with a gun-for-hire group accused of conspiring to kill the senior corrections official the following month.

The allegations in the ITO concerning Dosanjh and Singh have not led to charges, nor have they been tested in court.

Nishwant Dosanjh's lawyers provided this photo of their client and told CBC News in a statement that Dosanjh has co-operated with police, maintains her innocence and had no part in the attempt on the senior corrections official's life. (Submitted by Kim Schofield and Miranda Brar)

In a statement, Dosanjh’s lawyer, Kim Schofield, told CBC News her client has co-operated with police, maintains her innocence and had no part in the attempt on the senior corrections official's life.

Schofield says she hired an independent digital forensics expert to review the "data dump" she received of Dosanjh's seized cell phone. The lawyer says the expert found no photos or chat discussions relating to the attempted hit.

"There is absolutely nothing to connect her to that incident," wrote Schofield.

Singh has been held at TSDC since his October 2024 arrest amid allegations he acted as an accomplice in a drug-smuggling organization led by accused cocaine kingpin Ryan Wedding. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)

CBC News contacted Singh's lawyer for comment, but did not receive a response before publication. In an emailed statement in June, Singh's lawyer, Brian Greenspan, said his client had not been charged with any offence in Canada, months after the execution of the February warrants.

Singh has been held at the Toronto jail since his October 2024 arrest amid allegations he acted as an accomplice in a drug-smuggling organization allegedly involving killings and led by accused cocaine kingpin Ryan Wedding.

Singh is fighting extradition to California.

Inmate connected to 4 men charged in Project South: ITO

Investigators also connected Singh with others charged in Project South. According to the ITO, Singh was associated with four of the civilians charged in the corruption probe, including Elwyn Satanowsky, Da Costa and Dequon Lemonious.

Satanowsky is accused of arranging several shootings connected with the probe. He deposited money into Singh's inmate trust account and he spoke to Singh on the phone more than 300 times between the beginning of January and mid-September 2025, according to the ITO.

Elwyn Satanowsky is charged with arranging this September 2025 shooting at a house in Vaughan, Ont., as part of the Project South investigation. (York Regional Police)

Police intercepted communications between Da Costa and Singh through TSDC's inmate telephone system.

Lemonious is charged with conspiracy to murder the senior corrections official. The ITO identifies him as someone "who plans and structures violent criminal activity" within a gunmen-for-hire group.

In an intercepted phone call, Keajean Doman, an alleged enforcer in the group also charged in the conspiracy, blames Lemonious for "plays" that resulted in his incarceration. Doman was arrested last September after allegedly carrying out a shooting related to Project South in Vaughan, Ont.

Other intercepts connect Singh and Lemonious by way of them both speaking to, or about, a former cellmate of Singh's who's in custody on a different range at TSDC, according to the ITO.

CBC News contacted lawyers for Satanowsky and Lemonious for this story but neither provided a comment before publication.

World.title: Australian athlete apologizes for racing with diarrhea, forfeits the Beijing competition she won
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Hyrox athlete who started a global uproar after soiling herself and leaking feces at the popular indoor fitness competition has apologized for continuing to race, and forfeited her win.

"I want to offer my sincere apology to the people of China, my fellow competitors, the spectators and the Hyrox organizers for what happened during the race in Beijing," Australian Joanna Wietrzyk wrote in a statement posted to Instagram Thursday morning.

"Looking back, I regret the decision to not have stepped off the track. I recognize that I should have made a different choice."

Wietrzyk explained she felt " completely fit and healthy at the start of the race, with no reason to expect any illness." She added that, "on reflection," she decided to retroactively forfeit her win and the points she earned.

"I know my actions had an impact beyond myself, and I am genuinely sorry to everyone who was affected."

The graphic images of world record holder Wietrzyk competing with feces running down her legs at Saturday's Hyrox in Beijing have sparked debate about the health and safety of competitors versus the mentality that a win is a win, no matter the cost.

Footage showed Wietrzyk continue to push through her events using communal equipment such as ropes, sandbags, rowing machines and medicine balls, and doing burpees and lunges on a shared indoor track. She was the pro women's champion with a time of 1:01:23, beating the U.S.'s Alyssa McElheny by about 45 seconds.

"Go hard or go home … a win is a win," Wietrzyk posted — then later deleted — on Instagram after the event along with a selfie in what appeared to be a hospital bed, according to multiple news outlets.

McElheny has not yet made a public comment about the competition. CBC News has reached out to her press team.

Meanwhile, multiple media outlets report that Wietrzyk's major sponsor, Puma, is distancing itself from the athlete by quietly removing "Joanna Wietrzyk x PUMA" clothing items from its website.

But a spokesperson for Puma says there's "no change" to their partnership with Wietrzyk, telling CBC News in a statement Thursday that some landing pages were "unintentionally taken offline."

On social media, people have flooded the brand's comments with plays on "Puma," such as "Pooma," "Poopma" and "Poo Ma Pants."

Hyrox refunding affected participants

As the incident went viral, online commenters were quick to point out the health risks for other competitors, with many people saying Wietrzyk should have quit or Hyrox should have disqualified her. Others are calling on Hyrox to refund the other competitors or offer them compensation.

On Wednesday, Hyrox China announced it was refunding the entry costs to more than 1,000 participants affected by the incident, according to the South China Morning Post. A spectator at the event told the outlet that feces was visible on the track about 30 minutes after Wietrzyk started her race, causing several runners to slip.

Other athletes who competed in the same race described having to use equipment smeared with feces.

On Monday, Hyrox co-founder Moritz Fürste wrote in an Instagram statement that the organization has since changed its rules to prevent similar situations from happening again.

Its official rulebook already lists penalties for other bodily fluids, noting that spitting or clearing of nostrils onto the floor is strictly prohibited. Until this week, there was no mention of penalties for feces contaminating the race course.

"I am learning from this experience and will carry those lessons with me, including remembering that there is more to life than racing and knowing when it is right to step away," Wietrzyk wrote in her apology.

She added that she will be taking some time to "recover, reflect and look after myself and my family away from the noise."

World.title: Calgary man handed 12-year prison sentence for sexually assaulting 3 vulnerable women
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A Calgary man who targeted and sexually assaulted several vulnerable women who worked in Calgary’s sex trade has been sentenced to 12 years in prison.

Mantha, 62, was convicted of six offences in April: sexually assaulting three women — one of whom he drugged, and another he suffocated and assaulted with a weapon — as well as uttering threats against a fourth woman.

On Thursday, Justice Judith Shriar imposed the lengthy prison term following sentencing arguments last month where prosecutor Dominique Mathurin argued for a 10 to 13 year term while defence lawyer Justin Dean asked the judge to consider a five to seven year sentence.

“The road to today has been long,” said Mathurin in an interview after the sentencing decision.

“We are so grateful to each of the victims for coming forward and giving their testimony, which takes immense bravery and without whom a conviction would not have been possible.”

Prosecutor Dominique Mathurin credits Richard Mantha's victims for their brave testimony in helping to secure convictions. Mantha was sentenced to 12 years in prison. (Meghan Grant/CBC)

Mantha's victims were four women who struggled with drug addiction at the time. A publication ban protects the identities of three of the victims.

'Honoured to be standing here'

A fourth, Aimee Ert, successfully applied to the court to have the publication ban on her identity lifted.

In April 2022, Matha attacked Ert at his rural trailer. She managed to get away from him, running toward the highway, where she collapsed on the roadside. A passerby helped get her to hospital.

Ert was in court Thursday as the sentencing decision was delivered and said she was “feeling some closure.”

“I feel honoured to be standing here for the women who couldn’t,” said Ert, who recently celebrated being sober for four years.

Aimee Ert thanks Const. Steve Hill with the Calgary Police Service's victim assistance unit for his support over the years. (Meghan Grant/CBC)

In handing down the sentence Thursday, Shriar noted that Ert’s victim impact statement was “one of the most moving this court has ever heard.”

“I felt heard,” said Ert, reacting to the judge’s words.

“I felt that everything that I had experienced throughout my entire life, being an addict and the trauma that we experience … I was able to try to take that out and have it heard and create a positive impact from it.”

Anti-social personality disorder

Mantha was arrested in April 2023 after a massive police search of his rented rural property, where he lived in a trailer inside a quonset about 16 kilometres east of Chestermere, Alta.

His trial started in January 2024 and faced several lengthy delays because he fired two sets of lawyers and then had two health incidents, including a stroke, which has left him unable to speak.

During the trial, court heard that Mantha targeted women on the Forest Lawn stroll, a prostitution area in the southeast neighbourhood along 19th Avenue.

Shriar noted that a report prepared by a psychiatrist during the trial found that Mantha has an anti-social personality disorder, a disregard for others and lacks remorse for his actions.

Mantha has just over five years credit for the time he served pending trial, leaving six years and nine months left on his sentence.

World.title: Manitoba adopts permanent daylight time after survey suggested overwhelming opposition to clock changes
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Manitobans no longer need to remember to spring forward or fall back one hour on their clocks.

Daylight time will be in place permanently, Premier Wab Kinew announced in a news release Thursday.

This change means clocks will not revert to standard time on Nov. 1.

Manitoba joins several other provinces and territories that have adopted or are moving toward a permanent time, including British Columbia, Yukon, the Northwest Territories, Alberta and Saskatchewan.

Just six months ago, Kinew said his government was too busy with more important matters to consider changes to the clocks.

He was asked about it in early March, shortly after B.C. announced it intended to remain on daylight time permanently.

He later softened his stance, suggesting it may be time to revisit the issue for Manitoba.

In April, Alberta announced plans to table legislation to cement a move to permanent daylight time. Days later, the Northwest Territories said it will also end time changes. Yukon has been on permanent time since 2020 and Saskatchewan since 1966.

In May, Manitoba launched a survey, asking the public to weigh in the issue. For those who did want to see the twice-annual changes halted, the survey asked if they preferred to stay on standard or daylight time.

On Thursday, the province said nearly 72,000 votes were submitted in its survey, with 92 per cent of respondents saying they wanted to see an end to seasonal time changes. Among respondents, 58 per cent preferred permanent daylight time and 34 per cent sided with standard time.

In its news release at the time the survey launched, the province included a link to an analysis by Manitoba Health, which concluded that eliminating the time change would be better for population health.

The National Research Council of Canada's map of Canadian time zones. (National Research Council of Canada)

The report says loss of sleep is the "most immediate consequence" of the spring clock change, when clocks have moved forward an hour. The amount of time a person spends sleeping drops slightly in the week following, with adolescents particularly vulnerable, the report says.

Disruption of sleep and circadian rhythm following the spring shift have been linked to short-term increases in cardiovascular events, injuries and traffic collisions, as well as reduced well-being, according to the report.

Historical data from Manitoba Public Insurance shows a 20 per cent increase in collisions on the province's roadways following the spring change when compared to all other Mondays, with loss of sleep and biological clock disruption being contributing factors, according to Manitoba Health.

'Should have chosen standard time'

Moving to a permanent time "would remove the acute risks" that come from switching twice a year, the report says.

But one researcher says the province should have adopted permanent standard time rather than daylight time.

Inna Rabinovich-Nikitin, an assistant professor with the University of Manitoba's department of physiology and pathophysiology, says moving to permanent daylight is not the right decision for people's health.

"Our body has an internal circadian clock … and when we're moving to daylight savings time, it doesn't align with the light and dark cycles outside, and that basically makes us feel like we're always jet-lagged," she said.

"It's better not to change the time twice a year, but between daylight savings time and standard time, we should have chosen standard time."

However, a doctors' advocacy group said it supports the move to permanent daylight time.

Although permanent standard time might offer the closest alignment to natural circadian rhythms, permanent daylight time provides other health and societal benefits, particularly more usable sunlight in the late afternoon and evening, Doctors Manitoba said in a written statement Thursday.

WATCH | Here's how ending clock changes will impact Manitoba: Sunrise at 3 a.m.? How ending time changes would affect Manitobans | Duration closed caption 3:11 Premier Wab Kinew says the days of Manitoba changing the clocks twice a year are numbered. How would adopting permanent daylight time or permanent standard time change things in Manitoba? CBC weather specialist Riley Laychuk explains.

Manitoba enacted the Official Time Act, bringing provincewide daylight time into effect on May 12, 1963. It set the start of daylight time as the first Sunday in April, continuing until the last Sunday in October, when clocks fell back to standard time.

Daylight time was extended in 2007, starting the second Sunday in March and continuing until the first Sunday in November, to match U.S. changes.

Concern in northern Manitoba

Winnipegger Declan Shroeder, who runs Winnipeg Daylight Tracker — a "novelty account" on X — said changing clocks twice a year is "just something that's become archaic."

He supports the province's move, saying he appreciates daylight more in the evening than in the morning.

"The winters are so long and crushing in Manitoba that I really relish the idea of having the sun up till 9:30 or 10 p.m. in the summer."

But Joe Stover, who lives in Churchill, said parents in northern Manitoba are worried about their kids getting to school, now that the sun will rise there after 10 a.m. in the winter.

"Kids will be going to school when it's pitch black," he said, though he's not surprised by the support for the change.

"I'm all for democracy. It's what the people wanted, and so we'll reap what we sow either way," he said.

He hopes the province will review the change in about a year.

"I just hope that people aren't stubborn about it [and] have an open mind, whether you're for this or against this."

World.title: Court imposes strict conditions on Colombia’s military air strikes if minors are present
World.content:
A Bogota court imposed strict conditions on Colombia’s military authorities if they want to carry out air strikes on illegal armed groups in places where victims of forced recruitment are present.

The ruling of Bogota’s 34th Family Court lifted a suspension on the strikes that had been imposed earlier this month in response to a lawsuit.

The court imposed the following conditions on air strikes to evade violating International Humanitarian Law, which prioritizes the rights of child victims of forced recruitment over the success of military operations.

Don’t assume minors are legitimate targets because they form part of an illegal armed group

Intensify the verification and cross-checking of available information on the possible presence of minors at potential targets

Explicitly include this assessment to the legal and operational assessment of the attack

Assess the foreseeable risk of an attack on the lives and integrity of the minors

Examine the existence of less harmful means, methods, timing or operational alternatives that would allow the achievement of a comparable military advantage

Rigorously apply the principles of distinction, precaution, and proportionality before authorizing and executing the operation

Integrate

The court additionally ordered family welfare institute ICBF to be integrated into military operations and strengthen the pathways for disengagement, restoration of rights, comprehensive care, and reintegration of children and adolescents who are victims of recruitment, with a differentiated and territorial approach.

The court asked the Ombudsman and the Inspector General’s Office to monitor compliance of the orders issue to maximize the protection of children’s rights.

The lawsuit had been filed in a successful attempt to protect children against the violence President Abelardo de la Espriella sought to unleash on illegal armed groups that refused to demobilize.

World.title: US maintains Colombia “failed demonstrably” in fighting drug trafficking
World.content:
The United States President Donald Trump maintained that Colombia “failed demonstrably during the previous 12 months to make substantial efforts to adhere to their obligations under international counternarcotics agreements.”

In an annual reviews, Trump stressed that the South American country maintains its an unwilling drug trafficking country “solely due to the incompetence and chaos produced by the previous far-left government.”

“If, as expected, Colombia makes progress on aggressive coca eradication and dismantling its narcoterrorist networks over the coming year, I will consider lifting the country’s ‘failed demonstrably’ status,” said the US president.

President Abelardo de la Espriella “has pledged to lead an aggressive campaign against coca cultivation and cocaine production, which reached record levels under the failed socialist policies of his predecessor,” Gustavo Petro, according to Trump.

Colombia is poised to resume its place as our foremost security partner in the hemisphere, and the country’s military, police, prosecutors, and courts now finally have a worthy champion in President de la Espriella. US President Donald Trump

De la Espriella, who took office in August, informally joined the US Government’s Shield of the Americas program in an attempt to increase cooperation between Trump’s conservative and far-right allies in the region.

As part of his counternarcotics efforts, the Colombian president tried to increase air strikes on so-called “narcoterrorist” groups, but was forced to stop this by a court to protect minor forced recruitment victims.

The National Police announced a pilot aerial fumigation program, but this was also suspended by a court because of health and environmental concerns.

The State Department vowed to seek $1 billion dollar in aid, but has yet to ask Congress for these funds while allegedly dealing with the world’s highest number of deaths caused by the consumption of illicit drugs.

World.title: Colombia’s statistics chief sacked for claiming Petro did not manipulate statistics
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella sacked his statistics chief because he claimed he found no anomalies in labor statistics presented by the administration of former President Gustavo Petro.

In a press statement, De la Espriella’s press secretary said that DANE director Ricardo Valencia was sacked for claiming “that he had not found any anomalies in the DANE indicators for the month of July, figures compiled during the final month of the previous administration.”

Valencia made that claim “without any in-depth audits having been conducted beforehand,” according to the press secretary.

It is essential for the National Government to conduct a rigorous review of the information received and to ensure that the data on which strategic decisions for the country are based fully reflect the economic and social reality of Colombians. President’s Office

The former DANE director was sacked days after the President’s Office canceled another statistics press conference that are common because of the agency’s regular updates on the state of the Colombian economy

July’s labor statistics confirmed claims by the previous government that unemployment dropped to record lows after Petro raised the minimum wage.

De la Espriella has insisted that the country’s economy is in crisis contrary to evidence, which indicated Petro increased economic growth in his last half year in office.

World.title: Colombia’s social organizations and labor unions announce national strike in November
World.content:
Some 1,500 representatives of social organizations and labor unions agreed to begin organizing an anti-government national strike that should take place throughout Colombia either on November 11 or on November 20.

The organizations agreed to the mass mobilization during the National Gathering for the Defense of Life, Dignity, Democracy, Peace, Sovereignty, and Social Reforms that had been organized by labor unions in the capital Bogota.

The first and fundamental decision of the Meeting is to declare the most radical opposition to the illegitimate government of Abelardo de la Espriella because of the course it has imposed on the country—one of subordination to the interests of U.S. imperialism and alignment with the agenda of the international far right—which constitutes a direct threat to national sovereignty, democracy, and the rights won by the Colombian people, and an undeniable shift toward fascism. Social organizations and labor unions

In a statement, the organizations said that the national strike will be preceded by regional protests on October 10 and 14 that will seek to generate momentum for the national strike.

Indigenous organizations will additionally organize a Day of Indigenous, Afro and Popular Resistance on October 12.

A final date for the national strike has yet to be defined.

The organizations decided to call a strike to protest the government’s security and defense policy, the ending of peace processes with illegal armed groups and in defense of social reforms that had been implemented by former President Gustavo Petro.

The protests additionally seek to express solidarity with the people of Palestine, western Sahara, Iran, Bolivia and Venezuela, and reject US imperialism in the Americas.

We must categorically reject the interference of U.S. government officials in the formulation of domestic policies under the guise of so-called friendly aid, which in reality masks the ambition to intensify overexploitation, extractivism, territorial control, and the presence of foreign troops on our soil. Social organizations and labor unions

The organizations agreed to “prepare, through the most intense and massive agitation and propaganda campaign, a national strike.”

World.title: Judge suspends Colombia’s aerial fumigation pilot
World.content:
A Putumayo from the southern Putumayo province suspended the government’s announced resumption of the aerial spraying of coca, ordering information that would allow “a sufficiently informed decision on the merits.”

Earlier this week, the National Narcotics Council (CNE) ordered the National Police to restart the aerial fumigation of coca, the base ingredient for cocaine, “as a controlled, limited, temporary, and evaluable experimental phase, the implementation of a pilot plan for the eradication of illicit crops through aerial spraying using a manned aircraft and the formulated product Glufosinate Ammonium 200 SL.”

The National Police subsequently said that the 10km2 pilot area was located in Putumayo, a province inside the Amazon forest.

These announcements triggered a local foundation to sue the administration, claiming that the plans to do a pilot were in violation of the 2015 ban on aerial fumigation and threatened both locals and the environment.

The judge agreed and ordered the administration of President Abelardo de la Espriella to provide information on the environmental and health risk involved in the aerial spraying with glufosinate ammonium.

The potential implementation of the pilot plan before gathering and analyzing the studies, documents, and technical evidence cited by the administration itself as the basis for the decision could render the requested constitutional protection ineffective and jeopardize the possibility of reaching a sufficiently informed decision on the merits; Indeed, the combination of the announced imminence of the measure, the current lack of essential information needed to understand its territorial, social, and environmental scope, and the particular ecological sensitivity of the department of Putumayo necessitates preventive action aimed at preserving the effectiveness of this constitutional action. Putumayo court

The suspension of the aerial spraying comes days after De la Espriella promised US Secretary of State Marco Rubio that he would resume aerial fumigation, a notoriously ineffective way to get rid of coca.

World.title: Colombia announces new aerial fumigation pilot program
World.content:
Colombia’s National Narcotics Council (CNE) ordered the National Police to restart the aerial fumigation of coca, the base ingredient for cocaine.

In a resolution, the CNE ordered “as a controlled, limited, temporary, and evaluable experimental phase, the implementation of a pilot plan for the eradication of illicit crops through aerial spraying using a manned aircraft and the formulated product Glufosinate Ammonium 200 SL.”

In a public statement, the National Police’s counternarcotics unit said that the 10km2 pilot area was located in Putumayo and would not affect indigenous and afro-descendant communities, who would need to be asked permission.

The exclusion of environmental protection zones and protected areas, zones associated with bodies of water, rivers, and other environmentally sensitive areas is contemplated, as well as those territories that, in accordance with current regulations and the corresponding technical studies, must be excluded. National Police Counternarcotics

The purpose of the pilot program is to “evaluate the effectiveness of aerial spraying, as well as its application under the established technical and operational conditions, said the police.

The police stressed that “this experimental phase does not constitute the resumption, adoption, or definitive authorization of a widespread or nationwide aerial spraying program,” which was banned by the Constitutional Court in 2015.

In order to resume aerial fumigation, health and environmental authorities must sign off on the program and the police would only be allowed to use airplanes with the approval of the court and local communities.

President Abelardo de la Espriella vowed to resume aerial spraying more than 330,000 hectares while on campaign and after taking office last month as part of his hardline approach to organized crime.

Former President Ivan Duque also vowed to resume aerial spraying, but failed to comply with the norms established by the court.

World.title: Court orders Colombia’s government to remove images of slain “narcoterrorists”
World.content:
A Bogota judge ordered Colombia’s government to remove images and videos of President Abelardo de la Espriella walking through the remains of slain suspected guerrillas from its social media accounts.

The judge also ordered the government to remove images and videos of the body bags containing the lifeless remains of four members of organized crime group ACSN who were killed in La Guajira.

According to the judge, the images could be harmful to minors.

The decision was celebrated by congressman Santiago Osorio (Green Alliance), who sued the government over the controversial social media posts.

The State and the National Government cannot engage in a contest with crime to see which of the two is the most cruel; in this regard, the Office of the President of the Republic, Mr. Abelardo de la Espriella, were ordered to promptly remove images that may have reached the cell phones of children across the country, showing a state displaying corpses as trophies. Congressman Santiago Osorio

Th publications were previously rejected by the Ombudsman’s Office, whose director, Iris Marin, urged the government not to “compete with armed groups over who instills the most fear, who humiliates the adversary the most, or who turns death into a display of power.”

In the first video, De la Espriella and Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora walked through rows of body bags, displaying the remains of 23 alleged members of FARC dissident organizations EMC who were killed in the southern Guaviare province.

Among those killed in Operation Azarias were two minor victims of forced recruitment by the guerrillas.

The videos sought to promote the government’s hardline security policy, which vows to kill “narcoterrorists” who refuse to surrender.

World.title: US, Colombia sign memorandums of understanding amid “rebirth” of relations
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio hailed the “rebirth” of bilateral relations as they signed memorandums of understanding on nuclear energy and rare earths.

The two leaders met in Barranquilla, where De la Espriella lives, as part of Rubio’s tour through allied countries in the Andean region.

The president and the secretary of state hailed the improvement of ties that were severely disrupted when former President Gustavo Petro was in office.

During a joint press conference, Rubio stressed the need for security in the region, claiming that “the same networks, the same criminal groups that, although they commit their crimes here, they also commit crimes in the U.S., and they damage our people.”

De la Espriella said that as part of the “Barranquilla Agreements,” he asked the US for support for his hardline security policy.

We have proposed to the government—and today I reiterated this proposal to the secretary—the 21st-Century Patriot Plan to modernize aircraft, radars, drones, helicopters, anti-drone systems, air defense, mobility, intelligence, cyber defense, special forces, and maintenance and operations. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president promised to “start spraying, we are going to target the laboratories, the precursors, the trafficking routes, the drug trafficking kingpins, the armed narco-terrorist organizations—we are going after the money launderers, their criminal assets, and those international networks that pose a grave danger not only to the hemisphere but also to humanity.”

Rubio did not openly commit any US support other than the memorandums of understanding.

The unbinding agreements were part of Rubio’s wish list as the US seeks new sources for rare earths and miners that can be processed outside of China, which the US Government sees as its rival.

With the nuclear energy agenda, Colombia seeks to “strengthen its capacities” with US support. Both governments “reaffirm their commitment to international development and the peaceful use of nuclear energy.”

In order to create policy regarding the memorandums, De la Espriella would need congressional support, which he has yet to seek openly.

World.title: Evacuations ordered in Chile as wildfires run amok
World.content:
Chile’s National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response (Senapred) Wednesday ordered the evacuation of 14 communes in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía, including Nacimiento, Purén, and Contulmo, which have all been particularly affected by the forest fires.

In messages broadcast through the Emergency Alert System (SAE), the authorities also called on residents to leave their homes to avoid further damage to their health.

It has already been a week since the first wildfires ran amok in south-central Chile despite efforts to contain them. High temperatures, dryness, and strong winds add to the plight of local people and some 5,600 firefighters deployed in the area while helping flocks in from abroad.

”We are entering this part of the week which is the most complex. Today, tomorrow, and the day after we have an alert for high temperatures in several regions of the country that has mobilized a very large effort (…) to prevent the fires from spreading,“ Interior Minister Carolina Tohá said regarding the 311 active fires, of which 89 are being fought. The Senapred also said 180 fires were under control, and 309,747 hectares have been affected.

”If the temperature rises and the wind increases we can indeed have more problems, and we already have many fires,” Spanish Lieutenant Colonel Carlos Javier Martín Traverso told AFP. Traverso’s Air Operations Section of the Military Emergency Unit (UME) arrived in Chile on Sunday to join the firefighting efforts.

Over 309,000 hectares have been consumed in the regions of Maule, Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía with the death toll standing at 24, plus 2,180 people injured as 1,180 houses were destroyed, leaving 5,560 people homeless.

There seems to be a seamless scientific consensus that fires are the result of human actions, either by intentionality or carelessness, although the drought that has hit Chile for 13 years adds to the aggressiveness of the fires.

In this scenario, President Gabriel Boric Font has announced a curfew in the areas of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía where a state of catastrophe is in force, in order to guarantee the security and tranquility of

the families affected by the crisis. Defense authorities working on the sites will determine the restriction’s schedule.

“We have 24 people dead nationwide, three are from Santa Juana and we do not want there to be even one more,” Boric told reporters after visiting the area.

The number of fatalities was updated to 24 after two bodies were determined to belong to people who had died before the fires broke out.

Meanwhile, Biobío Governor Rodrigo Díaz said he was certain about “people criminally setting fires.”

“I have reports from police, firefighters, of people who have been setting fires. I do not have indications, but certainties, we need more patrols,” he insisted in a radio interview.

“We have fire outbreaks at the southern exit of Contulmo, different places where fires were set 300 meters away from each other, I could see it, nobody told me about it. The mayor of Mulchén told me how fires were lit in the four cardinal points, I have reports from the police, the Fire Department, from people who have been setting fires. I do not have indications, but certainties, we need more patrols in the area,” he explained.

President Boric’s Regional Delegate Daniela Dresdner said eight people had been arrested for “irresponsible and suspicious attitudes with respect to the setting of fires. This was due to citizen complaints and patrols by the Navy.”

“We are asking that all these conducts be denounced and we are filing a lawsuit for all these denunciations to [be] prosecute[d],” she added.

The Biobío Regional Prosecutor’s Office called on the citizenry to e-mail all data regarding criminal behavior to fiscaliaincendios@gmail.com, including pictures, videos, audios, or written information as to the probable causes of the fires, which will be handled confidentially. (Merco Press)

World.title: Chile’s wildfires death toll reaches 24
World.content:
Chilean authorities spoke Sunday of 24 fatalities, nearly 1,000 people injured, and some 800 houses destroyed in the past five days by wildfires spreading fast in amid a highly-irregular heat wave with strong winds and temperatures above 40°C in areas 500 km south of Santiago.

The death toll reached 24 after the death of one of the injured people who had been hospitalized in Angol, Undersecretary of the Interior Manuel Monsalve explained. “The risk situation in the country remains” in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía, and in certain localities of the central region of Maule, he said. A red alert was also decreed Sunday in communes of the southern regions of Los Ríos and Los Lagos due to the appearance of new fire outbreaks. He also pointed out that 26 of the 997 people injured were in serious condition.

“I came home from work and I was already without anything, without a house. I was left on the street, with my arms crossed, now with my son, and my wife, in a tent. I have no fodder for my animals,” a resident of the town of Purén, in the Araucanía region, told Televisión Nacional de Chile (TVN).

Meanwhile, President Gabriel Boric Font attended the wake of a firefighter in the town of Coronel. ”Chile is crying with you. I am here to tell you that you are not alone, that the family of Yesenia (Muñoz, the deceased firefighter) will not be alone,” he said.

According to Chile’s National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response (Senapred), the number of fires being fought went down from 87 to 51. “We are experiencing a small window of improving weather conditions during Sunday and Monday. That means that we are not with extremely high temperatures,” Monsalve said.

Undersecretary Monsalve also told reporters that 10 people have been arrested for their responsibility in starting some of the fires for which the red alert was still maintained. Of the total number of fires, 22 occurred Sunday for a total of 283 active fires, of which 151 were under control and 71 are being fought.

Given the magnitude of the fires in size and number, international help has been summoned. “We have just sent a plane to Chile with a contingent of the Military Emergency Unit to collaborate in extinguishing and controlling the fires that are raging in the country. All our support to the Chilean people,” tweeted Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez.

Chile’s Foreign Ministry also said assistance was being coordinated with Argentina, Brazil, Ecuador, the United States, and Mexico, while Boric’s administration has declared a constitutional state of catastrophe in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío and La Araucanía, to speed up additional resources while restricting free transit and involving military forces to contain the disaster.

In 2017, another chain of fires destroyed some 460,000 hectares, left 11 people dead, nearly 6,000 injured, and more than 1,500 homes burned.

Monsalve also warned that this week high temperatures will continue, as well as the risk of low humidity and strong gusts of wind, which will make it difficult to extinguish the flames. – MercoPress

World.title: Parts of Chile under red alert for major forest fires in central region
World.content:
