World.title: Azerbaijan urges expanding cooperation of partner states to address global challenges
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 17. Chief of the State Security Service (SSS) of Azerbaijan, Colonel-General Ali Naghiyev emphasized the importance of further expanding among the partner states to address global challenges.

This was reported by the Press Service of the State Security Service following Naghiyev’s speech at the 28th Meeting of the Conference of Special Services Agencies of Turkic-Speaking States, held in Kazakhstan, attended by the delegation led by the SSS chief.

According to the report, during the speech, Naghiyev highlighted new global and regional challenges arising from contemporary geopolitical processes, including the severe consequences that ongoing large-scale military conflicts have inflicted on the operation of transport corridors. The speech identified the recruitment of citizens as mercenaries for military operations—as well as the smuggling of weapons, ammunition, and explosives out of combat zones—as serious threats to the security environment that exacerbate the crime situation.

Noting the adverse effects of ongoing crises in the Middle East—including the blockade of strategic straits—on global trade, energy security, and the global economy, the Head of the Service emphasized that no state can remain insulated from these unfolding events amidst current uncertainties. He underscored the necessity of further expanding the exchange of experience and information among the partner states to ensure reliable national security and to address emerging challenges through a unified stance.

At the meeting, where the global situation was assessed and necessary steps to ensure regional security amidst modern challenges were discussed, a final document covering the relevant issues was signed.

World.title: Wilsons Prom's Sealers Cove track reopens after five years
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

At the southernmost point of mainland Australia, Yiruk Wamoon, or Wilsons Promontory, holds a special place in the hearts of many.

Each year, thousands of hikers make the pilgrimage to "The Prom", plunging into the isolation and solitude of the park's many walking trails.

But for the better part of five years, a vast swathe of its famed bushland has been closed to the public.

Battered by successive storms, the Sealers Cove walking track was shut, limiting access to some of the park's most iconic coves and beaches.

The trail reopened today, just in time for what rangers hope will be a busy summer at the national park.

But the road to repair was a tale straight from the pages of Swiss Family Robinson, including helicopters, barges, and a temporary camp and mess hall in the swamp to get the job done.

Everything, including the kitchen sink

Wilsons Prom is one of Parks Victoria's most popular parks, with about 600,000 visitors annually.

The Sealers Cove boardwalk has been around since the late 1970s, and was hit by a major flood in 2011. A decade later, it was battered by three successive storms and needed a complete rebuild.

The Victorian government allocated $4.8 million to rebuild a 2-kilometre stretch of the boardwalk, on top of a $23 million investment in the Wilsons Promontory Revitalisation Project.

Wilsons Promontory National Park is located on the southernmost tip of Australia's mainland. (Supplied: Parks Victoria)

The track's remote location was a major challenge for engineers and park rangers.

Wilsons Prom area chief ranger Brett Mitchell said the rebuild was an opportunity to repair the infrastructure for future generations.

"We've got 2 kilometres of boardwalk we needed to rebuild that's basically in a swamp," Mr Mitchell said.

Brett Mitchell expects the reopening of Sealers Cove to lead to an influx of visitors. (ABC News: Madeleine Stuchbery)

The broken boardwalk was removed, after which a dedicated team began the major planning and approvals process to get the new infrastructure in place.

Stephen Erickson is a director and project manager at Envirotechniques, which was responsible for the boardwalk project. He led the team of engineers and builders camped at the solitary cove for weeks on end.

They worked alongside traditional owners, Parks Victoria scientists and rangers to remove the damaged boardwalk and assess the area.

But with zero vehicle access to Sealers Cove, getting materials and crew onto the site was the first challenge Mr Erickson faced.

A mess hall, tool shed, and hot showers were available as part of a temporary camp set up for the construction crew at Sealers Cove. (Supplied: Parks Victoria )

"It's 9.5 kilometres from Telegraph Saddle to the site by walking track, or you can get there by boat typically out of Port Welshpool, or you can get there by helicopter," he said.

Up to nine people at a time were working on a rotating roster.

The crew would work up to 10 days straight at the remote camp, which featured a mess tent, dining and kitchen area, a machinery tool storage area and even hot showers.

Envirotechniques construction crew work on the new Sealers Cove boardwalk project. (Supplied: Parks Victoria )

They packed everything, including the kitchen sink.

"It was fairly important to try and provide the best facilities that we could," Mr Erickson said.

"The prom is unique, and it's well-loved by many Victorians.

" To be actually working in that environment, it does feel challenging but it's also very rewarding. "

The Sealers Cove boardwalk has been closed since 2021 due to storm damage, but has since been rebuilt. (Supplied: Parks Victoria)

Worth the wait

From removing materials, wading through swamps, or just the reality of living in an isolated camp environment, the boardwalk repair team lived and breathed their task.

The new boardwalk is built of fibre-reinforced plastic, and now sits about 30cm higher in anticipation of rising sea levels.

It has been a long journey, Mr Mitchell said, but worth the wait.

"It's a really special area of the park and a really popular area, so to have the boardwalk reopened and have our southern circuit reopened is a magnificent achievement from everyone concerned," he said.

"Our visitation is increasing every year, but to have that iconic southern circuit fully reopened with full access back to Sealers Cove, we're anticipating a huge influx of visitors and hikers back to that site."

Mr Erickson said he will never forget waking up to the sight of whales in the cove and the sounds of the bush each morning.

"There was a large family of kookaburras who used to put out their distinctive laugh early in the morning at dawn. We would be listening to the crashing waves on Sealers Cove through the night," he said.

"The mood and the weather and the wildlife that we saw out there were quite special."

World.title: Drug drivers will face higher fines under new Queensland laws
World.content:
Drivers with a drug present in their blood or saliva will face higher fines under new laws passed in the Queensland parliament.

From December, penalties for drug driving and combined drink-and-drug driving offences will increase.

The state government had said these reforms were an evidence-based response to rising road trauma and were informed by experts, crash data, and enforcement trends.

Transport Minister Brent Mickelberg said there was "no silver bullet" to reducing the road toll but that the broad reforms aimed to increase road safety.

"The increased penalties will better reflect the seriousness of the offending and send a clear message that dangerous behaviour is unacceptable," he told the House on Thursday.

Queensland transport minister Brent Mickelberg said he makes "no apology" for introducing tougher penalties for drug and drink driving. (ABC News)

"I make no apology for taking a strong position against drink and drug driving."

Mr Mickelberg said the road toll had increased by 35 per cent between 2019 and 2024.

"These are more than growing statistics. These are brothers, sisters, mothers, fathers and friends that are no longer with us," he said.

"That is why the Crisafulli government is working on multiple fronts to get people home sooner and safer."

Under the new laws, offenders driving with a relevant drug in their saliva will face a fine of up to $4,835 and lose their licence for a minimum of two months.

Those drugs are methylamphetamine, cocaine, MDMA or tetrahydrocannabinol, also known as THC.

Brent Mickelberg says the government is taking a "strong position against drink and drug driving." (ABC News: Anzaya Karim)

A driver who tests positive to drugs and has an illegal blood alcohol concentration will face a maximum fine of $5,699 and a licence disqualification for at least three months.

Under current state laws, there are no minimum fines for drink or drug driving offences.

Mr Mickelberg had previously said that, in some cases, these court-imposed fines had been lower than penalties for other offences, such as mobile phone use or not wearing a seatbelt.

Under the new reforms, there will be a minimum court-imposed fine for drink and drug driving.

The legalisation also included a new immediate six-month licence suspension framework for drivers detected travelling more than 40 kilometres per hour above the speed limit.

State parliament also passed a raft of other reforms, aimed at cracking down on dangerous driving, on Thursday night.

A Queensland government crackdown on drink driving will also introduce harsher laws for drug driving. (ABC News: Elizabeth Pickering)

These changes featured increasing the maximum penalty for motor vehicle offences which result in death or grievous bodily harm from 16 years to 25 years and expanding mandatory imprisonment requirements for serious and repeat dangerous driving offenders.

During the debate on the bill, Shadow Transport Minister Bart Mellish said the Labor Opposition welcomed the government's recognition of the importance of road safety.

But he said the new reforms fell short.

"Instead of striking the right balance between public safety and individual rights, the LNP government uses road safety as a crutch to justify measures unsupported by evidence to remove judicial discretion and disadvantage everyday Queenslanders," he told State Parliament on Thursday.

Concerns raised over medicinal cannabis

In a submission on the bill, Alcohol and Drug Foundation's (ADF) state manager Martin Milne said changes would negatively impact people "simply" taking their legal medicinal cannabis prescriptions.

He also raised concerns that THC could remain detectable in saliva for up to three days after use.

RACQ general manager for advocacy Joshua Cooney told a parliamentary committee that he supported the bill's combination of stronger consequences, intervention and behaviour change measures.

"We're not here to stand against the use of medicinal cannabis. We're here to advocate for improved road safety," he said in July.

During the debate, Mr Mickelberg acknowledged the concerns raised over legal medicinal cannabis prescriptions users.

He said the Queensland Drug Driving Review, commissioned by the former government, found that there was "no scientifically reliable THC threshold or impairment-based roadside test that accurately distinguishes impaired from unimpaired drivers".

"The review also identified broader concerns about medicinal cannabis prescribing practices, medication misuse, illicit THC products and the increasing crash risks associated with THC," Mr Mickelberg said.

He said until those matters were addressed, "the safety of all road users must remain our primary consideration".

World.title: How Swans rebuilt their midfield to challenge for premiership
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Rome wasn't built in a day and neither is an AFL midfield.

But instant construction was seemingly the task for the Sydney Swans in the wake of suspending five key players after last month's post-match incident at the Pullman Hotel in Melbourne.

While the suspensions were the catalyst for major change, smaller moves had been afoot in the weeks and months beforehand.

No midfield has been hotter than the Swans over the past five games. Sydney has gone from a league-average side across the middle to perhaps being the best.

This is despite losing three-time All-Australian Isaac Heeney, fellow superstar Chad Warner and premiership player James Jordon.

Two weeks ago, Sydney surprised the AFL by comprehensively beating reigning premiers Brisbane.

That victory was largely driven by this makeshift force in the middle dynamically (and aggressively) moving the ball while protecting their defence.

Instead of star power, the Swans are relying on structure and balance to drive them deeper into the finals.

System against talent

There's long been a debate in the footy world about system against talent. The Swans have placed themselves firmly in the camp of the former.

In their first game after the suspensions, Sydney tried new combinations, testing them in real footy.

It was an indication coach Dean Cox was exploring how the available talent would fit the much-vaunted system, a message he had been preaching all year.

"One thing we want to make sure is that we are a system-based team and role-focused team," Cox said of covering injuries to Heeney and Gulden in March.

It's the changes to the frontline that are most visible. Sydney relied heavily on Heeney, Warner and Jordon to drive their midfield engine.

Those three accounted for about half of their midfield centre-bounce contributions, let alone their impact around the ground.

But that role focus may have made it easier to solve for replacing the suspended stars and perhaps finding a better balance along the way.

Pieces of the puzzle

Midfield balance is often a delicate beast.

If a team is too aggressive, it can be beaten back the other way in transition.

Too passive or defensive, and you can struggle for territory and scoreboard pressure.

As a result, replacing Heeney, Warner and Jordon required some lateral thinking.

Excluding ruck Brodie Grundy, arguably the most important player is James Rowbottom.

Shuffled in and out of different roles, Rowbottom's flexibility within and between games has become a strength.

"I just do what the team needs," Rowbottom told reporters ahead of the qualifying final against the Lions.

"I sort of have done that for the last eight years or so. My role's been ever-changing this year.

"I've played a lot of half-forward, a lot of midfield, a bit of wing."

However, Rowbottom does his best work hunting the ball, and his opponent, at the bottom of packs and contests.

Rowbottom sits sixth all-time for tackles per game.

In the past fortnight, he has applied the clamps with 56 pressure acts over the two games, which is a league-leading rate.

He's unafraid to do the dirty work to make his teammates look better.

The reignited star

Two years ago, there were few more valuable young players in the league than Errol Gulden.

However, two injury-struck years dulled his star. It took just a month and a half for that supernova to reignite.

Since their round-20 win over cross-town rivals GWS, Gulden has quickly re-emerged as Sydney's attacking focal point.

Few see angles and hit potential kicks on the field better than Gulden.

As a result, the Swans look to get the ball into Gulden's hands more often than any other player in the league.

Gulden doesn't just blaze away. He's second among midfielders and sixth overall for retained metres gained, normally the specialty of defenders landing safer kicks.

In every way, Gulden finds ways to advance the ball with threat.

Without Heeney and Warner, Gulden is getting even more opportunity with ball in hand. This has improved their overall ball use and added more danger to their impressive attack.

Like all players, Gulden does have flaws.

While his attacking side is nearly unmatched, he is far from a defensive powerhouse.

At just 175 centimetres tall, he can be muscled out and pushed off balance when unable to use his speed.

It means his impact is best realised next to bigger bodies willing to do the hard yards.

The converted defender

While Jai Serong made last year's VFL Team of the Year at Hawthorn, he was unable to crack the stellar Hawks defence or in a wing role.

Given this, few expected Serong to be thrown into the heart of the contest.

But, in need of a defensive boost around contest and considering his aerobic ability, the Swans decided to explore the concept of using Serong as an inside midfielder.

His arrival at stoppage in round 22 accompanied a heavier dose of Gulden at the middle, with Serong further protecting the elite ball-user.

With Serong in the heat of battle, the Swans have become a dominant stoppage force.

He not only provides a safety blanket but has done damage off his own boot, much like Rowbottom.

Young gun

Like many young players in good teams, former first round pick Angus Sheldrick had to bide his time with short stints on the edges of the midfield rotation.

Sheldrick has firmly established himself as an impact player, both as a regular sub last year and on limited time this season.

But he has been able to make that time count, focusing those minutes on high impact-stoppage play.

He is able to cover the gaps of the other three with minimal drop-off so far.

The second layer

Often the pinch isn't felt in the front line when changes are made. Instead, it's beyond the main group where depth is really tested.

The Swans are suddenly fielding a slew of names only briefly seen at the top level. Billy Cootee, Tom Hanily, Jesse Dattoli and Caiden Cleary have made leaps in relatively unsung roles around the outside midfield and high half-forward.

Pressure, holding position and supporting structures have been the order of the day. These players, hungry and well-educated, are tasked with forming the outside layer and impacting post clearance.

Along with more senior figures, such as Tom Papley, Jake Lloyd, Braeden Campbell and the potentially returning Justin McInerney, they have helped control the middle of the ground.

Formidable Dockers

In the Swans' path to the grand final stands self-proclaimed minor premier "underdogs" Fremantle.

The Dockers, with a midfield led by Serong's brother Caleb, can equally pile the points on and defend with aplomb.

Winning territory through the middle is critical for the Swans' chances of staying alive one more week. But it's an area that the Dockers have been susceptible to in the past.

The Swans may have had an advantage in the element of surprise against Brisbane. Few knew exactly how Sydney would set up.

But Fremantle may have more of an idea now, unless Cox and the Swans have yet another surprise up their sleeves.

World.title: Victorian TAFE teachers working seven unpaid hours on average each week
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Early education teacher Elizabeth Chiarelli loves training the next generation of childcare workers in her TAFE classes.

"You meet a lot of talented students," Ms Chiarelli said.

"Some are changing careers completely."

But Ms Chiarelli said since the introduction of the Free TAFE program, bigger classes have meant less time to work with individual students, many of whom have additional needs, such as language, literacy and numeracy support.

"[It's meant] different types of students where you require more contextualised learning for each student," she explained.

"That can be really difficult sometimes."

Elizabeth Chiarelli says the Free TAFE program has led to larger classes and reduced teaching capacity. (ABC News: Sacha Payne)

Free TAFE started in Victoria in 2019, with the state government paying fees to encourage students to take on vocational studies in high-demand industries.

It rolled out nationally with the assistance of the federal government four years later.

More than 80 free courses are now available in Victoria, in areas like construction, agriculture, finance, hospitality, health and aged care.

But teachers say the increase in enrolments has not been met with a commensurate increase in resources, leaving staff to fill the gaps.

New research from independent think tank Per Capita, commissioned by the Australian Education Union (AEU), shows Victorian TAFE has the lowest funding per hour of education delivered in the country.

Data compiled in the report, pictured from highest to lowest funding per hour in the following table, shows that funding in Victoria is nearly $2 below the national average.

Jurisdiction Approx. expenditure/hr (2024, real $) Difference from national average Trend ACT $31.92 +$10.56 Above average Tasmania $26.70 +$5.34 Above average Northern Territory $26.13 +$4.77 Above average New South Wales $23.15 +$1.79 Above average South Australia $22.33 +$0.97 Near average National average $21.36 - Comparator Western Australian $20.96 -$0.40 Near average Queensland $19.90 -$1.46 Below average Victoria $19.44 -$1.92 (lowest) Persistently lowest

AEU Victorian president Justin Mullaly warns the funding deficit is threatening the state's ability to fill crucial skills shortages.

"It means that the instructional time — so the time that TAFE students spend in class — has been cut time and time again," Mr Mullaly told the ABC.

"And it means that teachers don't have enough time to actually provide their students with the skills and the education that they need."

Justin Mullaly says too many Victorian TAFE teachers are working extra hours without pay. (ABC News)

Teachers working unpaid hours

The report found Victoria's TAFE teachers are working an average of seven unpaid hours every week, which equates to up to $108.7 million in unpaid wages across the workforce every year.

It states that nearly 60 per cent have considered leaving TAFE.

"Our TAFE teachers on average are working almost a whole day a week unpaid and that's because they're trying to do the right thing by students," Mr Mullaly said.

Report author Wesa Chau said the government funding model, which pays subsidies per student enrolment hour, means TAFEs cannot rely on revenue to plan courses.

"Currently the funding goes towards the enrolment hours of students, which is the delivery hours," she said.

"But there are other things that need to be done."

Per Capita's Wesa Chau authored the report. (Supplied)

TAFE accounting and bookkeeping teacher Teghan Day said a shortfall in funding hours meant students were often left to do work on their own, which is difficult for courses where practical skills are required.

"What that ultimately means is teachers across Victoria are focused on delivering the content, making sure that we cover that essential knowledge for our students," she said.

"But often it doesn't leave enough time for students to be able to actually apply that.

"Students [have to] do work outside of class and they don't necessarily have the resources or the tools and equipment at home, especially when you look at trades and hands-on areas."

Teghan Day says the funding shortfall puts more pressure on students. (ABC News)

Funding opinions differ

The report recommends changing the per hour enrolment model to "block funding" per course while raising the per hour rate as an interim measure.

lt also recommends linking any expansion in the Free TAFE program to commensurate funding.

But the peak body for independent tertiary providers argues that government funding should be aimed at students, not institutions.

Felix Pirie, CEO of the Independent Tertiary Education Council of Australia, is calling for a review of government funding for vocational training.

Loading...

He thinks students should also be given the opportunity to study for free in the private sector.

"[Students] don't have an opportunity to undertake training with the support of government unless they go to a specific type of institution that may very well not suit their needs," he said.

"I think we should invest in students that go to independent providers … whether that's private not-for-profits, whoever that might be."

The CEO of the Victorian TAFE Association, Alex White, is calling for more campuses and classrooms alongside an increase in funding for subsidised TAFE places.

Alex White says better infrastructure is needed across Victorian TAFEs. (ABC News: Kyle Harley)

"Our population is increasing and the skills demands that Victoria is facing in the future — whether it's for clean energy, health, cyber security — are enormous," he said.

"There's going to be about 1.4 million new workers over the next 10 years in Victoria and TAFE is the only way that we can train such a large number of people in the skills that our economy needs."

Mr Pirie said it was "not an either-or proposition".

"We can't go down the path of only funding or investing in a particular provider type, whether it be TAFE or just an independent provider."

Free TAFE was first introduced in Victoria in 2019. (Supplied: Unsplash)

Fight 'not about pay'

The Shadow Minister for Jobs and Skills, Bridget Vallence, told the ABC that a Coalition government would work collaboratively with TAFE teachers to strengthen the state's vocational education and training system, but did not say whether that would include an increase to TAFE funding.

"The state relies heavily on TAFE teachers to educate and skill up Victorians and provide them with the qualifications they need to get decent jobs and help grow our economy," Ms Vallence told the ABC.

A government spokesperson told the ABC that Free TAFE had been a "game-changer", with more than 278,900 students commencing a free course.

"Our TAFE teachers are world-class and we'll always back them which is why in the most recent TAFE Teachers Agreement we delivered pay rises, better leave provisions and more time for assessment and planning," the spokesperson said.

The latest union campaign follows a protracted battle with the state government to reach a pay deal for public school teachers and education support workers.

But Justin Mullaly said this fight was not about pay for teachers.

"This is about making sure that we've got our TAFEs funded in a way that meets the ultimate needs of students."

World.title: Charles 'giddily elated' on night Diana was killed, her brother claims
World.content:
Princess Diana's brother has accused King Charles III of sounding "giddily elated, like a lottery winner" on the night his ex-wife was killed in a car crash almost three decades ago.

The explosive claim came in Charles Spencer's soon-to-be-released memoir, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, an excerpt of which Britain's Daily Mail published on Thursday, local time.

Among several complaints about the royal family's behaviour at the time of his sister's death, Earl Spencer gave his account of the night of the 1997 crash.

"Unlike my other callers, who were stunned, barely able to articulate their condolences and offers of help, he [Charles] sounded giddily elated — like a lottery winner, I remember thinking at the time," the excerpt read.

"He let me know he had informed William and Harry of their mother's death, first thing that morning, in their bedrooms at Balmoral. It all sounded strangely matter-of-fact, given the enormity of the disaster.

"Looking back now, I suspect the prince's first reaction must have been to think more of how this event might free him to marry the woman he loved, rather than appreciating the loss of one he did not. It can be hard to feel too much sympathy for an ex-spouse, or those who care for them profoundly, after bitter divorce."

Charles Spencer, left, speaks to Harry, the Duke of Sussex, in 2021. (Pool: Dominic Lipinski via Reuters)

The claims continue a war of words between Earl Spencer and Buckingham Palace that erupted earlier this week, when the first details of the book were made public.

Among several disparaging assertions, Earl Spencer alleged King Charles had told him "we'll forget her soon enough" in the days after Princess Diana was killed.

In response, a palace spokesperson said: "While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgement and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss."

Royal commentators have described the rebuke as the most pointed statement they had seen from a British monarch in years.

Buckingham Palace is yet to respond to Earl Spencer's latest claims.

King Charles and Queen Camilla step out in London. (Reuters: Hollie Adams)

Princess Diana and King Charles — who was not on the throne at the time — divorced in 1996. Charles married Queen Camilla, with whom he had been having a long-running affair, in 2005.

The extract of Earl Spencer's book released on Thursday included several bombshell allegations, including that:

Diana told him Charles had squeezed her waist and said, "Oh, a bit chubby here, aren't we?" in the days after their engagement.

Diana had confided in a friend that, on the eve of her wedding day, Charles had told her he was happy to marry her, but that he did not love her.

Diana "in her later years" had driven herself to the cliffs at Beachy Head in East Sussex "more than once" to take her own life, but that "her love for her sons stopped her from going further".

While Diana's deteriorating mental health, including a well-documented eating disorder, has been a matter of public knowledge for several years, Earl Spencer's direct and personal attacks linking them to King Charles are new.

The claims he makes in it have continued a devastating period for the royal family, which has included a public and ongoing rift between the king's two sons, William and Harry, as well as a police investigation into the monarch's brother, Andrew, who has been accused of child sex offences, which he denies.

In the past two years, Charles has also been treated for an undisclosed type of cancer, as has his daughter-in-law, Princess Catherine, who has recovered.

"It is only going to get worse; this is one extract that's being released from the book next week. One. I mean whatever else is in there is going to be explosive," royal commentator Afua Hagan told the ABC.

"Buckingham Palace is definitely going to be in damage control, and they have to be because Charles Spencer has always been so loyal to Princess Diana in her life and in her death, and he has really kept it in for a long time — all these things he has wanted to say."

Earl Spencer's book is expected to be released next week.

World.title: Shirt brand owner shares fix to get thousands of Temu dupes taken down
World.content:
When Warwick Levy learned copies of his T-shirts were being sold on Temu, he did not know how to handle it.

The Sydney-based owner of Lonely Kids Club, a genderless graphic tee company, hoped the problem would go away.

It did not.

"It got to a point where our entire website was scraped, and we have thousands of designs … so all our designs were on Temu," Mr Levy said.

" Our top selling designs were on there like 10, 20, 30, 40 times from different sellers, all with lots of sales attributed. "

The copies hurt sales; the bestselling "get in the van" shirt — featuring a drawing of the Healthy Harold giraffe — suddenly became significantly less popular.

The Get in the Van shirt is one of the most popular designs. (Supplied: Lonely Kids Club)

"At the time we thought maybe it's just gone stale. But then once it got removed [from Temu], it picked back up almost immediately," Mr Levy said.

Like many other small designers in Australia who have found their work copied by overseas giants, Mr Levy did not have the time or money to take the fight to court, and was unsure what government bodies would be able to support him.

"I'm a very small self-funded business without any sort of capital or investors, that sort of thing just didn't feel feasible," he said.

He reached out to Temu and was directed to its Intellectual Property (IP) Violation form — but the problems did not stop there.

"I spent like half an hour, 40 minutes going through and putting in data and then right before the end, where you then click to submit, it just disappeared; the whole window vanished, and then I lost all my work," he said.

"I tried it again, spent another 40 minutes and then again, it disappeared.

"I really stressed out because I was like, 'I've lost, like, my work twice; I feel very helpless in this situation, and I don't know what's going on'".

Warwick Levy operates his business from a studio in Artarmon, Sydney. (Supplied: Warwick Levy)

Mr Levy launched his business in 2011 working out of his bedroom, and now has a studio-warehouse in Artarmon where he collaborates with artists and has a focus on ethical, local production.

"It felt like I let [the artists] down because the work was stolen from my website and so that was my responsibility to remove it," he said.

Once Temu began selling copies, Mr Levy got complaints from customers about receiving low-quality garments, not realising they had purchased duplicates.

"We actually had one person not that long ago sort of say like, 'why would I buy this design from you when everyone's selling it?'" Mr Levy said.

"I say, 'Well, first of all, it's our design. No one else is meant to be selling it. Everyone else has stolen it.'"

Do you know more? Contact Liana Walker at walker.liana@abc.net.au

The workaround

After struggling to successfully navigate Temu's IP violation portal on different browsers, he found a workaround to complete the form.

Mr Levy said he started by having the information needed for the report prepared in a separate document. Then he opened the IP form in an incognito window, signed in and never closed the tab.

By acting fast, he was able to get the form through to the final stage. After that, he says it took days before he received a confirmation.

Some of the listings Warwick Levy submitted to Temu for violating content. (Supplied: Warwick Levy)

Mr Levy realised complaining about trademark violation sped up the process, and he says eventually the copies were removed — taking just over a week.

A Temu spokesperson said they had promptly removed the listings in question after the Lonely Kids Club's reports were received.

"Sellers are required to comply with applicable laws and platform policies, and those found to violate our IP policies are subject to enforcement actions, including listing removal, account suspensions, or permanent bans," the spokesperson said.

In the hope of helping other designers, Mr Levy has shared detailed instructions on how to get violating Temu listings taken down on the Lonely Kids Club website, and has since added software to his website to help prevent design theft.

Support from fans

Mr Levy said while he still finds copies of his work online, it is not at the same scale as Temu.

Throughout the process, the small business owner received great support from his fans, releasing a "How shit is Temu" tee that became very popular.

Small Australian designers copied by Shein Small Australian fashion designers say it is too time-consuming to continue to ask Shein to take down copies of their designs.

"People did come out saying, 'I would never buy it from Temu again. Thanks for telling us and we'll make sure that we report it wherever we can as well,'" Mr Levy said.

"It was really sweet."

He said he would like to see a hub created to support Australian designers impacted by IP violation.

World.title: These tiny crocodiles may be at risk, but they can't be listed as 'threatened'
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

The Northern Territory is synonymous with big open skies and humungous crocodiles.

But high in Arnhem Land's remote sandstone escarpments you will also find Australia's smallest snapping handbags.

It's here, more than 100 kilometres up the Liverpool River, that freshwater crocodiles only grow half as long as their downstream neighbours.

Since this population of "pygmy crocodiles" was first reported in Western science in the 1980s, there has been debate over whether the isolated reptiles were a different species.

"Species status can have major conservation implications," wildlife geneticist Jaime Góngora of the University of Sydney said.

" If these crocodiles were a separate species, they would likely require their own conservation assessment and management plan. "

But a new study published in Ecology and Evolution by Professor Góngora and colleagues that compared the genetics of different populations of freshwater crocodiles concluded they were one species.

Professor Góngora said the genetic differences in the small Liverpool River crocodiles was no greater than that found between freshwater crocodiles (Crocodylus johnstoni) that lived in other river systems.

"They are a unique population, but we did not find strong evidence that they are a separate species," he said.

While not a new species, Professor Góngora said pygmy crocodiles represented an ecological form of freshwater crocodile adapted to isolated escarpments.

He said this could warrant more protection for the Liverpool River crocodiles and a second population of small crocodiles in the Bullo River.

"Those adaptations are valuable and worth conserving," Professor Góngora said.

Why are they so small?

The small size of pygmy crocodiles compared to other freshwater populations is thought to be an example of "phenotypic plasticity", a phenomenon whereby a species develops different characteristics based on where it lives.

"A simple example is that identical plants can grow tall and lush in good soil but remain small and stunted in poor soil," Professor Góngora said.

"They are still the same species, but they respond differently to different conditions."

Centre for Crocodile Research managing director Sally Isberg, who was not involved with the study, said their small size came from adapting to smaller water pools on the escarpment, where less prey was available compared to down river.

"They've been able to mature at a smaller size because obviously the end goal is to pass on your genes," Dr Isberg said.

Discerning crocs from logs the challenge for AI trial Researchers are trialling artificial intelligence to detect crocodiles in north Queensland waterways, but its success depends on human training to ensure accuracy.

The original survey that described the Liverpool River's pygmy crocodiles found them in the upper reaches of the river past natural barriers, like waterfalls, where there weren't any large fish species.

The surveyors found the largest mature female pygmy crocodiles were between 1.07 metres and 1.12m long, and a male was 1.18m.

Elsewhere in the NT, female freshwater crocodiles mature at about 1.5m and grow up to 2m in length. While males mature at 1.6m to 2m and reach 2.5m.

Professor Góngora said freshwater crocodiles were known to grow larger in habitats with more permanent water and more abundant food.

For example, in the catfish-filled Lake Argyle in Western Australia, freshwater crocodiles have been recorded reaching lengths of about 3m.

Freshwater crocodiles living in Lake Argyle have been found to reach about 3m in length. (iNaturalist: Alan Bell/Freshwater crocodile/CC BY 4.0)

Do pygmy crocodiles need more conservation effort?

Dr Isberg said there was a point of alarm a few years ago for Bullo River pygmy crocodiles when cane toads, which can kill predators when ingested, moved through the region.

The exact state of the two pygmy crocodile populations is unclear, with no current population estimates.

Professor Góngora said there were high levels of inbreeding in the Liverpool River population compared to other crocodiles in the genetic study.

"That is not surprising given how isolated these crocodiles are," he said.

" Inbreeding can reduce genetic diversity, which may make populations less resilient to environmental change and other threats. "

Professor Góngora said more research was needed to understand the extent of inbreeding and whether it was affecting their long-term health, survival and ability to adapt to future challenges.

He said future research directions included more genetic sampling of the Bullo River crocodiles, studies on movement patterns and connectivity of the two populations between river systems, and ecological research into food availability, habitat quality and how the pygmy crocs responded to environmental pressures.

"Together, that would help us better understand how isolation and evolutionary processes are shaping these crocodile populations," Professor Góngora said.

In the meantime, he said conservation agencies could identify pygmy crocodiles as "unique management units" and prioritise them for monitoring, threat mitigation and recovery actions.

Cassius the croc stuffed for new exhibit The world's largest crocodile in captivity until its death last year is going on display in Far North Queensland.

A spokesperson for the flora and fauna division of the NT Department of Lands, Planning and Environment told the ABC in a written statement the concept of an "ecological" species was interesting, "but would likely apply to isolated populations of many species".

The spokesperson said the new study confirmed pygmy crocodiles were not genetically distinct enough to be a subspecies or separate species of freshwater crocodile.

"This means that they could not legally be listed as a threatened species," they said.

The spokesperson said the remote pygmy populations were naturally protected from many threats.

But they also noted the spread of cane toads was a problem for all freshwater crocodiles.

"There are currently no effective measures to reduce the impacts of cane toads at a landscape scale, although there is some very promising research in the development of 'Peter Pan' tadpoles."

World.title: Diesel 'crack spread' filling refiners' coffers as conflict cuts margins
World.content:
It is a long way from the Red Sea to grain farmer Adrian Roles' property in regional New South Wales, but the Middle East conflict is having a major impact on his harvest.

The wheat and sheep farmer said the price of diesel, pesticides, herbicides and even shipping to his property just outside Wagga Wagga have all increased.

Crude oil, which is the base product for diesel, has surged over $US105 per barrel, up from around $70 per barrel before the conflict.

The prices swings are taking a toll.

"So it's costing us, on the bottom line, about 40 per cent of our profitability," he said.

World scrambles for diesel

For farmers like Mr Roles the pressures from the conflict in the Middle East look likely to continue, according to Commonwealth Bank head of commodities Vivek Dhar.

The war's closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world's oil normally flows, has left much of the world scrambling for commodities like diesel.

"The market is screaming for that diesel right now," Mr Dhar said.

Pipelines that bypass the strait have alleviated some of the pressure but have been damaged in the conflict.

Mr Dhar said only about half the amount of crude oil from before the war is being exported from the Persian Gulf.

Oil tankers in and near the Strait of Hormuz are being attacked during transit. (AP/ISNA)

He believed the price of diesel would soon be more than the market would be able to stomach, with attacks on Russia's diesel refineries worsening the global shortage.

"So basically whatever's coming out of the Strait is what you have," he said.

Refiners are not letting a crisis go to waste, with the profit margin per barrel, known as the "crack spread", increasing from around $24 to $69.

Australia is particularly vulnerable to those price swings as it imports around 80 to 90 per cent of its diesel.

Farming is a particularly volatile industry with slim profit margins. (ABC News: Jostina Basta)

Mr Roles, who is also chair of the New South Wales Farmers Grain Committee, said "it's not like we can pass on these additional costs".

"We sell into a global commodity market, so we're price takers as well," he said.

"We're basically taking the international price."

It is not just diesel that is pushing up costs for farmers.

The rising price of fertiliser and pesticides which are made from petrochemicals, using oil products, has cut into their margins as well.

Volatile fuel prices the real problem

That cost of rising fuel prices flows into the rest of the economy, and businesses have to pay more to transport their products, Container Transport Alliance Australia's director Neil Chambers said.

Neil Chambers says the rising costs of transport will make it harder for businesses to ship their products. (Supplied: Scott Jewell)

"The price [of diesel] has risen dramatically, over 50 per cent, and that puts a great strain on cash flow," Mr Chambers said.

He said transport businesses were immediately passing higher fuel prices onto their customers.

"We haven't got a fuel supply crisis, we have a fuel cost crisis," he said.

One example of the pressures is at Butler Freight Services, based adjacent to Australia's busiest container port in Melbourne.

Before the conflict, transport companies like Butler would update their fuel surcharge, a fee on top of standard costs, once a month or every few months.

"Currently it's once every week. That's because of the volatility in fuel pricing," Mr Chambers said.

That means fuel increases are being passed down the supply chain and through to the eventual consumer much more quickly.

Track the latest petrol and diesel prices around Australia See what's happening with petrol and diesel prices near you, updated constantly.

That is unlikely to change, according to Mr Chambers.

"It's going to be a number of years of higher fuel prices," he said.

Fuel prices worsen inflation

Transportation impacts the cost of almost all goods, so the potential for diesel prices to further drive up inflation is real.

Inflation, the speed of price rises, is already above the rate the central bank wants to see, between 2 and 3 per cent a year.

For the year to July prices rose at 3.6 per cent, the same speed as the previous month.

Sarah Hunter says the RBA isn't underestimating the impact of higher diesel prices on inflation. (ABC News)

Speaking earlier this week, Reserve Bank chief economist and assistant governor Sarah Hunter called the Middle East crisis "the big unknown" in the global economy.

"Clearly prices have tracked up [and] just recently that is flowing into the local economy," she said.

Dr Hunter said regional areas were "more exposed" to the shock than people who lived in cities.

With no end in sight to the conflict, it meant higher prices, lower profit margins and more economic pain.

"We don't underestimate that," she said.

World.title: Larissa Lambert, Australia’s empress of R&B, is ready for her close-up
World.content:
Larissa Lambert: “You’ve just got to get to a place of not giving a f---, and that’s when it all flows out.”

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

If R&B has been perennially overlooked in Australia, Larissa Lambert has been its best-kept secret. The 30-year-old has a voice so warm and vibrant it could melt your butter, fry your pancakes, boil your coffee – the full breakfast. It’s the kind of thing a religious person might call “a gift from God”. When did she know she had it? “This is so cliche but, honestly, I knew since I could f---ing talk,” Lambert says with all the bluntness that’s made her a social media favourite. “I have memories of my family and people at school sitting around me being like, ‘do it again!’, and I’d sing a line and they’d be like, ‘whoa!’ So I knew, like, ‘I’m good at this’. There was no doubt about it. I had no plan B. I was like, ‘I’m gonna be a singer’.” More than a decade into her career, with viral successes and plaudits from superstars like SZA and Justin Bieber to her name, she’s finally releasing her long-awaited debut album, Yearning. Filled with her effortless vocals, production flourishes that flitter between Y2K nostalgia and club trends, and writing that coolly probes her desires and insecurities, the album is a cohesive triumph. It begs the question: why did it take so long? “I just never felt like I was ready,” says Lambert. “I was always like, ‘people are expecting so much from me’, so it needed to feel authentic. It needed to be me.” Wearing black leather pants, her pierced septum gleaming, Lambert looks every bit the star as we speak in a room the size of a confessional in Virgin Music’s offices in inner-Sydney’s Chippendale. We’re barely 10 minutes into the interview when she begins to outline the harrowing challenges that, at least partly, skewered the timeline to her debut. Three years ago, Lambert suffered psychosis following withdrawals from an addiction to prescription Valium. “My brain basically just went f---ing haywire. It took me a whole year to get back to normal,” she says. “During a psychosis, your whole world is flipped. I just felt hopeless. It’s f---ing scary.



“It’s like a panic attack on steroids. Everyone’s different with how they experience psychosis; some people can be aware they’re in it and some people can completely black out. I understood what was going on but you’re in an intense state of paranoia, you have intrusive thoughts, your moods are up and down. Writing was the only thing that was keeping me sane.” She’d been through drug psychosis before, years prior when she was 22. “That was from an edible, actually, because even marijuana is a big trigger for psychosis. If your family has a history of mental health issues you should never touch it,” she says. She’s more protective of herself now. “No substances, I’m 100 per cent sober,” she says. “I used to have a very addictive personality and I couldn’t say no, couldn’t turn down the party phase. Growing up, it was always like that. “The music industry, artists, creatives – we’re so addicted to escapism, especially if you come from not the best upbringing. You tend to emotionally regulate through substances. In my case, that’s what it was. I never knew how to deal with my emotions, so I would smoke to get out of them or take some sleepers to mellow out. “It’s so toxic, man, and it catches up to you. It caught up to me. So I’m 100 per cent sober, straighty-180 now. Maybe a little sip of wine here and there, but otherwise … I can’t, it’s not worth it.” Lambert had been working at a pizza shop in her home town, Rio Bravo in Ballarat – “incredible pizza, one of my favourite jobs I ever had” – when she scored her first break. At 16, a scout from The X Factor, then airing on the Seven Network, phoned, inviting her to an artist development camp after seeing videos she’d posted on Facebook of herself singing on her bedroom floor. “I thought it was a scam,” Lambert recalls. “He was like, ‘we’ve got this camp, it’s $500’. I was like, you’re f---ing joking.” After verifying the call was legit, she used funds she’d been saving to buy a laptop to accept the offer. Her boss at the pizza shop paid for her flights to Sydney. “He was a blessing,” says Lambert. At the camp, she was successfully recruited into the girl group Paris Inc.



“It was fun. It felt like training,” Lambert recalls of her time on The X Factor. “I needed it for my confidence. I used to be really, like, inwards. Being in the girl group helped me come out of my shell.” In 2019, after Paris Inc split, Lambert received interest from the States; a girl who was working with R&B star Jeremih – famed for his DJ Mustard-produced smash Don’t Tell ’Em, still a barbershop staple – found her on Instagram and pitched her to the singer. “He took me under his wing,” says Lambert. “He mentored me about how the States works, the culture, the people, certain flows and how to add more pockets to my songs. I’m so grateful for him. He wanted to sign me at the time but I ended up turning it down because I wanted to stay independent.” Larissa Lambert’s debut album, Yearning, has been a long time coming. Even now, Lambert remains an independent artist. She must’ve had major labels chasing her for ages? “Oh yeah, I’ve had an offer from pretty much every single label, but it’s always just been a standard label deal,” she says. What does that mean? “It means they’ll give you a label deal out of the 1980s where there’s nothing – literally, less than minus – in your favour,” she says, laughing. Her current arrangement with Virgin Music is a distribution deal, where she owns her masters and licenses them to the label for a set period. “Virgin were the only label that respected me, understood the vision and listened,” Lambert explains. “With a lot of the major labels, you’re just another TikTok viral sensation they’re gonna sign, and if you pop off, you pop off. I feel like labels have lost the art of developing an artist.” When labels approached her in the past, being a young artist, how did she know the deals weren’t in her best interests? “My intuition, I guess. It just never felt right.”



She pauses and recalibrates. “Actually, you know what it was? It’s because I went viral before I ever signed anything, so I started seeing my cheques!” she says with a laugh. “And knowing that a label would take 80 per cent of my earnings just to say they have me but not do anything for me? I was like, that is stupid, you’re not taking my money!” Back in 2021, a cover she sang of SWV’s Weak went “stupid viral” on TikTok. “Someone from the Philippines, and Indonesia as well, they started a dance trend to it. All these different trends took off. It was like a tree branch. It just kept going.” Lambert once said the viral cover made her “a lot of money”, enough to keep her career going. How so? “Well, I dropped the full cover on Spotify and then, you know, you make money from the master percentage. But then all the publishing obviously goes to SWV. So they made a good chunk off me, too!” She’d lucked into the exact kind of virality record labels employ entire departments to manufacture. “Yeah, and you can’t,” says Lambert. “You can definitely make a song viral if you put millions of dollars into it but is it gonna stick, though? Authentic viral is so special but no one knows the f---ing recipe. If I did, I’d go viral every time.” The experience gave her a unique insight into industry machinations, which was significant when record labels came calling. “They literally take 80 per cent of your earnings – it’s crazy! Like, how are you supposed to live? Off a tiny advance that’s supposed to last you three years? It doesn’t make sense. In my opinion, if you’re an artist and you sign to a label, you shouldn’t be working a nine-to-five. You should be able to put all your time and focus on your music and have an advance that will last you,” she says. “But, like, it’s a risk on both sides because labels are also risking a lot of money on certain artists, so I get it. But that’s why I chose to stay independent with a distro deal, and I vouch for that for any up-and-coming artists as well. It’s good because it forces you to learn every angle, so you’re never getting taken advantage of.”



On social media, Lambert’s gift has earned praise from SZA, Bieber and Ty Dolla $ign, a case of game recognising game. Do such co-signs translate into anything tangible? “Like, does it bring people to me?” Lambert asks. “Oh, of course. Especially when they’ve shared my stuff, they put on so many new listeners. But just having the recognition from them is crazy. The fact that my idols are seeing me and appreciating me? It’s a huge pat on the back to let me know I’m doing something right.” It makes it even more intriguing that she didn’t release her debut album sooner. Any other young artist would’ve been convinced to capitalise on the moment while there’s heat. “I know, I look back and I wonder if I could have, but I don’t think it would have worked,” says Lambert. The key to unlocking her album, she says, was linking up with executive producer Khaled Rohaim. Rohaim – a Grammy-nominated Sydney producer who has worked with stars including Rihanna, Doja Cat and The Kid Laroi – had long had Lambert in his sights. “He was trying to get me to leave the girl group when I was 17 and I was like, ‘who is this guy?’,” Lambert says, laughing. “I had no idea what he’d done but he actually has some of the most insane credits. Eventually I ended up doing a session with him three years ago, and we’ve been inseparable ever since.” The album’s emotional through line lies in its title. “Yearning” is a term that has had a cultural blow-up this year, a buzzword that’s defined a generation’s pushback against the casual nonchalance of online dating. It’s also long been the central emotion in R&B, from Jodeci’s Feenin’ to Kehlani’s Folded. “It’s about letting go of ego, bringing back authenticity and longing and openness,” says Lambert of her album’s message. “We’re in such a culture of being independent and being within yourself, and it’s toxic because we’re not meant to be like that. It makes people go insane and get depressed.”

World.title: Briggs, Australia’s most beloved rapper, goes hardcore
World.content:
Briggs, with Big Noter bandmate Steve Smith (drums): “I’ve always done something different, so this shouldn’t be such a surprise.”

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

As a solo artist and one half of ARIA-winning duo A.B. Original (with Trials), Yorta Yorta artist Adam Briggs has long been one of Australia’s most acclaimed and popular rappers. But he has a simple response for anyone who might be confounded by his sudden, and unexpected, pivot to hardcore punk. “Those imaginary lines of ‘you can’t do this’ and ‘you shouldn’t do that because you do this’? First of all, I’ll do what the f--- I want,” he says with a laugh from his home in Melbourne. “Second, I do things I’m passionate about and that I have my heart in. I just wanted to do something different. I wanted to make a different kind of record and just explore. “If you look at my career and the things I’ve done, I’ve always done different shit. I’ve done rap, comedy, written kids’ books, written episodes of TV. I’ve acted in films, I’ve acted in TV. I’ve always done something different, so this shouldn’t be such a surprise.” The perfectly titled Songs in the Key of Wrestling is Briggs’ debut hardcore album with his new band Big Noter (the band also features Steve Smith on drums, with Leigh Davies on guitars and Craig Strain on bass). If the sonic delivery is different, the tenacity is signature Briggs. Over thunderous riffage, opener My Genocide preaches collective liberation; It’s All Good Til It’s Not questions moral complacency; and Identity celebrates pride in self-determination. Album closer What’s the Matter with Adam? is a rhetorical dig at our mental health crisis.



“There are all these sick people, so at some point the system has failed,” says Briggs. “Even for me, I’m looked at as some kind of well-off dude, but for me to be able to get in to see a psych, it’s taken nearly 18 months. Some people don’t have the capacity and the facilities to wait that long.” What prompted him to seek mental health treatment? “Just trying to be a better person, man, that’s all. I’m not an emergency case, I don’t hear voices and stuff,” he says with a laugh. “I’m a fortunate person and I get to express myself in a lot of interesting ways, and I’m forever grateful for that, but I don’t measure my personal success as the benchmark for where we’re at as a society and as a community. If my mates are struggling, so am I. “People will talk about going to see their personal trainer and whatever, but there’s a stigma around seeking therapy or seeking mental health treatment. The sooner we equate physical health and mental health as one and the same, the better off we’re all going to be.” ‘It’s the same moral code and the same values, which to me is the most important part of anything I do.’ It’s immediately clear on Songs in the Key of Wrestling that no matter the genre, righteous fury remains the driving force behind Briggs’ creative expression. His work is a literal manifestation of John Lydon’s famous claim that “anger is an energy”. “For sure, but I have to balance it with humour,” Briggs says, pointing to songs like What Ya Swingin’ At and Big Noter (recorded with Idles singer Joe Talbot) that revel in brash braggadocio.



“It’s meant to be over-the-top, like an action movie, the kind of stuff we grew up on. Because the thing is, when I’m angry, bro, I can’t focus. I’ve got to be Zen when I write, I’ve got to be calm to focus, and that’s when the anger comes through. But even when they’re angry, these songs are fun. Because there’s a release to it. Finally, you get to breathe.” Hip-hop and hardcore have always lived side by side for Briggs. As a ’90s kid growing up in Shepparton in country Victoria, Rage and Recovery were his gateways to heavy music. “Scratch the Surface by Sick of It All, that was a huge one for me,” Briggs recalls. “And then I found Terror’s One with the Underdogs EP when that dropped. That was very much my kind of shit.” Born in the streets and community halls and fuelled by alienation, hip-hop and hardcore have always shared more similarities than differences. It’s Public Enemy sporting Minor Threat tees. Ice-T fronting Body Count. Even Beastie Boys were a hardcore band before they bought an 808 drum machine. From hip-hop to hardcore: “The boundaries are imaginary, bro. They don’t exist,” says Briggs. Aaron Lee Noyes “And Sick of It All are a band from Queens, you know what I mean?” adds Briggs. “I hung out with them for a bit, and Lou [Koller, the Sick of It All singer, who died in July] – rest in peace, legend – was telling me stories about seeing Kool G Rap outside his high school. They were up on all their rap shit because they’re all from the same ’hood.” Even today’s biggest hip-hop stars, like Travis Scott and rage-rappers Playboi Carti and Ken Carson embrace the overlap. Look at their gigs and they resemble hardcore shows: there’s a circle pit going, kids are stage-diving and slam-dancing, complete release. “The boundaries are imaginary, bro. They don’t exist,” says Briggs of the genre switch. “It’s what I felt doing this Big Noter record. It’s the same message, it’s just how I’ve chosen to deliver it. Not much really had to change. It’s the same moral code and the same values, which to me is the most important part of anything I do.”



In a nod to the overlap, he recruited some famous friends to appear on the album. On What’s the Matter with Adam?, Tom Morello of iconic rap-rockers Rage Against the Machine contributes a typically blistering guitar solo that sounds like turntablism-meets-Space Invaders. On the interlude A Message from Chuck, Briggs gets his friend Chuck D of Public Enemy to deliver a few words shouting out Yorta Yorta Nation and calling out January 26. “I wanted to pay homage to rap because I didn’t want to create this idea that I was leaving hip-hop,” Briggs says. “When I wrote a kids’ book I wasn’t leaving hip-hop. When I was writing for Disenchantment with Matt Groening I wasn’t leaving hip-hop. But suddenly I shift genres and I’ve left something behind? Nah, that’s not it. “Having Chuck on the record is just an acknowledgment of the community he’s been a part of as well,” Briggs adds, noting Public Enemy’s famous link-up with heavy music stalwarts Anthrax on 1991’s Bring the Noise. “He sent it back with multiple takes and I was like, sick.” It did, however, create one lasting bit of light-hearted concern. “I was saying to a mate, like, in this world of AI, I bet a lot of people will think I just got this AI Chuck D to shout out Shepparton and Yorta Yorta Nation,” he says, laughing. “But f--- it because I know what’s what. A lot of the things I do on my albums and in my career are solely for me, so I don’t even trip.”

World.title: Risky business: Why it’s time to take Tom Cruise seriously again
World.content:
CultureMoviesThe Verdict Risky business: Why it’s time to take Tom Cruise seriously again Jamie Tram September 18, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

I can vividly recall the first time I encountered Tom Cruise: not at the movies or on the living room TV, but in a viral edited GIF of him smothering Oprah with force lightning. For most of the 21st century, following a slew of disastrous TV appearances (not least this famously antagonistic exchange with Peter Overton on 60 Minutes), Cruise’s public reputation has fallen somewhere between megalomaniac and meme. Audiences no longer believe in Cruise as an exceptional everyman, an emblem of America’s conscience, or an international sweetheart. Instead, we’ve come to embrace him as cinema’s hardest working action star. Tom Cruise in Digger. Warner Bros The Mission: Impossible series, which began as a slick Brian De Palma thriller (and only Cruise’s second action role), has since ballooned to a multibillion-dollar phenomenon off the unhinged spectacle of its middle-aged lead actor confronting his mortality in a barrage of cartoonish, real-life stunts. Even for sceptics, there does appear to a universal pleasure (schadenfreude?) in watching a fabulously wealthy man break his ankle on camera for our entertainment. But with the franchise frontman closing the book on the last two decades of blockbuster showmanship and pivoting back to ambitious original fare (see: his upcoming apocalyptic comedy Digger), it’s time we also returned to recognising him seriously as one of our greatest dramatic actors.



Let’s just get this out of the way: the popular notion that Tom Cruise is somehow more of a maladjusted weirdo narcissist than any other celebrity of his calibre, from Brad Pitt to Johnny Depp, is simply PR smoke and mirrors. We are frankly better off abandoning the idea that anyone who’s churned through the machinery of Hollywood since their youth, with a net worth exceeding half a billion dollars, is remotely normal. Even before the confluence of publicity disasters in the mid-2000s (the inevitable result of replacing his long-time publicist with his sister), the pre-millennium Cruise would not have been a graceful fit for our current era of hyper-online, smoothed-over movie stardom. Over the decades, Tom Cruise has deftly moulded his inescapable star persona into an array of idiosyncratic, often subversive performances that illuminate the culture around him. Looking back at his breakout performances as Joel in Risky Business and Maverick in Top Gun, his façade of effortless cool, shaded by two of the most recognisable sunglasses in pop culture, is noticeably stretched tight over an obsessive, constantly over-compensating attitude. This is, after all, a man who tops out at 170cm. That Cruise, the actor, is so transparently eager to impress his audience and outdo his peers – even as a young, relative unknown, he cast off his lucrative Brat Pack association to chart his own course – it made him the perfect Reagan-era leading man. Risky Business, The Color of Money, and even the much-maligned Cocktail set the stage for a young, 20-something Cruise to craft the prototypical grindset bro: a sweaty, vacuously charming protagonist who trades his innocence for the promise of unimaginable wealth.



By proving he could hold his own against an ageing Paul Newman in Money, Cruise also established a winning template that saw some variation of a jacked-up young gun square off with Hollywood legends (including Dustin Hoffman, Robert Duvall and Jack Nicholson) of an older generation. Any Tom Cruise movie is, of course, destined to be consumed by its leading man, but what’s less appreciated is his generosity as a collaborator who coaxes out tantalising new qualities from his co-stars. Notably, Hoffman and Newman both won Academy Awards for Best Actor in their films starring alongside Cruise. In the 1990s, Cruise committed himself to some of the greatest on-screen crashouts committed to celluloid. Where the depths of his arrogance, neuroses and insecurities were hinted at in earlier movies, this decade on screen unravelled his once-bulletproof star persona to perversely captivating ends. Eyes Wide Shut lampooned male impotence; Interview with the Vampire unleashed an immortal with an endlessly self-destructive drive; Magnolia curdled his familiar bravado into loathsome entitlement in his prescient depiction of a showboating pick-up artist. Jerry Maguire can be seen as Cruise’s most direct attempt at reckoning with his status as one of Hollywood’s biggest stars. Playing the titular sports agent who inconveniently develops a conscience, he actively grapples with the dichotomy between Tom Cruise the smarmy bullshit artist and Tom Cruise the human being. At his core, Cruise excels at playing someone trying very, very hard to be normal – and when the pretence slips, his talent at going nuclear is virtually unparalleled. In a movie stuffed with famous quotes, it’s worth noting this one line that would loom over his transition into middle-age: “24 hours ago, man, I was hot. Now, I’m a cautionary tale.” Tom Cruise stars in Digger. Warner Bros

World.title: ASX set to rise, Wall Street climbs as oil prices slide and pressure from the bond market eases
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to rise, Wall Street climbs as oil prices slide and pressure from the bond market eases Stan Choe September 18, 2026 — 5:18am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

US stocks are rising and recovering most of their losses for the week. Falling oil prices and easing pressure from the bond market helped Wall Street reverse many of its moves from the prior day, when the Federal Reserve hiked its main interest rate for the first time in years and suggested more may be ahead as it tries to get the nation’s high inflation under control. Wall Street’s benchmark index is on track for just its second gain in the last nine sessions. Bloomberg The S&P 500 climbed 1.1 per cent and was on track for just its second rise in the last nine days. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 358 points, or 0.7 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite was 1.6 per cent higher. The Australian sharemarket is set to rise, with futures at 4.57am AEST pointing to a gain of 57 points, or 0.7 per cent, at the open. The ASX added 0.4 per cent on Thursday. The Australian dollar was stronger at US71.11¢.



Stocks got a boost after the price for a barrel of Brent crude oil slid 1 per cent to $US104.79. That’s down sharply from the nearly $US110 it reached earlier in the week on worries that the war with Iran will keep oil bottled up in the Middle East instead of going to customers worldwide. Brent is of course still much more expensive than the $US72 per barrel that it cost earlier this year, but Thursday’s slide helped pull yields lower in the bond market and removed some pressure on stocks. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.95 per cent from 5.01 per cent late Wednesday. Related Article Aviation Qantas ground staff set to strike over ‘Joyce-era’ bargaining agreements Higher yields make it more expensive for everyone to borrow money, from the US government to people looking to buy houses to businesses wanting to build data centers. That in turn slows the economy. The Fed on Wednesday raised the short-term interest rate that it controls, the federal funds rate, by a quarter of a percentage point for its first hike in more than three years. Officials also indicated at least one more increase may be coming this year and that the Fed may then keep the federal funds rate high through next year.



The signals sent Wall Street on a roller coaster. Stocks initially held onto their gains from earlier in the day after the Fed made its announcement Wednesday. They then slid sharply before recovering a chunk of the losses before trading ended for the day. On the upside for markets, the shift to higher interest rates built confidence that the Fed is committed to getting inflation back to its target of 2 per cent. Questions had begun to bubble in the summer about whether it would feel pressure from President Donald Trump, who is calling for lower interest rates. And the short-term cost of pain for the economy could be worth it if it gets inflation under control following years of staying too high. On the downside for markets, higher rates undercut prices for stocks and other investments. When investors are earning more in interest from owning bonds, which are considered safer investments, they’re less willing to pay high prices for other kinds of investments. That’s beyond the effect higher rates have on slowing the economy in hopes of removing fuel for inflation. Some reports on Thursday signalled the US economy may be strong enough to withstand higher interest rates. One said fewer US workers applied for unemployment benefits last week. Another said that manufacturing growth in the mid-Atlantic region was stronger than economists expected. Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said on Wednesday that a strengthening economy is one of the reasons Fed officials moved to raise interest rates after keeping them on hold earlier this year.



He also cited “geopolitics,” along with the threat that increases in prices it’s causing could filter out and push up inflation elsewhere. That’s likely a nod to the war with Iran and its effect on oil prices. On Wall Street, stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry continued to rebound following their worldwide slide on Monday. Nvidia climbed 2.6 per cent, and Advanced Micro Devices rose 6.5 per cent. That was even though OpenAI disclosed six more reports of “unexpected or concerning” behaviour in AI models. Leaders of the AI industry over the weekend called for a slowdown in development to address safety issues for humanity. Related Article Opinion

Racism My accent is unremarkable. But it has almost certainly helped me Millie Muroi Economics Writer Stocks of several homebuilders also rose, even though a report showed the industry broke ground on fewer new homes last month than economists expected. The housing industry has been one of the hardest hit by the climb for the 10-year Treasury’s yield, which topped 5 per cent this week for the first time since 2023 and has sent mortgage rates higher.



Thursday’s ease in yields helped offer some support, and D.R. Horton rose 1.5 per cent, while PulteGroup added 0.8 per cent. Rival Lennar wavered throughout the day and was most recently down 0.1 per cent after reporting weaker profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected. In stock markets abroad, indexes rose across much of Europe following a weaker finish in Asia. London’s FTSE 100 rose 1.2 per cent after the Bank of England decided to keep its interest rates on hold. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: Driverless metro trials step up a gear as target opening date looms
World.content:
NationalNSWSydney Metro Driverless metro trials step up a gear as target opening date looms Matt O'Sullivan September 18, 2026 — 5:05am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The green light has been given for trials of driverless trains without a supervisor keeping watch on board along the final section of Sydney’s $30 billion M1 metro line a month out from the targeted opening date. It marks a step forward in the rigorous process to gain approval for passenger services on the 13-kilometre stretch of metro line between Sydenham and Bankstown. Confidential Sydney Metro documents have cited “mid-October” as the most recent target date for the opening. The opening of the southwest section of the M1 will hinge on final approval for passenger services by the country’s rail regulator. The opening of the metro line between Bankstown and Sydenham hinges on approval from the national rail regulator. Sitthixay Ditthavong The Office of the National Rail Safety Regulator said that once all the evidence and documentation supporting the safety case for the Southwest Metro section was received, and its due diligence had been completed, the application for accreditation could be finalised and granted.



The watchdog said it would assess the final application as quickly as possible, but noted that it “requires sufficient time to undertake the work”. Related Article Sydney Metro Surge in demand for Sydney’s metro trains leaves passengers waiting “As with other projects of this type, the final assessment, ahead of services beginning, will be to verify that all risks to safety have been identified and that the appropriate systems and processes are in place and working to manage these risks effectively,” it said. Two years ago, the Minns government announced the planned date for the opening of the M1 line’s city-section between Chatswood and Sydenham a month out, only to be forced to delay it by several weeks because it had not secured approval from the national regulator. Transport Minister John Graham said he wanted to give communities an opening date they could rely on, and that depended on the independent regulator’s important work. “This is not a tick-and-flick exercise. This a real-life, independent safety assessment process,” he said.



Graham said the delivery of data and documentation to the national rail regulator was an “iterative process and is in line with planned milestones”. He confirmed that the line’s operator, Metro Trains Sydney, had gained approval on Thursday for trial running of driverless operations without a supervisor on board the trains to step in if required. The metro station at Bankstown is at the southwest end of the 66-kilometre M1 line. Sitthixay Ditthavong The final stage of the M1 line has added complexities such as mechanical gap fillers between curved platforms and driverless trains. Ibises and other wildlife entering the rail corridor have regularly triggered a detection system. Sydney Metro said documents would continue to be submitted to the rail regulator “over the coming weeks in line with planned milestones as part of the progressive assurance process”.





In mid-2018, the former Coalition government told commuters that the line would need to be closed for three to six months. Even before it closed in September 2024, the Minns government said the shutdown might last longer than its earlier estimates of 12 months.
