World.title: Labour's proposed corporate homicide charges welcomed by Pike River Mine families
World.content:
Labour promises to introduce a corporate homicide offence carrying a punishment of life imprisonment, if it's elected.

Families of those killed in the Pike River Mine disaster have long campaigned for the charge.

Labour workplace relations and safety spokesperson Jan Tinetti said New Zealand had a sobering record on health and safety at work.

"We have some of the highest workplace deaths in the developed world," she said.

"This is a glaring hole that we don't have as a deterrent for those people, those employers that are not ensuring that there's strong health and safety provisions in their workplace."

Under the party's proposed law, a person or company could be found guilty, if they had a legal duty of care, and exposed anyone to a risk of death or serious injury, and if someone then died.

An individual could be sentenced to life in prison and companies could be fined up to $10 million.

Tinetti hoped that would be enough incentive for companies to strengthen health and safety practices, so no prosecutions would be necessary.

The United Kingdom had 30 convictions since the offence was introduced in 2008, she said.

Tinetti said Labour had worked with unions, employers and families of the Pike River victims on the policy.

"We all remember those 29 men and we do not want to see that happen again in this country," she said.

"This could be the deterrent that would have stopped or could have stopped that happening, but it is hard to say in hindsight."

'Fantastic' - Pike River campaigner

In 2010, a methane-fuelled explosion ripped through the Pike River coal mine on the South Island's West Coast, killing 29 workers.

Sonya Rockhouse's 21-year-old son Ben was one of them.

She and Anna Osborne, who's husband Milt also died, had since campaigned for tougher health and safety laws, including a corporate manslaughter charge.

Rockhouse said Labour's policy was "fantastic" and hoped to see it eventually introduced into law.

"If we had had corporate homicide or corporate manslaughter, we wouldn't be where we are now," she said.

"It's too late for us... but at least we can leave a legacy of knowing that those that come in the future will be far better off in the workplace."

She hoped the threat of life in prison or a big fine would be enough to make change.

"I think the majority, it will make them think twice about making sure that health and safety is a priority in their companies," she said.

"People who are in charge and who knowingly don't make the workplace safe, they need to be held to account."

Rockhouse said her work would never be done, and she and Osborne, among others, would push governments of any stripe to ensure people were kept safe at work.

They recently rallied against an overhaul of health and safety laws, which they warned would risk a workplace disaster.

The minister in charge, Brooke van Velden, said the bill offered commonsense changes that increased certainty, eased compliance costs and improved safety.

World.title: Woman describes father's death after nine hours in waiting room
World.content:
Kiwis who have experienced the disastrous effects of an overloaded healthcare system are challenging politicians to explain how they will right the ship.

Tayla Horsburgh, whose father Brent Horsburgh died at Waikato Hospital after nine hours in the waiting room, was among those gathered in Auckland's Three Kings for a community meeting on Thursday night to mark World Patient Safety Day.

"In addition to the hospital being over 100 percent capacity, they were also four doctors down and two nurses down during the afternoon shift," she recalled about the day her father died.

"Mum received a call from the hospital at one in the morning, saying he had collapsed and they were doing CPR and to get to the hospital as quickly as we could."

Tayla, alongside her sister Jordyn and mother Tracey, were told to wait in the family room.

"In the meantime, there was a nurse standing at the door and mum said to her 'can you just tell me if he's okay', and she said 'yep'," Tayla said.

"The doctor then came in moments later, and told us they could not resuscitate him and he had passed away. This was such a horrible experience and that nurse gave us a false sense of hope."

Fellow panelist Bernie Braithwaite had survived with multiple myeloma, a type of blood cancer, for fifteen years.

"After the Christchurch earthquakes I went to donate blood and quickly moved to donating plasma," he said.

"About two months into that I got a note from the blood service saying they had seen an irregularity."

One of the drugs he needed to survive wasn't funded by Pharmac.

Tayla Horsburgh's father died at Waikato Hospital after waiting for hours in the ED. Supplied/ Waikato Hospital

"That drug, which is now funded by Pharmac, at the time it was not, it's a drug called lenalidomide. It cost me $22,000 for a three-month supply," he said.

"Every time I picked up a little capsule, it was $458, you don't want to drop it down the sink, I can tell you. Your hand shakes a bit when you stick it in your mouth, at $458."

He urged the politicians in the audience - representatives from each major party, except for Te Pāti Māori - to view medicine as an investment rather than a cost.

"As long as we continue with a cost approach rather than an investment approach, we'll never build a valid case for not just making step-change but making leap-change in how we fund not just medicines but the health system in general," he said.

"If you can fund and continue to keep people as vital and contributing members of society, they'll return a hell of a lot more than they'll cost you."

He later asked the politicians what they would do to address gaps in Pharmac's coverage, and whether they would commit to a long-term bipartisan approach.

"We're very proud of our policy to close the medicines gap with Australia," ACT's Auckland Central candidate Antonia Modkova said.

"The ACT Party is proposing to increase the portion of the health budget spent on medicines by one percent each year until 2033 to close the medicines gap."

Opportunity's Northcote candidate Cody Marsh, a former paramedic, said bipartisanship was central to the party's healthcare policy.

"We want cross-party agreement. It's the only way this is going to survive consecutive governments," he said.

Plunket nurses facing unprecedented workload in 'healthcare crisis' Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

"Policies like ACT's, we're willing to work with them on that, but I think we also need to understand where you're taking that funding from. Where is that money being taken from?"

National's Carlos Cheung, the MP for Mt Roskill, echoed the call for bipartisanship.

"We are from different parties, and we have different approaches to the healthcare system, but at the end of the day we all want a better health system for every single person here," he said.

Labour's Phil Twyford, the MP for Te Atatū, didn't commit to a specific policy.

"We do need to spend more on medicines, and we'll have something to say closer to the election when the government has opened its financial books," he said

"Labour is a big supporter and always has been of Pharmac because of the potential for it to deliver, and the record of it delivering value for money."

Gareth Hall, who lost his 16-year-old daughter Maddy to suicide, asked the panel what they would do to keep mentally ill children safe.

"We need a better community response to support parents, to support children, and people who actually know more than just empathy but how to wrap around the support that's needed," NZ First's Glendene candidate Alfred Ngaro said.

Green Mt Albert candidate Ricardo Menéndez March said his party would expand youth services throughout the country.

"These are critical services that help actually support young people, especially those who may have a complicated relationship with their parents," he said.

World.title: Improving safety on West Auckland rail crossings will take decades
World.content:
At peak times, 12 trains pass through the Glenview Road crossing every hour. Within six months, that will increase to 16 trains per hour.

It is estimated it will cost around $3 billion and take 30 years to make rail crossings safer across West Auckland.

This week, Aucklanders have been celebrating the opening of the City Rail Link, but work on a critical part of the rail system has barely started.

Residents in one West Auckland community say they have been pleading for changes to a level crossing that is a major safety concern, but that could be decades away.

The level crossing on Glenview Road in Glen Eden is one of 21 places across West Auckland where roads, footpaths and rail lines intersect.

At peak times, 12 trains pass through every hour, and within three to six months, that will increase to 16 trains per hour.

Emily Simes and Heather Tanguay from Glen Eden Residents' Association say the Glenview Road level crossing and intersection needs urgent attention. RNZ / Erin Johnson

Glen Eden Residents' Association chair Heather Tanguay said the road around the crossing gets clogged and cars are backed up down the road. With the increasing frequency of trains, that's only going to get worse, she said.

"Of all the business that we've conducted since the residents association started, this area here has been the priority."

Tanguay said residents had known for years that making the level crossing safe would be "complicated and difficult".

But closing the crossing entirely is not practical. The rail line goes through the middle of the suburb: the town centre and houses are on one side, a school, the fire station and the largest cemetery in the country are on the other side, along with more homes.

Residents' association member Emily Simes said when the school day finishes at Glen Eden Primary the level crossing and intersection "just go crazy", and at peak times it's busy with traffic, pedestrians, "and good luck trying to bike".

"The safety of this intersection is paramount, and it needs a proper solution absolutely as soon as possible."

The rapid increase in housing intensification in recent years means "it makes no sense to push this out further decades", Simes said.

In preparation for the City Rail Link and more frequent trains, 16 crossings have been closed or replaced across Auckland in the past decade.

Three pedestrian bridges have been built in East and South Auckland in the last year, and work is underway on three road bridges in Takaanini. That work is expected to cost around $800 million.

Funding for level crossing replacements across West Auckland is yet to be sorted.

Glen Eden station is right beside the level crossing, which further complicates any changes, Auckland Transport says. RNZ / Erin Johnson

Waitākere ward councillor Shane Henderson said the west was intensifying rapidly and could not be forgotten.

"... the Henderson-Massey area in particular has taken the most resource consents of any area of Auckland over the entire super city history. Those populations have exploded and will keep exploding.

"We deserve the investment that comes with that. We deserve to produce a fantastic life for people out there and part of that is helping them get around."

Safety was a "huge" part of why that investment needed to happen quickly, he said.

"We've had some tragic incidents on the (western) line, and we've lost lives and my heart goes out to everyone affected."

Auckland Transport says there's "no easy options" for West Auckland's level crossings, and this one at Glenview Road is "complex". RNZ / Erin Johnson

Last week, a school boy died after being hit by a train near Baldwin Avenue station.

"We can't afford to be losing lives on our network. That's a call to action for this work to make it as urgent as possible," Henderson said.

Keenan Matthes died when he was struck by a train in Rānui in 2017 while out for a run.

His mother, Karamea Matthes, told RNZ the risk to pedestrians could be prevented by removing pedestrians from rail tracks.

"I believe pedestrians and tracks do not go together...because trains cannot stop in an instant, trains run much faster. We are pushing for more of them, not just during peak times, but throughout the day."

Matthes said she knew separating trains and pedestrians was expensive.

"That's something that we can work towards, and a future where there is no public on tracks, I can't wait for that to happen."

Karamea Matthes says she can't wait for a future where people and trains are separated. RNZ / Erin Johnson

Auckland Transport head of level crossings Tom Willetts said options were being developed to replace or remove rail level crossings from Maungawhau to Swanson.

"There are no easy options. These crossings are often located in densely populated areas, and there are a number of challenging trade-offs and impacts on local communities to consider, ranging from changes to current journeys to construction disruption and impacts on properties."

AT is currently talking to the public about proposed options to replace level crossings between Kingsland and Mount Albert, where the first increase in train frequencies is expected to be needed for growing passenger numbers, Willetts said.

Shane Henderson would like to see Glen Eden and Rānui included in the early discussions.

"They need to be part of that inner-West conversation... At the very least, locking in time frames, locking in funding."

Willetts said investigations were continuing for options from Avondale to Swanson, which were expected to be made public in early 2027.

The timing of the work will depend on funding from council and central government, he said.

At Glenview Road, clear road markings and signage would make an immediate difference, Heather Tanguay said.

Willetts said the area was a priority for short-term improvements to keep traffic flowing and improve safety.

However, as Tanguay is already aware, solving the level crossing conundrum is "difficult".

"The close proximity of the West Coast Road intersection to the rail line makes options such as overbridges or trenches difficult to build due to geometric constraints.

World.title: Student transience falls to lowest point in more than a decade
World.content:
More than 2000 children changed schools twice or more last year - the lowest number of transient students the country has seen in more than a decade of records.

Education Ministry figures showed 1958 moved school twice, 134 moved three times, 36 had four school moves and one child moved schools five times or more.

That dropped the rate of transience to a low of 2.7 in every 1000 children, down from 2.9 the previous year and well below the rate of about five per thousand that prevailed in the mid-2000s.

The ministry said transience was associated with lower achievement at school.

"A study found that school movement had an even stronger effect on educational success than residential movement. There is also evidence that transience can have negative effects on student behaviour, and on short-term social and health experiences," it said.

Māori children had the highest rate of transience at 5.8 per 1000, and accounted for just over half of last year's transient children (1127).

Transience rates were particularly high in Northland (9.3), West Coast (9.1), and Manawatū-Whanganui (7.5).

The ministry's figures also included cumulative transience for a group of 61,593 students who started school in 2020.

By last year, 7537 of that cohort (12.2 percent) had moved schools twice or more.

World.title: Athlete Joanna Wietrzyk apologises for continuing HYROX race after soiling herself
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Australian athlete Joanna Wietrzyk has apologised for continuing to compete in a HYROX competition in China having soiled herself.

Wietrzyk experienced the medical episode during the contest last weekend in Beijing, and went on to win, but has now retroactively withdrawn from the race and handed back all points earned.

The incident went viral on social media, with videos of her continuing the race shared widely.

HYROX, a popular fitness competition launched in Germany in 2017, sees competitors combine running with multiple workout station challenges, including sandbag lunges, burpees, sled pushes and rowing using shared equipment.

The athletics brand, which came under fire over health and safety standards, has since apologised for "not reacting immediately" over the incident.

Wietrzyk, who has faced questions over her decision to continue, has now issued a social media statement.

Joanna Wietrzyk shared an apology online on Thursday, withdrawing and handing back points from the race she won. (Instagram: @joannawietrzyk)

"I want to offer my sincere apology to the people of China, my fellow competitors, the spectators and the HYROX organisers for what happened during the race in Beijing," she said in a post on Instagram.

"I felt completely fit and healthy at the start of the race, with no reason to expect any illness,

" Looking back, I regret the decision to not have stepped off the track. I recognise that I should have made a different choice. "

In the statement, Wietrzyk said she had chosen to retroactively withdraw from the race and hand back the points she earned from competing.

Within the HYROX elite framework, athletes accumulate ranking points based on their placement and finishing time. The points contribute to national and global ranking systems.

"I know my actions had an impact beyond myself, and I am genuinely sorry to everyone who was affected," she said.

"I am learning from this experience and will carry those lessons with me, including remembering that there is more to life than racing and knowing when it is right to step away.

"On reflection, I have decided to retroactively withdraw from the race and forfeit the points I earned."

Joanna Wietrzyk (middle in black top) has issued an apology. (Instagram: joannawietrzyk)

Rules changed after backlash

The incident attracted intense criticism of HYROX's health and safety standards.

HYROX co-founder Moritz Fürste had earlier taken to Instagram to apologise "to all who were directly or indirectly involved".

Social media posts about the incident during the HYROX race in Beijing. (Weibo, RedNote and Douyin)

"HYROX made a mistake by not reacting immediately during the race," he added in a statement on Instagram.

"In the end it is my job to foresee these potential incidents — and I did not."

HYROX apologises after athlete soiling The apology comes after different arms of the organisation tried to explain how the situation was managed after the competition went viral online.

He said new event procedures and rules were being drawn up to "prevent situations like this from happening again".

The rules now state that if a "racer's blood, vomit, urine, or faeces poses a welfare or contamination risk to the racer or to other racers, a Race Director may withdraw the racer from the race on medical grounds".

Before the rule change, competitors were penalised for littering, spitting, or clearing their nostrils onto the race course, which some online described as a double standard.

World.title: Court battle looms for Socceroos star after drug test
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Cristian Volpato is set for a court battle with the Socceroos star's lawyer confirming he will challenge charges that he was driving with cocaine in his system.

The 22-year-old returned a positive roadside reading for cocaine after he was pulled over by police on Sydney's Anzac Bridge on July 24.

He had been driving at 109 kilometres per hour in a 60km/h zone.

He later underwent independent testing at a private clinic, where it was claimed he returned a negative reading.

However, Volpato was then sent for a secondary oral fluid test by police, which again confirmed a positive result for cocaine.

He copped a $722 fine as a result of the second positive test, but on Thursday his lawyer Paul McGirr confirmed to AAP that he had elected to take the matter to court.

Volpato has maintained his innocence, insisting he never knowingly ingested the substance.

He also undertook a test when he returned to Italy, which was negative, his club side Sassuolo said.

The Sydney-born player was a late inclusion for the Socceroos' World Cup campaign after switching his international allegiance from Italy to Australia on the eve of the tournament.

In a statement provided to AAP, a Football Australia spokesperson confirmed the organisation was aware of reports concerning Volpato and a "traffic matter currently subject to a police process".

"As the matter is ongoing, it would not be appropriate for Football Australia to comment further at this time," the spokesperson said.

Regardless, the positive reading on Volpato's secondary police test could have major ramifications for his availability heading into January's Asian Cup.

Sources have previously told AAP that Volpato could be hauled before FA's disciplinary and ethics committee, where the sport's governing body has the power to suspend him from national team action.

The 22-year-old is currently playing in Serie A with Sassuolo but is sidelined with a right leg injury sustained against Bologna this month.

AAP

World.title: 'Cinema' expected as rival wingers go to battle one last time
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Robert Toia will have a front-row seat to the last instalment of the battle between teammate Mark Nawaqanitawase and Ronaldo Mulitalo, and the Sydney Roosters centre is bracing himself for more box-office entertainment.

"Cinema, that's what I expect — [another chapter in] an ongoing battle and I think if we get the win that will top it off," Toia said.

Saturday's sudden-death semifinal could be Nawaqanitawase's last in the NRL, with the 26-year-old former Wallabies star switching back to the 15-man code with Japanese side Saitama Wild Knights.

Few could have imagined the impact Nawaqanitawase would have had in rugby league when he crossed codes after the Paris Olympics.

There have been highlights in just about every game — be it his grubber ahead and tip toe down the sideline against Canterbury last season that was named try of the year, or last weekend's tap-ahead intercept before climbing off the deck and racing away to score against Penrith.

"It's pretty hard to stay alert because you don't know what's going to happen," Toia said.

"I didn't expect him to do what he's been doing, I think he has shocked everyone."

Nawaqanitawase's long-running on-field feud with the sledge-happy Mulitalo — the pair of wingers openly admire each other off it — has made Roosters-Sharks games fixtures to savour.

"There's a bit of competitiveness there but I think that is what makes the game so great — it's the best of the best going at it with each other," said Roosters forward Siua Wong.

Toia's opposite number KL Iro said of Mulitalo: "He can get personal at times but after the game he always makes sure he clears it up straight away and shakes his hand.

"He loves getting in the mix, he's a huge competitor."

Nawaqanitawase has made the switch to rugby league look easy, having won caps for the Kangaroos, played State of Origin for NSW and scored 41 tries in 44 games for the Roosters.

The Roosters and Sharks battle on Saturday night from the Sydney Football Stadium.

AAP

World.title: Canberra is the greatest mystery of the NRLW finals
World.content:
Of all the teams in the fight for the NRLW premiership, Canberra shapes as the ultimate wildcard.

Ahead of the first finals series in club history, the Raiders are a difficult puzzle to solve; for themselves and opponents alike.

Darrin Borthwick's side enter the finals in fifth place with a 6-5 record that belies a strange tendency that developed over the season: more than any other team in the league, they play to their opponent's level.

Can anyone stop the Roosters in the NRLW? After completing the most dominant regular season in NRLW history, the big question around the Sydney Roosters is simple: can anyone hope to stop them?

The Raiders have a winning record against fellow top six teams, highlighted by a 28-4 win over third-placed Broncos, comfortably the Brisbane team's biggest ever NRLW loss.

They even put the gloves up against powerhouses Gold Coast and Sydney Roosters, losing to the two competition heavyweights by a combined 10 points, finishing close enough in both games that they would fancy their chances in a rematch.

But as easily as the Raiders can be inspired by the challenge of taking on the big dogs, they can be complacent when facing teams they should handle easily.

Canberra dropped games to stragglers Parramatta, North Queensland and Cronulla throughout the season, costing them a home final.

As they prepare to head to Campbelltown to take on Wests Tigers in tomorrow night's sudden-death final, they are still trying to work themselves out as they head into the deep waters.

"I've found we've lifted for those bigger teams. We've spoken about that, that we need to believe we can win because if we get that down, our effort and our fight will come," said captain Zahara Temara.

"For some of the other teams who aren't as high on the ladder, we've matched them in terms of effort, and that's disappointing. But we know we can lift for the big teams."

It is an unorthodox way for Canberra to live, but now that only big teams are left, the Raiders' record against the top sides makes them perhaps the best candidate to break open the Roosters-Titans hegemony at the top.

Canberra will lean heavily on Zahara Temara's experience through the finals. (Getty Images: Scott Gardiner )

Temara's experience will be crucial for Canberra, with the clever halfback one of the few Raiders with an extensive finals pedigree, having won a premiership with the Roosters in 2022.

That was the 29-year-old's third grand final, and she admits she took the team's success for granted in the earlier years, something she is desperate to ensure does not happen to her Raiders teammates this time around.

"Something I wish someone told me in those early years at the Roosters was how hard it is to have regrets. I took it seriously, but not as seriously as I could have," said Temara.

"It's hard to make the finals. It's extremely hard to win a grand final, and with the position we're in now, I want them to have no regrets, to realise how we can make history."

That perspective was reinforced by former Roosters teammate and current Canberra co-captain Simaima Taufa, especially after their losing effort in the 2020 grand final.

The Raiders will be without gun lock forward Simaima Taufa tomorrow night. (Getty Images: Mark Nolan)

The sight of the whole-hearted Taufa after the match has never left Temara, and inspires her to this day.

"She gave it her everything, and I didn't feel like I did," said Temara.

"We were all disappointed, but I tell her all the time now I couldn't look at her because I knew I hadn't done everything I could for her and the team.

"I still took it seriously. I just wish I took it as far as she did."

With Taufa sidelined due to suspension, there will be even more responsibility on Temara's shoulders tomorrow night.

The Tigers are polar opposites of the Raiders: they beat every side that missed the finals, but went 1-4 against the other play-off teams, with their sole success coming via a one-point win over Newcastle.

But there are similarities too. The joint venture is also playing in its first finals match, and given Raecene McGregor's form at halfback, the team will also lean heavily on an experienced playmaker to show the way.

Inside Tigers remarkable NRLW turnaround Few expected much from Wests Tigers in this year's NRLW competition, but after winning as many games this season as the rest of their history combined they've proved the doubters wrong ahead of a maiden finals push.

To add to the intrigue, this is a rematch only seven days in the making. The two sides met last Friday night at Leichhardt with the Raiders grinding out a 22-10 victory.

Winger Mackenzie Wiki and centre Leianne Tufuga, who was crowned the club's player of the year, both played blinders as Canberra's strike out wide carried the day.

It ensured the Tigers would enter the finals on the back of consecutive losses, but Temara understands how dangerous they still can be when the stakes are highest.

"Their fight stood out," said Temara

"They were down on the scoreboard, but their fight and hunger to keep coming at us was hard to manage. We got lucky with some errors and penalties that kept the momentum for us."

World.title: Croc-inhabited Fitzroy River gets green light for 2032 Olympic rowing
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

After months of fierce debate, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) has approved rowing and canoe sprint events on Rockhampton's Fitzroy River for the 2032 Brisbane Olympic and Paralympic Games.

The central Queensland river will host the events despite concerns over its suitability, including its crocodile inhabitants.

Premier David Crisafulli said the doubters had been proven wrong with today's announcement.

"The IOC assessment for the site is complete," Mr Crisafulli said.

" The Fitzroy has passed with flying colours. It's official. Signed, sealed and delivered. "

International rowing bodies had questioned the location's suitability for competition. (Supplied: Rockhampton Regional Council)

It comes after World Rowing and Paddle Worldwide also backed an independent technical assessment of the Rockhampton flatwater course.

The Games Independent Infrastructure and Coordination Authority (GIICA) and internationally renowned marine engineering experts WaterProof Marine Consultancy and Services B.V. (WaterProof) completed a comprehensive, independent technical assessment of the Fitzroy River.

The assessment included extensive on-water investigations and modelling to understand how the course would perform under a range of conditions, weather patterns, water levels and flood risk at both Games time and throughout the period leading into the event.

Loading...

Having reviewed the assessment, World Rowing president Jean-Christophe Rolland and Paddle Worldwide president Thomas Konietzko endorsed the central Queensland waterway.

Mr Rolland said it could provide a safe, fair and consistent field of play suitable for Olympic and Paralympic rowing and canoe sprint competitions.

"Based on the extensive analysis undertaken, we now know that the Fitzroy River is capable of providing fair competition conditions during the period of the Games, consistent with the requirements of Olympic and Paralympic rowing," he said.

A future Olympic dream is taking shape on the Fitzroy River, where young rowers could one day compete for their country on their hometown course. (Supplied: Rockhampton Regional Council)

Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleije told state parliament "it's a win for regional Queensland".

"The experts have confirmed it. World Rowing and Paddle Worldwide have endorsed it," he said.

" Rockhampton is good for rowing and rowing is good for 2032 and beyond. "

Rowing Australia and Paddle Australia today acknowledged the completion of the independent technical assessment of the field of play for the Rockhampton flatwater course.

The assessment included detailed surveys of the riverbed and competition course. (Supplied: Rockhampton Regional Council)

"This assessment forms part of the full project validation report," a Rowing Australia spokesperson said.

"Rowing Australia looks forward to the completion of this full report and will continue to support key stakeholders involved in the venue planning process for the Brisbane 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games."

Brisbane 2032 president Andrew Liveris said "thorough and robust" assessments had been undertaken on the Fitzroy River before it was given the tick of approval.

Game on Rocky

Rockhampton Mayor Tony Williams welcomed the confirmation of the Fitzroy River as the venue for rowing at the 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games.

Tony Williams has thanked the state government for its support of Olympic rowing in the city. (ABC Capricornia: Jacob Gamble)

"This endorsement proves what we've always known. That Rockhampton's Fitzroy River will be the perfect venue for rowing at the 2032 Games," he said.

"Rockhampton is ready for the world stage. Now it's time to get to work and secure the infrastructure and opportunities that will benefit our community long after the Games have ended."

Queensland senator and National Party leader Matt Canavan, who first championed the Fitzroy River as an Olympic venue, said it was a great day for central Queensland.

The Fitzroy River has faced intense scrutiny since it was selected as a venue for the Brisbane 2032 Olympics. (Supplied: Rockhampton Regional Council)

"The Fitzroy River is one of the most beautiful parts of our country. It's an iconic Australian river," he said.

" It's been a tough fight, and some people had not wanted rowing to be outside of south-east Queensland. "

But Tom Sharp, mayor of rival rowing location Scenic Rim, dismissed today's announcement, and said there was still a long way to go for Rockhampton as a host city.

"You've got the financial assessments, you've got the overlays for the visitors, spectators, you've got the accommodation assessments, you've got the rowers themselves," he said.

"We're only at the starting blocks and Rocky's only starting to catch up to Scenic Rim."

The Rockhampton rowing facility will host the Queensland Schools' Championship regatta this weekend. (Supplied: Rockhampton Fitzroy Rowing Club)

The Queensland premier said GIICA would now proceed with the detailed planning, design and construction of the Rockhampton site.

He also told state parliament there would be no widening or dredging and that the Fitzroy Barrage was Rockhampton's "secret weapon".

While the river has passed an independent technical assessment, the region will require more accommodation to support an influx of athletes and visitors in 2032.

"Rockhampton knows how to host major events. It already hosts tens of thousands of people for Beef Week and Rockynats, and the Games will deliver extra accommodation for the future," Mr Crisafulli said.

The Fitzroy River has been used as a venue for Australian rowing team training camps over the years. (ABC Capricornia: Alice Roberts)

Rowing Queensland chief executive Anthea O'Loughlin also welcomed the outcome of the technical assessment, as the Rockhampton venue prepared to host more than 800 young rowers for the Queensland Schools' Championship Regatta this weekend.

"This is an important step to provide certainty to our athletes and community as we progress towards 2032," Ms O'Loughlin said.

"We note the references in the statement to legacy and investment in the sport and look forward to further information on this as it develops."

Sarah Black says the Olympics will bring a great legacy. (ABC Capricornia: Katrina Beavan)

President of the Rockhampton Fitzroy Rowing Club, Sarah Black, was ecstatic when the ABC broke the news to her that Rockhampton had been given the final seal of approval from the IOC.

"We've known that the course here is fantastic, but to have that international endorsement for the technical assessment is just fantastic news for us here in Rockhampton," she said.

Capricorn Enterprise chief executive Mary Carroll said today's announcement was a major milestone for central Queensland and an opportunity to deliver lasting economic, tourism and community benefits for the region.

"Commercial in confidence discussions have been proceeding positively with major investors to this region who I strongly believe will be able to deliver new hotel accommodation, an athletes' village and legacy infrastructure including world-class rowing and canoeing facilities," she said.

World.title: Greene to leave Giants ahead of expected move to Cats
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

The GWS Giants have confirmed Toby Greene will leave the club to potentially join Geelong ahead of the 2027 season.

The Giants released a brief statement on Thursday morning, announcing Greene's intention to return to his home state of Victoria.

Greene has told the Cats he wants to join the club from next season.

"The Giants have been advised by Toby Greene of his intention to move back to Victoria for family reasons with a view to joining the Geelong Football Club," the statement read.

Giants chief executive Dave Matthews told SEN radio Greene was leaving with the club's wishes.

"That's the decision he has made and we certainly respect that," Matthews said.

"He's been a celebrated figure at our club, a very important person and I know this has been a really tough decision, one he's largely made for family reasons."

Toby Greene (second from right) was a foundation player at the Giants. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Mark Kolbe)

The 32-year-old has been offered a lucrative three-year deal to join Geelong.

Greene can join the Cats as an unrestricted free agent once the free agency period opens on October 2.

"We are really excited Toby wants to join the Geelong Football Club," Cats executive general manager of football, Andrew Mackie, said in a statement.

"We know this was a significant decision for Toby and his family, and we recognise what the Giants have meant to him and respect the contribution he has made to their club.

"We are looking forward to helping Toby write the next chapter of his career at the Cats."

Last week, Greene spoke about his talks with the Cats.

"With Geelong, I've had an open discussion," Greene said last week.

"Told them what I think about and what I wrestle with and they then explained what it would look like for me.

Zak Butters nominates Bulldogs as preferred club Port Adelaide's three-time best and fairest winner announces his desire to join the Victorian team.

"Geelong would be a lot less travel and more time for family. They discussed aspects of the role and how it would look in the team."

The news comes after Zak Butters chose the Western Bulldogs, instead of the Cats, as his preferred destination following his exit from Port Adelaide.

Greene was a foundation player at the Giants, spending 15 seasons at the club.

He debuted in 2012 and kicked 450 goals across 282 senior matches.

Greene won the club's best and fairest award twice and is a three-time All-Australian.

He was named Giants' co-captain in 2022 before becoming the sole skipper the following season.

World.title: Broncos NRLW stars credit 'Princey blow-up' for season turnaround
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Brisbane Broncos NRLW stars Romy Teitzel and Tamika Upton insist an emotive half-time address from coach Scott Prince was the catalyst for the team's return to form.

The defending premiers host Newcastle in an elimination final on Saturday at Brisbane's Langlands Park.

They enter the match on a three-match winning streak, which followed a mid-season slump.

The Broncos' last loss was a 28-20 defeat to the Gold Coast Titans on August 23.

Broncos, Titans record wins The Broncos thrash the Warriors to hit peak form before the finals, while the high-flying Titans beat the Knights in the concluding round of the minor premiership.

It was their third consecutive defeat.

Trailing 14-4 at half-time in that match, TV footage showed Prince laying down the law in no uncertain terms.

"We are a great team with great standards and we weren't living up to them," Teitzel said.

"We deserved every single word that he threw at us.

"The response comes from having a lot of respect for Princey and believing in his game plan.

"Everything is driven from that respect factor and believing in what he is trying to drive here at the Broncos."

Following the loss to the Titans, the Broncos beat Parramatta 44-10 and St George Illawarra 24-16, before thrashing the Warriors 52-18 at home last Sunday.

Tamika Upton says the players have deep respect for their coach, Scott Prince. (Getty Images: Jason McCawley)

Broncos captain Upton said Prince, who coached the team to the premiership last year, told the players home truths they needed to hear.

"We had a few little things we had to fix, and we weren't doing it, hence the Princey blow-up," Upton said.

"To be honest, we are used to it. He is a very passionate coach. That's the thing, we are all competitors."

Upton said she and her teammates had enormous respect for Prince, who captained the Wests Tigers to the 2005 NRL premiership during his decorated playing career.

"I would rather him be yelling at us than not speaking to us," she said.

"Honestly, you feel that because he was a player.

"When he is talking like that, you feel the energy, and you respect that a lot because he has been there and done it before.

"He wouldn't do it if he didn't care. I respond to that."

AAP

World.title: WTA Finals hoped to become 'Super Bowl of women's sports'
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

The season-ending WTA Finals will be held in North Carolina for at least three years from 2027, as the tour seeks to take greater control of its flagship event amid financial concerns.

The finals, featuring the season's top-eight singles players and doubles ​teams, will be played in Charlotte at the venue which hosts the Hornets NBA team.

WTA chair Valerie Camillo said the tour wanted to build ‌the finals into the "Super Bowl of women's sports".

Camillo said the WTA would operate the event itself rather than rely on the type of outside-promoter arrangement previously used.

"The WTA will be taking greater ownership and control of the event and investing ⁠alongside our partners," Camillo said.

Financial details ​of Charlotte's package were not disclosed ‌ahead of a planned announcement by local partners.

Rybakina downs Sabalenka for US Open title Elena Rybakina already took Aryna Sabalenka's world number one ranking, now she takes her US Open title as well.

Camillo said it represented a "meaningful investment" that gave the WTA confidence to commit to the city.

The move follows the WTA's decision to relocate the November 2026 finals to Indian Wells, California, after ending an agreement under which Riyadh had hosted the event with the backing of Saudi Arabia's Public Investment ​Fund.

British newspaper The ‌Telegraph reported last week internal WTA projections showed the tour could run out of cash next year and move into debt by autumn 2027 if its spending pattern continued.

The report said the WTA expected operating ⁠losses of $US23 million ($32 million) in 2026 and cited the loss of ‌revenue associated with the Saudi finals deal ‌as a major contributor.

Camillo said 2026 was a transitional year and the tour was tightening spending while absorbing ‌the unexpected cost of moving the finals to Indian Wells.

The WTA has not yet set prize money for the 2027 finals.

Camillo said equal prize money remained an important goal, but added the tour was considering alternatives, including ⁠a profit-sharing model with players.

"We want this event to be built together with the players," she said.

"Why stop at equal prize money?"

The WTA also plans to establish a greater operational presence in Charlotte as it builds the event.

Reuters

Tech.title: Xbox’s clever disc-to-digital feature was 15 years in the making
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

When Xbox announced a new feature last month that lets you digitize existing physical game collections, I immediately thought of the Xbox One. Disc-to-digital seems like a clever new feature for Xbox, perfectly timed as a response to Sony killing PlayStation discs. But the reality is that it has been 15 years in the making and is now a big part of Xbox’s ongoing game preservation efforts.

Ahead of the launch of the Xbox One in 2013, Microsoft made a key decision to uniquely identify discs. Sources familiar with Microsoft’s plans tell me the company was exploring the idea of true Xbox digital ownership in 2011, including digital gifting, recycling digital games, and the ability to swap discs at retail stores in exchange for a digital version. Some of those original Xbox One plans leaked out online, and many others have remained secret for more than a decade.

Microsoft’s Xbox One launch hinted at some of these ideas, too. The console was originally supposed to be always online, to enable Microsoft’s vision of digital game sharing, and more. Microsoft walked back those plans after a messy and confusing Xbox One launch created a backlash to the always-online requirement. But some of those original digital ideas are now starting to come to life in different ways.

Microsoft’s decision to essentially embed a serial number on the discs that Xbox consoles can read has allowed it to launch disc-to-digital, a method that lets you turn a physical Xbox One disc into a digital copy simply by slotting it into a disc drive. A decision made 15 years ago has resulted in this useful feature and may well lead to true digital ownership in the coming years.

It’s not something Sony can copy, either. Unless the PlayStation maker has been quietly adding metadata to its discs over the years, it will have to find another method to help PS5 owners move their physical collections over to the digital era.

Microsoft thought ahead, not necessarily to disc-to-digital, but just about identifying discs so it was ready for when console games moved into an all-digital era. That era looks like it’s right around the corner, especially now that Sony has announced it’s killing PlayStation discs in 2028. Both Microsoft and Sony also ship digital-only variants of their consoles, and it’s clear from game sales numbers that most titles are purchased digitally these days.

I fully expect Microsoft to follow Sony and eventually scrap Xbox discs, especially as the number of authorized manufacturers capable of producing physical media continues to shrink. That’s largely because almost every other form of media, from music to movies, has moved on from optical discs. The big difference with Xbox, though, is that Microsoft has always been obsessed with game preservation.

In the same year that disc-to-digital is launching, Microsoft is also bringing original Xbox and Xbox 360 games to PC. The company has also spent years working on its backward compatibility program, to get as many games from the Xbox and Xbox 360 eras working on modern Xbox consoles. Game preservation is a central part of Project Helix, the next Xbox that could play every Xbox game ever made.

It’s not an easy task to pull off game preservation, either. There are the complex technical challenges that need to be overcome, alongside licensing issues and the business challenges from publishers that decide how a game should be sold.

Some of those technical challenges mean that not every single Xbox One disc will work with this new disc-to-digital feature. That could be because some early discs simply didn’t get pressed with the unique identifier. Microsoft warned its internal Xbox testers that “it all depends on how and when the disc was manufactured and it may not have the features we need for this program.”

Discs that are slightly damaged might also not work with disc-to-digital, but run just fine otherwise. That’s why it’s important that Xbox is launching this right now — physical media decays over time.

The licensing and business challenges are far more complicated. Publishers need to agree to disc-to-digital, and some could hold back. It appears that most are on board, and even Ubisoft games started showing up recently. We’ve seen a number of other games come online since Microsoft’s announcement, and the company has been clear that more will follow.

The next challenge beyond disc-to-digital is solving digital ownership. If all we really own of a digital game is a license, I hope that one day those licenses can move freely across devices and platforms. I want to buy a single copy of a game and have that license follow me across Xbox, PlayStation, Nintendo, and PC. I also want to be able to gift or sell that license on different marketplaces, just as we’ve been able to do with physical discs at retailers for decades.

Microsoft envisioned this true digital ownership future 15 years ago, and it has gradually taken steps toward making it a reality. I hope Xbox can eventually pull it off, but the solution will require publishers and platform owners to agree on a shared system for how game licenses are bought, transferred, gifted, and resold. That’s a much bigger challenge than simply getting rid of the disc.

The pad
