Tech.title: Soundboks Rider Party Speaker Review: Loud and Durable
Tech.content:
The Soundboks Rider looks like no other portable speaker I've tested. It resembles something you'd find on stage at a concert rather than at your next barbecue. Its restrained design is almost the antithesis of the flashy, LED-pulsing party speakers you might find from brands like JBL or Samsung.

The build quality is impressive, confidence-inspiring, and clearly made to last. It's built like a tank, with a steel front grille, silicone rubber ball corners, and a thick plastic cabinet. During a drop test, I was frankly more worried about the speaker breaking my stairs than my stairs breaking the speaker. Another win for longevity is the replaceable battery—it charges via USB-C, and you can swap it in and out in seconds. This feels like a speaker you could have for decades.

While smaller than Soundboks' other speakers, it is still much larger than your average Bluetooth unit, and a bit awkward to carry with its single carry-grip on one corner. I would have loved to see two carry handles, one on each side. That would make the Rider easier and more flexible to carry, similar to the Sony ULT Field 7.

Unlike the larger Soundboks Mix and Soundboks 4, this is meant to be a stand-alone speaker—it does not have Soundboks' wireless multi-speaker connectivity (SKAA TeamUp), a speaker stand mount, or additional inputs (read: XLR).

Loud and Clear

Soundboks speakers can get loud, and despite the Rider being the smallest in the brand's lineup, its audio output is astonishing. I was frankly scared to turn this speaker up to max volume (11 on the dial, IYKYK).

Tech.title: People Are Pissed Off and Ready to Own Their Shit
Tech.content:
The train blasts through right as Louis Rossmann starts to speak. This has happened several times already at the event he’s hosting on a Friday night in San Jose, California. All the speakers before him patiently paused when the train on the nearby tracks roared by, its loud horn blaring, then resumed talking. But Rossmann is mid-sentence in his rapid-fire delivery about the topic he’s fiercely passionate about, and he doesn’t stop. He shouts over the train.

This is the penultimate stop of the Own Your Shit tour, a US-wide odyssey of events this summer put on by ownership advocate and YouTuber Louis Rossmann and his advocacy nonprofit Fulu. Around 80 people have crammed into the narrow side porch of a brewery. The final event will be in Silver Springs, Maryland, on October 1.

Before Rossmann spoke, panels featured an advocate from the Electronic Frontier Foundation, students from San Jose State University’s Fixit workshop, and a leader of the Fisker Owners Association, a group of vehicle owners who refuse to let their cars die. The main call to action is to kill a very specific piece of legislation: Section 1201 of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act. Enacted in 1998, this section of the DMCA prohibits bypassing digital restrictions and locks enabled by a product manufacturer.

Ostensibly, the legislation was meant to ensure device security. Ownership and repair advocates have long criticized it for helping companies put software locks on devices and then charge owners for access to their own hardware. Rossmann, along with fellow advocate Kevin O’Reilly, started Fulu to pay out bounties for people who can disable digital locks on a device, even if there are legal consequences.

“How many people here enjoy it when they get threats of lawsuits?” Rossmann asks during the San Jose event. “Raise your hand.” Maybe four or five hands go up, including a grinning Rohit Chopra, the former director of the federal Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. “I enjoy when people try to sue me,” Rossmann says. “When they send me threats, I literally frame them.”

His presentation bounces through his various ownership- and repair-oriented fights. He calls out companies like Amazon, which removed books from people’s Kindles, and home pipe leak detector company Roost, which discontinued stand-alone Wi-Fi products to the dismay of its users. He criticized Apple, Sony, wheelchair companies, and BMW, which recently ran ads for the new Spider-Man movie on their customers’ dashboard screens. He accuses companies of adding paid subscriptions to their products after customers buy them as a form of “ransomware.”

It’s a righteous screed that feels infectious in the crowd. People cheer and call out their own ownership issues. Rossmann is a preacher at the pulpit of people pissed off by subscription services, the steady decline of physical media, and the inability to fix their stuff.

The Own Your Shit tour comes as people grow increasingly angry with companies like Sony ending physical disc support and deleting digital items in customers’ libraries. (Google has recently done something similar and deleted a user’s copy of The Lord of the Rings.) Amazon just ended support for its perfectly fine older Kindles. People feel squeezed by economic pressures as devices get more expensive and want to hang onto their devices longer.

Katharine Trendacosta, a director of policy and advocacy at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, spoke at the event to call out the way companies have turned just about everything into subscription services users have to pay for. “They get the subscription and our data,” Trendacosta says. “It's a win-win for them and a lose-lose for us.”

Tech.title: ‘Fast & Furious’ Takes a Victory Lap With a Ferociously Fun Roller Coaster
Tech.content:
Toward the end of my college days, I harbored a not-so-secret crush. She and I carried on a mild flirtation, dancing around the possibility of more, but it wasn’t until she found out I’d never seen The Fast and the Furious that she gave me an opening.

“What?!” she exclaimed. “It’s my favorite movie!” So we made plans to watch it at her dorm the next day. Even if I didn’t like it, I reasoned, the experience would constitute a worthy reversal of the trope about men forcing testosterone-soaked action movies on their girlfriends. I’ll spare you the details of what happened that afternoon, but it may come as no surprise that I gave the film an enthusiastic five-star review.

In the 25 years since the launch of the franchise, F&F has massively capitalized on such runaway infatuations. The big, bald, sleeveless blockbusters serve as monuments to America’s demented car culture, product placement (Corona, anyone?), and the ambiguously defined bonds of “family”—pronounced “fambly.” With their high-octane set pieces that ignore all known physics, leavened by subpar acting and threadbare storylines, the films invite us to submit to some reptilian part of our brain that cares only for power and speed.

Which is why the series was ideal inspiration for Universal Studios Hollywood’s new foray into cutting-edge outdoor roller coasters. On Wednesday, the long-anticipated Fast & Furious: Hollywood Drift opened to the public, offering parkgoers the chance to hop into replicas of the movies’ muscle cars—including Dom Toretto’s 1970 Dodge Charger R/T—that spin and soar along more than 4,000 feet of track at speeds of up to 72 miles per hour. (A different version of the ride is slated to debut at Universal’s Florida park next year.)

The day before, select media and content creators had the chance to experience the attraction without the inconvenience of waiting in line, and I’m pleased to report that it didn't disappoint: I rode it three times in a row and could have gone back for more. Its four launch sections and three corkscrew inversions made for a whip-fast adrenaline rush, augmented by revving motor noise from seat-mounted speakers. In Dom’s lead car, you can even detect the braking resistance as you slide into a drift. I hollered with glee throughout each circuit, making sure to occasionally shout “TOLUCA LAKE,” the name of the affluent neighborhood next door; residents have been very upset about all the screaming.

Tech.title: The EU Wants to Break Up Kids and Their Chatbots
Tech.content:
The EU plans to ban chatbots from simulating emotions or interpersonal relationships in interactions with anyone under the age of 18 as the bloc tries to stop children from developing emotional dependencies on the technology.

The rules will be part of the EU Kids Act, proposed on Thursday, which includes similar restrictions on minors’ access to social media and video-sharing platforms. Children under 13 will be banned from accessing chatbots without their guardians’ supervision, and digital platforms will have to build child-safety protections into their products or face fines of up to 6 percent of total worldwide turnover, according to a draft of the legislation seen by WIRED.

Chatbots operating in the EU will also not be allowed to retain memory of interactions between separate conversations under the new rules, since the Commission worries this could lead to systems accumulating sensitive data of minors over time and potentially reinforcing harmful interaction patterns.

Providers of online social networking sites, video-sharing platforms, and games should not automatically activate or encourage the use of AI chatbots on their services, the proposed law will also stipulate. That includes not pinning AI companions and general conversational chatbots at the top of a minor’s contacts list, it says—as had been done by Snapchat.

The proposal is limited to AI companions and general conversational chatbots seen by the Commission to pose serious risks to minors’ health, safety, and well-being. Simeon de Brouwer, a policy adviser at the Brussels-based advocacy group European Digital Rights, welcomes the chatbot measures, but tells WIRED it doesn’t make sense to restrict them to young people only. “Don’t we all deserve to be protected from AIs designed to be addictive, from AIs which create emotional dependencies, or from AI features which are activated and pushed by default onto users?” The EU says its Digital Fairness Act, due to be unveiled later this year, is expected to propose clampdowns on addictive design more widely.

Tech.title: Hundreds of Election Deniers Will Be on the Ballot This November
Tech.content:
On November 3, when voters across the US go to the polls, almost 200 election deniers will be on the ballot. Many of them have repeatedly undermined the very process they are participating in, and they will be looking to win some of the most powerful elected positions in the country—positions that would help determine how voting goes in future elections.

Following the primaries, there will be 197 election deniers on the ballot for congressional and statewide races in the midterms across 43 states, according to new data shared exclusively with WIRED by States United Action, a nonpartisan nonprofit that supports state officials in protecting elections.

These numbers include a sitting US congressman who voted against certifying the 2020 election results; a former state representative who integrated QAnon conspiracy theories into election denialism; and local election officials who have actively sought to undermine election results by pushing baseless conspiracy theories about noncitizen voting.

But for election experts and officials, one of the biggest concerns ahead of the midterms is the possibility that these election deniers could obtain oversight of the 2028 presidential election process. The data shows there are already 27 election deniers in 20 states who hold a statewide office with election oversight, like secretary of state or attorney general—positions that allow the holder to set voting rules or prosecute those they believe are cheating at the ballots. In November, 33 election deniers will seek to secure similar positions in states across the country.

“All Americans should be concerned if people who are trying to undermine trust in elections and trying to interfere in the election process are taking positions of responsibility over elections,” Wendy Weiser, vice president for democracy at the nonprofit Brennan Center for Justice, tells WIRED. “We've seen in recent years an increasing number of election deniers taking some positions of public trust. As the numbers increase, it just increases the risk to our election system. This really is an attempt to corrode the system from within.”

The huge roster of election deniers on the ballot in November has also been emboldened by a groundswell of local groups and individuals who have been working for years to promote baseless claims about mail-in voting, noncitizen voter fraud, and rigged voting machines.

And from the top, President Donald Trump has increasingly pushed election-denial conspiracy theories, according to data gathered by States United Action. The group’s data shows that 60 percent of Trump’s statements referencing elections since the 2024 election include an explicit claim of fraud, rigging, or theft. That percentage has risen to 84 percent in the second quarter of 2026.

"The election-denial movement is more powerful than ever, and it's a direct threat to our freedom to vote,” Joanna Lydgate, CEO of States United Action, tells WIRED. “Election deniers are embedded at every level of government, pushing conspiracy theories from positions of real power.”

WIRED is keeping a close eye on many of these impactful races featuring election deniers. Here are five of the midterm races featuring election deniers that WIRED and States United Action are tracking:

The Michigan Senate Race

In the wake of the 2020 election, former US representative Mike Rogers slammed Trump’s efforts to persuade Georgia’s secretary of state to change the election results as “more gangster than presidential.” He was also unequivocal in his assessment of Trump’s role in the attack on the Capitol on January 6, 2021: “You’re damn right you had responsibility for this,” Rogers said at the time.

But now, seeking a return to Congress as the Republican nominee for Senate in Michigan, Rogers appears to see election denialism as a winning campaign strategy. “I am thankful for President Trump’s commitment to transparency. The news coming out of the White House tonight is deeply troubling—especially that of a voter fraud scheme right here in Michigan,” Rogers wrote on X moments after Trump delivered a conspiracy-filled speech about election fraud, including a long-debunked claim about fraud in Michigan.

Tech.title: Bose Just Dropped New Sport Open Earbuds and Ultra Open Earbuds (2nd Gen)
Tech.content:
Bose’s original Ultra Open Earbuds were released more than two years ago and sparked the proliferation of a new style of open earbuds that resemble clip-on earrings. I’d been waiting for the Ultra Open Earbuds (2nd Gen) to arrive, and now they’re finally here, with improved sound, voice-calling performance and battery life, Bose says.

While the updated buds carry the same elevated $299 list price as their predecessor, the company has also unveiled its completely new Sport Open Earbuds that cost $199 and have a different design than the original Ultra Open Earbuds. Both new buds are available for preorder Sept. 19 and ship Oct. 1.



Bose Ultra Open Earbuds (2nd Gen) highlights

According to Bose, the Ultra Open Earbuds (2nd Gen) feature new drivers, allowing them to play louder and deliver deeper bass. Like Bose’s QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds (2nd Gen), as well as its QuietComfort Ultra Headphones (2nd Gen) and QuietComfort Headphones (2nd Gen), they’re also equipped with the company’s TrueSpatial technology with head-tracking for Immersive Audio, which now includes a Cinema mode. They look very similar to the original, with a slightly upgraded version of the original’s “cuff-clip form factor” that a lot of other people found quite comfortable.

Bose

Available in black, white smoke and “limited-edition” cherry chocolate or olive green colors, they have an IPX4 rating (splash-resistant) and are rated for up to 9 hours of battery life (that’s up from 7 hours), though that number drops if you engage Immersive Audio.

Thanks to their secure fit and open design, the Ultra Open Earbuds worked well for running and biking, and the new version is also suitable for sporting activities, though Bose is billing the lighter Sport Open Earbuds as more durable and “purpose-built for active use,” with an even more secure fit.

Bose Sport Open Earbuds highlights

The Sport Open Earbuds look similar to Shokz OpenDots 2 earbuds, which also sell for $199. Bose says they “combine a secure cuff-style fit with soft silicone construction, IP54 sweat, splash and dust resistance, tactile controls and rich open audio, all while keeping listeners naturally aware of their surroundings.”

The Bose Sport Open Earbuds have an IP54 rating and come in three color options. Bose

The Sport Open Earbuds don’t support Bose’s Immersive Audio feature and are rated for up to 7 hours of battery life. They’re available in three colors: black, white smoke and “limited-edition” eucalyptus green (that same color is available for Bose’s recently released QuietComfort (2nd Gen) headphones).

My quick take

I haven’t tried the new buds yet, but I’ll be receiving review samples in advance of their Oct. 1 ship date and will post full hands-on reviews of them.

A lot has changed in the clip-on earbuds market since Bose first released the Ultra Open Earbuds in February 2024, with dozens of new clip-on models available, many of them at far lower prices than $300. While I suspect the Ultra Open Earbuds (2nd Gen) will be among the best-sounding open earbuds and certainly a good premium option in the category, I also think we’ll see these buds on sale fairly frequently; $300 just seems too high to pay for a pair of clip-on earbuds. (Apple’s new AirPods 5 don’t fit as securely as either of these open buds, but they do feature active noise canceling and start at $129.)

The Sport Open Earbuds have a lightweight cuff-clip form factor. Bose

As for the Sport Open Earbuds, I’ll see how they compare to the Shokz OpenDots 2, Anker Aero Clip 2 and Baseus’ XC1 clip-on earbuds ($100), which feature Sound by Bose. Like the Ultra Open Earbuds (2nd Gen), I also expect the Sport Open Buds to see regular discounts to compete with all the new premium sport clip-on buds hitting the market, many of which feature improved sound and voice-calling performance.

Tech.title: The US Military Can’t Stop Talking About Space Weapons
Tech.content:
After decades of silence, the US military is suddenly chatty on the topic of space weapons.

Earlier this week, Air Force Secretary Troy Meink revealed at the Air, Space & Cyber Conference in Maryland that the US has fielded “on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the Joint Force against hostile adversary action.” The next day, Chief of Space Operations Gen. Douglas Schiess echoed the same message.

Two days later, I listened to Gen. Stephen N. Whiting, the commander of the US Space Command, put his own spin on the space weapons announcement during the Advanced Maui Optical and Space Surveillance Technologies Conference.

“The Joint Force retains on-orbit space control weapons fully capable of defending the United States and its interests against hostile adversary actions,” Whiting said.

Whiting did not elaborate on what those weapons are, if they’d target objects in space or on Earth or how long they’ve been active.

“We need the ability to affect targets,” he told a group of reporters after his address. “The discussion that we’ve had over the last couple days just highlights that we have those capabilities.”

The idea that the US is fielding space weapons didn’t come as a huge surprise to anyone in the industry. The shock was the timing. Why are Washington’s top commanders suddenly broadcasting the militarization of space this week?

“I still don’t get it. Why now?” said Victoria Samson, chief director of space security and stability, Secure World Foundation. “Russia and China are going to look at this as continued evidence that the US is a bad actor in space. This makes our job of getting international participants to sign on to our vision of responsible behavior in space that much harder.”

I sat down with Whiting and a group of reporters to ask these questions. But like the other commanders discussing space weapons this week, he largely declined to get into specifics.

Military officials blame China and Russia

In the meeting with reporters after his address, Whiting pointed to China and Russia as the first countries to deploy space weapons.

“China and Russia have developed and fielded counter-space weapons, the whole range of kinetic and nonkinetic capabilities,” he said. “That is not in doubt, and that has happened.”

Russia used a ground-based missile to blow up one of its own defunct satellites in 2021, an event that created more than 1,500 pieces of debris larger than a softball and likely hundreds of thousands of smaller pieces. China has also deployed similar antisatellite weapons in the past – most notably a 2007 incident that created the largest debris cloud in history.

While there haven’t been confirmed instances of China and Russia deploying orbital weapons against adversaries, the experts I spoke with at AMOS said aggressive behavior is commonplace, including actions that look like data siphoning from adversary satellites or communications jamming.

“Between China and Russia on orbit, this is happening all the time,” said Jason Ruggieri, a director at COMSPOC, a company that tracks objects in space. “We can’t make an assessment when they have a close approach with a satellite about what exactly they were doing, but we can make assumptions based on open-source intelligence.”

What do space weapons look like?

When I polled space experts at AMOS about what type of weapon the US military officials are referring to, communications jammers was the most common answer.

“The Russians and Chinese are thought to have them. It seems pretty obvious,” said Samsen. “Before this, the US had three declared offensive counter-space capabilities — all jammers. Those are like intro to counter-space capabilities or basic stepping stones. So if it was like that on Earth, I don’t know why it wouldn’t be that in space.”

Both China and Russia swiftly condemned the US for escalating tensions in space.

“We urge the US side to stop expanding its military capabilities and preparing for war in outer space,” Chinese ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said in response to Meink’s comments. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov also called on Tuesday to keep space “free of any weapons.”

Whiting framed this week’s flurry of announcements as the logical conclusion to a decade of militarization in space.

“Uniformed warfighters have capabilities to be able to defend American interests in their domain. That is not a controversial statement for those who operate in the air or at sea, on the land or in cyber. But it may be a new statement for us in space,” he said. “It is all about normalizing the domain as a place that we defend American interests.’

President Donald Trump has made dominance in space a priority during his second stint in office. On Aug. 20, he set a target of “1,000 launches and reentries every year” by 2030, many of which would deliver military payloads to orbit. For comparison, 2025 saw 193 launches in the US – 85% of which were from SpaceX, according to BryceTech.

A week after taking office in 2025, Trump also directed the Department of Defense to create a Golden Dome missile defense system using thousands of satellites that would be equipped with orbital weapons. The Congressional Budget Office estimated that it would cost $1.2 trillion to develop and operate over 20 years.

None of the military officials said what kind of space weapon the US has deployed already, but an official who spoke to The Washington Post on the condition of anonymity said it could be a weapon that would allow the military to take out an enemy’s satellite if it’s being used to target American troops or a US satellite.

“US allies and partners are going to say, ‘Oh, if the US thinks it needs weapons in space, we probably do too.’ And it will proliferate,” Samsen said. “Truly it’ll be an arms race in space.”

Tech.title: Having Trouble Loading Pizzas Into the Oven? Your Peel May Be the Problem
Tech.content:
Chances are, if you own a pizza oven, have stood near a pizza oven or have uttered the words “pizza oven” in the vicinity of your phone, it’s likely that the almighty algorithm has delivered up a steady stream of pizza oven accessories, from pizza oven stands to sizzler platters to pizza peels in every style and shape.

If you have cursed in the vicinity of your phone while trying to launch a pizza into your pizza oven without inadvertently creating a calzone, chances are even better that Big Internet Brother has targeted you for a sliding pizza peel. If, after dozens of practice launches, you haven’t mastered the art of the traditional wood or perforated metal pizza peel, even with all-powerful semolina flour gliders, you may be very tempted by the ease promised by such a tool as a sliding pizza peel.

The Best Pizza Ovens, Tested by CNET See at CNET

But is it worth it? Or is it just the Temu-niverse capitalizing on your desire for a homemade pizza that doesn’t come with a side of anxiety and despair? Reader, the temptation was too strong. I checked one out, and here’s the lowdown on what you can expect from a sliding pizza peel.

How does a sliding pizza peel work?

A sliding pizza peel costs $30 to $40 on Amazon. Pamela Vachon/CNET

A sliding pizza peel is essentially a lightweight wooden pizza peel with a manual conveyor belt attached. Rather than thrusting a stationary peel under your entire pie, you only need a small edge of maneuverability to start. Once the sliding peel gets a little purchase on the raw pizza dough, you pull the cloth slide toward you by its handle while pushing the wooden board underneath.

To launch the pizza with a sliding pizza peel, reverse the process: Use the handle on the cloth glider to push, sliding the pizza into the oven while pulling the sturdy board out from underneath it.

Cloth, you say? Well, not exactly. The conveyor mechanism moves like fabric, but think of it more like a nonstick baking mat. Many are made of woven fiberglass with a polytetrafluoroethylene coating, which is nonstick but still grips enough to hold raw or cooked pizza dough. It’s frankly like a flimsier Silpat or not unlike an oilcloth table covering.

PTFE, in case you’re wondering, is related to per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances. Yes, we’ve worked hard to avoid PFAS; however, the material’s pliability doesn’t encourage chipping, and it is also replaceable. The wooden board itself admittedly also spares every expense without the heavy lifting required of other wooden pizza peels — this is made from raw, lightweight bamboo.

Sliding pizza peel best practices

I practiced with naked dough. Pamela Vachon/CNET

While a sliding pizza peel may seem like a cure-all, if, like me, you adore what your pizza oven offers but still struggle with pizza peel mechanics, it still requires practiceof its own —and caution. As with more traditional pizza peels, it cannot undo other mistakes, such as poorly constructed, too warm pizza dough or an overloaded pie. You can still calzone-ify your pizza, even with a sliding pizza peel.

Unlike a traditional pizza peel, which lets you push and pull simultaneously, the sliding pizza peel’s primary handle is also very short, meaning you kind of have to get (uncomfortably) close to the mouth of the oven to use it.

The fact that none of these seemingly magic wands are produced or branded by any major pizza oven manufacturer should serve as a caution. (Pizza oven manufacturers probably just want you to become a bona fide pizzaiolo, confidently using the legitimate tools of the trade; they are clearly not trying to encourage the use of these cheap devices.)

Various sliding pizza peels are purportedly heat-resistant up to a certain temperature (which varies). Many pizza ovens, however, can reach temperatures much hotter than those sliding peels are designed for.

Loading a raw pie into the oven is one of the trickiest parts of at-home pizza making. Pamela Vachon/CNET

More than one user on various online pizza oven forums reported that the nonstick belt of a sliding pizza peel melted onto the hot pizza stone. Others, however, called the device an absolute game changer. Either way, using a sliding pizza peel requires you to launch quickly, which again requires practice, probably best done outside your actual pizza oven. (Your oven-oven with a removable pizza stone? A much lower-stakes practice arena.)

My experience with a sliding pizza peel

Because of the peel’s modest length, you have to get uncomfortably close to the oven during launch. Pamela Vachon/CNET

I have been an enthusiastic pizza oven user since one came into my life, but I still haven’t mastered the mechanics of either a traditional wood or perforated metal pizza peel. I slightly prefer metal, but either way, pizza attempt number one always results in a folded disaster. My crime, apparently, is wanting the kind of thin pizza crust a 20-year-old New Yorker demands. The thinner the pizza, the harder to launch.

I can attest that the sliding pizza peel did make it easy to pull the pizza off the cutting board where I shaped the dough and applied toppings. Despite feeling cheaply made, the mechanics are inarguable. I achieved a crust thinness I truly couldn’t with the other models.

While you have to get close to the heat to deposit it, I haven’t earned any burns or scars from trying. Repeated launches in a very hot pizza oven also didn’t seem to affect the fabric slide, but then again, I was prepared to move extremely fast to avoid a crisis—and to get away from the heat.

Success, if not exactly centered. Pamela Vachion/CNET

In case it merits saying, a sliding pizza peel is entirely unnecessary for pulling pizza out of a pizza oven. In fact, I would caution against it since it really relies on setting the peel down on the pizza stone, never mind the fact that you really have to get your hand inside the oven in the starting position for pulling a pizza onto it. Once a pizza is fully cooked and the dough is sturdy, even a thin pizza can be collected with a more traditional pizza peel anyhow.

A traditional pizza peel is still best for pulling pies from the oven. Pamela Vachon/CNET

The verdict on a sliding pizza peel? Proceed with caution. And practice.

Ultimately, the average price of sliding pizza peels available online is about $30. Even with mixed reviews, it’s a fairly low-stakes gamble to see whether one improves how often you use your big-ticket pizza oven.

Tech.title: Another Miserably Hot Summer Is Nearly Over. NOAA Says It’s the Worst on Record
Tech.content:
If you sat around at any point this year and wondered why it felt so much hotter than normal, it’s because it actually was. According to a new report from NOAA, summer 2026 is the hottest on record, beating out the prior holders of the crown, a tie between 2021 and 1936.

Per NOAA, the average temperature across the continental US was 75.6 degrees Fahrenheit, with daytime maximum temperatures averaging out at 88.6 degrees. Both of those are the warmest since the beginning of recorded temperatures in the US. Most of this extra heat was concentrated in the southern and western portions of the US, while the Midwest, Great Lakes region and northeastern areas all saw near or slightly above average temperatures.

Some areas have it worse than others. Arizona had its second-hottest summer on record, trailing only 2024. However, the desert state still experienced an average of 97 degrees, with 39 days with temperatures over 110 degrees and 121 days over 100 degrees. The state is expected to add to those totals heading into the last couple of weeks of September.

Alaska and Hawaii weren’t left out of the party. Both of those states experienced their third-warmest summers on record.

To add insult to injury, nearly 60% of the country is also in drought conditions, according to the US Drought Monitor. NOAA says that the Ohio Valley and parts of the Midwest had good rain but virtually everywhere else received less rain than average. Somewhat ironically, two years ago, the script was flipped, and both of those regions were in drought conditions.

“Persistent heat domes and drought conditions were key factors in the widespread above-average temperatures observed during 2026,” Karin Gleason, chief of the monitoring section at NOAA’s National Centers for Environmental Information, told CNET in an email. Gleason says that the jet stream, which is the strong wind in Earth’s atmosphere that functionally dictates the weather, was skewed toward high pressure in the US, trapping heat and causing extended heat domes. Pair that with drought conditions, which allowed “solar energy to heat the dry ground and air more efficiently,” and you have the ingredients for one hot summer.

The unseasonable warmth is going to continue

Hurricane Lowell hit Ni’ihau and Kaua’i. It’s the first hurricane to directly hit Kaua’i since Hurricane Iniki in 1992. NOAA

Summertime heat is often oppressive, but it’s not the only season this year that is slated to have warmer-than-average temperatures. NOAA released another report showing that 2026’s El Niño is strengthening, and is 90% likely to continue doing so into winter 2026 to 27. That means the US — and many other parts of the Northern Hemisphere — are in for an unseasonably warm autumn and winter.

El Niño is a normal weather pattern caused by warmer-than-average conditions in the central and eastern Pacific Ocean every two to seven years and can last up to 18 months. However, the current one began forming in June and has risen to the rank of “super” El Niño, a media-only name that NOAA doesn’t use, which indicates that this year’s El Niño is reaching historic levels.

It changes weather patterns all across the world, and is to blame for the uptick of hurricane threats in Hawaii, the lack of hurricane threats in the Atlantic, and higher-than-average temperatures for Americans across the country. Experts predict that El Niño is going to last until February 2027 at least, leading to a warmer winter, but also an increased chance of extreme weather, not unlike the winter storm that buried much of the US under up to a foot of snow in January. Warmer doesn’t necessarily mean that it won’t be cold enough for snow.

And you’re paying for all of it

With temperatures reaching record highs, it’s no surprise that utility bills likely did too. Analysts warned that electricity demand could spike over the summer of 2026. Those increases definitely happened, as the US Energy Information Administration showed that fossil fuel prices were up virtually all summer, with the one hopeful stat being that solar, wind and hydroelectric power generation were up while fossil fuel usage was down compared to 2025.

Data about the actual impact to consumer bills isn’t out yet, but early estimates show that the nationwide average bill went up by 4%, with some areas reaching as high as 10%, including Detroit, Baltimore, and Washington DC. A few major cities saw a decline, but most places saw some sort of increase.



Most of these costs aren’t coming from an increase in usage from everyday people in their homes. According to the EIA, homes used 1,500 terawatt-hours (TWh) of electricity in 2025, which is up a small amount from the 1,400 TWh that residents used in 2005. That means people are using less than 10% more power today than they were back when Hollaback Girl by Gwen Stefani ruled FM radio stations.

By contrast, data centers used approximately 70 TWh in 2015. They more than doubled that number to 176 TWh in 2023 and are up to 448 TWh in 2025, with expectations that the number is going to increase to 980 TWh by 2030. That means data center energy usage went up by 272 TWh in just three years, versus 100 TWh in residential homes over 20 years. The amount of power used by data centers in 2026 is still unknown, but based on the frequency at which they’re being built, it’s hard to imagine that data center energy usage is going down.

The human cost is also rising. According to the World Health Organization, heat-related deaths worldwide have increased by 85% between the year 2000 and 2021, and a recent NPR investigation found that the number of deaths influenced by heat in the US is far higher than the official CDC figures. All of those data sources indicate that heat-related deaths are increasing in the face of global climate change, including approximately 35,000 excess deaths from Europe’s back-to-back heat waves during summer 2026.

Tech.title: 3 iPhone 18 Pro Upgrades That Will Make My Life as a Frequent Traveler Easier
Tech.content:
I’ve traveled all over the world with the iPhone 17 Pro Max during the past year, but I think the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max have made the right changes for someone like me who’s constantly on the go. The new Pro phones debuted last week at the company’s “Surprise and Shine” event, and I think three new features in particular will solve the gripes I’ve had with my orange 17 Pro Max as a traveling companion.

While I am in awe of the Ceramic Shield 2 durability that impressively protected my screen, I wouldn’t call it the best travel phone. It gets warm to the touch in hot weather and doesn’t offer the same pleasing camera experience as Android heavyweights like the Vivo X300 Ultra, Xiaomi 17 Ultra or the Oppo Find X9 Ultra. That’s why I’m stoked for the camera upgrades on Apple’s new models.

But I’m most excited about two comparatively minor upgrades, too. The expanded Dynamic Island capabilities and a redesigned vapor chamber appeal to me as someone who is constantly on the move and needs glanceable information. Here’s why I think these upgrades might tempt me to upgrade to the 18 Pro Max.

More glanceable information in the Dynamic Island

The Dynamic Island is smaller on the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max (right) than last year’s 17 Pro Max (left). Patrick Holland/CNET

When I’m on the go, I’m almost always jumping between multiple apps. One minute it is Flightly to track my flights, another minute I’m checking routes on Google Maps and then waiting for my Uber ride to arrive. On my iPhone 17 Pro Max, the Dynamic Island tracks two Live Activities, but I need to swipe between the three apps to multitask. Apple is changing this with its new Pro iPhones.

With the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, the new Dynamic Island can expand to show up to three live activities simultaneously. It doesn’t stretch all the way to the screen edges. Instead, you get one main activity on the Dynamic Island with smaller circular icons on either side.

A preview of the three activities to be tracked by the Dynamic Island. Screenshot by CNET/Apple

This won’t change the way you use your iPhone, but I expect it to make multitasking easier with glanceable info right on top of your iPhone. The small icons likely won’t provide much information, but if I can get a navigation arrow alongside my Flighty updates and ETA for Uber rides, I’m sorted. The two icons also serve as shortcuts to open those apps, offering faster access than manually switching apps — which is common when I’m juggling my flight information while getting out of that rideshare vehicle.

A redesigned vapor chamber for better cooling

The iPhone 18 Pro has a larger vapor-cooling chamber. Screenshot by CNET/Apple

My iPhone 17 Pro Max gets warm to the touch when I’m navigating and using the camera app on my photo walks. It drains the battery faster than usual. That’s why I’m excited about the iPhone 18 Pro Max’s improved ability to keep itself cool during intensive periods like my constant photography.

The iPhone 18 Pro has a “next-generation” vapor chamber that’s three times the surface area of the one in the iPhone 17 Pro. Apple redesigned the phone’s interior so its A20 Pro processor can connect directly to the vapor chamber, which is claimed to continuously cycle deionized water throughout the system for “significant” improvements in cooling performance.

Theoretically, all of this could allow the A20 Pro chip to sustain higher performance for longer periods. I imagine it helping keep the phone cool on extended camera usage and navigation, and delivering longer battery life.

You can see the aperture physically open and close on the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max. Patrick Holland/CNET

Pro controls to take control of my photos

I’m not a professional photographer, but I love taking photos. I’m into street photography and portraits, and the iPhone 18 Pro’s new upgrades seem fantastic, at least on paper. While variable aperture would allow me to control the amount of light hitting the sensor, I’m more excited to try the Pro Controls.

So far, I’ve relied on third-party apps to take motion-blur photos, but I can finally do so within the iPhone 18 Pro’s Camera app itself. Apple is adding the ability to adjust the shutter speed from the viewfinder.

The new Pro controls will let you customize your camera and photo-taking experience by adding manual control options for changing the white balance, using a histogram to check exposure levels, changing the shutter speed and manually adjusting the aperture between four options (ƒ/1.48, ƒ/1.8, ƒ/2.8, and ƒ/4.0 f-stops).

Pro controls on the iPhone 18 Pro can help capture more creative photos without needing any third-party apps. Screenshot by CNET/Apple

These Pro controls will allow me to take full control of how my image looks, rather than relying on Apple’s auto mode or processing to decide everything for me.

Sure, most Android phones have had this feature for years, which is why I carry an Ultra phone alongside my iPhone on9 every trip. However, the iPhone 18 Pro could finally make me ditch the second camera phone and carry just one device for my casual photography.

These three upgrades have me stoked for the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max. The redesigns that get me more glanceable information around the Dynamic Island, camera improvements that give me more control over my photography and improvements that will hopefully keep the phone from getting too warm will have an immediate impact on how I use the phone while running around the world.

Tech.title: What Is Copilot? Everything You Need to Know About Microsoft’s AI Tools
Tech.content:
Since OpenAI’s ChatGPT launched in November 2022, tech companies have poured billions of dollars into generative AI. Microsoft joined forces with OpenAI for a multiyear, multibillion-dollar investment. One of the results of this partnership was the creation of Microsoft’s own AI tool, Copilot.

If you’ve spotted Copilot in Windows, then opened Word and found it there too, you might wonder whether they’re the same thing. Microsoft certainly gets its mileage out of the name.

Copilot launched in 2023 as a successor to Bing Chat – which, in a way, evolved from Cortana, though it used a different underlying technology. But you get my point. Microsoft’s virtual assistants have had a long evolution.

Microsoft did have a couple of false starts with AI, though, like its Recall feature, which was quickly dropped from the Copilot Plus PC launch before eventually reaching those computers in April 2025.

So, what exactly is Microsoft Copilot? It’s an AI assistant, a chatbot, an app and increasingly an agent that can carry out tasks for you. The umbrella term Copilot can be a bit confusing, so let’s explore what it means in its applications and how you can use it.

The branding breakdown

Copilot is Microsoft’s branding for various AI-powered tools embedded across its ecosystem, including in Windows, Edge, Bing, Microsoft 365 (all the Office apps), Teams, GitHub and security tools. You can also download the Copilot app on your iOS, Android and Mac devices, or use it in a web browser.

Microsoft has begun bringing its personal and work experiences together. Its updated Copilot app became available in August 2026. The app previously called Microsoft 365 Copilot is now called Microsoft Copilot, with features that depend on your account and subscription.

The branding has also expanded to PCs as Microsoft rolled out an AI laptop, Copilot Plus PC. Many newer Windows laptops come with a dedicated Copilot key that lets you jump straight into your AI assistant with one press on a keyboard. But you don’t need a Copilot Plus PC to use the chatbot.

How Microsoft Copilot works

Copilot uses large language models to write text, search the web, summarize emails, generate code, automate tasks and assist you across the apps you probably already use. It also generates and edits images.

Microsoft Copilot/Screenshot by CNET

Microsoft says its system uses models from Microsoft, OpenAI and other developers, rather than just one model powering every feature.

When Copilot searches the web, it can include links to the sources behind an answer. Those links help you check its work, because all AI tools hallucinate, and even the most confidently delivered answer can still be wrong.

You can chat with Copilot for free, but you’ll need to sign in if you want it to save your chat history or keep a longer conversation going. Some versions also let you choose which AI model to use, though the options vary by plan.

On Windows, Copilot runs as a standalone app. You can control its file-search permissions and summon it with the optional “Hey Copilot” wake word or, if your keyboard has it, with a Copilot key.

Edge also includes Copilot, offering contextual assistance like summarizing articles or comparing products while you browse.

Copilot vs. other AI chatbots

Because it’s an AI chatbot, you can compare Copilot to ChatGPT, Grok, Perplexity, DeepSeek and Anthropic’s Claude. These all offer chat interfaces where you enter prompts and get responses, though their capabilities now extend beyond basic conversation.

As an AI assistant, it resembles how Google’s Gemini works across its software products, but Copilot is more tightly embedded into productivity tools. Meta AI is also integrated across its social platforms, but it’s more suited for casual and creative use.

If you spend much of your day in Word and Outlook, being able to ask for help inside those apps could save you some copying and pasting. For example, instead of asking ChatGPT to write an email and then copying it into Outlook, Copilot lives inside Outlook and generates the draft using your email history and context.

That convenience depends on having the appropriate access. The free assistant and the Copilot features included in a Microsoft 365 subscription aren’t interchangeable. A work account can also come with restrictions set by your employer.

Some products carrying the name Copilot serve different purposes. GitHub Copilot helps with software development, while Copilot Studio lets organizations build and manage AI agents.

What can Microsoft Copilot do?

Microsoft Copilot/Screenshot by CNET

When you use Microsoft 365 Copilot, the AI draws from the context of your files and data, like calendars or chats (with your permission), to generate content or provide suggestions.

In Word, it can draft, edit and summarize documents. In Excel, it can build formulas, analyze data and generate charts. It’ll whip up a deck for you in PowerPoint based on a prompt or a Word doc. Outlook Copilot drafts emails and summarizes threads. In Teams, it can generate meeting summaries and pull context from chats you weren’t paying attention to (we’ve all been there).

Copilot Voice lets you have a spoken conversation instead of typing. Copilot Vision lets you share a screen, app or supported camera view and ask questions about what you’re seeing. You could ask it to walk you through an unfamiliar app without having to describe every button.

That said, Vision provides guidance, but it doesn’t click buttons or enter text for you. Microsoft’s current Vision guide lists Microsoft 365 Personal, Family or Premium subscriptions as a requirement and says availability can vary during rollout, including on mobile.

You can use Copilot Imagine to create images from descriptions or upload an image and ask Copilot to change it. A cool feature is that if you choose a preset restyle option, as I did in the image below with Anime Keyframe, Copilot produces the complete prompt for you. You can then tweak the image according to your preference.

Microsoft Copilot/Screenshot by CNET

For studying, Microsoft describes Copilot Learn as a way to create practice tests and flashcards. It’s a more useful starting point for revision than asking the chatbot to do your homework.

Microsoft has also moved into AI that carries out tasks on your behalf. Introduced in February 2026, Copilot Tasks is a consumer feature that uses its own computer and browser to handle background jobs. It’s still in preview, and you can join a waitlist.

In the updated Copilot app, Cowork is designed for longer, multistep work, such as creating or editing Microsoft 365 documents, managing your email, calendar and files, working with websites and running scheduled or event-driven tasks. Cowork is generally available for work accounts, while the personal version remains in preview and requires an eligible Microsoft 365 subscription. Microsoft says it asks for approval or hands control back before completing sensitive actions, including making purchases and sending messages.

Following OpenAI’s footsteps with ChatGPT Health, Microsoft introduced Copilot Health, a separate space that can draw on your medical records and wearable data. It can help you understand that information or prepare for a doctor’s appointment, but it can’t diagnose conditions or prescribe medication.

How much does Copilot cost?

Copilot has a free version with usage limits. You don’t need a Microsoft 365 subscription to start chatting, but paid plans add AI features inside Microsoft’s apps and larger allowances.

Microsoft 365 Personal costs $10 a month.

Microsoft 365 Family costs $13 a month.

Microsoft 365 Premium costs $20 a month and includes Researcher and Analyst.

Microsoft 365 Pro costs $100 a month and offers the highest usage limits. Despite the similar name, this is different from the older standalone Copilot Pro subscription.

The included paid AI benefits on Family, Premium and Pro can’t be shared with other household members.

One change could catch returning users off guard: Microsoft retired the consumer Copilot’s Deep Research feature in August 2026. Researcher is a separate experience available with Premium and Pro. Don’t assume an older guide promising free Deep Research still applies.

Business Copilot licenses are priced separately. So are GitHub Copilot and Copilot Studio.

Privacy concerns

AI tools integrated into the software we use daily can quietly blur the line between helpful and intrusive. Installing Copilot doesn’t give it unrestricted access to your computer, but what it can use depends on the permissions you grant and the services you connect. You still have to decide how much personal or work information you’re comfortable sharing for the sake of convenience.

Ashique KhudaBukhsh, professor of software engineering at Rochester Institute of Technology, who specializes in AI and Natural Language Processing and also previously worked as a software developer for Microsoft, says the tech giant’s security standards are pretty high.

But he also admits: “As the AI tools increasingly operate across diverse platforms, there is an elevated risk that the data may bleed from one system into another.”

He says vulnerable groups, like senior citizens, should be educated and trained so they are up to speed on the risks of AI and can protect themselves until there is more regulatory oversight of this.

But KhudaBukhsh also notes there are some common misconceptions about AI and privacy.

“AI systems are [not] intrinsically invasive,” he explains, since “many of these systems are built with privacy by design principles.”

Microsoft changed its training policy with the updated Copilot app. For personal accounts, the company says conversations and file contents aren’t used to train foundation models. The same applies to Copilot in Microsoft 365 apps for home.

Older guides may still tell you how to opt out of training, but those instructions apply to the previous version.

Copilot can save your chat history and remember preferences. You can review or delete saved memories and turn memory off, but doing so won’t erase anything already saved.

Like every AI tool CNET has reviewed so far, it’s not perfect. But if you’re already using Microsoft software, Copilot could make your daily workflow easier. If you mainly want help polishing a paragraph or answering occasional questions, try the free version before adding another subscription to your monthly bills.

As KhudaBukhsh says, “It could be very convenient to use technology, but at the same time, we need to be very mindful of what we are sharing, and if we are understanding the trade-off between convenience and security.”

Tech.title: Here Are All the Ways You Can Customize Your iPhone’s Lock Screen
Tech.content:
Patrick Holland/CNET

Over the last few years, Apple’s major iOS updates have introduced a lot of ways to customize your iPhone to better suit your preferences. One part of your device that has gotten more customization options than others is your lock screen.

When Apple released iOS 18 back in 2024, you were given the ability to remove or change the controls on your lock screen — a welcome improvement if you’ve ever accidentally turned on your flashlight while pocketing your phone. Then, iOS 26 let you move your lock screen widgets, increase the size of your clock and give your lock screen wallpaper a 3D spatial effect. Now, iOS 27 lets you shrink the size of your lock screen’s clock.

Here’s how to bring these changes to your lock screen and what to know about each one.

Change the size of your lock screen’s clock

With iOS 27, you can shrink or expand the size of your lock screen’s clock. Enabling tiny clock moves the time to to the top of your lock screen next to the date. The expanded clock takes up about a third of my iPhone 16 Pro’s screen at most, which I love because if I place my phone on a table, I can easily see the time, even without my glasses.

If you want the minuscule or big clock on your lock screen, you’ll have to enable either option. Here’s how to shrink your lock screen’s clock in iOS 27.

1. Tap Settings.

2. Tap Wallpaper.

3. Tap Customize under the lock screen you want to adjust.

4. Tap your clock.

5. Tap the rectangle in the top right corner of the menu across the bottom of your screen.

Screenshot by Zach McAuliffe/CNET

Your lock screen clock will then shrink and move to the bar across the top of your screen. Tap that same button and your clock will go back to the size it was before.

Here’s how to expand the clock on your lock screen.

1. Tap Settings.

2. Tap Wallpaper.

3. Tap Customize under the lock screen you want to adjust.

Your clock will have a thicker tab in the bottom right corner of its outline. Tap and drag this down to expand your clock to your desired size.

Screenshot by Zach McAuliffe/CNET

Then tap the clock to choose a Glass or Solid design, and adjust the color, thickness and opacity of the Liquid Glass design. It’s important to note after changing the clock’s size, you can’t change the font. Only the far left clock font can be expanded for now, but maybe Apple will expand this to other fonts in a future iOS update.

Screenshot by Zach McAuliffe/CNET

Your lock screen’s widget dock can have a new home

You can also move your lock screen’s widget dock. This lets you place the dock near the bottom of your lock screen, right above your controls.

To move your lock screen’s widget dock, go to Settings > Wallpaper and tap Customize under the lock screen you want to adjust. Then, tap and drag the widget dock to the bottom of your lock screen.

Screenshot by Zach McAuliffe/CNET

If you expand your lock screen’s clock, your widget dock will automatically be placed near the bottom of the screen, and you can’t place it anywhere else on your screen.

Spatial effects come to wallpapers

Your lock screen’s wallpaper also gets a fun, 3D effect that Apple calls a spatial scene. When enabled, spatial scenes add depth to elements in your wallpaper — and pictures — making them appear to pop out at you. As you move your iPhone around, those elements will move, too.

To turn your lock screen wallpaper into a spatial scene, go to Settings > Wallpaper, then tap Customize for the lock screen you want to work with. Tap the hexagon near the bottom-right corner of your screen, and your iPhone will turn the wallpaper into a spatial scene.

Screenshot by Zach McAuliffe/CNET

It’s important to note that spatial scenes only work with photos, not with the wallpapers Apple provides, such as those in the Weather and Emoji collections.

Controls get some color

A pretty small change iOS 26 brought to your lock screen is changing the color of the controls near the bottom of your screen. This change is enabled automatically, so you just have to add a colorful control, or create your own, to bring a pop of color to your lock screen.

Screenshot by Zach McAuliffe/CNET

Make your lock screen your own

Apple has slowly loosened its grip on your iPhone’s lock screen, giving you more freedom to customize its appearance and how you use it over the years.

Being able to expand or shrink your clock, move the widget dock to more than one position and being able to give your wallpaper a 3D effect are just a few ways you can create your own experience on your iPhone. These features could be improved — like giving you more freedom in where you can place your widget dock — but I expect Apple to keep adding ways to customize your iPhone’s lock screen in the future.

For more on iOS, here’s what you should know iOS 27 and everything iOS 26 brought to your iPhone.

Tech.title: I Tested New Keurig Milk Pods for Instant Frothy Lattes
Tech.content:
I’d wager most American coffee-drinkers have sampled a Keurig brew. If you don’t already own one of the single-serve coffee makers, perhaps your aunt shared a cup during the holidays, or there’s one in the office break room. Intuitive to use, easy to maintain and long-lasting, the appliance offers terrific practicality. Simply pop in a pre-bought coffee pod, hit a button and watch a cup pour out.

Courtesy of The Milk Pod, such easy extraction now extends to dairy, too. Compatible with Keurig brewers, these single-serve capsules produce rich-textured milk with a single push. Impressively, the pods are shelf-stable for 15 months and don’t even require refrigeration. Currently available in three classic coffee flavors — plain, vanilla and caramel—they’re made with milk powder and natural ingredients. Rather than just hot milk, the dairy’s composition turns out frothy, yielding a latte-like consistency. It’s an intriguing addition to Keurig’s already expansive pod selection.

Coffee and milk, all at the press of a button

Milk Pods load in just like normal pods. Nikita Ephanov/CNET

Unlike a milk frother or steam wand, the pods require minimal instruction. They insert right into the K-Cup slot, no adjustment necessary. The Milk Pods entail no specialized setup; I was already sampling the dairy only minutes after opening the box.

As I brewed with Milk Pods one morning after the next, the initial ease continued. It’s recommended to brew the milk before the coffee, both to a six-ounce size, so the two liquids fit into a standard mug. As long as I didn’t accidentally press the wrong volume (my Keurig offers 6-, 8- and 10-ounce settings), I couldn’t make any mistakes.



Really, the only slight annoyance with the setup is the constant need to refill the water. My Keurig has a 30-ounce water tank, which means I need to top it up at half capacity. During only the second round of coffee, the brewer pinged me to take the reservoir to the sink, an upkeep that didn’t take much effort. Functionality-wise, the pods are remarkably easy. Pouring cold dairy out of the fridge is the easiest milk-integration technique. It’s hard to imagine a more consumer-friendly system.

Convenience is cool and all, but how do the pods taste?

Milk comes out hot and frothy, ready to be mixed with coffee. Nikita Ephanov/CNET

From dozens of seasonal K-Cups to various brand partnerships, Keurig capsules number in the hundreds. I sampled the Milk Pods with a generic brand of K-Cup from a local grocery store. Filled with dark-roasted coffee, the capsule brewed into a strong, lightly bitter-tasting brew – exactly the kind of flavor profile I’d dilute with milk. My chosen K-Cup wasn’t espresso-style, so the consistency resembled drip coffee.

Still, all three Milk Pods added a pleasant thickness to my Keurig coffee. The plain capsule lent the coffee a neutral creaminess, reminiscent of a latte, but nevertheless distinguishable from standard milk. The mouthfeel and taste reminded me of creamer, albeit with a more natural dairy character. Unlike the satisfying micro-bubbles in freshly steamed dairy, I picked up a smidge of powdery solids on my tongue. The cup wasn’t disappointing, but I still prefer the frothiness of fresh milk.

After you run a milk pod through the system, you simply load your coffee of choice. Nikita Ephanov/CNET

The bolder character of the flavored pods made the dehydrated downside less noticeable. I preferred the caramel of the two, which offered a complex nutty bitterness that paired well with my coffee. Sweet yet not saccharine, the pod reminded me of a well-made caramel candy. The vanilla capsule overpowered my coffee more, yielding a strong vanilla-syrup-like flavor. I could see this pod pairing better with other K-Cups, perhaps elevated even further in an iced latte. Overall, I found the Milk Pods pretty impressive for a shelf-stable product, but not quite cafe-quality.

In favor of shelf stability

Comparing the Milk Pods with fresh dairy reveals some differences, but you also have to consider convenience. The year-long durability, combined with no need for refrigeration, makes the pod worth stocking, even if it’s not a daily option.

Over several weeks of trialing the capsules, I left town and came back. The Milk Pods meant I didn’t need to worry about a carton left spoiling in the fridge. Plus, the morning after I returned, I didn’t need a bleary-eyed shopping run for my morning latte, either. I’d be happy to come across Milk Pods in a setting like an Airbnb or hotel. Given the self-contained ease of use, the pods align well with Keurig’s ecosystem. I could also see myself brewing the milk into a K-Cup of black tea or hot chocolate, making it a versatile Keurig option.

Milk Pods cost a dollar each, roughly the same as a coffee K-Cup. Nikita Ephanov/CNET

Thinking about cost

Consumed day to day, coffee costs add up. A hot latte from a cafe averages well over $5, and even home-brewing can dent the grocery budget. A K-Cup capsule and a Milk Pod cost $1 each, for an affordable $2 drink. Especially since you can buy a Keurig K-Mini machine for as little as $50, switching to this setup can save you money on coffee out in under a month. Plus, a Keurig requires minimal expertise, so you won’t need to learn how to make coffee.

Still, with a bit more effort, you can find better-priced coffee and milk options. On average, a gallon of milk retails for $4.30, with 21 six-ounce servings of dairy — that’s just over 20 cents per cup. You will need to steam the milk yourself. Handily, though, Keurig sells a $9.50 frother for the task. Fresh milk takes more effort — but to my taste, the flavor and texture are better. Not to mention, warming fresh dairy yourself lets you try out alternative milks as well as milks with varied fat compositions. Want a touch of sweetness in your cup? You can always grab a bottle of syrup and mix in a pump or two.

I wouldn’t switch to Keurig brewers specifically for this milk product, but Milk Pods are a convenient option and may be worth buying if you already use a Keurig. They’d also be handy to have on hand when you’ve run out of milk but are too bleary-eyed to make a morning run to the market.
